<PB N=v>
<C>PREFACE</C>
<SHL>
<P><SC>The Shakespeare</SC> Club,&mdash;&lquo;many millions strong&rquo; as <SC>Christopher
North</SC> says,&mdash;is made up of readers of Shakespeare and students of
Shakespeare. All are readers, and some at times students. When
reading Shakespeare, we resign ourselves to the mighty current, and
let it bear us along whithersoever it will; we see no shoals, heed no
rocks, need no pilot. Whether spoken from rude boards or printed
in homely form, the words are Shakespeare's, the hour is his, and a
thought of texts is an impertinence.
<P>But when we study Shakespeare, then our mood changes; no
longer are we &lquo;sitting at a play,&rquo; the passive recipients of impres-
sions through the eye and ear, but we weigh every word, analyse
every expression, sift every phrase, that no grain of art or beauty
which we can assimilate shall escape. To do this to our best advan-
tage we must have Shakespeare's own words before us. No other
words will avail, even though they be those of the wisest and most
inspired of our day and generation. We must have Shakespeare's
own text; or, failing this, the nearest possible approach to it. We
shall be duly grateful to the wise and learned, who, where phrases
are obscure, give us the words which they believe to have been
Shakespeare's; but, as students, we must have under our eyes the
original text, which, however stubborn it may seem at times, may
yet open its treasures to our importunity, and reveal charms before
undreamed of.
<P>This original text is to be found in the First edition of his
Works, published in 1623, and usually known as the <SC>First Folio</SC>,
which was presumably printed from the words written by Shake-
speare's own hand, or from Stage copies adapted from his manu-
scripts. Be it that the pages of this First Folio are little better
than proof-sheets, lacking supervision of the author or of any other,
<PB N=vi>
<HE>vi <I>PREFACE</I></HE>
<P>yet &lquo;those who had Shakespeare's manuscript before them were
more likely to read it right than we who read it only in imagi-
nation,&rquo; as Dr <SC>Johnson</SC> said. Even grant that the First Folio is,
as has been asserted, one of the most carelessly printed books ever
issued from the press, it is, nevertheless, the only text that we have
for at least sixteen of the plays, and condemn it as we may, &lquo;still is
its name in great account, it still hath power to charm&rquo; for all of
them. Can any good reason be urged why, in this present play at
least, we should not, in the hours devoted to study, be it remem-
bered, have the text of the First Folio as our guide? Is there not
every reason why we should? If misspellings occur here and there,
surely our common-school education is not so uncommon that we
cannot silently correct them. If the punctuation be deficient, surely
it can be supplied without an exorbitant demand upon our intel-
ligence. And in lines incurably maimed by the printers, of what
avail is the voice of a solitary editor amid the Babel that vociferates
around, each voice proclaiming the virtues of its own specific? Who
am I that I should thrust myself in between the student and the
text, as though in me resided the power to restore Shakespeare's
own words? Even if a remedy be proposed which is by all acknow-
ledged to be efficacious, it is not enough for the student that he
should know the remedy; he must see the ailment. Let the ail-
ment, therefore, appear in all its severity in the text, and let the
remedies be exhibited in the notes; by this means we may make
a text for ourselves, and thus made, it will become a part of our-
selves, and speak to us with more power than were it made for us
by the wisest editor of them all&mdash;it may be &lquo;an ill-favoured thing,
sir,&rquo; but&mdash;it will be &lquo;our own.&rquo;
<P>Impressed with this belief, I have in this volume abandoned the
plan, heretofore followed in this edition, and instead of giving a
modernised text, have reproduced the First Folio, reprinting it from
my own copy with all the exactitude in my power, scanning it letter
by letter, and have recorded in the Notes the various readings of all
other critical editions. For a fuller exposition of what I have done,
o<*> left undone, in this regard, and in regard to the text in general,
I must refer to p. 460 of the Appendix.
<PB N=vii>
<HE><I>PREFACE</I> vii</HE>
<P>I have long been of the opinion that in the interpretation of Shake-
speare's plays, our first appeal, and perhaps our last, should be made
to the dramatic instinct, as it has been termed, with which eminent
Actors are especially endowed. To see <SC>Kean</SC>, it has been said, was
to read Shakespeare by &lquo;flashes of lightning.&rquo; Yet how seldom do
we find in Shakespearian Commentaries any reference to the dramatic
rendering of a character, or of a passage, by an eminent Actor. This
is, however, not altogether the fault of the Commentators. All who
have read much of the Biographies of Actors will, I think, agree with
me in the regret that explicit, specific descriptions of their acting are
so meagre. Of vague generalisations, conveying no definite ideas, we
have a superfluity; but of the tones, or looks, or emphasis on par-
ticular words or lines there is a plentiful lack. What help is given
to us by the information that nothing could surpass the fervour of
<SC>Garrick's</SC> wooing as Romeo, or that <SC>Mrs Siddons</SC> was wonderfully
tragic as Lady Macbeth? What we require is the report like that
of an eye-witness whose record is taken on the spot; then we shall
know Romeo's every tone and look when rich music's tongue unfolds
imagined happiness. There are, however, scattered here and there,
explicit definite descriptions of the treatment by eminent Actors of
various passages; those which I deemed worthy of preservation I
have recorded in the Commentary. At my solicitation my friend,
<SC>Mr Edwin Booth</SC>, wrote out for me, in an interleaved copy of this
play, much of his &lquo;business;&rquo; I cannot but think that to others his
notes will be as interesting and as valuable as I have found them.
It is to be borne in mind for his sake that the notes were made
with no view to their being printed.
<P>It cannot be but that, in the selection of notes for an edition like
the present, an editor, working single-handed, must be influenced
by his own tastes and predilections. I can honestly say, however,
that if I have been single-handed I have been also single-eyed,&mdash;
single-eyed to the one object of elucidating the text. We do not
go to Shakespeare to study grammar or scanning, but we study his
grammar that we may understand him, and arrange the scansion,
that every charm which rhythm can yield may be his, as of right.
<PB N=viii>
<HE>viii <I>PREFACE</I></HE>
<P>Hence the prominence which I have given to all grammatical and
verbal criticism; which is to be regarded solely as a means to an
end. Without a complete understanding of the words the meaning of
the whole sentence will be lost,&mdash;and is not the meaning of Shake-
speare the very butt and sea-mark of our utmost sail? It is as con-
tributors towards this object that I regard Actors, and have, therefore,
recorded their interpretations. Herein the selection of notes for this
volume has been influenced by my own preference. &lquo;It is impossible,&rquo;
says <SC>Dr Johnson</SC>, &lquo;for an expositor not to write too little for some,
&lquo;and too much for others. He can judge what is necessary only by
&lquo;his own experience; and how long soever he may deliberate, will at
&lquo;last explain many lines which the learned will think impossible to be
&lquo;mistaken, and omit many for which the ignorant will want his help.
&lquo;These are censures merely relative, and must be quietly endured.&rquo;
<P>Since these words were written, a hundred and twenty years ago,
what numberless busy &lquo;expositors,&rquo; high and low, wise and simple,
learned and ignorant, clerk and lay, at home and abroad, have been,
down to this hour, poring over every Act, and Scene, over every line,
and syllable! Is there anything left for us to explore or to discover?
&lquo;Gentlemen,&rquo; said <SC>Dr Barclay</SC> in one of his Edinburgh Lectures,
&lquo;Anatomy may be likened to a harvest-field. First come the reapers,
&lquo;who, entering upon untrodden ground, cut down great store of corn
&lquo;from all sides of them. These are the early anatomists of modern
&lquo;Europe. Then come the gleaners, who gather up ears enough from
&lquo;the bare ridges to make a few loaves of bread. Such were the anat-
&lquo;omists of the last century. Last of all come the geese, who still
&lquo;continue to pick up a few grains scattered here and there among the
&lquo;stubble, and waddle home in the evening, poor things, cackling
&lquo;with joy because of their success. Gentlemen, we are the geese&rquo;
<P>The next play in this edition, if there ever be one, will be, prob-
ably, <I>The Merchant of Venice.</I>
<P>To my Father, the <SC>Rev. Dr Furness</SC>, be my thanks pressed down
and running over for all that he has done for me, especially for his
translation of my selections from the German in the Appendix.
<P>H. H. F.
<P><SC>March</SC>, 1886

<CC><P>1. <SC>Scene</SC>.] <SC>Fechter</SC>: A street in Venice&mdash;on the right a house with practicable
door and window. Night. <SC>Booth</SC>: Venice. A dark street. Full stage.
<P>2. The bracketed numbers and letters [310 <I>a</I>, etc.] indicate the page and column in F<SUB>1</SUB>.
<P>4. <B>Neuer]</B> <SC>Coleridge</SC> (<I>Notes</I>, &amp;c., p. 247): Admirable is the preparation, so truly
and peculiarly Shakespearian, in the introduction of Roderigo, as the dupe on whom
Iago shall first exercise his art, and in so doing display his own character. Roderigo,
without any fixed principle, but not without the moral notions and sympathies with
honour, which his rank and connections had hung upon him, is already well fitted and
predisposed for the purpose; for very want of character and strength of passion, like
wind loudest in an empty house, constitute his character. The first three lines happily
state the nature and foundation of the friendship between him and Iago,&mdash;the purse,&mdash;as
also the contrast of Roderigo's intemperance of mind with Iago's coolness,&mdash;the cool-
ness of a preconceiving experimenter. The mere language of protestation,&mdash;&lquo;If ever
I did dream of such a matter, abhor me,&rquo;&mdash;which, falling in with the associative link,
determines Roderigo's continuation of complaint,&mdash;&lquo;Thou told'st me, thou didst hold
him in thy hate,&rquo;&mdash;elicits at length a true feeling of Iago's mind, the dread of con-
tempt habitual to those who encourage in themselves, and have their keenest pleasure
in, the expression of contempt for others. Observe Iago's high self-opinion, and the
moral, that a wicked man will employ real feelings, as well as assume those most alien
from his own, as instruments of his purposes:&mdash;&lquo;And, by the faith of man, I know my</CC>

<P>4. <B>me]</B> <SC>Knight</SC> believes that by the emphasis falling on &lquo;me,&rquo; as here in the F, the
expression is somewhat more in Roderigo's vein, and that the omission of <I>Tush</I> was
not accidental.
<P>6. <B>this]</B> <SC>Hudson</SC>: The intended elopement. Roderigo has been suing for Desde-
mona's hand, employing Iago to aid him in his suit, and paying his service in advance.
The play opens pat upon her elopement with the Moor, and Roderigo presumes Iago
to have been in the secret of their intention.
<P>7. <B>But]</B> <SC>Knight</SC>, the first editor to proclaim an absolute trust in the First Folio,
and to give a reason for the faith that was in him, here at the very outset offers
battle. <SC>Steevens</SC>, following the Qq, had said that, &lquo;the Folio suppresses the
oath '<I>sblood.</I>&rquo; The use of the word <I>suppresses</I> seems to cast a slur; and <SC>Knight</SC>
is instantly on hand, &lquo;but Steevens does not tell us,&rquo; he says, &lquo;what the Folio does
besides. It accommodates the rhythmical arrangement of the sentence to the sup-
pression of the oath. This is certainly not the work of some botcher coming after the
author. Such instances of right feeling and good taste, in the omission of offensive
expressions, constantly occur throughout this play in F<SUB>1</SUB>. In the Qto such offensive
expressions are as constantly found. The modern editions cling to the Qto in this
particular, upon the supposition that in the Folio the passages were struck out by the
Master of the Revels. The Master of the Revels must have been an exceedingly
capricious person if he thus exercised his office in 1623, and thus neglected it in 1622.
We have not a doubt, seeing that the structure of the verse is always accommodated to
the alteration, that every such change was made by the author of the play. It was not
that the Master of the Revels was scrupulous in the use of his authority with F<SUB>1</SUB>, and
negligent with Q<SUB>1</SUB>, but that both Qto and Folio were printed at a period when the Stat-
ute of 1604 [<I>Qu.</I> 1605?] for restraining the profane use of the sacred name in stage-
plays, had fallen into neglect. But the Qto was printed from an early copy of the play
which existed before the Statute came into operation. The Folio contains the author's
additions and corrections. This would be a sufficient reason, if there were no other,
for preferring the text of the Folio in this as well as in other matters.&rquo; <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. i)</CC>

<P>14. <B>Off-capt]</B> That is, says <SC>Theobald</SC>, stood cap in hand, soliciting him. So in
<I>Ant. &amp; Cleo.</I> II, vii, 64: &lquo;I have ever held my cap off to thy fortunes,&rquo; and in <I>Tim.</I>
IV, iii, 212: &lquo;And let his very breath, whom thou'lt observe, Blow off thy cap.&rquo; <SC>Jen-
nens</SC> suggests that we are not to suppose that the Great ones <I>often</I> begged Othello, cap
in hand, to promote Iago, and adds, &lquo;'tis very likely the original reading was <I>Off'd
cap.</I>&rquo; The reading of the Qq, says <SC>Ritson</SC> (p. 225) is &lquo;nonsense;&rquo; whereas an &lquo;inti-
mate knowledge of the Qq&rquo; convinces <SC>Malone</SC> that &lquo;they ought not without very
strong reason to be departed from.&rquo; No such strong reason appears to him here, prob-
ably because to him as well as to all who adopt <I>oft capped</I>, <SC>Mason's</SC> explanation seems
conclusive, namely that &lquo;to <I>cap</I> is to salute by taking off the cap. It is still an academic
phrase.&rquo; <SC>Knight</SC> comes to the defence of F<SUB>1</SUB>, and, admitting that <I>to cap</I> in ancient
academical phrase meant to take the cap off, and that it is so used by other early Eng-
lish authors, as in Drant's <I>Horace</I>, 1567, yet, asks Knight, &lquo;is <I>oft capp'd</I> supported by
the context? As we read the whole passage, three great ones of the city wait upon
Othello; they &ldquo;off-capp'd,&rdquo;&mdash;they took cap-in-hand,&mdash;in personal suit that he should
make Iago his lieutenant; but he evades them, &amp;c. He has already chosen his officer.
Here is a scene painted in a manner well befitting both the dignity of the great ones
of the city and of Othello himself. The audience was given, the solicitation was hum-
bly made, the reasons for refusing it courteously assigned. But take the other reading,
<I>oft</I> capp'd; and then we have Othello perpetually haunted by the three great ones of
the city, capping to him and repeating to him the same prayer, and he perpetually deny-
ing them with the same bombast circumstance. Surely this is not what Shakespeare
meant to represent.&rquo; <SC>White</SC> (ed. i) suggests that &lquo;capped&rquo; seems &lquo;to have meant to
keep the cap on, not to take it off. For example: &ldquo;And this of Paull, that a man
should neither pray nor preach capped, or with his head covered, is also cleane abol-
ished.&rdquo;&mdash;Cranmer's <I>Confutation of Unwritten Verities</I>, 1582, p. 62.&rquo; But <SC>Dyce</SC> (ed.
iii) is not convinced, and after quoting Malone, opposes White with a definition from
Coles's <I>Latin Dict.:</I> &lquo;To cap a person, <I>coram aliquo caput aperire, nudare.</I>&rquo; [I</CC>

<P>17. <B>bumbast]</B> <SC>Nares</SC>: Originally cotton. Hence, because cotton was commonly
used to stuff out quilting, &amp;c., <I>bombast</I> also meant the stuffing of clothes, &amp;c. Hence
applied to tumid and inflated language. [Cotgrave gives: Cottoner. <I>To bumbast, or

<P>17. <B>Circumstance]</B> <SC>Reed</SC>: That is, circumlocution. See <I>Greene's Tu Quoque</I>

a bombast circumstance. F<SUB>1</SUB> distinctly separates, <I>for, certes, says he</I>, from <I>nonsuits my
mediators.</I> Othello, according to <I>Iago's</I> calumnious assertion, says the truth only to
himself.
<P>19. <B>Non-suites]</B> <SC>Lord Campbell</SC> (p. 112): Here is a striking instance of Shake-
speare's proneness to legal phraseology. <I>Nonsuiting</I> is known to the learned to be the
most disreputable and mortifying mode of being beaten; it indicates that the action is
wholly unfounded on the plaintiff's own showing, or that there is a fatal defect in the
manner in which his case has been got up; insomuch that Mr. Chitty, the great special
pleader, used to give this advice to young barristers practising at <I>nisi prius:</I>&mdash;&lquo;Always
avoid your attorney when nonsuited, for till he has a little time for reflection, however
much you may abuse the Judge, he will think that the nonsuit was all your fault.&rquo;

<CC><P>19, 20. <B>For . . . officer]</B> <SC>Theobald</SC>, following <SC>Pope</SC> in the omission of <I>For</I>, was
the first to mark <I>Certes . . . officer</I> as a quotation. Of the edd. who follow the QqFf,

<P>19. <B>certes]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: That is, certainly, in truth. <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Lex.</I> s. v.) says that
here, and in <I>Hen. VIII:</I> I, i, 48, &lquo;certes&rquo; is a monosyllable, an assertion which I am
afraid must be marked as one of the very few errors which that admirable lexicographer
has made. An English ear will readily guide the present line with <I>certes</I> as a dis-
syllable, and the line in <I>Hen. VIII</I>, &lquo;One, certes, that promises no element,&rquo; is scanned
by reading &lquo;promises&rquo; as a dissyllable, a contraction of which <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Vers.</I> p. 62)
gives numerous examples. The very many instances of &lquo;certes&rquo; as a dissyllable in
Spenser alone would teach us to contract, in Shakespeare, almost any other word in
the line rather than that. [I am now half inclined to agree with Schmidt. 1887.]&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>21. <B>Arithmatician]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: So, in <I>Rom. &amp; Jul.</I> Mercutio says: &lquo;one that
fights by the book of arithmetic.&rquo; <SC>Malone</SC>: Iago means to represent Cassio not as a
person whose arithmetic was &lquo;<I>one, two</I>, and the <I>third</I> in your bosom,&rquo; but as a man
merely conversant with <I>civil</I> matters, and who knew no more of a squadron than the
<I>number</I> of men it contained. <SC>Singer</SC> thinks that Iago refers to Cassio as a man whose
knowledge of military evolutions was drawn entirely from books on tactics, wherein
&lquo;the movements requisite to change from line to column, &amp;c. are worked out numeri-
cally on the base of a tactical unit.&rquo; C. A. <SC>Brown</SC> (<I>Sh.'s Autobiog. Poems</I>, p. 110),
in his essay to prove that Shakespeare had visited Italy, says that there was good
reason why Cassio, the Florentine, should be derisively termed by Iago &lquo;a great arith-
metician,&rquo; &lquo;a counter-caster&rquo; with his &lquo;debtor and creditor.&rquo; &lquo;A soldier from Florence,
famous for its bankers throughout Europe, and for its invention of bills of exchange,
book-keeping, and everything connected with a counting-house, might well be ridiculed
for his promotion, by an Iago, in this manner.&rquo;

<CC><C>[22, 23. <B>&lquo;Florentine, (A Fellow almost damn'd in a faire Wife).&rquo;</B>]</C>
<P>his Heaven on Earth, that he idoliz'd her, and that he forgot to think of Happiness in
an After-state, as placing all his Views of Bliss in the single Enjoyment of her. In

and that as Cassio was unmarried, there must be some mistake in giving him a wife; but

would treat with scorn and ridicule. Wherefore Hanmer reads &lquo;a fellow almost damn'd

<SC>Tyrwhitt</SC> (p. 2): The great difficulty is to understand in what sense any man can
be said to be &lquo;almost damn'd in a fair wife&rquo; or &lquo;a fair phyz.&rquo; I cannot find any ground
for supposing that either the one or the other has ever been reputed to be damnable
sins in any religion. There is the same expression in <I>Mer. of Ven.</I> I, i, 98: &lquo;If they
should speak, would almost damn those ears, Which, hearing them, would call their
brothers fools.&rquo; And there the allusion is evident to the Gospel-judgment against those
who call their brothers fools. I am inclined, therefore, to believe that the true reading
here is: &lquo;A fellow almost damn'd in a fair <I>life</I>,&rquo; and that Shakespeare alludes to the
judgment denounced in the Gospel against those <I>of whom all men speak well.</I> The
character of Cassio is such as would be very likely to draw upon him all the peril of
this denunciation, literally understood. Well-bred, easy, sociable, good-natured, with
abilities enough to make him agreeable and useful, but not sufficient to excite the envy
of his equals or to alarm the jealousy of his superiors. In several other passages Iago
bears his testimony to the amiable qualities of his rival. Conf. &lquo;the daily beauty of his
life,&rquo; V, i, 22. I will only add that however hard or far-fetch'd this allusion (whether
Shakespeare's or only mine) may seem to be, Archbishop Sheldon had exactly the
same conceit when he made that singular compliment to a nephew of Sir William
Temple, that &lquo;he had the curse of the Gospel, because all men spoke well of him.&rquo;
<SC>Heath</SC> (p. 551) adopts Theobald's &lquo;Florentine's,&rquo; and &lquo;apprehends the meaning to be
that, notwithstanding Iago had a fair wife, he had little chance for going to heaven,
as by the watchfulness of his jealousy he made it extremely difficult for her to do her
part toward sending him thither.&rquo; <SC>Jennens</SC> in his text marks the line as an <I>Aside</I>,
and, retaining the parenthesis, reads &lquo;A fellow's almost damn'd in a fair wife!&rquo; In
his note, after condemning Theobald's emendation, and asserting that Hanmer's is
simply equivalent to saying that &lquo;Cassio's a damn'd handsome fellow,&rquo; he upholds
his own text by pleading that he has &lquo;only supplied an <I>s</I> after &ldquo;fellow;&rdquo;&rquo; and by
supposing that &lquo;Shakespeare meant the line to be spoke apart, expressing a sudden
motion of jealousy in Iago on naming Othello and Cassio, of both of which that he
was jealous appears from II, iii. And Iago's meaning is, &ldquo;To be married to a hand-
some woman (as I am) is almost as bad as being damn'd; as the number of her ad-
mirers will doom the husband to a state of perpetual jealousy.&rdquo;&rquo; <SC>Tollet</SC> (<I>Var.</I>'78):

<P>creature that had you a fair wife of that sort you would condemn her. <SC>Bibliothecar.
Chetham</SC> (<I>Ibid.</I>): Your second correspondent [Workard] in this passage is undoubtedly
right in his emendation, but not, I think, in insisting on unity of idea. The strife is not
that of the battlefield, but of the election. &lquo;A fellow [who would have been] almost
damn'd In a fair strife.&rquo; <SC>Arrowsmith</SC> (p. 38) [whose interpretation will be found,
I think, to have been foreshadowed by Martinus Scriblerus, and by <G>*d</G>.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]: Hard
above all has been the fate of &lquo;in;&rquo; let but Iago say that for soldiership his com-
rade Cassio is &lquo;a fellow almost damned in a fair wife&rquo;&mdash;that his qualifications for
the post of lieutenant would be almost discreditable in a woman; let him add
withal, as though on set purpose to preclude every chance of being misunderstood,
that Cassio possesses no more strategic knowledge than a &lquo;spinster,&rquo; when lo! a
goodly troop of commentators, clerk and lay, bishop and bookseller, lawyer and anti-
quary, critic professional and critic amateur, home-born and outlandish, men who have
read much and men who have read nothing, swarm forth to bury this simple remark
under a pile of notes, that from first to last contain not an inkling of its purport. . . . .
The words are to be taken circumscriptly, not sent gadding after Bianca, or no one
knows who; their meaning must be sought and found within the compass of the line
in which they stand. Had Shakespeare written &lquo;a fellow almost damned in a raw
lad,&rquo; the dullest brain could scarcely have missed the imputation that Cassio's military
abilities would be almost disallowed, condemned as hardly up to the mark in an inex-
perienced boy; or had the words run, &lquo;a fellow almost damned in an old maid,&rquo; then,
though it might not be understood how an officer, after Iago's report, of Cassio's in-
capacity, should be almost damned in one of her sex and condition, she at any rate
could not, like the &lquo;fair wife,&rquo; have been discovered at Cyprus in a young courtesan.
Or not altering a syllable, with only a slight change in their order, let us place the
words thus: &lquo;a fellow in a fair wife almost damned;&rquo; by this disposition of them the
reader is pinned to their true construction; the alliance between Cassio and the fair
wife is closer than the commentators suspected; they harp upon conjugal union, Iago
speaks of virtual identity; they seek the coupling of two persons in wedlock, he con-
templates an embodiment of the soldiership of the one in the condition of the other,
and so incorporated he pronounces it to be &lquo;in a fair wife&rquo; almost reproveable; adding,
in the same vein, that it was no better than might be found in &lquo;a spinster.&rquo; To dwell
on this point longer would be to upbraid the reader's understanding. [Of Arrowsmith's
explanation <SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. iii) says: &lquo;Though it may appear to some to be rather forced and
obscure, I am far from asserting it to be wrong.&rquo;] <SC>Forsyth</SC> (<I>Shakspere</I>, &amp;c., p. 107):
As contrasted with Staunton's and similar glosses, our proposal is simplicity itself. It
consists in throwing out the word &lquo;wife&rquo; as a misprint very easily made, and by a differ-
ence in pointing (to which, as all know, neither the early Qq nor the Ff paid much
attention) to read thus: &lquo;A fellow almost damned; in a fair <I>strife</I> That never,&rquo; &amp;c.....
The greatest deficiency of the expositors, in our humble view, has been their inability
to compare the author with himself, and if this is intelligently done in the present case,
there can be small doubt of the result. <SC>Earl of Southesk</SC> (<I>Saskatchewan</I>, p. 413):

<CC><P>or damn'd in a <I>form o' wax</I>&rquo; is harmonious with the context, and agrees with Iago's
contemptuous references to Cassio. <SC>Hudson</SC> (ed. iii) reads <I>wight</I> in his text instead
of &lquo;wife,&rquo; which, he thinks, &lquo;cannot be explained to any fitting sense but by methods
too subtile and recondite.&rquo; Of all the readings hitherto offered he prefers Capell's <I>face.</I>
&lquo;It suits the occasion and the speaker very well; for Iago dwells much on Cassio's hand-
someness of person; recurs to it again and again; and builds his scheme partly on that
circumstance, as if he longed to make it the ruin of Cassio, sure enough. On the other
hand, however, Iago's thought may well have been that Cassio was badly damaged by
the fascinations of a handsome mistress; thus referring to the amorous intrigue with
Bianca, which comes out so strongly in the course of the play. So I am satisfied we
ought to read <I>wight.</I> It seems to me a very natural and fitting word for the place; and,
if spelled phonographically, <I>wite</I>, might easily be misprinted &ldquo;wife;&rdquo; and Iago seems
rather fond of using it scoffingly in reference to women. It may not be amiss to note
that Iago's talk about Cassio is full of contempt. Surely a reading that requires an
explanation so forced as Arrowsmith's may well be distrusted. It has set me more
than ever against the old text.&rquo; <SC>John Hunter</SC>: Cassio is here regarded as about
to marry his mistress, Bianca, whose charms, it would seem, were such as to make
this world a paradise for him, and thus put him in danger of forfeiting the happiness
of the world to come. The notion is founded on the parable of Dives and Laz-
arus: &lquo;Son, remember that <I>thou in thy life-time receivedst thy good things</I>, and like-
wise Lazarus evil things; but now he is comforted, and thou art tormented.&rquo;&mdash;Luke
xvi, 25. Cf. <I>Mer. of Ven.</I> III, v, 78-83. <SC>Bulloch</SC> (<I>Studies</I>, p. 248): The line is a
concentrated essence of Iago's opinion of Cassio's soldiership. It is, as it were, spoken
by the bye, and amplified in the speech. I therefore propose &lquo;almost damn'd in <I>war-
fare life.&rquo; Warfare</I> does not occur in Shakespeare, though it does in our English
Bible. <SC>Crosby</SC> (<I>Robinson's Epit. of Lit.</I>, 15 Mar. 1879) justifies F<SUB>1</SUB> by interpreting
&lquo;in&rquo; as equivalent to <I>on account of</I>, and &lquo;wife&rquo; as <I>woman in general.</I> Thus: &lquo;a fellow
who is willing to go to perdition&mdash;almost sell himself to the devil&mdash;for a beautiful
woman.&rquo; R. M. <SC>Spence</SC> (<I>N. &amp; Qu.</I> 1879, 5th, xi, 383): I offer: &lquo;A fellow all must
damn in affairs wise.&rquo; Iago says, that all who are wise in military affairs must con-
demn the appointment of a man who knows nothing of war, but &lquo;bookish theorie.&rquo;
F. A. <SC>Leo</SC> (<I>Shakespeare-Notes</I>, p. 116, 1885) finds, as far as the sound is concerned,
that &lquo;damn'd in&rquo; could have been &lquo;very easily misunderstood for <I>tempting</I>,&rquo; and that
the <I>ductus literarum</I> would readily explain &lquo;almost&rquo; as <I>at most;</I> and therefore pro-
poses, as suiting the requirements of sound, of sense, and of letters: &lquo;A fellow, <I>almost
tempting</I> a fair wife.&rquo; [In conclusion I merely re-echo Dr Johnson's words: &lquo;This
is one of the passages which must, for the present, be resigned to corruption and ob-
scurity. I have nothing that I can, with any approach to confidence, propose.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>22-27. <SC>Coleridge</SC> (<I>Notes</I>, &amp;c., 248): Let the reader feel how by and through the
glass of two passions,&mdash;disappointed vanity and envy,&mdash;the very vices of which he is
complaining are made to act upon him as if they were so many excellences; and the
more appropriately, because cunning is always admired and wished for by minds con-
scious of inward weakness; but they act only by half, like music on an inattentive
auditor, swelling the thoughts which prevent him from listening to it.

<P>31. <B>others]</B> <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> i, 233) notices the remarkable frequency in F<SUB>1</SUB> of the

with the MSS. of the Elizabethan Age, may, perhaps, be able to explain its origin.
Were it not for the different degrees of frequency with which it occurs in different parts
of the F,&mdash;being comparatively rare in the <I>Comedies</I> (except, perhaps, in <I>Wint. Tale</I>),
appearing more frequently in the <I>Histories</I>, and becoming quite common in the <I>Trage-
dies</I>,&mdash;I should be inclined to think it originated in some peculiarity of Shakespeare's
handwriting.&rquo; [See <I>Lear</I>, V, iii, 258. Walker gives the following nine instances, in
this play, of this interpolation as he considers it, viz: the present passage, where &lquo;others&rquo;
appears as <I>other</I> in Qq; &lquo;eares&rquo; in F<SUB>1</SUB> as <I>eare</I> in QqFf, I, iii, 245; &lquo;likings,&rquo; QqFf, III,

&lquo;scuses&rquo; in Ff as <I>scuse</I> in Qq, IV, i, 93; &lquo;behauiors,&rquo; Ff as <I>behauior</I> in Qq, IV, i, 119.
To these nine instances a tenth may be added: &lquo;Thicks-lips,&rquo; F<SUB>1</SUB>, as <I>thick lips</I> in Qq,

from this list we eliminate the three words wherein the Ff and the Qq agree, and
wherein no critic but Walker has found the <I>s</I> superfluous, viz: <I>likings, horrors</I>, and
<I>sorrowes</I>, and add the fourth, <I>warres</I>, which only Capell changed to <I>war</I>, we shall have
seven instances remaining where this <I>s</I> is found in the Ff, but not in the Qq. If then
Walker's adumbration of the cause of this <I>s</I> be accepted, viz: that it originates in some
peculiarity of the writing of that hand which left &lquo;scarse a blot in his papers,&rquo; this
manifest distinction between the two copies adds a vindication, by no means insig-
nificant, of the superior authority of the First Folio.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>35. <B>Auntient]</B> J. D. (<I>N. &amp; Qu.</I> 1879, 5th, xii, 4): The common interpretation of this
word is that it means an ensign, in the double sense of standard and standard-bearer.
So our older Dictionaries explain it; Cotgrave has: &lquo;<I>Enseigne</I>, an ensigne, auncient,
standard-bearer.&rquo; The explanation is correct as far as it goes, but is not sufficiently
precise. The ancient was a banner bearing an heraldic device, the token of ancient or
noble descent, borne by a gentleman or leader in war. &lquo;Lord Westmorland his ancyent
rais'd, The dun bull he rais'd on hie.&rquo;&mdash;<I>The Rising in the North.</I> &lquo;Master, master,
see you you faire ancyent, Yonder is the serpent and the serpent's head.&rquo;&mdash;Perey's
<I>Rel.</I> (ed. 1867) i, 303. The servant recognized by this device that the ship belonged
to Duke John of Austria. The word was, however, used to denote one who was con-
nected with some blazon of this kind, whether as an attendant to a standard or to
some gentleman who had armorial bearings. In the English edition of the <I>Janua
Linguarum Trilinguis</I>, by J. Comenius, 1662, it is said, that &lquo;the standard-bearers
carrie the standards in the midst of the troops, whom the ancients march before with
hangers;&rquo; the Latin is, &lquo;quos pr&aelig;cedunt antesignani cum romph&aelig;is&rquo; (p. 245). The
word <I>antesignanus</I> is explained by Ducange as one &lquo;qui pr&aelig;ibat vexillo ad illius cus-
todiam.&rquo; In Anchoran's <I>Gate of Tongues Unlocked</I> (ed. 1639), which is based on the
work of Comenius, the passage runs thus: &lquo;whom the lieutenants precede or go before
with long two-handed swords&rquo; (p. 143). From these instances it is easy to see how
the word came to mean a personal attendant or body-squire, who, says Fosbrooke (<I>Ant.</I>
ii, 752), &lquo;had the care of the things relating to the person of the knight, carried his
master's standard, and gave the catchword in battle,&rquo; an office often borne by men of
honourable descent. This is the meaning of the word in <I>Othello.</I> Iago was the per
sonal attendant of the Moor in a military capacity, in modern language, his aide-de-</CC>

<P>41. <B>Stood]</B> <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 361): The subjunctive (a consequence of the old inflection)
was frequently used, not as now with <I>would, should</I>, &amp;c., but in a form identical with
the indicative, where nothing but the context (in the case of past tenses) shows that it
is the subjunctive. In the present instance, if it be asked, what is the difference be-
tween &lquo;stood&rquo; here and &lquo;would have stood&rquo; I should say that the simple form of the
subjunctive, coinciding in sound with the indicative, implied to an Elizabethan more
of <I>inevitability</I> (subject, of course, to a condition which is not fulfilled). &lquo;Stood&rquo;
means &lquo;would certainly have stood.&rquo; The possibility is regarded as <I>an unfulfilled fact</I>,
to speak paradoxically. Compare the Greek idiom of <G>i(/na</G> with the indicative.
<P>42. <B>Affin'd]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: Do I stand <I>within</I> any such <I>terms</I> of propinquity, <I>or</I> relation
to the Moor, as that it is my duty to love him? <SC>Staunton</SC>: By any moral obligation
am <I>bound</I>, &amp;c. [See II, ii, 243.]

<CC><P>worthless of birds,&mdash;<I>daws</I>, which are treated with universal contempt. &lquo;Shakespeare

be here referred to with contempt, or without dignifying the allusion.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>] <SC>Harting</SC>
(p. 119): The Jackdaw (<I>Corvus monedula</I>) has not been so frequently noticed by Shake-

<P>71. <B>am]</B> <SC>Jennens</SC>: This signifies I am not that inwardly which I am outwardly, or,
I am not what I seem to appear to be. Pope has here turned poetry into prose. <SC>Hud-
son</SC>: Iago probably means &lquo;I am not what I <I>seem</I>,&rquo; but to speak thus would not smack
so much of the peculiar dialect with which he loves to practise on the dupe. <SC>Maginn</SC>
(p. 268): Can these last words be intended as a somewhat profane allusion to the title
by which the Almighty reveals himself to Moses? <I>Exod.</I> iii, 14. I <SC>Am that I am</SC> is
the name of the God of truth. <I>I am not what I am</I> is, therefore, a fitting description
of a premeditated liar.
<P>72. <B>fall]</B> I can recall no instance in this play where <SC>Knight</SC> (&lquo;Good Knight,&rquo; as
Douglas Jerrold said his epitaph should be) displays more ingenuity in extracting a
meaning from a misprint in F<SUB>1</SUB>, than in this word, and not only a meaning, but a hidden
beauty thoroughly Shakespearian. &lquo;<I>Full</I> fortune,&rquo; says Knight, &lquo;means simply <I>how for-
tunate he is.</I> But the F<SUB>1</SUB> conveys a much more Shakespearian idea. If the Moor can
carry it thus,&mdash;appoint his own officer, in spite of the great ones of the city who capp'd
to him, and, moreover, can secure Desdemona as his prize,&mdash;he is so puff'd up with his
own pride and purposes, and is so successful, that <I>fortune owes him a heavy fall.</I> To
<I>owe</I> is used by Shakespeare not only in the ancient sense of to <I>own</I>, but in the modern
sense of <I>to be indebted to, to hold</I> or <I>possess for another.</I> Fortune here owes the thick-
lips a fall, in the same way that we say, &ldquo;He owes him a good or an evil turn.&rdquo; This
reading is very much in Shakespeare's manner of throwing out a hint of coming calam-
ities.&rquo; <SC>Steevens</SC> cites &lquo;full fortune&rquo; as used in <I>Cymb.</I> V, iv, 110, and <SC>Malone</SC> adds
another instance in <I>Ant. &amp; Cleo.</I> IV, xv, 24.
<P>72. <B>Thicks-lips]</B> For the spelling, see note on &lquo;others,&rquo; line 31.
<P>72. <B>owe]</B> &lquo;To <I>owe</I> in ancient language is to <I>own</I>,&rquo; says <SC>Steevens</SC>; &lquo;very true,&rquo;
says <SC>Pye</SC>, &lquo;but do not explain it so often.&rquo;

<P>83, 84. <SC>Warburton</SC>: This is not sense, take it which way you will. If &lquo;night and
negligence&rquo; relate to &lquo;spied,&rquo; it is absurd to say, &lquo;the fire was spied by negligence.&rquo; If
&lquo;night&rquo; and &lquo;negligence&rquo; refer only to the time and occasion, it should then be <I>by night</I>
and <I>thro' negligence.</I> Otherwise the particle <I>by</I> would be made to signify <I>time</I> applied
to one word, and <I>cause</I> applied to the other. We should read, therefore, &lquo;Is <I>spred</I>,&rquo; by
which all these faults are avoided. [<SC>Staunton</SC> queries if Warburton be not right.]
<SC>Edwards</SC> (p. 144): The plain meaning is,&mdash;not the fire was spied by negligence, but
&mdash;the fire, which came by night and negligence, was spied. And this double meaning
to the same word is common to Shakespeare with all other writers, especially where the
word is so familiar a one, as this in question. Ovid seems even to have thought it a
beauty, instead of a defect. <SC>Johnson</SC>: The particle <I>by</I> is used equivocally; the same
liberty is taken by writers more correct: &lquo;The wonderful creature! a woman of reason!
Never grave <I>out of</I> pride, never gay <I>out of</I> season.&rquo; M. <SC>Mason</SC>: This means &lquo;during
the time of night and negligence.&rquo; <SC>Knight</SC> thinks that had the parenthesis of F<SUB>1</SUB> been
adopted, all discussion might have been saved. <SC>Delius</SC> interprets it, &lquo;according to
Shakespeare's use of the copulas, as equivalent to <I>nightly negligence</I> or <I>negligence by
night</I>, and qualifying &lquo;fire.&rquo; [Surely night is the cause that a fire takes place without
being observed; it is because of night that the fire is neglected. Could we not here
use <I>from</I> quite as well as <I>by?</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>89. <B>Bra. Aboue]</B> <SC>Booth</SC>: Brabantio should be seen through the open window at
his look or papers; this would account for his appearance, instead of his servants, at
this &lquo;terrible summons.&rquo; Iago should keep in shadow during this.

<CC><P>indeed is in the text so set down? <SC>Booth</SC>: This should indeed be so spoken, im-

<P>114. In this line <SC>Knight</SC> silently adopts <I>spirit</I> of Qq, and retains &lquo;their&rquo; of the Ff.
I think it would have been better had the change been reversed; &lquo;spirits&rquo; in the plural,
thus used, is quite Shakespearian.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>118. <B>Grange]</B> <SC>Warton</SC>: That is, you are in a populous city, not in a lone house,
where a robbery might be easily committed. &lquo;Grange&rquo; is properly the farm of
a monastery, where corn (Lat. <I>granum</I>) is reposited. But in Lincolnshire, and in
other Northern counties, every lone house, or farm which stands solitary, is called a
<I>grange.</I> <SC>Steevens</SC>: Conf. <I>meas. for Meas.</I> III, i, 278, &lquo;at the moated grange resides
this dejected Mariana.&rquo; <SC>Knight</SC> refers to the picture of neglected loneliness, which
this &lquo;moated grange&rquo; in <I>Meas. for Meas.</I> suggested to Tennyson, in those verses which
are familiar to us all.
<P>122. <B>deuill]</B> <SC>Gould</SC> (p. 84): Actors usually commit the ludicrous mistake of bring
ing down the emphasis plump on &lquo;devil,&rquo; as if the highest motive for serving God were
the devil's bidding! J. B. Booth said: &lquo;that will not serve <I>God</I>, if the devil <I>bid</I> you,&rquo;
giving the plain meaning, that the devil's bidding was no argument <I>against</I> serving God.
<P>123. <B>Ruffians]</B> <SC>Staunton</SC>: Here employed in its secondary sense of <I>roisterer,
swash-buckler</I>, and the like, though its primary meaning was, undoubtedly, <I>pander;</I>
Latin &lquo;leno,&rquo; the Italian &lquo;roffiano.&rquo;
<P>124. <B>Nephewes]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: Here, like Lat. <I>nepos</I>, it signifies a grandson, or any
lineal descendant, however remote. <SC>Boswell</SC>: The word <I>grandson</I> never occurs in
Shakespeare. <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Gloss.</I>): &lquo;Nephew,&rquo; like cousin, was formerly used with great
laxity. See <I>1 Hen. VI:</I> II, v, 64, where <I>nephew</I> ought to mean <I>cousin.</I> <SC>Halliwell</SC>
appositely cites the fact that Shakespeare in his Will speaks of his grand-daughter, Eliz-
abeth Hall, as his <I>niece.</I> [See Richardson's <I>Dict.</I> for manifold citations, from Robert
of Gloucester down, where <I>nephew</I> is used for grandson or lineal descendant. Cooper's
<I>Thes.</I> &lquo;Nepos: the sonne or daughters sonne, a nephew.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]</CC>

<CC><P>was just approaching to, or just past, that it was doubtful whether at that moment it
stood at the point of midnight, or at some other less equal division of the twenty-four
hours; which a few minutes either before, or after, midnight would be. So in <I>Macb.</I>
III, iv, 126: &lquo;What is the night? <I>Lady M.</I> Almost at odds with morning, which is
which.&rquo; <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 435: <I>And</I> is omitted. Cicero says, that the extreme test of a
man's honesty is that you can play at odd and even with him in the dark. And per-
haps &lquo;odd-(and-)even&rquo; here means, a time when there is no distinguishing between
<I>odd</I> and <I>even.</I>

<P>138. <B>Gundelier]</B> <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Vers.</I> p. 218) shows that, just as <I>pioneer, engineer,

did not write &ldquo;gundeler&rdquo; (&ldquo;gondoler&rdquo;), he certainly intended the word to be so pro-
nounced.&rquo; <SC>Abbott</SC> does not include this word in the list which he gives (&sect; 492) of the
class referred to by Walker, but places it under &lquo;apparent Alexandrines&rquo; (&sect; 497), and
contracts it <I>gond</I>(<I>o</I>)<I>lier.</I> Walker's treatment is, I think, the better.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

<CC><P><I>to.</I> The idea of the entire surrender of Desdemona to Othello is intended, which &lquo;in&rquo;
certainly conveys, even better than <I>on.</I> There are, assuredly, instances where <I>in</I> is
used where we should now use <I>on</I>, as in Gen. i, 22; Matt. vi, 10, also <I>1 Hen. VI:</I> I,
ii, 2 (all cited in <I>Bible Word-Book</I>), where, however, the phrase &lquo;in the earth,&rquo; is im-
mediately connected with &lquo;in the heavens,&rquo; and is not, therefore, exactly parallel with
the present instance. See &lquo;in your owne part,&rquo; I, iii, 91, <I>post.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>149. <B>extrauagant]</B> Used by Shakespeare three times and uniformly in its classical
sense of <I>wandering, vagrant.</I>
<P>149. <B>wheeling]</B> <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii) adopts <I>wheedling</I> from his (MS), as it is &lquo;just the
epithet that would be applied by Roderigo to Othello, who had cajoled and cheated
Brabantio out of his daughter.&rquo; <SC>Singer</SC> (<I>Sh. Vind.</I> p. 279): Even could Collier adduce
an instance of <I>wheedling</I> before the reign of Charles II., it would be difficult to per
suade us to displace &lquo;wheeling;&rquo; for, connected, as it is, with &lquo;extravagant,&rquo; it is no
doubt used like the Italian &lquo;girevole,&rquo; with its secondary meaning of <I>inconstant, un
steady.</I> That <I>wheedling</I> should have been suggested, makes it certain that Collier's
(MS) in this instance lived not earlier than the last century. <SC>Staunton</SC> says, that he
would prefer <I>whirling.</I> <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Lex.</I>) thinks that from meaning &lquo;to fetch a com-
pass,&rquo; as in <I>Cor.</I> I, vi, 19, it came to mean &lquo;to err about,&rquo; as here and in <I>Tro. &amp; Cress.</I>
V, vii, 2.
<P>156. <B>dream]</B> <SC>Coleridge</SC> (<I>Notes</I>, &amp;c. 249): The old careful senator, being caught
careless, transfers his caution to his dreaming power at least. <SC>Booth</SC>: This dream is
to the superstitious Italian convincing proof of what he is told, and accounts for his
sudden belief in his friend's treachery.

<CC><P><I>speare Jahrbuch</I>, 1879, xiv, 174) gives a curious list of the Inns of Venice in Othello's
day, of which history has preserved the names, as follows: &lquo;<I>al Selvadego, allo Sturione,
al Cavaletto, al Capello, alle do</I> (<I>due</I>) <I>Spade, alla Campana, al S. Giorgio</I> or <I>al Flauto,
al Lion bianco, al Gambaro, alla Luna, all' Aquila nera, alla Corona, all' Angelo, alla
Torre</I>,&mdash;but <I>al Sagittario</I> has not yet been discovered. The most probable supposition
is,&rquo; continues Th. Elze, &lquo;that it was an imaginary name devised by Shakespeare, which
we should be as little likely to discover as <I>The Pegasus</I> in Genoa, where the Pedant
lodged with Baptista in <I>Tam. of Shr.</I> IV, iv, 5. A certain appropriateness in the
names and characters is not lacking: the soldier lives in the <I>Sagittary</I>, the Pedant in
the <I>Pegasus.</I>&rquo; <SC>Rolfe</SC> disposes of Knight's assertion, that this was the Arsenal. &lquo;It
appears,&rquo; he says, in his Notes ad loc. &lquo;from I, ii, 53, below, that Othello was not at his
usual lodging, and the messengers of the Senate had not known where to find him.
Cassio also asks &ldquo;What makes he here?&rdquo; which implies that he was in an unfamiliar
place. Note also what Othello says, in I, iii, 143. If the Arsenal had been the
&ldquo;place,&rdquo; no guide to it would have been necessary.&rquo; In an <I>Addendum</I> on p. 210,
Rolfe still more emphatically disproves Knight's remark: &lquo;We cannot find any evi-
dence that the Arsenal at Venice was ever called &ldquo;the Sagittary;&rdquo; probably this is a
mere conjecture of Knight's. The figure mentioned by Knight is not &ldquo;over the gates,&rdquo;
but is one of four statues standing in front of the structure. It represents a man hold-
ing a bow (not &ldquo;drawn&rdquo;) in his hand, but is in no respect more conspicuous than its
three companions. If Shakespeare was ever in Venice he probably saw the statue (if
it is as old as the gateway, which was built in 1460), but we cannot imagine why it
should suggest to him to call the place <I>the Sagittary.</I> That word means not an ordi-
nary archer, but a <I>Centaur</I> with a bow, as in the familiar representations of the zodiacal
sign Sagittarius. This is its sense in the only other passage in which Shakespeare uses
it, <I>Tro. &amp; Cress.</I> V, v, 14: &ldquo;the dreadful Sagittary Appals our numbers.&rdquo; That <I>the
Sagittary</I> in the present passage cannot be the Arsenal is, however, sufficiently clear
from I, iii, 143, 144. The Arsenal was by far the largest and most prominent public
building, or collection of buildings, in all Venice, its outer walls being nearly two miles
in circuit. To suppose that anybody in the employ of the government would need the
help of Iago in finding the place is absurd.&rquo;
<P>177. <B>despised]</B> <SC>Warburton</SC>: We should read <I>despited</I>, i. e. vexatious. <SC>Heath</SC>:
Brabantio very properly calls the remaining part of his life a &lquo;despised time,&rquo; since the
ill-conduct of his only daughter, in matching herself to an adventurer so much beneath
her birth and rank, could not, in his apprehension, but draw great contempt on himself.
<SC>Johnson</SC>: &lquo;Despised time&rquo; is <I>time of no value;</I> time in which &lquo;There's nothing serious
in mortality, The wine of life is drawn, and the mere dregs Are left this vault to brag
of,&rquo; <I>Macb</I> II, iii, 89. <SC>Steevens</SC>: Again, in <I>Rom. &amp; Jul.</I> I, iv, 110: &lquo;a despised life
closed in my breast.&rquo;</CC>

<CC><P>181. <B>deceaues]</B> May it not be permitted here to &lquo;frolic in conjecture,&rquo; and suggest
that the printer has accidentally substituted an <I>s</I> for a <I>d</I>, and that we should read <I>de-
ceaued</I>? Even if we adopt the reading of Q<SUB>1</SUB>, I should prefer <I>they deceaued</I> to &lquo;thou
deceiuest.&rquo; In both cases a certain symmetry of the sentence is preserved in the alter-
nation of thought, which is first fixed on the daughter, and then on the Moor, then
recurring to the daughter, then to the Moor and the daughter both together, then to
the daughter, and then to them both together again.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>186. <B>blood]</B> <SC>Booth</SC>: With emotion, as with Shylock: &lquo;my own flesh and blood to
rebel!&rquo;
<P>188. <B>Is]</B> See <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 335, for instances where the quasi-singular verb <I>precedes</I>
the plural subject. This usage Abbott explains on the ground, that when the subject is
as yet future, and, as it were, unsettled, the third person singular might be regarded as
the normal inflection. Such passages are very common, particularly in the case of
&lquo;There is.&rquo;
<P>188. <B>charmes]</B> <SC>Booth</SC>: In your study of this play bear in mind the superstition
that pervades it. Even Othello, while sneering at it, humours it when Desdemona is
brought before the Duke as a witness against him; and he has faith in the &lquo;antique
token&rquo; and the sword of &lquo;ice-brook's temper.&rquo; Reflections like these help the actor to
<I>feel</I> the character he assumes.
<P>189, 190. <B>By . . . abus'd]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: By which the faculties of a young virgin
may be infatuated and made subject to illusions and false imagination.</CC>

<CC><P>darkness of the night, which alwaies emboldeneth men to naughtinesse; and that there

<P>14. <B>Magnifico]</B> <SC>Tollet</SC>: &lquo;The chiefe men of Venice are by a peculiar name called
<I>Magnifici</I>, i. e. Magnificoes.&rquo;&mdash;Minsheu [s. v. <I>Magnificent.</I> Minsheu adds: Et Aca-

<P>16. <B>double]</B> <SC>Warburton</SC>, followed by <SC>Theobald</SC> (not <SC>Capell</SC>, as <SC>Knight</SC> says),
interpreted this as signifying <I>as large, as extensive</I>, equivalent to the Greek <G>diplou_s</G>,
and cited Dioscorides and Theocritus. Whereupon Dr <SC>Johnson</SC> thus improved the
occasion: All this learning, if it had even been what it endeavors to be thought, is, in
this place, superfluous. There is no ground for supposing, that our author copied or
knew the Greek phrase; nor does it follow, that, because a word has two senses in
one language, the word which in another answers to one sense should answer to both.
<I>Manus</I>, in Latin, signifies both a <I>hand</I> and <I>troop of soldiers</I>, but we cannot say, that
&lquo;the captain marched at the head of his hand;&rquo; or, &lquo;that he laid his troop upon his
sword.&rquo; It is not always in books that the meaning is to be sought of this writer, who
was much more acquainted with naked reason and with living manners. &lquo;Double&rquo; has
here its natural sense. The president of every deliberative assembly has a <I>double</I> voice.
In our courts the chief justice and one of the inferior judges prevail over the other two.</CC>

<CC><C>[16. <B>&lquo;As double as the Dukes.&rquo;</B>]</C>
<P>because the chief justice has a <I>double</I> voice. Brabantio had in his effect, tho&rquo; not by
law yet by <I>weight</I> and <I>influence</I>, a voice not <I>actual</I> and <I>formal</I>, but <I>potential</I> and ope-
rative, as <I>double</I>, that is, a voice that when a question was suspended would turn the
balance as effectually <I>as the Duke's.</I> &lquo;Potential&rquo; is used in the sense of science; a
caustic is called a potential fire. <SC>Malone's</SC> studies in early Venetian polity played
him false here; so far from the Duke's having a &lquo;<I>double</I> voice,&rquo; it appears from
Thomas's <I>History of Italy</I>, 1560, that it was exactly what he had not: &lquo;Whereas,&rquo; says
Thomas, &lquo;many have reported, the duke in ballotyng should have <I>two voices;</I> it is
nothinge so, for in giving his voice he hath but one ballot, as all others have.&rquo; Nothing
discouraged, Malone at once surmises that &lquo;Shakespeare might have gone on this re-
ceived opinion, which he might have found in some other book. Supposing, however,
that he had learned from this very passage that the Duke had <I>not</I> a double voice in the
Council of Seven, yet as he had a vote in each of the various Councils of the Venetian
State (a privilege which no other person enjoys,) our poet might have thought himself
justified in the epithet which he has here used; and this circumstance, which he might
have found in a book already quoted, Contareno's <I>Commonwealth and Government of
Venice</I>, 1599, was, I believe, here in his thoughts: &ldquo;So great is the prince's authoritie,
that he may, in whatsoever court, adjoine himselfe to the magistrate therein, being presi-
dent, as his colleague and companion, and have equal power with the other presidents,&rdquo;
&amp;c., p. 41. Again, p. 42: &ldquo;Besides this, the prince hath in <I>every Councell</I> equal author-
itie with any of them, for one suffrage or lotte.&rdquo; Thus we see, continues Malone, though
he had not a double voice in any one assembly, yet as he had a vote in all the various
assemblies, his voice, thus <I>added</I> to the voice of each of the presidents of those assem-
blies, might with strict propriety be called <I>double</I> and <I>potential.</I>&rquo; <SC>Steevens</SC>: <I>Double</I>
and <I>single</I> anciently signified <I>strong</I> and <I>weak</I> when applied to liquors, and perhaps to
other objects. In this sense the former epithet may be employed by Brabantio, and the
latter by the chief justice speaking to Falstaff: &lquo;Is not your wit single?&rquo; Here the
phrase may, therefore, only signify that Brabantio's voice, as a magnifico, was as forcible
as that of the Duke. <SC>Henley</SC>: &lquo;The double voice&rquo; of Brabantio refers to the opinion,
(which, as being a magnifico, he was no less entitled to, than the duke himself), <I>either</I>,
of nullifying the marriage of his daughter contracted without his consent; <I>or</I>, of sub-
jecting Othello to fine and imprisonment for having seduced an heiress. <SC>Pye</SC> [does
one reader in a thousand know or remember, that Pye is a predecessor of Tennyson as
Poet-Laureate?&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]: Surely the obvious purport of the passage is that Brabantio,
from his popularity and wealth, has effectually such a weight in the Senate as gives
him a power equal to the double vote conferred by the constitution on the duke.
<SC>Knight</SC>: It is clear that Shakespeare did not take the phrase in a literal sense; for,
if he had supposed that the duke had a double voice as duke, he would not have as-
signed the same privilege to the senator Brabantio. <SC>Delius</SC>: If what Brabantio says
has as much weight as what the duke says, his voice must be twice as potential as that
of the other nobles, i. e. as double as the duke's. <SC>Hudson</SC>: &lquo;A voice potential or
powerful <I>as much so as</I> the Duke's.&rquo; <SC>Jourdain</SC> (<I>Philol. Soc. Trans.</I>, 1860, p. 142):
This is an historical mistake made by a typographical error; the &lquo;as&rquo; should be <I>of.</I>
The Duke had not a double voice, but the members of the Council of Three had very
nearly such, as the following will show:&mdash;&lquo;Next vnto the Duke are three called the
Signori Capi or Cai, whiche outwardly seeme inferioure to the Duke, and yet are of
more auctoritee than he. For theyr power is so absolute that if there happen cause
why, they maie arrest the Duke.&rquo;&mdash;<I>The historie of Italie</I>, by William Thomas, 1549.</CC>

<CC><P>directly opposite to the poet's meaning. So in <I>Lear</I>, III, i, 14, &lquo;unbonneted he runs.&rquo;
Othello means to say, that his birth and services set him upon such a rank that he may
speak to a Senator of Venice with his hat <I>on</I>, i. e. without showing any marks of defer-
ence or inequality. I, therefore, am inclined to think Shakespeare wrote: &lquo;May speak,
<I>and bonnetted</I>,&rquo; &amp;c. Or, if any like better the change of the negative <I>un</I>, in the cor-
rupted reading, into the epitatic <I>im</I>, we may thus reform it: &lquo;May speak <I>imbonnetted</I>,&rquo;
&amp;c. [This last conjecture was withdrawn by Theobald (ed. ii), but proposed anew by
Steevens, without credit.] <SC>Johnson</SC>: Pope's emendation may as well be <I>not putting
on</I> as <I>not putting off</I>, the bonnet. <SC>Steevens</SC>: <I>Bonneter</I>, says Cotgrave, is to put off
one's cap. So in <I>Cor.</I> II, ii, 30. Mr Fuseli explains this passage as follows: &lquo;I am
his equal or superior in rank; and were it not so, such are my demerits, that, unbon-
neted, without the addition of patrician or senatorial dignity, they may speak to as
proud a fortune,&rquo; &amp;c. &lquo;At Venice the <I>bonnet</I>, as well as the toge, is a badge of aris-
tocratic honours to this day.&rquo; A. C. (in <I>Var.'21</I>): &lquo;Unbonneted&rquo; is uncovered, re-
vealed, made known. See a similar expression in II, iii, &lquo;you <I>unlace</I> your reputation.&rquo;
<SC>Coleridge</SC> (<I>Notes</I>, &amp;c., p. 250): Theobald's argument goes on the assumption that
Shakespeare could not use the same word differently in different places; whereas I
should conclude, that as in the passage in <I>Lear</I> the word is employed in its direct
meaning, so here it is used metaphorically; and this is confirmed by what has escaped
the editors, that it is not &lquo;I&rquo; but &lquo;my demerits&rquo; that may speak &lquo;unbonneted,&rquo;&mdash;without
the symbol of a petitioning inferior. <SC>Staunton</SC>: The import we take to be,&mdash;my ser-
vices when revealed (<I>unbonneted</I>) may <I>aspire</I> or <I>lay claim to</I> (<I>may speak to</I>) as proud
a fortune as this which I have attained. Even with Fuseli's interpretation it is indis-
pensable for the integrity of the passage that &lquo;speak to&rquo; be understood in the sense
just mentioned of <I>aspire</I> or <I>lay claim to.</I> <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Lex.</I>): Perhaps the meaning is
simply: I may say so with all courtesy and humility, and Othello's words must, per-
haps, be accompanied by a corresponding gesture, as the writing of F<SUB>1</SUB> seems to imply,
by placing the word &lquo;unbonnetted&rquo; in a parenthesis. <SC>White</SC> (ed. ii): The question
of manners in Shakespeare's time as to the hat seems very difficult. The remembering
courtesy, the off-capping, and the unbonneting are quite incongruous. No attempt to
reconcile these expressions has been at all successful.

<CC><P><I>curl'd</I> by nature. <SC>Johnson</SC>: &lquo;Curled&rquo; is <I>elegantly and ostentatiously dressed.</I> He
had not the hair particularly in his thoughts. <SC>Steevens</SC>: Shakespeare evidently

the same expression in his <I>Just Italian</I> [but as was said before, parallel expressions

expressly mentioned, and the epithet &lquo;curled&rquo; is added as characteristic of a person
of the highest rank: &lquo;Let him have time to tear his curled hair.&rquo; [See notes in
<I>Lear</I>, III, iv, 84, &lquo;A Serving-man, proud in heart and mind; that curled my
hair.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>85. <B>Deareling]</B> <SC>Knight</SC>: This Saxon word is used in a plural sense. <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Re-
marks</I>, p. 233): The fact is, the <I>s</I> has been omitted in the Folio by a mistake of the
compositor. In Shakespeare's time <I>dearling</I> could never have been used as a plural.
That even Spenser (who antiquated his language more than any of his contemporaries)
did not venture to employ such an archaism, is proved by the following from his <I>Hymne
in honour of Love:</I>&mdash;&lquo;in a Paradize Of all delight, and ioyous happie rest, Where they
doe feede on Nectar heauenly wize, With <I>Hercules</I> and <I>Hebe</I>, and the rest Of <I>Venus</I>
dearlings, through her bountie blest.&rquo;
<P>87. <B>Guardage]</B> <SC>Rolfe</SC>: Guardianship, used by Shakespeare nowhere else.
<P>88. <B>to feare]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: To terrify, as in <I>3 Hen. VI:</I> V, ii, 2, &lquo;a bug that fear'd
us all.&rquo; The line is redundant in measure. It might originally have ran, &lquo;Of such as
thou: to fear, not to delight.&rquo; <SC>Malone</SC> takes &lquo;fear&rquo; to be a substantive, and used for
the object of fear; but <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 405, more correctly explains the phrase as an ellipsis,
common among Elizabethans, after <I>will</I> and <I>is</I>, e. g. &lquo;I will to the weird sisters.&rquo; &lquo;I
must to Coventry.&rquo; &lquo;I am to thank you for it,&rquo; i. e. I am <I>bound</I> to thank you for it; s<*>
here &lquo;such a thing as thou (a thing <I>fit</I>) to fear (<I>act.</I>), not to delight.&rquo;
<P>89. <B>Judge me]</B> <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 365, Let the world judge for me. This optative use
of the subjunctive, dispensing with &lquo;let,&rquo; &lquo;may,&rquo; &amp;c., gives great vigour to the Shake-
spearian line. [It is doubtful if &lquo;me&rquo; be here the Ethical Dative, as in I, i, 53: &lquo;Whip
me such honest knaues,&rquo; or &lquo;He plucked me ope his doublet,&rquo; <I>Jul. C&aelig;s.</I> Brabantio calls
upon the world really to judge him and his position, which he immediately proceeds to
state.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>90. <B>practis'd]</B> Very frequently used, as here, in the sense of plotting, with arts or
magic. See <I>Lear</I>, III, ii, 57: &lquo;Has practis'd on man's life.&rquo;
<P>91. <B>Minerals]</B> In <I>Ham.</I> IV, i, 26, &lquo;a mineral&rquo; means a <I>mine</I>, but in <I>Cymb.</I> V, v, 50,
in the present passage, and in II, i, 330, it is used in the sense of a drug or mortal
poison.</CC>

<CC><P>92. <B>weakens Motion]</B> <SC>Theobald</SC> suggested and adopted <I>weaken notion.</I> &lquo;That
is, her <I>apprehension</I>, right <I>conception</I> and <I>idea</I> of things, <I>understanding, judgment;</I>
and supported the change by the apposite passage, &lquo;his notion weakens,&rquo; <I>Lear</I>, I, iv,
221. <SC>Capell</SC> thought Theobald's change was &lquo;open to no objections.&rquo; <SC>Malone</SC> and
<SC>Steevens</SC> approved of Hanmer's text, seeing that <I>motion</I> is used afterward in I, iii,
364, in the same sense, and also in <I>Cymb.</I> II, v, 20; <I>Ham.</I> III, iv, 72; <I>Meas. for
Meas.</I> I, iv, 59; and because, as Malone said, there was &lquo;good reason to believe that
the words <I>weaken</I> and <I>waken</I> were in Shakespeare's time pronounced alike.&rquo; &lquo;The
objection to Theobald's &ldquo;notion,&rdquo;&rquo; continues Malone, &lquo;is that no opiates or intoxicating
potions or powders of any sort can distort or pervert the <I>intellects</I>, but by destroying
them for a time; nor was it ever, at any time, believed by the most credulous that <I>love-
powders</I>, as they were called, could <I>weaken the understanding</I>, though it was formerly
believed that they could <I>fascinate</I> the <I>affections;</I> or, in other words, <I>waken</I> motion.
Brabantio afterward asserts, &ldquo;That with some mixtures powerful o'er the <I>blood</I> He
wrought upon her.&rdquo; Shakespeare, in almost all his plays, uses <I>blood</I> for passion.
And one of the Senators asks Othello, not whether he had <I>weakened</I> Desdemona's
<I>understanding</I>, but whether he did &ldquo;by indirect and forced courses subdue and <I>poison</I>
this young maid's <I>affections.</I>&rdquo;&rquo; <SC>Ritson</SC> (p. 227), however, satisfactorily vindicates the
Folio, thus: To &lquo;weaken motion&rquo; is to <I>impair the faculties.</I> It was till very lately,
and may be still an opinion, that philtres or love potions have the power of perverting,
and of course weakening or impairing, both the sight and judgement, and of procuring
fondness or dotage toward any unworthy object who administers them. And by
<I>motion</I> Shakespeare means the senses which are depraved and weakened by these
fascinating mixtures. <SC>Staunton</SC> thinks that this view is expressly contradicted by
what Brabantio has just said: that Desdemona was &lquo;so opposite to marriage,&rquo; and he
&lquo;therefore readily accepts the easy emendation Hanmer offers. Brabantio's grievance,
it is plain, was not that Othello had, by charms and medicines, abated the motions
of Desdemona's sense, but that he had aroused and stimulated them.&rquo; R. M. <SC>Spence</SC>
(<I>N. &amp; Qu.</I>, 1879, 5th, xi, 383): Twice elsewhere in this Act &lquo;motion&rquo; means <I>emotion;</I>
the <I>usus loquendi</I> thus warrants me to regard <I>emotion</I> as the meaning of the word in
this passage also; if so, then Hanmer's <I>waken</I> must indubitably be adopted. [Truly
does <SC>Knight</SC> say of this passage that the notes, here very much abridged, of the Com-
mentators are neither satisfactory in a critical point of view, nor edifying in a moral
one.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>99. <SC>Booth</SC>: Now Othello's friends draw. Othello stands between the two parties
with sheathed scimetar held up; its crescent shape lends a little Oriental atmosphere to
the picture. 'Tis harmless.
<P>101. <B>Cue]</B> In <I>Ham.</I> II, ii, 534, <SC>Wedgwood's</SC> definition is quoted: &lquo;The last words
of the preceding speech, prefixed to the speech of an actor in order to let him know
when he is to come on the stage. From the letter Q by which it was marked, &ldquo;be-
cause,&rdquo; says Butler, <I>Eng. Gram.</I>, 1634, &ldquo;it is the first letter of <I>quando</I>, when, showing
when to enter and speak.&rdquo;&rquo; [Note Q<SUB>1</SUB> in Textual Notes.] <SC>Skeat</SC> now gives a differ-
ent derivation; he says, &lquo;that an actor's <I>cue</I> seems to be the same word as <I>queue</I>, as
signifying the last words or tail-end of the speech of the preceding speaker. Oddly
enough, it was, in this sense, sometimes denoted by Q; owing to the similarity of the
sound.&rquo;
<P>102. <B>Whether]</B> This passage is cited by <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Vers.</I> 106) as one of the many
instances in which <I>hither, whether</I>, &amp;c. are printed as dissyllables, where the verse indi-
cates that they are monosyllables. Cf. <I>Macb.</I> I, iii, 111; <I>Ham.</I> III, ii, 193; <I>Lear</I>, II,
i, 53, also in <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 466.
<P>105. <B>direct Session]</B> <SC>Hudson</SC>: The language is rather odd, and, perhaps, some-
what obscure; but the meaning probably is, till the time prescribed by law and by the
regular course of judicial procedure.</CC>

<P>121. <B>Pagans]</B> <SC>Theobald</SC>: Would Brabantio infer, if his private injury were not
redressed, the Senate should no longer pretend to call themselves Christians? But
pagans are as strict and moral as the most regular Christians in the preservation of pri
vate property. Difference of faith is not concerned, but mere human policy. I there-
fore read <I>pageants</I>, i. e. if we let such injurious actions go unpunished our statesmen
must be slaves, ciphers in office, and have no power of redressing, be things of mere
show and gaudy appearance only. <SC>Steevens</SC>: I believe the morality of either Chris
tians or pagans was not in our author's thoughts. He alludes to the common con-
dition of all blacks, who come from their own country both <I>slaves</I> and <I>pagans;</I> and
uses the word in contempt of Othello and his complexion. If this Moor is now
suffered to escape with impunity, it will be such an encouragment to his black country-
men, that we may expect to see all the first offices of our state filled up by the <I>pagans</I>
and <I>bondslaves</I> of Africa. <SC>Heath</SC> (p. 534). It is certain from this very play that the
Moor had been both a <I>bondslave</I> and a <I>pagan</I>, though at that time he was neither.
<SC>Malone</SC>: In Shakespeare's time <I>pag in</I> was a very common expression of contempt</CC>

<CC><P>2. <SC>Lloyd</SC>: Central in the First Act is the scene in the Council Chamber; and the
consideration, by the Duke and Senators, of the news from Cyprus is no mere surplus-
age; it strikes a tone of dispassionate appreciation of evidence and opinion that domi-
nates all the succeeding scenes of agitation and disorders. From inconsistent intel-
ligence, the main point of agreement is carefully adopted for further examination,
notwithstanding predisposition to underrate it; intelligence, otherwise of good author-
ity, is condemned as fallacious from collateral indications; and lastly, thus prepared for,
the last courier has full credence, and the critical circumstances once understood action
follows at once. Othello is dispatched that very night. The same solid perspicacity
distinguishes the reception of the complaint of Brabantio.
<P>3. <B>composition]</B> <SC>Warburton</SC>: That is, consistency, concordancy.
<P>3. <B>this Newes]</B> <SC>Skeat</SC> (<I>Dict.</I> s. v.): The form <I>newes</I> does not seem to be older
than about <SC>a. d.</SC> 1500. It is nothing but a plural formed from <I>new</I> treated as a subs.,
so also <I>tidings.</I> It is a translation of F. <I>nouvelles</I>, plural of <I>nouvelle</I>, new (Cotgrave);
so also Lat. <I>nova</I> = new things, i. e. news. [From a rough calculation by means of Mrs
Cowden-Clarke's <I>Concordance</I>, I find that Shakespeare uses this word in the singular
more than three times as often as in the plural.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>7. <B>Hundred fortie]</B> <SC>White</SC> (ed. i): I think it not improbable that this passage
stood, as the rhythm requires: &lquo;My letters say a hundred seven galleys. <I>Duke.</I> And
mine a hundred forty. <I>2 Sen.</I> Mine, two hundred.&rquo; <SC>Purnell</SC>: The occasional omis-
sion of the conjunction in numerals may be a relic of the French usage (cent-quarante).
<P>10. <B>the ayme]</B> <SC>Warburton</SC>: Where there is no better ground for information
than conjecture. <SC>Johnson</SC>: The reading of Q<SUB>2</SUB> has a sense sufficiently easy and com-
modious. Where men <I>report</I> not by certain knowledge, but by <I>aim</I> and conjecture.
[For other instances of its use in the sense of <I>guess, conjecture</I>, see <SC>Schmidt</SC>, <I>Lex.</I></CC>

<CC><P>56. <B>To]</B> <SC>Malone</SC> interprets the text of the Qq, for those who adopt it, as meaning:
&lquo;tell him we wish him to make <I>all possible haste</I>;&rquo; and adds that all messengers in the
time of Shakespeare were enjoined, &lquo;Haste, haste; for thy life, post haste.&rquo;
<P>61. <B>Ottoman]</B> <SC>Malone</SC>: It is part of the policy of the Venetian state never to
entrust the command of an army to a native. &lquo;To exclude, therefore, (says Contareno,
trans. by Lewkenor, 1599) out of our estate the danger or occasion of any such ambi-
tious enterprises, our ancestors held it a better course to defend the dominions on the
continent with foreign mercenary soldiers, than with their home-bred citizens.&rquo; Again:
&lquo;alwaies they do entertain in honourable sort with great provision a <I>captaine generall</I>,
who alwaies is a <I>stranger borne.</I>&rquo; <SC>Reed</SC>: So in Thomas's <I>Hist. of Italy</I>, p. 82: &lquo;By
lande they are served of straungers, both for generalls, for capitaines, and for all other
men of warre; because theyr lawe permitteth not any Venetian to be capitaine over
an armie by lande: Fearing, I thinke, C&aelig;sar's example.&rquo; <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Lex.</I>) queries
whether this be used here as an adjective or substantive; <SC>Rolfe</SC> inclines to think it is
the former.
<P>62. <SC>Booth</SC>: The Duke should be busy with papers or conferring with the Senators,

<CC><P>of our Cinque-ports, where the Baily and his Fisher-men are knocking their heads together
on account of some Whale, or some terrible broil upon the Coast. But to show them
true Venetians, the maritime affairs stick not long on their hand; the public may sink
or swim. They will sit up all night to hear a Doctors Commons, Matrimonial, Cause.
And have the Merits of the Cause at large laid open to 'em, that they may decide it
before they stir. What can be pleaded to keep awake their attention so wonderfully?
Never, sure, was <I>form of pleading</I> so tedious and so heavy, as this whole scene and
midnight entertainment.

persuaded, therefore, that <I>set</I> of the Qq is right.

<CC><P>107. <B>vn-varnish'd u]</B> This is a noteworthy and praiseworthy attempt at correcting
a typographical error: &lquo;vn-varnish'd&rquo; should be spelled <I>vn-uarni$h'd.</I> In aiming at
correcting it by the substitution of the <I>u</I> for the <I>v</I>, the compositor forgot to remove the
<I>v</I>, and put <I>u</I>, with unusual accuracy, within seven letters of its true place.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>108. <B>my. . .Loue]</B> That is, &lquo;the whole course of my love.&rquo; This construction,
plain enough here, sometimes gives rise to difficulty: see &lquo;your sovereignty of reason,&rquo;
<I>Ham.</I> I, iv, 73; &lquo;his means of death,&rquo; <I>Ib.</I> IV, v, 207; &lquo;my better part of man,&rquo; <I>Macb.</I>
V, viii, 18, and many other examples in <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 423.
<P>109. <B>What]</B> The preposition <I>with</I>, which is here omitted, as in so many other in-
stances of adverbial expressions of time, or of manner (see <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 202), the F<SUB>2</SUB> sup-
plied after &lquo;daughter,&rquo; line 112, &lquo;The editor of that edition,&rquo; says Dyce (ed. iii), &lquo;not
knowing that, according to the earlier phraseology, such an addition was unnecessary
for the sense.&rquo; Doubtless through inadvertence, <SC>Grant White</SC> (ed. ii) says that <I>with</I>
was &lquo;recklessly omitted.&rquo; Cf. &lquo;The interim having weighed it,&rquo; <I>Macb.</I> I, iii, 154; &lquo;shall
. . . .More suffer and more sundry ways,&rquo; <I>Ib.</I> IV, iii, 48; &lquo;Which time she chanted,&rquo;
<I>Ham.</I> IV, vii, 179. <SC>Delius</SC> thinks that <I>with</I> was omitted, because the preceding line
in the parenthesis ended in &lquo;withal.&rquo;
<P>112. <SC>Rymer</SC> (p. 101): All this is but <I>Prcamble</I>, to tell the Court that He wants
words. This was the Eloquence which kept them up all night, and drew their atten-
tion in the midst of their alarms. One might rather think the novelty and strangeness
of the case prevail'd upon them: no, the Senators do not reckon it strange at all. In-
stead of starting at the Prodigy, every one is familiar with <I>Desdemona</I>, as he were her
own natural Father, rejoice in her good fortune, and wish their own several Daughters
as hopefully married. Should the Poet have provided such a Husband for an only
daughter of any noble Peer in <I>England</I>, the Black-amoor must have chang'd his Skin,
to look our House of Lords in the face.

<CC><P>118. <B>main'd]</B> In reference to this misprint <SC>Dyce</SC> says, that he does not mean to
defend it when he observes that in <I>2 Hen. VI:</I> IV, ii, 172, we have the provincialism
in Cade's speech: &lquo;mained,&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> lamed.
<P>119. <B>Perfection]</B> To <SC>Theobald</SC> the expression <I>perfection erring</I> seemed a contra-
diction. &lquo;I have ventured,&rquo; he says, &lquo;to imagine that our author wrote &ldquo;<I>Affection</I> so
could err.&rdquo;&rquo; <SC>Dr Johnson</SC>: The objection is childish; &lquo;perfection&rquo; is used here, as
almost everywhere else, for a high degree of excellence.
<P>121. <B>practises]</B> That is, <I>stratagems, treacherous plots</I>, very frequently thus used.
Cf. &lquo;a pass of practice,&rquo; <I>Ham.</I> IV, vii, 139; &lquo;my practices ride easy,&rquo; <I>Lear</I>, I.
ii, 172.
<P>127. <B>more wider]</B> Is not this to be preferred to &lquo;more certain&rquo; of the Qq? A wide
and open proof seems to stand in clear contrast to thin, narrow shows and trivial con-

<P>163. <B>Antars]</B> <SC>Pope</SC>: French, grottoes. <SC>Johnson</SC>: Caves and dens. <SC>Chalmers</SC>,
(<I>Supp. Apol.</I>, 464), whose learning was rather tickle o' the sere, has on this line a good
specimen note: &lquo;Shakespeare by no very uncommon quibble has used the expressions
&ldquo;anters vast&rdquo; and &ldquo;desarts idle&rdquo; in one sense, when he meant another. The progress
of the word &ldquo;anters&rdquo; seems to be this: anters, aunters, aventers, adventures; and
hence the word &ldquo;anters&rdquo; came to signify, in the language of Yorkshire, <I>strange things</I>
or <I>strange stories.</I> So in a disputation <I>bytwene a Chrystens mon and a Jew</I>, written
before the year 1300: &ldquo;Hur schull we longe abyde Auntres [adventures] to hear.&rdquo;
The play on &ldquo;desarts idle&rdquo; consists in confounding &ldquo;desart&rdquo; for a <I>wilderness</I> with
<I>desert</I> for merit; and <I>deserts idle</I>, or unworthy desert, might be deemed desert, <I>sine
pulvere.</I>&rquo;
<P>163. <B>idle]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: Every mind is liable to absence and inadvertency, else Pope
