tators that <I>wild</I> might add a feature of some import, even to a desert; whereas, <I>sterile</I>
leaves it j<*>st as it found it, and is (without a pun) the <I>idlest</I> epithet which could be
applied. <*>pe, too, had an ear for rhythm; and as his reading has some touch of
Shakespeare, which the other has not, and is besides better poetry, I should hope that
it will one day resume its proper place in the text.</CC>

with the most wondrous Tales; [lines 163-169 are here quoted]. Seriously, 'twas a
woful Tale! unfit, one wou'd think, to win a tender Fair-one. It's true, the Poet suf-
ficiently condemns her Fancy; and makes her (poor Lady!) pay dearly for it in the
end. But why, amongst his <I>Greek</I> names, he shou'd have chosen one which denoted

change their natural Inclination for fair, candid, and courteous Knights into a Passion

plain and literal sense, prevails strongly at the present time. Monsters and Monster-
lands were never more in request: And we may often see a Philosopher, or a Wit, run
a Tale-gathering in those <I>idle Desarts</I>, as familiarly as the silliest Woman or the merest
Boy. <SC>Warburton</SC>: Discourses of this nature made the subject of the politest conver-
sation, when voyages into, and discoveries of, the new world were all in vogue. So,
when the Bastard Faulconbridge in <I>King John</I>, describes the behaviour of upstart great-
ness, he makes one of the essential circumstances of it to be this kind of table-talk.
The <I>fashion</I> then running altogether this way, it is no wonder a young lady of quality
should be struck with the history of an adventurer. <SC>Johnson</SC>: Whoever ridicules
this account of the progress of love, shows his ignorance not only of history, but also
of nature and manners. It is no wonder that, in any age or in any nation, a lady&mdash;
recluse, timorous, and delicate&mdash;should desire to hear of events and scenes which she
could never see; and should admire the man who had endured dangers and performed
actions, which, however great, were yet magnified by her timidity.

most natural wish, to be the very hero himself before whose feet smooth success is
strewed, as it had been before Othello's? Is it unusual to hear a girl express the wish
that she were a man? It was not in this wish that Othello detected the &lquo;hint,&rquo; but in
the &lquo;Friend that loved her.&rquo; If Desdemona had expressed the wish to Othello's face,
that Heaven had made a husband for her just like Othello himself, I doubt if the latter,
or any one else, would have softened the expression into a &lquo;<I>hint.</I>&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>192. <SC>Lewes</SC> (<I>On Actors</I>, &amp;c., p. 5): Even in earlier and better days there was
much in [Kean's] performance of Othello which was spasmodic, slovenly, false. The
address to the Senate was very bad. He had little power of elocution, unless when
sustained by a strong emotion; and this long, simple narrative was the kind of speech
he could not manage at all. He gabbled over it, impatient to arrive at the phrase:
&lquo;And this was all the witchcraft I have used. Here comes the lady, let her witness
it.&rquo; His delivery of this &lquo;point,&rquo; always startled the audience into applause by its
incisive tone and its abrupt transition; yet nothing could be more out of keeping with
the Shakespearian character. Othello might smile with lofty disdain at the accusation
of witchcraft, or rebut it calmly, but not make it the climax of a withering sarcasm,&mdash;
attacking the word &lquo;witchcraft&rquo; with high and sudden emphasis, and dropping into an
almost disrespectful colloquialism as the lady appeared. Indeed, throughout the First
and Second Acts, with the exception of occasional flashes (as in the passionate fervour
with which he greets Desdemona on landing at Cyprus), Kean's Othello was rather
irritating and disappointing,&mdash;arresting the mind, but not satisfying it. From the
Third Act onwards, all was wrought out with a mastery over the resources of ex-
pression such as has been seldom approached. In the successive unfolding of these
great scenes he represented with incomparable effect the lion-like fury, the deep and
haggard pathos, the forlorn sense of desolation alternating with gusts of stormy cries
for vengeance, the misgivings and sudden reassurances, the calm and deadly reso-
lution of one not easily moved, but who, being moved, was stirred to the very depths.</CC>

<CC><C>[245. <B>the bruized heart was pierc'd through the eares</B>].</C>
<P><I>wounded.</I> True, so it does sometimes; but it is also used in a good sense, as here, for
touching, affecting, comforting, as with music, the &lquo;bruised heart&rquo;&mdash;&lquo;the ear-piercing
fife.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Piec'd</I> is a wretched emendation; who ever talked of <I>piecing</I> a bruise? <SC>Sir
Joshua Reynolds</SC>: Shakespeare was continually changing his first expression for
another, either stronger or more uncommon; so that very often the reader, who has
not the same continuity or succession of ideas, is at a loss for its meaning. Many of
Shakespeare's uncouth, strained epithets may be explained by going back to the ob-
vious and simple expression, which is most likely to occur to the mind in that state.
I can imagine that the first mode of expression that occurred to the poet was this:
&lquo;The <I>troubled</I> heart was never cured by words.&rquo; To give it poetical force, he altered
the phrase: &lquo;The wounded heart was never reached through the ear.&rquo; <I>Wounded</I> heart
he changed to <I>broken</I>, and that to &lquo;bruised,&rquo; as a more common expression. <I>Reached</I>
he altered to <I>touched</I>, and the transition is then easy to &lquo;pierced,&rquo; i. e. thoroughly <I>touched.</I>
When the sentiment is brought to this state, the commentator, without this unravelling
clue, expounds <I>piercing the heart</I> in its common acceptation <I>wounding the heart</I>, which,
making in this place nonsense, is corrected to <I>pieced the heart</I>, which is very stiff, and,
as Polonius says, <I>is a vile phrase.</I> <SC>Steevens's</SC> thoughts turn to surgery, and he sug-
gests that as inflammation sometimes results from a <I>bruise</I>, a cure can be effected only
by &lquo;piercing&rquo; or lancing. <SC>Malone</SC>: &lquo;Pierced&rquo; is merely a figurative expression, and
means not <I>wounded</I>, but <I>penetrated in a metaphorical sense;</I> thoroughly affected.
[Malone here gives a dozen citations from Shakespeare, Spenser, Marlowe, and <I>The
Mirrour for Magistrates</I>, which merely show that what is <I>pierced</I> is <I>penetrated;</I> while
the need is, in this instance, of examples in proof that <I>piercing</I> can mean, what Jen-
nens rightly says it means, viz.: penetrating with a soothing or consoling power. Of
Malone's many quotations only four are in this sense quite germane, viz.: &lquo;Honest plain
words best pierce the ear of grief,&rquo; <I>Love's Lab.</I> V, ii, 763; &lquo;With sweetest touches
pierce your mistress' ear,&rquo; <I>Mer. of Ven.</I> V, i, 67; &lquo;Nor thee, nor them, thrice noble
Tamburlane, Shall want my heart to be with gladness pierc'd,&rquo; Marlowe's <I>Tambur-
lane</I>, Part First, I, ii; &lquo;Whose [Melib&oelig;e's] sensefull words empierst his hart so neare
That he was rapt with double rauishment,&rquo; <I>Faerie Queene</I>, Bk VI, ix, 233 (ed. Grosart).
Another example Malone gives from Spenser, where, as he says, &lquo;we have the very
words of the text,&rquo; with the implication that the drift is parallel, which I do not think
is the case. It is in the description of <I>Sclaunder</I>, Bk IV, viii, 231: &lquo;<I>Her words. . . .
Which passing through the eares, would pierce the hart</I> And wound the soule it selfe
with grief vnkind: For like the stings of Aspes, that kill with smart, Her spightfull
words did pricke, and wound the inner part.&rquo; Malone quoted only the words which
are italicized, probably in all honesty, and the trifling matter would not have deserved
attention had not Knight, and Staunton, and even Dyce, been misled into citing the
passage, assuredly without looking it up; the two former, unfortunately, without ac-
knowledgement to Malone. Hudson cites it, but had verified it. <SC>Purnell</SC> says, that
we must &lquo;take the word here as meaning merely reached.&rquo; <SC>Bailey</SC> (ii, 107), whose
notes life (or at least, my life) is, alas, too short to cite in full, and whereof the
felicity is not always in direct ratio to their length, proposed as an emendation, which
he is &lquo;quite sure is far more likely to have been Shakespeare's language&rquo; than
either &lquo;pierced&rquo; or &lquo;pieced&rquo;: &lquo;That the bruis'd heart was <I>plaster'd</I> through the ear.&rquo;&mdash;
<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>276. <B>I loue]</B> <SC>Knight</SC>: Desdemona's love remains, and though the <I>did</I> of the Qq
assists the rhythm, it enfeebles the sense. <SC>Cowden-Clarke</SC>: Desdemona is gentle
even to timidity; but, like many women whose gentleness has been wrought into timid-
ity by a too rigid strictness of their elders, she is capable of singularly bold action and
of self-assertion on occasion. Her independent act in leaving her father's house, and
in marrying the man of her choice, is precisely characteristic of the one, and her present
speech is an eminent specimen of the other. Encouraged by loving treatment, she is
capable of moral strength; chilled by severity, she is a moral coward.</CC>

<CC><P>277. <SC>Edwards</SC> (<I>Canons</I>, &amp;c., p. 144): &lquo;Downright violence,&rquo; means the unbridled
impetuosity with which her passion hurried her on to this unlawful marriage; and
&lquo;storm of fortunes&rquo; may signify the hazard she thereby ran of making shipwreck of
her worldly interest. Both very agreeable to what she afterwards says: &lquo;to his hon-
ours and his valiant parts Did I my soul and fortunes consecrate.&rquo; <SC>Heath</SC> (p. 557):
That is, my entrance upon the fortunes I have chosen in that violent manner of pro-
ceeding as if I had taken them by storm. <SC>Johnson</SC>: &lquo;Violence&rquo; is not <I>violence suf-
fered</I>, but <I>violence acted.</I> Breach of common rules and obligations. Perhaps the Qto
has the true reading. M. <SC>Mason</SC> cannot understand the &lquo;storm of fortunes&rquo; with &lquo;for-
tunes&rquo; in the plural, and asserts that we should read either &lquo;scorn of fortunes,&rquo; or
&lquo;storm of Fortune,&rquo; the latter meaning &lquo;not the injuries of Fortune, but Desdemona's
own high-spirited braving of her.&rquo; <SC>Steevens</SC>: The same mistake of <I>scorn</I> for &lquo;storm&rquo;
occurs in the old copies of <I>Tro. &amp; Cress.</I> I, i, 35: &lquo;as when the sun doth light a
scorn.&rquo; <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Remarks</I>, &amp;c., p. 234) believes that <I>scorn</I> of the Qto was &lquo;no doubt
right;&rquo; but as an editor he preferred &lquo;storm.&rquo; He cites a passage, which Mason had
cited before him, from B. and Fl.'s <I>Honest Man's Fortune</I>, IV, i: &lquo;where we find,&rquo; says
Dyce, &lquo;according to the old eds., &ldquo;He'll laugh and <I>storm</I> you,&rdquo; &amp;c., while the ex-
cellent MS. of that play in my possession affords the true reading: &ldquo;He'll laugh and
<I>scorn</I> you,&rdquo; &amp;c.&rquo; <SC>Singer</SC>: &lquo;Storm&rquo; seems to be used intensively of violence, &lquo;the
stormy violence I have used against my fortunes.&rquo; <SC>Hudson</SC>: The meaning, probably,
is the state or course of life which the speaker has boldly ventured upon in forsaking
the peaceful home of her father to share the storms and perils, the violences and
hardships, of a warrior's career. <I>Scorn</I> will not cohere with <I>violence</I>, unless by making
it express a quality of Desdemona herself, not of her fortunes. She evidently means
the violence and storm of fortunes which she has <I>braved</I> or <I>encountered</I> in marrying
the Moor, and not any thing of a violent or scornful temper in herself. <SC>Rolfe</SC>: The
bold action I have taken, and the stormy fortunes I have voluntarily encountered, in
order to marry him.

might, to herself, speak of the &lquo;amorous rites,&rquo; but for Desdemona to do so before the
Senate of Venice! impossible. Would it not, then, be better to read <I>parts?</I> She had
just said, that it was &lquo;for his honours and his valiant parts&rquo; she loved him.

<CC><P>288, 289. I do not think that the Qq here give us a reading which is of essential
importance. There is a tone of humble, almost servile, entreaty in &lquo;beseech you,&rquo;
which jars a little on the dignified, &lquo;unbonneted&rquo; bearing of Othello throughout this
cene.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>291, 292. <B>heat . . . defunct]</B> <SC>Theobald</SC> was the first to note the obscurity of this
passage, which, as it had been theretofore printed, he pronounced a &lquo;period of as stub-
born nonsense as the editors have obtruded upon poor Shakespeare throughout his
whole works;&rquo; the difficulty lay, he thought, in the word &lquo;defunct,&rquo; which &lquo;signifies
nothing else either primitively or metaphorically&rquo; than <I>dead;</I> and Othello could not
mean to say that &lquo;appetite was dead in him,&rquo; because he afterwards says, &lquo;I am de-
clined Into the vale of years; yet <I>that's not much.</I>&rquo; Wherefore Theobald changed
&lquo;defunct&rquo; to <I>distinct</I>, and paraphrased the passage thus: &lquo;I do not beg her company
with me, merely to please myself; nor to indulge the heat and affects (i. e. affections)
of a new-married man, in my own distinct and proper satisfaction, but to comply with
her in her request and desire of accompanying me.&rquo; Shakespeare, he adds, uses
&lquo;affects&rquo; for <I>affections</I> in several other passages which are cited. <SC>Upton</SC> (p. 183),
reading &lquo;the young affects&rquo; in parenthesis, says that &lquo;defunct&rquo; is &lquo;not to be taken
strictly here as signifying absolutely dead, but almost so; or from the Latin <I>defunctus</I>,
it might mean, discharged from youthful appetite, and proper to his age and character.
So afterwards (II, i, 262), Iago says, &ldquo;there should be loveliness in favour, sympathy
in years, manners, beauties, all which the Moor is <I>defective</I> in.&rdquo; Now, if any alter-
ation be proposed, instead of &ldquo;defunct&rdquo; the properest word seems <I>defect:</I> &ldquo;In my
<I>defect</I> and proper satisfaction,&rdquo; in which sense the Latins use <I>defectus.</I> Or what if,
with a slighter variation still, we read: &ldquo;Nor to comply with heat (the young affects
In <I>me</I> defunct) and proper&rdquo;? &amp;c.&rquo; <SC>Warburton</SC> paraphrases thus: &lquo;with that heat and</CC>

<P>new affections which the indulgence of my appetite has raised and created;&rquo; and then
dogmatically adds: &lquo;this is the meaning of &ldquo;defunct,&rdquo; which has made all the diffi
culty of the passage.&rquo; <SC>Johnson</SC>, whose note, wherein he follows Upton's &lquo;in <I>me</I> de-

received by Hanmer. Warburton's explanation is not more satisfactory: what made
the difficulty will continue to make it. &ldquo;Affects&rdquo; here stands not for <I>love</I>, but for
<I>quality</I>, for that by which anything is affected. &ldquo;I ask it not,&rdquo; says he, &ldquo;to please
appetite, or satisfy loose desires, the passions of youth which I have now outlived, or
for any particular gratification of myself, but merely that I may indulge the wishes of
my wife.&rdquo;&rquo; <SC>Steevens</SC>: In <I>The Bondman</I> (I, iii, p. 29, ed. Gifford) by Massinger is a

Timoleon is the speaker, and says to Cleon, &lquo;youthful heats, That look no further than

some accident changed places, and that the passage ought to read: &lquo;Nor to comply
with heat, the young affects; But to be free and bounteous to her mind, In my defunct
and proper satisfaction,&rquo; I would then recommend it to consideration, whether the
word &lquo;defunct&rquo; (which would be the only remaining difficulty) is not capable of a sig-
nification drawn from the primitive sense of its Latin original, which would very well
agree with the context. <SC>Tollet</SC>: I would propose: &lquo;In my <I>defenc't</I>, or <I>defenc'd</I>,&rquo;
&amp;c., i. e. I do not beg her company merely to please the palate of my appetite, nor to
comply with the heat of lust which the <I>young</I> man <I>affects</I>, i. e. loves and is fond of, in
a gratification which I have by marriage <I>defenc'd</I>, or inclosed and guarded, and made
my own property. . . . . I am persuaded that the word &lquo;defunct&rquo; must be at all events
ejected. <SC>Henley</SC>: Othello here supposes that his petition for the attendance of his
bride might be ascribed to one of these two motives: either solicitude for the enjoy-
ment of an unconsummated and honourable marriage, or the mere gratification of a
sensual and selfish passion. But as neither was the true one, he abjures them both:
&lquo;I therefore beg it <I>not</I> To please the palate of my appetite; <I>Nor</I> to comply with heat
(&mdash; &mdash;) and proper satisfaction.&rquo; The former, having nothing in it unbecoming, he
<I>simply</I> disclaims; but the latter, ill-according with his season of life, he assigns a reason
for renouncing: &lquo;the young affects In me <I>defunct.</I>&rquo; As if he had said, &lquo;I have out-
lived <I>that</I> wayward impulse of passion by which younger men are stimulated.&rquo; By
&lquo;young affects&rquo; the poet clearly means those &lquo;youthful lusts&rquo; which St. Paul admon-
ishes Timothy to flee from and the Romans to mortify. <SC>Malone</SC>: For the emendation
<I>disjunct</I> I am responsible. Some emendation is absolutely necessary, and this appears
to me the least objectionable of those which have been proposed. To the reading of
Upton &lquo;(the young affects In me defunct),&rquo; there are three strong objections. The first
is, the suppression of the word <I>being</I> before <I>defunct</I>, which is absolutely necessary to
the sense, and of which the omission is so harsh that it affords an argument against the
probability of the proposed emendation. The second and the grand objection is, that
it is highly improbable that Othello should declare on the day of his marriage that the
youthful affections were dead in him. He himself (as Theobald has observed) informs
us afterwards that he is &lquo;declined into the vale of years;&rquo; but adds at the same time,
&lquo;yet that's <I>not much.</I>&rquo; This surely is a decisive proof that the text is corrupt. My
third objection to Upton's regulation is, that by the introduction of a parenthesis, which
is not found in the old copies, the words &lquo;and proper satisfaction&rquo; are so unnaturally</CC>

<P>disjoined from those with which they are connected in sense, as to form a most lame
and impotent conclusion; to say nothing of the awkwardness of using the word &lquo;proper&rquo;
without any possessive pronoun prefixed to it. All these difficulties are done away by
retaining the original word &lquo;my,&rquo; and reading <I>disjunct</I>, instead of &lquo;defunct;&rquo; and the
meaning will be, &lquo;I ask it not for the sake of my <I>separate</I> and private enjoyment, by
the gratification of appetite, but that I may indulge the wishes of my wife.&rquo; <SC>Rann</SC>
(reading &lquo;the young affect's In me defunct&rquo;): &lquo;The tumult of such young desires is at
my time of life considerably abated.&rquo; Rann here anticipates <SC>Gifford</SC>, who in his note
on the passage in Massinger's <I>Bondman</I>, cited by Steevens, says: &lquo;&ldquo;Affects&rdquo; occurs
incessantly in the sense of <I>passions, affections:</I> &ldquo;young affects&rdquo; are, therefore, per-
fectly synonymous with <I>youthful heats.</I> Othello was not an old man, though he had
lost the fire of youth; the critics might, therefore, have dismissed that concern for the
lady, which they have so delicately communicated for the edification of the rising gen-
eration. . . . . I would wish the future editors of Shakespeare to consider whether he
might not have given <I>affect</I> in the singular (this also is used for <I>passion</I>) to corre-
spond with <I>heat.</I>&rquo; <SC>Knight</SC>: &lquo;Comply&rquo; may be used in the sense of <I>supply</I>, &lquo;affects&rquo;
are <I>affections</I>, and &lquo;defunct&rquo; does not necessarily mean <I>dead.</I> Tyrwhitt considers that
&lquo;defunct&rquo; may be used in the Latin sense of <I>performed.</I> As <I>function</I> has the same
Latin root, we would suggest that Shakespeare used &lquo;defunct&rquo; for <I>functional</I>, and then
the meaning is clear: &lquo;nor to gratify the young affections in my <I>official</I> and <I>individual</I>
satisfaction.&rquo; <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. i): &lquo;In my <I>defunct</I> and <I>proper</I> satisfaction&rquo; is merely &lquo;in
my <I>own dead</I> satisfaction&rquo; or gratification, the youthful passions or &lquo;young affects&rquo; being
comparatively &lquo;defunct&rquo; in him. For the sense, though not for the harmony of the
verse, it ought to have run &lquo;for my proper and defunct satisfaction;&rquo; and had it so
run, we doubt if so much ink would have been spilt and wasted upon it. It requires
no proof that &lquo;proper&rquo; was often used for <I>own.</I> <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Remarks</I>, p. 235) apprehends
that &lquo;few persons will be satisfied with Collier's explanation; nobody, assuredly, with
Knight's,&rquo; and then cites the passage already given from Massinger's <I>Bondman</I>, to-
gether with one from Fletcher's <I>Fair Maid of the Inn</I>, I, i, first cited by Gifford, to
show, as Gifford had already observed, how these lines of Shakespeare were under-
stood by his contemporaries. &lquo;They also show,&rquo; adds Dyce, &lquo;that Upton's alteration
of &ldquo;my&rdquo; to <I>me</I> is absolutely necessary.&rquo; Both Dyce and Gifford approve of Johnson's

absence, and for my own satisfaction.&rquo; For the use of <I>default</I> in this sense Jourdain
cites several examples. <SC>White</SC> (ed. i): Utterly unable either to explain this passage
or to suggest in what particular it may be corrupted, I leave it exactly as it appears in
the old copies. Of the page after page of comment which has been written upon it,
and the several conjectural attempts which have been made to modify it into intelligi-
bility, only Johnson's appears worthy of notice. . . . . That Shakespeare, although he
may very probably have written &lquo;comply with heat,&rquo; wrote &lquo;comply with proper satis-

been said about this passage, and asserts that nothing can be less felicitous than John-

meaning of the speaker, which yet seems plain enough.&rquo; &lquo;The epithet &ldquo;young&rdquo; does</CC>

<CC><P>I think, we may rest. The object of the speaker is attained; he has given us his
meaning. As a mere intellectual amusement we may inquire into the passage more
curiously, and rearrange the puzzle while retaining the sense; the pleasure and the
profit will, by the exercise, accrue to ourselves alone, with but little likelihood of ever
heading, except in imagination, a band of converts. Moreover, in the inexplicable pas-
sages in Shakespeare, like &lquo;the runaway's eyes,&rquo; &lquo;the dram of eale,&rquo; &lquo;Vllorxa,&rquo; the
present passage, and others, after the printers have borne all the obloquy which we can
heap upon them, might we not frown a little at Shakespeare himself? He must have
written rapidly. Would his fame be seriously impaired or stabbed to the centre, if we
cautiously whispered among ourselves that he now and then wrote carelessly?&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>294. <B>defend . . . soules]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC> says, and he has been followed by all editors
who have noticed the word, that &lquo;defend&rquo; here means to <I>forbid</I>, a meaning which it
undoubtedly bears in many passages; but it may be doubted if it be worth while to
reject here its ordinary meaning; if it has a military flavour it is certainly not inappro-
priate to Othello. <SC>Abbott</SC> gives <I>prevent</I> as its equivalent, which to me is scarcely better
than <I>forbid.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed. Collier</SC> (<I>Notes</I>, &amp;c., p. 451): &lquo;Good souls&rquo; become <I>counsels</I> in
the (MS). Othello would hardly apply &lquo;good souls&rquo; to the Duke and Senators of

upwards, that the Hawke may not see at all, and when the threed shall ware loose or

threed is put nearer to the beake. For a Sparrow-hawke should see somewhat back-
wardes, and a Falcon forwardes. The reas&otilde; is that if the Sparrow-hawke should see

fist, and seeing the companie of men, or such like, she would bate too much.&rquo; Sir

(<I>Bible Word-Book</I>, s. v. <I>Cieled</I>): The etymology of this word is obscured by the spell-

a room was to cover it with boards, or wainscotting, like Fr. <I>plancher.</I> To <I>seel</I> the eyes
of a hawk or dove (Fr. <I>siller</I> les yeux) was to sew up their eyelids. &lquo;What we now call

<P>298. <SC>Malone</SC>: &lquo;Speculative instruments,&rquo; in Shakespeare's language, are the <I>eyes</I>,
and &lquo;active instruments,&rquo; the <I>hands and feet.</I> As &lquo;seel&rquo; is here metaphorically used,
it applies very properly to the &lquo;<I>speculative</I> instruments;&rquo; but <I>foils</I>, of the Qq, agrees
better with &lquo;<I>active</I> instruments.&rquo; <SC>Knight</SC>: The modern editors have made up a text
between the Qto and Ff. They reject the <I>foils</I> of the Qto, and adopt the &lquo;seel&rquo; of
the Ff, while they substitute the <I>active</I> of the Qto for the &lquo;offic'd&rquo; of the Ff. Having
accomplished this hocus-pocus, they tell us that speculative instruments are the eyes,
and active instruments the hands and feet; that to &lquo;seel&rquo; is to close the eyelids of a
bird, which applies very properly to the speculative instruments, but that <I>foils</I> better
suits the active. It is their own work they are quarrelling with, and not that of the
author. Either reading is good, if they had let it alone. The speculative and <I>active
instruments</I>, which are <I>foiled</I>, are the thoughts and the senses; the speculative and
<I>offic'd instrument</I>, which is <I>seeled</I>, is <I>the whole man</I> in meditation and in action. When
the poet adopted the more expressive word <I>seel</I>, he did not leave the ugly anomaly
which the commentators have made. He took the whole man as an instrument, spirit-
ual and material, and metaphorically seeled the perceptions of that instrument. [Cf.
&lquo;no speculation in those eyes,&rquo; <I>Macb.</I> III, iv, 95.]

<P>323-325. <B>Looke . . . faith]</B> <SC>Coleridge</SC> (<I>Notes</I>, &amp;c., 251): In real life, how do
we look back to little speeches as presentimental of, or contrasted with, an affecting

men. <SC>Verplanck</SC>: The actors who have been most celebrated in the part, from Quin
to Cooke, are understood to have represented Iago as at least a middle-aged man. Yet
the incident of Iago's youth seems to add much to the individuality and intensity of the
character. An old soldier of acknowledged merit, who, after years of service, sees a
young man like Cassio placed over his head, has not a little to plead in justification of
deep resentment, and in excuse, though not in defence, of his revenge; such a man
may well brood over imaginary wrongs. The caustic sarcasm and contemptuous esti-
mate of mankind are, at least, pardonable in a soured and disappointed veteran. But
in a young man the revenge is more purely gratuitous, the hypocrisy, the knowledge,
and dexterous management of the worst and weakest parts of human nature, the reck-
lessness of moral feeling,&mdash;even the stern, bitter wit, intellectual and contemptuous,
without any of the gayety of youth,&mdash;are all precocious and peculiar; separating Iago
from the ordinary sympathies of our nature, and investing him with higher talent and
blacker guilt. <SC>Cowden-Clarke</SC>: It is remarkable that Shakespeare has here taken
pains to specify the exact age of Iago, as he has specified that of Hamlet. They are,</CC>

<CC><P>perhaps, the two most intellectual characters that our poet has drawn; and he has made
them nearly of the same age, as if at that period of life a man's intellect were at the
culminating point of activity and energy. . . . . Iago is a hard, cold-blooded, almost
vivacious scoundrel from inherent disposition, who uses his keen intellect with the
same fierce joy in its skill and power to destroy that he uses his sharp dagger or sword.
<SC>Hudson</SC> (<I>Introd.</I>, p. 22): Moreover Iago's youth goes far to explain the trust which
others repose in him; they cannot suspect one so young of being either skilled in vil-
lainous craft or soured by hard experience of the world; while his polished manners
and winning address gain him the credit of superior parts, without breeding any ques-
tion of his truth.
<P>346. <B>Gynney Hen]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: Anciently the cant term for a prostitute.
<P>350. <B>Vertue]</B> <SC>Coleridge</SC> (<I>Notes</I>, 251): This speech comprises the passionless
character of Iago. It is all will in intellect; and therefore he is here a bold partisan
of a truth, but yet of a truth converted into a falsehood by the absence of all the neces-
sary modifications caused by the frail nature of man. And then comes the last senti-
ment: &lquo;Our raging motions, our carnal stings, our unbitted lusts, whereof I take this
that you call&mdash;love to be a sect or scion!&rquo; Here is the true Iagoism of, alas! how
many! Note Iago's pride of mastery in the repetition of &lquo;Go, make money!&rquo; to his
anticipated dupe, even stronger than his love of lucre; and when Roderigo is com-
pletely won&mdash;&lquo;I am chang'd. I'll go sell all my land,&rquo; when the effect has been fully
produced, the repetition of triumph&mdash;&lquo;Go to; farewell; put money enough in your
purse!&rquo;

<CC><P>good linen it made. In many parts of England the young shoots are boiled and much
relished as food, and M. Soyer tried hard, but almost in vain, to introduce it as a most
dainty dish. In other points the nettle is a most interesting plant. Microscopists find
in it most beautiful objects; entomologists value it as a favourite of butterflies and other
insects, of which in Britain alone upwards of thirty varieties feed solely on the nettle-
plant, and it marks the progress of civilization by following man wherever he goes.
But as a garden plant the only advice to be given is to keep it out of the garden by
every means, where, if allowed, it would soon become a sad weed.
<P>353. <B>Lettice]</B> <SC>Ellacombe</SC> (p. 106): This excellent vegetable with its Latin name
came to us, probably, from the Romans. It was cultivated by the Anglo-Saxons, who,
in recognition of its narcotic qualities, called it &lquo;Sleepwort.&rquo; In Shakespeare's time the
sorts cultivated were very similar to ours, and probably as good.
<P>353. <B>Hisope]</B> <SC>Ellacombe</SC> (p. 97): The <I>Hyssopus officinalis</I> is not a British plant,
but it was held in high esteem in Shakespeare's time. It is now very little cultivated;
it has not much beauty, and its medicinal properties are not much esteemed; yet it will
always have an interest to readers of the Bible, though whether or not the hyssop of
Scripture is the <I>Hyssopus offic.</I> is still a question. It seems likely from the following
passage in Lyly's <I>Euphues</I>, that the plants were not named at random by Iago: &lquo;Good
gardeiners, in their curious knots, mixe Hisoppe with Time, as ayders the one to the
growth of the other; the one beeing drye, the other moyst&rquo; [p. 37, ed. Arber].
<P>353. <B>Time]</B> <SC>Ellacombe</SC> (p. 233): It is one of the most curious of the curiosities
of English plant names that the Wild Thyme,&mdash;a plant so common and so widely dis-
tributed, and that makes itself so easily known by its fine, aromatic, pungent scent that
it is almost impossible to pass it by without notice,&mdash;has yet no English name, and
never seems to have had one. Thyme is the Anglicized form of the Greek and Latin
<I>Thymum</I>, which it probably received from its use as incense in sacrifices; while its
other name, <I>serpyllum</I>, refers to its creeping habit. It is another curious point con-
nected with the name that <I>thymum</I> does not occur in the old English vocabularies.
Nor is even its Latin form found, except in the <I>Prompt. Parv.</I>, where it is &lquo;Tyme,
herbe, <I>Tima, timum</I>&mdash;Tyme, flowre, <I>Timus.</I>&rquo; It is thus a puzzle to know how it can
have got naturalized among us, for in Shakespeare's time it was completely naturalized.
It is as a bee-plant especially that the thyme has always been celebrated. See Ovid's
<I>Fasti</I>, v; Vergil, <I>Ed.</I> vii. The wild thyme can be scarcely considered a garden plant,
except in its variegated and golden varieties; but if it ever should come naturally in the
turf, it should be welcomed and cherished for its sweet scent.

<CC><P>378. <B>Locusts]</B> <SC>Warburton</SC>: Whether you understand by this the insect or the
fruit, it cannot be given as an instance of a delicious morsel, notwithstanding the exag-
gerations of lying travellers. The true reading is <I>loches</I>, a very pleasant confection
introduced into medicine by the Arabian physicians; and so very fitly opposed both to
the bitterness and use of Coloquintida. [Warburton's &lquo;very pleasant confection&rquo; be-
comes a &lquo;sirop tr&egrave;s-doux&rquo; in Le Tourneur's translation, which he poetically converts in
his text into &lquo;la manne des roseaux.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>] <SC>Beisly</SC> (p. 163): These &lquo;locusts&rquo; are
the fruit of the Carob tree (<I>Siliqua dulcis</I>). Gerarde in his <I>Herball</I> says: &lquo;The carob
groweth in Apulia, a province of Naples, and other countries eastward, where the cods
are so full of sweet juice that it is used to preserve ginger. It groweth also in sundry
places in Palestine, where there is such plenty of it that it is left unto swine and other
wild beasts to feed on. Moreover, both young and old feed thereon for pleasure, and
some have eaten thereof to supply and keep the necessary nutriment of their bodies.
This is of some called St. John's bread, and thought to be that which is translated
<I>locusts</I> whereon St. John did feed when he was in the wilderness. The fruit or cod is
called <I>Siliqua dulcis.</I>&rquo; <SC>Ellacombe</SC> (p. 113) says it is the fruit of &lquo;the <I>Ceratonia siliqua</I>,
a native of Southern Europe and the Levant. Its fruit contains a sweet pulp, and in
Spain and elsewhere it is fed to cattle. The Carob was cultivated in England before
Shakespeare's time. Its name survives in the <I>carat</I> of the jewellers, who in trading in
the East used the Carob beans for weighing small objects. Though the Carob tree did
not produce the locusts on which St. John fed, there is little doubt that the &ldquo;husks
which the swine did eat,&rdquo; and the prodigal son longed for, were the produce of the
Carob tree.&rquo;
<P>379. <B>Coloquintida]</B> <SC>Reed</SC>: This, says Bullein (<I>Bulwarke of Defence</I>, 1579), &lquo;is
most bitter, white like a baule, full of seedes, leaves like to cucummers, hoat in the
second, dry in the third degree.&rquo; He then gives directions for the application of it,
and concludes, &lquo;and thus do I end of coloquyntida, which is most bitter and must be
taken with discretion.&rquo;
<P>381. <SC>Purnell</SC>: The repeated reference to &lquo;money&rquo; is equivalent to &lquo;This is your
game. But you must be prepared to pay for it.&rquo;
<P>383. <B>delicate way]</B> <SC>Delius</SC>: That is, by adultery with Desdemona.</CC>

is explained by &lquo;extravagant and wheeling stranger,&rquo; I, i, 149. <SC>Ritson</SC> (p. 229): Here
is a collection of quibbles. By an &lquo;erring Barbarian&rquo; is meant not only a <I>roving Moor</I>,
but a <I>shallow, blundering brute;</I> and this character is set in opposition to that of a
<I>supersubtle Venetian woman.</I> The vow, he concluded, must needs be frail that was

<CC><P>Othello with his own wife hates him accordingly, and determines on revenge. <SC>Snider</SC>
(vol. i, p. 100): The true motive for Iago's hate is given here in this and in his suc-
ceeding soliloquies, since he would not be likely to announce his own shame or herald
his self-degrading suspicions. He considers that Othello has destroyed the chastity of
his wife. . . . . It is often taken for granted that his suspicions are wholly groundless,&mdash;
in fact, that he does not believe them himself. [In the Appendix will be found Sni-
der's theory that Othello's guilt in this regard is one of the hinges of the tragedy.&mdash;
<SC>Ed.</SC>] But that Iago is sincere in his belief cannot be consistently questioned. . . . .
With this interpretation there is a motive quite adequate for the subsequent vindictive
conduct of Iago; otherwise, he is an unnatural character,&mdash;a monstrosity. His slight
in regard to promotion would doubtless excite his enmity, but not an enmity sufficient
to involve Desdemona in destruction, or even Othello. To inflict worse than death
upon a man because he did not advance a subordinate when he could have done so is
altogether disproportionate to the offence, but to cause his wife to perish also is merely
horrible. Thus Iago is a monster, a wild beast, and needs no motive at all,&mdash;not even
neglect of promotion,&mdash;to bring on a rabid fit of cruelty. And what then becomes of
the artistic merit and beauty of this drama? . . . . The second motive is therefore the
true one, and at the same time is adequate. The family of Iago has been ruined by
Othello; now Iago, in his turn, will ruin the family of the destroyer of his domestic
life. Hence Desdemona is included in his retaliation. He thus requites the Moor
with like for like. His conduct is logical, and his revenge only equals the offence.
But there is absolutely no proportion between motive and deed if he involved Othello's
family in destruction merely because the latter would not promote him.

as a prophet.&rquo;
<P>416. <B>proper]</B> <SC>Booth</SC>: Not only <I>handsome</I>, but a <I>refined</I> and <I>dignified gentleman;</I>

<P>428. W. N. (<I>Memorials of Sh.</I>, p. 356): Shakespeare has shown great judgement
in the darkness which he makes to prevail in the first counsels of Iago. To the poet
himself all the succeeding events must have been clear and determined; but to bring
himself again into the situation of one who sees them in embryo, to draw a mist over
that which he had already cleared, must have required an exertion of genius peculiar
to this author alone. In so lively a manner does he make Iago show his perplexity
about the future management of his conduct, that one is almost tempted to think that
the poet had determined as little himself about some of the particulars of Iago's de-
struction.</CC>

<CC><P><SC>Rymer</SC>: For the Second Act, our Poet having dispatcht his affairs at Venice shews
the Action next (I know not how many leagues off) in the Island of Cyprus. The
Audience must be there too; And yet our Bays had it never in his head to make any
provision of Transport Ships for them. In the days that the Old Testament was Acted
in Clerkenwell by the Parish Clerks of London, the Israelites might pass through the
Red Sea; but alas, at this time we have no Moses to bid the Waters <I>make way</I>, and to
Usher us along. Well, the absurdities of this kind break no Bones. They may make
Fools of us, but do not hurt our Morals. <SC>Fechter</SC>: Cyprus: A Platform before the

<CC><P>10. <B>Mountaines]</B> In adopting the Qq, <SC>Pope</SC> evidently supposed that &lquo;mountains&rquo;
here referred, not to water but, to land; <SC>Theobald</SC> showed that Shakespeare refers to
&lquo;hills of seas&rquo; in this very Scene, line 215, and &lquo;liquid mountains&rquo; in <I>Tro. &amp; Cress.</I>,
and that he had abundance of classical authority for the simile, in Homer, and Vergil,
and Ovid; and that therefore &lquo;mountains&rquo; here refers to <I>waves</I>. Despite this clear ex-
position, <SC>Jennens</SC>, the sturdy follower of Q<SUB>1</SUB>, thinks that &lquo;the sense seems to require&rquo;
either Pope's text or his own, both founded on the Qto. In the <I>mes lt</I> of Q<SUB>1</SUB> he sees,
correctly, a typographical error for <I>melts</I>, and thus interprets the passage: &lquo;If it hath
ruffian'd so upon the sea as here at land, where the huge mountain melts away before
the storm, what ribs of oak can hold the mortise? Theobald did not consider the im-
propriety of <I>waves melting; clouds</I> have been said to melt indeed, but never <I>waves</I>
that I remember. I don't doubt that Shakespeare had the following passage of Scrip-
ture in his eye, &ldquo;The mountains melt at the presence of the Lord,&rdquo; &amp;c.&rquo;
<P>12. <B>Segregation]</B> <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Gloss.</I>): A separation, or dispersion. <SC>White</SC> (ed. ii):
The opposite of congregation; an extraordinary use of the word.
<P>13. <B>Foaming]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: The Qto offers the bolder image, i. e. the shore that
execrates the ravage of the waves. <SC>Delius</SC>: Even if <I>banning</I> were erased by Shake-
speare and &lquo;foaming&rquo; substituted, the former justifies &lquo;chidden&rquo; rather than <I>chiding.</I>
<P>14. <B>chidden]</B> <SC>Knight</SC>: How weak is the <I>chiding</I> billow <I>pelting</I> the clouds! but
the billow &lquo;chidden&rquo; by the blast is full of beauty. [Both <SC>Dyce</SC> and <SC>Schmidt</SC> give
to this word in this passage the meaning of &lquo;to sound, to resound, to echo&rquo; and &lquo;to be
noisy about,&rquo; and they refer in support to the Qto. But this definition contains, it seems
to me, but a small share of the full definition of &lquo;chidden.&rquo; I have searched in vain
for a passage in Shakespeare where &lquo;to chide&rquo; has the meaning <I>to sound</I>, and that
meaning alone; in every instance there is, it seems to me, the essential idea of <I>scold-
ing, brawling, contention</I> in all degrees, from &lquo;chiding as loud as thunder&rquo; to &lquo;the sweet
chiding of well-tuned sounds.&rquo; The &lquo;gallant chiding&rquo; which Hippolyta (<I>Mid. N. D.</I>
IV, i, 120) heard when Hercules and Cadmus bayed the bear in a wood in Crete, ap-
plies, I think, to the hunters scolding, urging on, the hounds; which Hippolyta after-
ward calls a &lquo;musical discord;&rquo; the &lquo;discord&rquo; was the brawling of the hunters, the
hounds, their followers, and the bear; the &lquo;music&rquo; was the softened echoes of it all
from &lquo;the skies, the fountains, every region near.&rquo; The essential idea of &lquo;chiding&rquo; is
there not merely &lquo;sound.&rquo; The &lquo;chiding nativity&rquo; of Marina (<I>.Per.</I> III, i, 32) was the
rude, brawling welcome to the world given to her by the contest of &lquo;fire, air, water
earth, and Heaven.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]</CC>

<CC><P>15. <B>Maine]</B> To <SC>Knight</SC> belongs the credit of giving the modern spelling and inter-
pretation of this word; his note is: What is &lquo;high and monstrous main&rquo;? We use
the word <I>main</I> elliptically; for the main sea, the great sea, as Shakespeare uses it, in
&lquo;'twixt the heaven and the main.&rquo; The main is the <I>ocean.</I> Substitute that word, and
what can we make of the passage before us? &lquo;the wind-shak'd surge with high and
monstrous <I>ocean.</I>&rquo; But adopt the word <I>mane</I>, and it appears to us we have as fine an
image as any in Shakespeare. It is more striking even than the passage in <I>Hen. IV.:</I>
&lquo;&mdash;the winds, Who take the ruffian billows by the top, <I>Curling</I> their monstrous heads.&rquo;
In the <I>high and monstrous mane</I> we have a picture which was probably suggested by
the noble passage in Job: &lquo;Hast thou given the horse strength? Hast thou clothed
his <I>neck</I> with thunder?&rquo; One of the biblical commentators upon this passage remarks,
that Homer and Vergil mention the mane of the horse; but that the sacred author, by
the bold figure of thunder, expresses the <I>shaking of the mane</I>, and the <I>flakes of hair</I>
which suggest the idea of lightning. The horse of Job is the war-horse, &lquo;who swal-
loweth the ground with fierceness and rage;&rquo; and when Shakespeare pictured to him-
self his <I>mane</I> wildly streaming, &lquo;when the quiver rattleth against him, the glittering
spear and the shield,&rquo; he saw an image of the fury of the &lquo;wind-shak'd surge,&rquo; and
of its very form; and he painted it with &lquo;high and monstrous mane.&rquo;
<P>17. <B>Guards]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: Alluding to the star <I>Arctophylax.</I> <SC>Steevens</SC>: I wonder
that none of the advocates of Shakespeare's learning have observed that <I>Arctophylax</I>
literally signifies &lquo;the guard of the Bear.&rquo; J. F. <SC>Marsh</SC> (<I>N. &amp; Qu.</I>, 1877, 5th, viii,
83): Both Johnson and Steevens are in error; and Shakespeare knew better than his
commentators what he was talking about when he spoke of the guards of the polc,
and not of the guard of the Bear. Arctophylax is not a synonym for the star Arcturus,
but for the constel&ldot;ation Bo&ouml;tes; and the Bear, of which he is the guard, or rather
keeper, is not the Little Bear, of which Polaris is the lucida, but the Great Bear, as will
be evident in the most cursory glance at a celestial globe. Arctophylax, whether it
mean the star or the constellation, has no connection with the Polar guards. They are
the two stars <G>b</G> and <G>g</G> Urs&aelig; Minoris, on the shoulder and foreleg of the Little Bear, as
usually depicted, or sometimes on the ear and shoulder. They were more observed in
Shakespeare's time than now for the purposes of navigation. Norman's <I>Safeguard of
Sailers</I>, 1587, has a chapter, &lquo;Howe to knowe the houre of the night by the Guards,&rquo;
&amp;c. They were even made the subject of mechanical contrivances for facilitating cal-
culation, one of which is described in <I>The Arte of Navigation</I>, trans. by Richard Eden
from the Spanish of Martin Curtis (or Cortez), 1561, consisting of fixed and movable
concentric circles with holes, through which to observe &lquo;the two starres called the
Guardians, or the mouth of the horne.&rquo; Further details will be found in Admiral
Smyth's <I>Cycle of Celestial Objects</I>, ii, 331, where is also cited Tap's <I>Seaman's Gram-
mar</I>, 1609, &lquo;containing still more upon the Guards;&rquo; and Hood's <I>Use of the Celestial
Globe</I>, 1590, deriving the name &lquo;from the Spanish word <I>guardare</I>, which is to beholde,</CC>

<P>30. <B>Verennessa]</B> <SC>Theobald</SC>, by simply altering the punctuation, was the first to
make this refer to the ship and not to Cassio, &lquo;who was no Veronese,&rquo; says Theobald in
his ed. i; &lquo;but we find from other passages in the play he was of Rome&rquo; (withdrawn
in ed. ii). &lquo;The vessel properly belonged to Verona, but was in the service of Venice.&rquo;
<SC>Heath</SC>: Shakespeare had no ship in his thoughts, but intended to inform us that
Cassio was of Verona, an inland city of the Venetian State. The word Veronese
should be pronounced after the Italian manner as a quadrisyllable. T. <SC>Warton</SC>: It
was common to introduce Italian words, and in their proper pronunciation then familiar;
see <I>Faerie Queene</I>, III, xii, 90: &lquo;And sleeues dependant <I>Albanese</I>-wyse.&rquo; The ship
was a Verones&eacute;, just as we now say a Hamburgher. Cassio was a Florentine. In this
speech the Third Gentleman, who brings the news of the wreck of the Turkish fleet,
returns to the tale, and tells the circumstances more distinctly. In his former speech
he speaks of &lquo;a noble ship of Venice,&rquo; and now he adds: &lquo;The very ship is just now
put into port, and she is a Verones&eacute;.&rquo; That is, a ship fitted out or furnished by the
people of Verona, a city of the Venetian State. <SC>Steevens</SC>: I believe we are all
wrong. Verona is an inland city. Every inconsistency may, however, be avoided if
we read <I>The</I> Veronessa, i. e. the name of the ship is the Veronessa. [While all the
critics thus far had stated that Verona was tributary to Venice, yet, having cited no
authority, they had apparently drawn the fact from the depths of their consciousness;
it was reserved for <SC>Malone</SC> to justify the assertion in a note, which is the only one
from the mass that <SC>Dyce</SC> quotes, as follows:] &lquo;Besides many other towns (says Con-
tareno), castles, and villages, they [the Venetians] possess seven faire cities; as Trevigi,
Padoua, Vicenza, <I>Verona</I>, Brescia, Bergamo, and Crema.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Commonwealth of Venice</I>,
1599. <SC>Knight</SC> retains the <I>Veronessa</I>, because &lquo;as a feminine it is applicable to a
ship.&rquo; <SC>Collier</SC>: The Third Gentleman has already said that the ship was &lquo;of Ven-
ice,&rquo; and it is not likely that he would assert just afterwards that she was a &lquo;Verones&eacute;;&rquo;
it seems much more probable that he would by mistake call Cassio, whom he did not
know, a &lquo;Verones&eacute;.&rquo; <SC>Singer</SC>: Whether a <I>Veronessa</I> signified a ship fitted out by
Verona, or designated some particular kind of vessel, is not yet fully established. But
as it has not hitherto been met with elsewhere, the former is most probably the true
explanation. <SC>White</SC> (ed. i): There is difficulty in either reading; but of the two
errors, one of which it is necessary to suppose on Shakespeare's part, a momentary for-
getfulness appears the more probable. <SC>Keightley</SC> (<I>Exp.</I>, 301): Another instance of
the poet's negligence or forgetfulness. . . . . Though the metre is perfect, it might be
better to insert <I>nam'd</I> or <I>one.</I> It is not likely that the ship was called &lquo;the <I>Veronessa.</I>&rquo;

<CC><P>Lieutenant,&rquo; &amp;c. <SC>Hudson</SC> adopts Daniel's suggestion. <SC>Rolfe</SC> agrees with White that
the confusion is perhaps due to a momentary forgetfulness on Shakespeare's part. <SC>Th.
Elze</SC> (<I>Sh. Jahrbuch</I>, xiv, 176): The word is clearly corrupt, but F<SUB>1</SUB> puts us on the right
track. Let the true word be &lquo;verrinessa,&rquo; and the changes, due to editorial lack of
knowledge, through &lquo;verennessa&rquo; and &lquo;Veronessa&rquo; to &lquo;Veronese&rquo; are easily under-
stood. Now although I cannot at the moment give an Italian authority for the noun
&lquo;verinessa,&rquo; yet there is the word &lquo;verrina&rquo; and the verb &lquo;verrinare,&rquo; which is an old
nautical term and still in use, equivalent in meaning to <I>tenebrare, perforare, traforare</I>,
that is, to &lquo;cut through,&rquo; to &lquo;cleave,&rquo; like the French <I>percer.</I> Wherefore the &lquo;noble
ship of Venice&rquo; was a <I>verrinessa</I>, &lquo;un perceflot.&rquo; [Is not this the exact equivalent
of the nautical term &lquo;cutter&rquo;? If only an instance of the use of the Italian word
could be produced, this vexed question would be settled for ever. As it is, Th. Elze's
explanation seems far more satisfactory than any other; but if a supersubtle compositor
forces us to choose between a lack of memory on Shakespeare's part and a lack of
geographical information, I prefer the latter. The nationality of a chance ship, men-
tioned once and never again, is of less moment than the nationality of an important
character; the same wind that can blow a ship to Aleppo can waft one from Verona.
Furthermore, how in the wild excitement of the moment could the Third Gentle-
man find out from what city of Italy Cassio came? That he was the lieutenant to
the warlike Moor might be revealed at a glance by some distinctive decoration of his
dress, such as the scarf of company, which always bore the Captain's colours.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

<CC><P>58, 59. <SC>Johnson</SC>: I do not understand these lines. I know not how <I>hope</I> can be
<I>surfeited to death</I>, that is, <I>can be increased, till it be destroyed;</I> nor what it is, &lquo;to stand
in bold cure;&rquo; or why <I>hope</I> should be considered a disease. Shall we read: &lquo;Therefore
my <I>fears</I>, not surfeited to death&rquo;? &amp;c. This is better, but it is not well. Shall we
strike a bolder stroke, and read thus: &lquo;Therefore my hopes, not <I>forfeited</I> to death,
Stand <I>bold, not sure</I>&rquo;? <SC>Jennens</SC>: Wishes may be called the food upon which hope is
very apt to surfeit; and to surfeit to death too, when there is no ground or foundation
to expect the thing hoped for. Hope is in perfect health where the grounds for it are
equal to the wish; but if the wish preponderate the grounds of expectation, hope is in
a sickly state. This was the case with Cassio; his wishes for Othello's safety were
greater than the probability of it, for he had left him on a dangerous sea; so his hope
was sick; but not sick to death, because the ship had a good pilot; this thought <I>phys-
ick'd</I> hope, and put it in a bold state of cure. <SC>Steevens</SC>: Presumptuous hopes, which
have no foundation in probability, may poetically be said to surfeit themselves to death,
or forward their own dissolution. &lquo;In bold cure&rquo; means in confidence of being cured.
<SC>Malone</SC>: It is not <I>hope</I> which is here described as the disease; those misgiving appre-
hensions which diminish hope are, in fact, the disease, and hope itself is the patient.
<SC>Henley</SC>: I believe that Solomon upon this occasion will be found the best interpreter:
&lquo;Hope deferred maketh the heart sick.&rquo; <SC>Knight</SC>: Hope upon hope, without reali-
zation, is a surfeit of hope and extinguishes hope. Cassio had some reasonable facts to
prevent his hope being &lquo;surfeited to death.&rquo; <SC>Collier</SC>: The meaning seems to be, that
Cassio's hopes are not destroyed by constant repetition and disappointment. <SC>Singer</SC>:
Therefore my hopes, not surfeited to death <I>by excess of apprehension</I>, stand in <I>confi-
dence of being cured.</I> <SC>Staunton</SC> (Note on <I>Ant. &amp; Cleo.</I> II, i, 38): As in our early
language to <I>expect</I> most commonly meant to <I>stay</I> or <I>wait</I>, so to <I>hope</I> on some occasions
was used where we should now adopt <I>to expect.</I> (Note on present passage): &lquo;Hopes&rquo;
here are <I>expectations</I> or <I>presentiments.</I> <SC>Cowden-Clarke</SC>: My hopes, not having
been utterly destroyed by reiterated false excitement and successive defeat, remain in
confident expectation of being fulfilled. <SC>Hudson</SC>: Cassio, though anxious, does not
despair; and the meaning of &lquo;stand in bold cure&rquo; seems to be, &lquo;my hopes, though near
dying, stay themselves upon, or are kept alive by, <I>bold</I> conjecture;&rquo; or, it may be, &lquo;are
confident of being cured.&rquo; I was for a while in doubt whether to read &lquo;not <I>suffocate</I>
to death&rquo; or &lquo;not <I>sick yet unto</I> death;&rquo; but on the whole preferred the former as involv-
ing somewhat less of change, and as being perhaps rather more in Shakespeare's man-
ner. D'<SC>Hugues</SC>: Il est clair cependant que les esp&eacute;rances s'ajoutant aux esp&eacute;rances,
sans &ecirc;tre jamais r&eacute;alis&eacute;es, constituent un trop plein (surfeit) d'esp&eacute;rances, qui fait &eacute;va-
nouir toute esp&eacute;rance. C'est la m&ecirc;me chose que Moli&egrave;re a voulu dire dans le fameux
sonnet d'Oronte: Belle Philis, on d&eacute;sesp&egrave;re Alors qu'on esp&egrave;re toujours. [These para-
phrases are all of them intelligible, and would be entirely satisfactory could we only
forget the text, which as it now stands is unintelligible to me, and I am willing to &lquo;say
ditto to&rquo; Dr. Johnson.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]</CC>

<P>74, 75. <SC>Warburton</SC>: It is plain that something very hyperbolical was here in-
tended. But what is there as it stands? Why this, that in the essence of creation
she bore all excellency. The expression is intolerable, and could never come from one
who so well understood the force of words as our Poet. The <I>essential vesture</I> is the
same as <I>essential form.</I> So that the expression is nonsense. For the <I>vesture of crea-
tion</I> signifies the <I>forms</I> in which created beings are cast. And <I>essence</I> relates not to
the <I>form</I>, but to the <I>matter.</I> Shakespeare certainly wrote: &lquo;And in <I>terrestrial</I> vesture,&rquo;
&amp;c. And in this lay the wonder, that all created excellence should be contained within
an earthly mortal form. <SC>Heath</SC> (p. 559): I entirely agree with Warburton that the
common reading is indefensible. . . . . I should rather suspect that the poet wrote:
<P>And in <I>the sensual</I> vesture,&rquo; &amp;c. The sense is, And within that vesture of the human
senses with which she is clothed by the Creator she is endued with every excellency.
<SC>Johnson</SC>: I do not think &lquo;essential&rquo; inexplicable; it seems to be used for <I>existent, real.</I>

<P>the <I>ingenious verse.</I> This is the best reading, and that which the author substituted
in his revisal. <SC>Steevens</SC>: I believe the word &lquo;tire&rquo; was not introduced to signify to

i, 64, Lorenzo calls the body &lquo;the muddy vesture of decay.&rquo; It may be observed that
<I>ingener</I> did not anciently signify one who manages the <I>engines</I> or <I>artillery</I> of an army,
but any <I>ingenious person</I>, any <I>master of liberal science.</I> Cf. Jonson's <I>Sejanus</I>, I, i: &lquo;No,
Silius, we are no good <I>ingeners</I>, We want the fine arts,&rquo; &amp;c. <I>Ingener</I>, therefore, may
be the true reading of this passage; a similar thought occurs in <I>Temp.</I> IV, i, 10: &lquo;For
thou shalt find she will outstrip all praise, And make it halt behind her.&rquo; In the Argu-

parently from the Latin, <I>ingenium.</I> <SC>Malone</SC>: Perhaps we should read: &lquo;Does tire

ceeded no further than to bare painting, and not arrived to the stupendous wonders of
your great <I>ingeniers.</I>&rquo; For a similar imagery to that in the first of these lines, see one
of Daniel's <I>Sonnets:</I> &lquo;Though time doth spoil her of her fairest vaile That ever yet
mortalitie did cover.&rquo; M. <SC>Mason</SC>: The reading of the Folio appears to have been,

which he has elsewhere used in a military sense. Daniel uses <I>ingeniate:</I> &lquo;Th' adul-

The text of the Folio presents no difficulty when we understand the word <I>ingener.</I>

<CC><C>[74, 75. <B>essentiall Vesture of Creation, Do's tyre the Ingeniuer.</B>]</C>
<P>reading of the Qto is given [in the text] with the full consciousness that it does not
represent the passage as Shakespeare left it, and in the belief that very probably he
did not write it at all. The attempt to make something of the Folio text by regarding
the last word as a misprint of <I>ingener</I>, i. e. artist, writer, ingenious person, I cannot but
regard as utterly futile. Possibly &lquo;tire&rquo; here means attire, and refers to &lquo;vesture;&rquo; it
may also mean weary, and have for its subject the word or phrase which is incorrectly,
or both incorrectly and imperfectly, represented by &lquo;ingeniuer.&rquo; For in <I>V. &amp; A.</I>,
Venus's tongue is called &lquo;the engine of her thoughts;&rquo; and in <I>Tit. And.</I> III, i, Mar-
cus styles Lavinia's tongue &lquo;that delightful engine of her thoughts.&rquo; Here Shake-
speare may have meant Cassio to say, that Desdemona's charms were beyond descrip-
tion either by pen or tongue. I am inclined to believe that the reading of the text [i. e.
the Qto] was substituted for the true, but illegible or incomprehensible, reading by the
transcriber of the passage who prepared the copy. <SC>Br. Nicholson</SC> (<I>N. &amp; Qu.</I>, 1865,
3d, viii, 43): The Qto text lacks a sufficient rise in hyperbole to conclude fitly the pre-
vious hyperbolic praises, and a poetical conclusion to the simile commenced in &lquo;vesture.&rquo;
In the Folio &lquo;tire&rquo; cannot mean <I>weary;</I> but as a verb suggested by &lquo;vesture,&rquo; and hav-
ing reference to it, it must be either the shortened form of <I>attire</I>, or formed (perhaps for
the nonce, as is not unfrequent in writers of that day) from <I>tire</I>, a head-dress; and this
either transitively or agentially in the sense of &lquo;arrange a head-dress,&rquo; or reflectively in
the sense of &lquo;to act as.&rquo; But if creation be represented as a vesture, it follows that
Desdemona, as a part of creation, should (agreeably to the last given meaning of &lquo;tire&rquo;)
be part of the dress; and giving the word this sense, we obtain the plain meaning cor-
responding with the reading of the Qto,&mdash;that creation being the vesture, she, Desde-
mona, is the tire, tiara, or crown of it, one who &lquo;tops all.&rquo; Again, if all creation be
represented as a vesture, it can only be as the regal robe of God its ingener or artificer;
hence we may consider ingeniver as the representative of some form of ingener; the
exact form is unimportant, but I would prefer the French, <I>ingenieur</I>, as this, printed
<I>ingenievr</I>, might easily have been changed by an ignorant compositor into <I>ingeniver.</I>
As to the probable origin of the phrase, I cannot but think that these two lines were
formed on the remembrance of Psalm cii, 25, 26: &lquo;Thou hast laid the foundation of
the earth, and the heavens are the work of Thine hands, . . . . they all shall wax old
as doth a garment, and as a vesture shalt Thou change them, and they shall be changed.&rquo;
This being combined with the thought of Desdemona as a pure daughter of Eve, the
last and therefore, according to the previous gradation of creation, the crowning work
of God. Combined, perhaps, with these, and assisting the association of the two, may
have been the remembrance of the ray, circlet, or &lquo;glory,&rquo; which surrounds the head
of sacred images or pictures, and the phrase &lquo;forasmuch as man is the glory of God.&rquo;
Possibly the reader who has not paid attention to the frequency with which Shake-
speare draws from Scriptural sources, and to the frequency with which these form his
phrases, may consider my remarks more subtle than sound; but the addition of the
word &lquo;essential&rquo; strongly corroborates them, and illustrates how fully and perfectly
Shakespeare elaborated a thought, and how comprehensively and succinctly he ex-
pressed it. Desdemona is represented as a being of purity and love, a female Abdiel
'mong Italian women; and hence Cassio is made to break out into such expression-
seeking praise as to call her the top of creation, as creation is &lquo;essentially&rquo; and with-
out &lquo;the accident&rquo; of sin, or as it was when it was beautiful before God and pronounced
to be very good. <SC>Keightley</SC> (<I>Exp.</I>, p. 301): It seems almost impossible to make
any good sense out of the Folio. &lquo;The essential,&rquo; &amp;c. means person, body, form.</CC>

<CC><P>i) reads <I>enscarp'd</I> and upholds the word: because Shakespeare never uses &lquo;steep&rquo; in
the sense of &lquo;plunge&rquo; or &lquo;submerge,&rquo; but always in that of &lquo;lave&rquo; or &lquo;soak,&rquo; which is
almost ridiculously inappropriate here; because &lquo;scarp&rquo; in Shakespeare's day meant
the inner slope of a ditch or intrenchment, then as now descriptive of shelving rocks:
and because <I>enscarped</I> might be easily mistaken for &lquo;ensteeped,&rquo; owing to the likeness
between <I>c</I> and <I>t</I> in the MS. of the early seventeenth century. <SC>Dyce</SC> in his ed. ii re-
minded White of Henley's reference to IV, ii, 60, and White adopted &lquo;ensteep'd&rquo; in
his ed. ii, and <I>enscarp'd</I> was heard of no more.

<CC><P>118. <B>Courtesy]</B> <SC>Coleridge</SC> (<I>Notes</I>, &amp;c., 254): Here is Cassio's warm-hearted, yet
perfectly disengaged, praise of Desdemona, and sympathy with the &lquo;most fortunately&rquo;
wived Othello; and yet Cassio is an enthusiastic admirer, almost a worshipper, of Des-
demona. Oh, that detestable code that excellence cannot be loved in any form that is
female, but it must needs be selfish! Observe Othello's &lquo;honest,&rquo; and Cassio's &lquo;bold
Iago, and Cassio's full guileless-hearted wishes for the safety and love-raptures of
Othello and &lquo;the divine Desdemona.&rquo; And also note the exquisite circumstance of
Cassio's kissing Iago's wife, as if it ought to be impossible that the dullest auditor
should not feel Cassio's religious love of Desdemona's purity. Iago's answers are the
sneers which a proud, bad intellect feels towards women, and expresses to a wife.
Surely it ought to be considered a very exalted compliment to women, that all the sar-
casms on them in Shakespeare are put in the mouths of villains. <SC>Booth</SC>: Kiss her
face; not, as is frequently done, her hand. Iago winces slightly, for he &lquo;suspects Cas-
sio with his nightcap.&rquo; I was once so irritated by Cassio's kissing the hand of Emilia,
despite directions at rehearsal, that I said &lquo;If she would give you so much of her
<I>hand</I>,&rquo; &amp;c., which staggered Cassio and set all the actors giggling.
<P>123 et seq. <SC>Rymer</SC> (p. 110): Now follows a long rabble of Jack-pudding farce be-
twixt Jago and Desdemona, that runs on with all the little plays, jingle, and trash below
the patience of any Country Kitchenmaid with her Sweetheart. The Venetian Donna
is hard put to 't for pastime! And this is all, when they are newly got on shore, from
a dismal Tempest, and when every moment she might expect to hear her Lord (as she
calls him) that she runs so mad after, is arrived or lost. And moreover &lquo;in a town of
war, the people's hearts brimful of fear.&rquo; Never in the World had any Pagan Poet his
Brains turned at this Monstrous rate. But the ground of all this Bedlam-Buffoonery we
saw in the case of the French Strollers, the company for acting <I>Christ's Passion</I>, or the
<I>Old Testament</I>, were Carpenters, Cobblers, and illiterate fellows; who found that the
Drolls, and Fooleries interlarded by them, brought in the rabble, and lengthened their
time, so they got money by the bargain. Our Shakespeare, doubtless, was a great Mas-
ter in this craft. These Carpenters and Cobblers were the guides he followed. And it
is then no wonder that we find so much farce and Apocryphal matter in his Tragedies.</CC>

<CC><P>132. <B>Huswiues]</B> <SC>White</SC> (ed. ii): In Shakespeare's day, and in some parts of Eng-
land still, <I>housewife</I> is pronounced <I>husif</I>, which has passed into <I>hussy</I>, with a half joc-
ular, half serious, implication of wantonness, which seems not to have been lacking
three hundred years ago. Indeed, perhaps, we should read here &lquo;hussies in your beds.&rquo;
<P>134. <SC>Jennens</SC>: Perhaps this speech should be &AElig;milia's; Iago's next speech seems
to require it. <SC>Collier</SC>: In a handwriting of the time it is given to Emilia in the
Duke of Devonshire's copy of Q<SUB>1</SUB>.
<P>138. <B>No]</B> <SC>Booth</SC>: Linger on &lquo;no,&rquo; with a significant side glance at her. All that
he says till he speaks &lquo;Aside&rquo; should be delivered humorously, to conceal his bitter-
ness, which his features occasionally reveal.
<P>140. <B>praise me?]</B> <SC>Horn</SC> (i, 340): Many a poet, heaping up tragic devices for
tragic ends, would have probably represented Desdemona as feeling an involuntary,
foreboding aversion to Iago; but even her very freedom from all forebodings is in
itself deeply tragic, and devised with a rare insight into character.

laws of the realm.&rquo; A statement of which may be seen in <I>The Student's Companion,

<CC><P>170. <SC>Steevens</SC>: The hint for this question, and the metrical reply of Iago, is taken
from a strange pamphlet, called <I>Choice, Chance, and Change, or Conceits in their Col-
ours</I>, 1606; when after Tidero has described many ridiculous characters in verse, Arno-
filo asks him, &lquo;But, I pray thee, didst thou write none in commendation of some worthy
creature?&rquo; Tidero then proceeds, like Iago, to repeat more verses. [It would not have
been worth while to cite this note of Steevens, had not <SC>Singer</SC> repeated it, without
acknowledgement, in both his First and Second editions. I never saw the pamphlet,
and dislike to depart from the safe rule of verifying all Steevens's citations, especially
those wherefrom Steevens asserts that Shakespeare &lquo;took hints,&rquo; assertions always doubt-
ful, frequently absurd, and here especially uncertain, in view of the date 1606.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>171. <B>put on]</B> <SC>Theobald</SC> could not understand how merit could put <I>on</I> the vouch
of malice. &lquo;I should rather think,&rquo; he says, &lquo;that merit was so safe in itself, as to repel
and put off all that malice and envy could advance to its prejudice.&rquo; He therefore
changed his text to &lquo;put <I>down.</I>&rquo; <SC>Warburton</SC>: The sense is, one that was so con-
scious of her own merit, and of the authority her character had with every one, that
she durst venture to call upon malice itself to vouch for her. This was some commen-
dation. And the character only of the clearest virtue; which could force malice, even
against its nature, to do justice. <SC>Johnson</SC>: To <I>put on</I> the vouch of malice, is to
assume a character vouched by the testimony of malice itself. <SC>Capell</SC> (p. 142): &lquo;Put
on&rquo; is&mdash;push on, push forward the unwilling; so that the sense is&mdash;push malice on to
vouch, dare it to give its testimony, say what it knows of her; this is the very force
of &lquo;put on&rquo; and &lquo;vouch,&rquo; and their explanation combin'd; and other comment than
this the passage does not require.
<P>173. &amp;c. <SC>Booth</SC>: These lines should be spoken as though composed on the spur of
the moment; not glibly, as though studied beforehand.
<P>173. <B>She that]</B> <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 268: Generally it will be found that <I>which</I> is more defi
nite than <I>that. Which</I> follows a name, <I>that</I> a pronoun. Sometimes <I>which</I> is used in
this sense to denote an individual or a defined class, while <I>that</I> denotes a hypothetical
person or an indefinite class, as here.</CC>

<CC><P>180. <B>To]</B> For the omission of <I>as</I> in relative constructions, see <I>Lear</I>, I, iv, 36, or
<SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 281.
<P>180. <B>Cods-head]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: That is, to exchange a delicacy for coarser fare. See
Queen Elizabeth's Household Book for the 43d year of her Reign: &lquo;Item, the Master
Cookes have to fee all the salmons' tailes,&rquo; &amp;c., p. 296. <SC>White</SC> (ed. ii): That is, to
give up the best part of a homely thing for the worst part of something very fine.
<SC>L&uuml;ders</SC> (p. 43) detects herein another, and f&uuml;r feinere Ohren weniger schmackhafte
Bedeutung. <SC>Purnell</SC>: By the despised salmon's tail he means Othello, whom she had
chosen in preference to the wealthy, curled darlings of Venice.
<P>182. <SC>Booth</SC>: A glance at Roderigo would imply that Desdemona is the &lquo;wight&rquo;
particularly referred to. Roderigo has long been an unnoticed follower. [Qu. Ought
not Roderigo to be disguised? Did not Iago tell him to defeat his favour with a
usurped beard? It seems almost impossible to suppose that Cassio had never met in
Venice, Desdemona's assiduous wooer, Roderigo, and yet see line 297 of this scene,
where Iago tells Roderigo that Cassio does not know him. Can this refer to anything
else than to his &lquo;defeated favour&rquo;?&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>183, 185. <B>were . . . Beere]</B> This rhyme is recorded merely in Ellis's <I>Early-Eng.
Pron.</I>, p. 965. It is hazardous to deny that a perfect rhyme is here intended, and yet
it seems to me that Iago pauses so long in search of one that Desdemona breaks in
with her question; and that Iago, thus spurred, rushes to his lame and impotent con-
clusion, where a defective rhyme would indicate its off-hand character, and supply a
dash of humour to counteract the bitterness. There is, however, authority elsewhere
for rhyming <I>were</I> and <I>beer.</I> In <I>Com. of Err.</I> IV, ii, 9-10, we have <I>were</I> and <I>here;</I> in
<I>R. of L.</I> 631, <I>were</I> and <I>appear;</I> in <I>Sonn.</I> 140, 5, <I>were</I> and <I>near;</I> but <I>were</I> rhymes with
<I>bear</I> in <I>Sonn.</I> 13, 6. Chapman frequently rhymes <I>here, were, there, cheer</I>, and <I>dear.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>185. <B>Chronicle]</B> In this word <SC>Johnson</SC> discerned an allusion &lquo;to the Roman prac-
tice of marking the jars with the name of the Consul. The appearance of such a
woman would make an era, but as the merit of the best woman is but small, that era
might be properly applied to the distinction of the different ages of small beer.&rquo; This
note was not repeated in either of the two editions which Dr Johnson and Steevens
afterwards edited. In its stead appeared the interpretation by <SC>Steevens</SC>, which has
been since then generally accepted, &lquo;of keeping the accounts of a household.&rquo;</CC>

<P>189. <B>Counsailor]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: This seems to mean not so much a man that <I>gives

<P>192. <SC>Coleridge</SC> (<I>Notes</I>, &amp;c., 254) calls attention in this speech to the importance
given to trifles, and made fertile by the villainy of the observer.
<P>192. <B>palme]</B> <SC>Booth</SC>: The hands of both should be ungloved. They seldom are so.

<P>208. <B>Warriour]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: In III, iv, 173, Desdemona calls herself an &lquo;unhand-

Ronsard frequently calls his mistresses <I>guerri&egrave;res;</I> and Southern, his imitator, is not
less prodigal of the same appellation. Had I not met with the word thus fantastically
applied, I should have concluded that Othello called his wife a &lquo;warrior&rquo; because she had
embarked with him on a warlike expedition, and not in consequence of Ovid's observa-
tion: &lquo;Militat omnis amans, et habet sua castra Cupido.&rquo; [Southern was not born until
nigh a half century after Shakespeare's death. Steevens's reading was so extensive,
his memory so tenacious, and his wit so ready, that we shall always owe him gratitude</CC>

<CC><P>231. <B>set downe]</B> <SC>Malone</SC>: Who can prove that <I>set down</I> [in opposition to <I>let
down</I>] was not the language of Shakespeare's time, when a viol was spoken of? To
<I>set</I> formerly signified to <I>tune</I>, though it is no longer used in that sense. <SC>Steevens</SC>:
To &lquo;set down&rquo; has this meaning in no other part of our author's works. However,
<I>virtus post nummos;</I> we have secured the phrase, and the exemplification of it may
follow when it will. <SC>Boswell</SC>: To &lquo;set down&rquo; has the same meaning as to <I>put down</I>,
to <I>lower.</I> Yet, as the phrase to <I>let down</I> is the usual phrase, and might be easily cor-
rupted, it was probably the true one. <SC>Cowden-Clarke</SC>: It is possible that &lquo;<I>set</I> down&rquo;
was formerly as much a technical musical phrase as &lquo;<I>let</I> down&rquo; is now. <SC>Hudson</SC>: It
is worth noting that Milton's Satan relents at the prospect of ruining the happiness
before him, and prefaces the deed with a gush of pity for the victims; whereas the
same thought puts Iago in a transport of jubilant ferocity. Is our idea of Satan's
wickedness enhanced by his thus indulging such feelings, and then acting in defiance
of them, or as if he had them not? or is Iago more devilish than he? <SC>Booth</SC>: This
should be spoken with calm assurance; not too pointedly. He knows he will make
the discord,&mdash;so does the audience.

<CC><P>313. <B>if you can]</B> <SC>Jennens</SC>: The sense requires <I>if I can;</I> Iago had brought the

reply, in fact, determines nothing; it suits equally well with either lection.

of lies, made manifest in the flesh, here speaks all but all the truth for once, to himself

<P>336. <B>Trash . . . trace]</B> <SC>Warburton</SC>: &lquo;A trifling insignificant fellow may perhaps
be called <I>Trash</I>, but the metaphor of hunting is not preserved. I suppose therefore
that the word is <I>brach</I>, which is a low species of hounds of the chase, and a term gen-
erally used in contempt. As to &ldquo;trace,&rdquo; <I>crush</I> of Q<SUB>1</SUB> is plainly a corruption of <I>cherish.</I>&rquo;
<SC>Warton</SC> was the first to suggest that <I>trash</I> should be substituted for &lquo;trace,&rquo; but he
was not strictly accurate in his definition of its technical meaning; he supposed that it
meant simply to <I>rate</I>, to <I>check</I>, and cited Caratach's reply to Nennius (<I>Bonduca</I>, I, i)
when Nennius taunted him with flying from the Romans: &lquo;I fled too; But not so
fast,&mdash;your jewel had been lost then, Young Hengo there; he <I>trash'd</I> me,&rquo; i. e., says
Warton, he <I>stopped</I> me. At last <SC>Steevens</SC> (1793) discovered the meaning of <I>trash</I>
which has since been generally accepted. &lquo;To <I>trash</I> is still a hunter's phrase, and sig-
nifies to fasten a weight on the neck of a dog, when his speed is superior to that of his
companions. . . . . &ldquo;Trash&rdquo; in the first instance in this line may be used to signify a
worthless hound, as the same term is afterwards employed to describe a worthless
female: &ldquo;I do suspect this trash&rdquo; (V, i, 108). It is scarcely necessary to support the
present jingle on the word, it is so much in our author's manner, although his worst.&rquo;
<SC>Knight</SC> upholds &lquo;trace,&rquo; but was misled in his interpretation. &lquo;Trash&rquo; and &lquo;trace,&rquo;
says Knight, &lquo;are used with perfect propriety. The &ldquo;trash&rdquo; is the thing <I>traced, put
in traces</I>&mdash;confined&mdash;as an untrained worthless dog is held, and hence the present
meaning of <I>trash.</I>&rquo; <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Remarks</I>, p. 237): Knight's explanation of &lquo;trash&rquo; is bo<*>
rowed from Richardson's <I>Dict.</I>, where we find: &lquo;A <I>trash</I>&mdash;anything (man, dog)
<I>trashed</I> or <I>traced</I> or confined in <I>traces</I>, that it may not, because it would, run or pursue
too fast, rashly; like an untrained dog; a worthless hound; hence it is anything worth-
less,&rquo; &amp;c. But in this explanation Richardson is undoubtedly mistaken; he gives to
<I>trash</I> a meaning which it never did and never could bear. When used as a huntsman
or dog-trainer's term, or metaphorically with an allusion to their practices, it invariably</CC>

<CC><P>signifies <I>the thing</I> <SC>which restrains</SC>: &lquo;Above this lower roome shall be your hunts-

a too forward dog, to check his movements. <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii) in justification of his
(MS.) says that &lquo;<I>trash</I> and <I>trace</I> were used somewhat synonymously, as a mode of
keeping back <I>braches</I>, i. e. dogs, who hunted too quickly. Iago speaks of Roderigo as

has been misprinted <I>trash.</I>&rquo; &lquo;Roderigo is cheeked or <I>trashed</I> by Iago for his quick
