likeness of <I>c</I> and <I>t.</I> <SC>Staunton</SC> cannot subscribe to Warburton's emendation <I>brach</I>,
&lquo;although persuaded that &ldquo;<I>trash</I> of Venice&rdquo; is a vitiation of what the poet wrote.
<I>Trash</I> signifying to <I>clog</I>, to <I>impede</I>, is surely the genuine word for &ldquo;trace&rdquo; of the
Folio.&rquo; <SC>Bailey</SC> (ii, 108): It is plain to me that the genuine reading is <I>leash</I>, i. e.
whom I hold in leash for the quick hunting of the Moor. <SC>Keightley</SC> (<I>Exp.</I> 302):
&lquo;The jingle,&rquo; Steevens says, &lquo;being in Shakespeare's manner.&rquo; Now to this I object&mdash;
first, that this was not Shakespeare's manner, for the apparent instances of it are mostly
printers' blunders; and, secondly, that Roderigo did not require to be <I>trashed</I> or checked
&lquo;for his quick hunting,&rquo; for he was always hanging back and ready to give up the chase
till urged on by Iago. This last objection also applies to &lquo;trace&rquo; in the sense of fol-
low or accompany. It would apply also, though in a less degree, to <I>train</I>, which would
yield a tolerable sense. On the whole, I think that Iago's words may have been <I>praise</I>,
which would suit his sneering, ironical tone. As to <I>brach</I>, though we frequently find it
used of a woman, I believe it was never applied to a man. <SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. iii): I give the
reading of Steevens, but I now (1865) entertain great doubts if it be what Shake-

here one of its commonest meanings; &lquo;<I>For</I> his quick hunting&rquo; does not mean, <I>because
of</I> his quick hunting' but <I>in order to</I> make him, <I>for the purpose</I> of making him, hunt

is strange that White should have missed the common meaning of the word &lquo;trace.&rquo; It
was Steevens who gave a bias to the word from which it never recovered until Halli-
well set it straight, whose note is as follows: &lquo;The meaning seems to be&mdash;if this wretched

<P>339. <B>right garbe]</B> Since <SC>Johnson's</SC> time, every modern editor, except <SC>Knight</SC>,
has preferred <I>rank</I> of the Qto, which Steevens interprets as meaning &lquo;<I>grossly</I>, i. e.
without mincing the matter,&rquo; and cites Marston's <I>Dutch Courtezan</I> [III, i], &lquo;Whether,
in the ranke name of madnesse,&mdash;whether?&rquo; To this meaning <SC>Malone</SC> adds, <I>lascivi-
ous</I>, as in <I>Mer. of Ven.</I> [I, iii, 81], &lquo;The ewes, being rank.&rquo; For &lquo;garbe&rquo; <SC>Steevens</SC>
cites, &lquo;as perhaps employed in the sense here required,&rquo; Chapman's <I>Odyssey</I> [xviii,
482] where &lquo;cheek-proud Melantho&rquo; rails at the disguised Ulysses: &lquo;Or 'tis like To
prove your native garb, your tongue will strike On this side of your mouth.&rquo; [Despite
this array of authority, I cannot but think the Folio has the true reading. Iago's plans
are not settled, all is &lquo;but yet confus'd,&rquo; details will depend on circumstances as they
arise; the main point is to get Cassio on the hip, and then abuse him to the Moor in
the right garb, in the best fashion, whatever that fashion may turn out to be. If <I>rank</I>
were the word here, I do not think that Iago would say &lquo;<I>the</I> rank garb,&rquo; as though
there were but one coarse way of dealing, but rather &lquo;in <I>a</I> rank garb.&rquo; Whether &lquo;garb&rquo;
is here used subjectively or objectively, as the style of address which Iago will himself
assume in approaching Othello or as the address which he will impute to Cassio, is
scarcely important; the question lies in the use of &lquo;right&rquo; or <I>rank.</I> I prefer the former.
It is, probably, the fear which Iago expresses in the next line that has influenced the
preference for <I>rank</I> over &lquo;right.&rquo; But this fear is only Iago's &lquo;motive-hunting&rquo; for
dieting his revenge on Cassio; it does not specify the manner of his revenge, all that,
as he expressly says, is but yet confused, which would hardly be true if he had already
decided that the garb in which Cassio was to be abused should be <I>rank.</I> For refer-
ences to &lquo;garb&rquo; see <I>Lear</I>, II, ii, 92. <SC>Singer</SC> (ed. ii) says that &lquo;rank garb&rquo; is merely
in the <I>right down</I> or <I>straightforward</I> fashion, and in support refers to &lquo;the right butter-
woman's <I>rank</I> to market,&rquo; which is about as apt as would be the familiar phrase in
which Hamlet's uncle refers to his own offence. An appropriate support of the Folio
is to be found in <I>Mid. N. D.</I>, where Helena says, &lquo;I am a right maid for cowardice,&rquo;
or in the &lquo;right butterwoman&rquo; in Singer's own quotation from <I>As You Like It.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<CC><P>what they are; that is, in being an overmatch for truth and Nature themselves. And
this soliloquy is, I am apt to think, Shakespeare's supreme instance of psychologic sub-
tilty and insight; as it is also Iago's most pregnant disclosure of his real springs of
action, or what Coleridge aptly calls &lquo;the motive-hunting of a motiveless malignity.&rquo;

wronged him in the way he intimates; he is merely seeking to opiate or appease cer-

<CC><P>phrases? But there is an instance in <I>Tro. &amp; Cress.</I> (I, ii, 24) where &lquo;addition&rquo; seems
to stand for characteristic quality or natural bent; it is where Alexander says that Ajax
&lquo;hath robbed many beasts of their particular additions; he is as valiant as the lion,

ble for &lquo;addition&rquo; to bear here, certainly with enough plausibility to remove it from a
black list of &lquo;stark misprints.&rquo; Each man is to betake himself to what sport or revel
his particular disposition leads him to indulge in; and if in &lquo;addition&rquo; a military flavor
be found, it is all the more appropriate among soldiers. <I>Addiction</I> is a cacophonous
word, never used by Shakespeare, except in one other passage.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

<CC><P>54. <B>Ile drink for you]</B> What does this mean? Is it that Iago will use any and

<P>56. <B>craftily qualified]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: Slyly mixed with water. [Cannot &lquo;craftily&rquo;
here mean <I>strongly, powerfully?</I> &lquo;I have drunk but one cup, and that was &ldquo;power-
ful weak,&rdquo; too.&rquo; The necessity of his &lquo;qualifying&rquo; his cup <I>furtively</I> is not clearly appa-
rent to me, when he confesses the action thus freely to Iago. To be sure, Cassio may
have accompanied the confession with a wink to indicate that he thought it a good
joke; but this jars a little with my conception of Cassio's character. I prefer to think
that he openly and freely qualified that first cup, and the innovation it wrought made
him forget to qualify the second among the lads of Cyprus.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<CC><P>71. <B>pottle-deepe]</B> <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Gloss.</I>): A pottle was a measure of two quarts (&lquo;A Pot-
tle, <I>Quatuor libr&aelig; liquidorum, congii Anglicani dimidium</I>,&rquo; Coles's <I>Lat. and Eng.
Dict.</I>), but frequently meaning a drinking-vessel without reference to the measure.
<P>72. <B>else]</B> <SC>Delius</SC> suggests, with great ingenuity, that this may have been meant for
<I>Ls</I>, the abbreviation of <I>Lords.</I> <SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. iii): In my former edition I followed the
Folio (comparing <I>King John</I>, II, i, 276: &lquo;Bastards and <I>else</I>&rquo;); but I now think it safer
to adhere to the lection of the Qq.
<P>73. <SC>Rolfe</SC>: That is, are sensitive with regard to their honour, or quick to take
offence at a supposed insult.
<P>74. <B>Elements]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: As quarrelsome as the <I>discordia semina rerum;</I> as
quick in opposition as fire and water. <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Lex.</I>): A pure extract, as it were,
the very quintessence of the isle.
<P>80. <B>Montano]</B> <SC>Booth</SC> doubts if Shakespeare meant to have Montano take part in
this carouse, and therefore makes him enter later from a different direction just in time
to see Cassio stagger off. <SC>Steevens</SC> felt the same impropriety; see his note line 85.
<P>81. <B>Consequence]</B> An instance of the omission of the plural <I>s</I> in words whose
termination has a plural sound. See <SC>Walker's</SC> <I>Vers.</I> Art. li, p. 243. This line is not
there noted. Or see <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 471.
<P>81. <B>dreame]</B> <SC>Theobald</SC> suggested and adopted <I>deem</I>, i. e. opinion, judgement.
<SC>Johnson</SC>: I rather read <I>scheme.</I> But why should &lquo;dream&rquo; be rejected? Every scheme
subsisting only in the imagination may be termed a &lquo;dream.&rquo;</CC>

<CC><P>84. <B>rowse]</B> <SC>Gifford</SC> (<I>The Duke of Milan</I>, Massinger, vol. i, p. 237, ed. 1805):
A &lquo;rouse&rquo; was a large glass (&lquo;not past a pint&rquo; as Iago [sic] says) in which a health
was given, the drinking of which by the rest of the company formed a <I>carouse.</I> Bar-
naby Rich is exceedingly angry with the inventor of the custom, which, however, with
a laudable zeal for the honour of his country, he attributes to an Englishman, who, it
seems, &lquo;had his brains beat out with a pottlepot&rquo; for his ingenuity. There could be no
<I>rouse</I> or <I>carouse</I> unless the glasses were emptied. In process of time both these words
were used in a laxer sense. [See <I>Ham.</I> I, ii, 127; I, iv, 8.] <SC>Booth</SC>: Don't be <I>drunk</I>,
but silly,&mdash;absurdly polite.
<P>85. <B>Souldier]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: If Montano was Othello's predecessor in the government
of Cyprus (as we are told in the Dramatis Person&aelig;), he is not very characteristically
employed in the present scene, where he is tippling with people already <I>flustered</I>, and
encouraging a subaltern officer, who commands a midnight guard, to drink to excess.
<P>87, &amp;c. <SC>Halliwell</SC>: This song appears to be referred to in <I>The Knave in Grain
new Vampt</I>, 1640: &lquo;<I>Fub.</I> The drawers have drawne him out, sir.&mdash;<I>Lod.</I> Clinke,
boyes.&mdash;<I>Toma.</I> Drinke, boys.&mdash;<I>Stult.</I> And let the cannikin clinke, boyes.&rquo; The song
itself does not appear to have been discovered. [This allusion I cannot find in Ingle-
by's <I>Centurie of Prayse.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]</CC>

<CC><P>106. <B>and-a]</B> Compare &lquo;He that has and&mdash;a little tiny wit,&rquo; <I>Lear</I>, III, ii, 74, and

<P>113. <B>awl'd]</B> This, the solitary indication of an unusual pronunciation, points, I

unscotifies it to it's injury: (<I>a</I>) in &ldquo;<I>take</I>,&rdquo; and what is call'd the diphthong in &ldquo;<I>auld</I>,&rdquo;
should have the Scottish twang with them, namely&mdash;our (<I>ah</I>) sounded broader; and to
make out the line's Iambi, the first syllable of &ldquo;<I>about</I>&rdquo; must have a small thesis, and
&ldquo;<I>thee</I>&rdquo; a full one.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC></CC>

<CC><P>126. &lquo;The habit which he [<SC>Kean</SC>] had acquired in early life, and which led to such
important results, viz.: that of closely observing the expression of the human face
whenever he had the opportunity, continued with him to the last. It was in a room at
the Castle one night that he was asked by a friend when he studied? Indicating a
man on the other side of the room, who was very much intoxicated, but who was
labouring to keep up an appearance of sobriety, he replied, &ldquo;I am studying now. I
wish some of my Cassios were here. They might see that, instead of rolling about in
the ridiculous manner they do, the great secret of delineating intoxication is the en-
deavour to stand straight when it is impossible to do so. The only man who ever
played the drunken scene in <I>Othello</I> properly was Holland.&rdquo;&rquo;&mdash;<I>Hawkins's Life of
Kean</I>, vol. ii, p. 360.
<P>129. <B>sinnes]</B> <SC>Booth</SC>: The traditional &lquo;business,&rquo; said to be Charles Kemble's, can-
not be improved upon. Cassio drops his handkerchief, and in his effort to recover it,
falls on his knees; to account for this position to his companions, he attempts to pray.
His clothes being awry, his sword has slipped to his right side, and this confuses him
for a moment as to which is his right or his left hand. Whatever you do here, do <*>t
delicately and with great seriousness, and show a readiness to fight any one who <I>thinks</I>
you're drunk. The more dignified your manner, the more absurd and yet correct your
performance will be.
<P>131. <B>right . . . left]</B> <SC>Purnell</SC>: A British soldier is not considered drunk if he
can go through his facings.</CC>

<CC><P>160. <B>ingraft]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: An infirmity <I>rooted, settled</I> in his constitution. <SC>Henley</SC>:
This explanation seems to fall short of the poet's meaning. The qualities of a tree are
so changed by being engrafted, that its future fruits are not such as would have natu-
rally sprung from the stock, but derive their qualities from the graft inserted in it.

nothing more than a printer's blunder, which F<SUB>2</SUB> corrects by making Montano say, &lquo;I
am hurt, but <I>not</I> to the death.&rquo; The true stage direction, for which &lquo;He dies&rquo; was, no
doubt, intended, is found in Q<SUB>2</SUB>, &lquo;He faints.&rquo; [It is not easy here to decide between

<CC><P>faints.&rquo; Assuredly Montano does not die; and it is difficult to see with what propriety
a man who had fainted could be adjured to stop fighting, both by Othello and Iago. If
these words be not a stage direction, but a part of the text, there is to Tollet's interpre-
tation this objection, viz.: that Montano was acting throughout in self-defence, as he
himself tells Othello, line 227, which he would have scarcely presumed to assert had
he renewed the attack with such bitterness before Othello's very eyes. This is one of
the passages, I think, where it will not do to inquire too closely. The dramatic action
demands a barbarous brawl, in which Montano shall be worsted, and latitude is given
to the actors to portray the extent of his discomfiture. I am not sure that <SC>Cowden-
Clarke's</SC> course of omitting the words altogether be not the wisest.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<CC><P>impart they did.&rquo; <SC>Malone</SC>: When David Rizzio was murdered in Edinburgh, the
Provost ordered the <I>common bell</I> to be rung, and five hundred persons were immedi-
ately assembled. So in Peacham's <I>Valley of Varietie</I>, where he is speaking of the use
of bells, &lquo;they call for helpe when houses in cities and townes are on fire; or when
there is any mutinie or uproare.&rquo; <SC>Halliwell</SC>: At the poet's native town, Stratford-
on-Avon, it has been the practice from time immemorial to ring the bell of the Guild
chapel on the alarm of fire being given. <SC>Alger</SC> (<I>Life of Forrest</I>, i, 308): From the
general group he [Forrest as Othello] turned to a single attendant who stood at his

Fechter almost screams in passion, rushing up the stage the while. Kean gave it calmly
and authoritatively, as a thing of course, and &lquo;more in sorrow than in anger.&rquo;

<P>201. <B>lookes]</B> An instance (cited by <SC>Walker</SC>, <I>Crit.</I> ii, 132) of <I>s</I> substituted for <I>st</I> in
the second person singular of the verb. Compare IV, ii, 207; V, ii, 79; and two other
striking instances: <I>Ham.</I> I, iv, 53: &lquo;That thou . . . . Revisits thus the glimpses,&rquo; &amp;c.,
and <I>Lear</I>, IV, vi, 160: &lquo;Thou hotly lusts to use her,&rquo; &amp;c. I think this usage should
be observed in even modern editions, when to give the full grammatical form would
result in harshness.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>204. <B>Quarter]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: In their quarters; at the&iacute;r lodging. <SC>Malone</SC>: That is,
on our station. So in <I>Timon</I>, V, iv, 60: &lquo;not a man Shall pass his quarter.&rquo; Their
station or &lquo;quarter&rquo; in the present instance was the guardroom in Othello's castle. It
cannot mean lodgings, for Montano and the Gentlemen had continued, from the time
of their entrance, in the apartment of Othello's castle, in which the carousal had been;
and Cassio had only gone forth for a short time to set the watch. On his return from
the platform to the apartment he meets Roderigo, and the scuffle ensues. <SC>Ritson</SC> (p.
230): Rather, <I>at peace, quiet</I>, or, as Johnson elsewhere explains it, &lquo;in friendship, amity,
concord.&rquo; They had been on that very spot (the court or platform before the castle)
ever since Othello le$t them, which can scarcely be called being in their <I>quarters</I> or at
their <I>lodging.</I> And, indeed, they could not have left it without being guilty of another
offence, as they were directed by Othello to keep the watch. <SC>Henley</SC> denies that the
phrase ever meant <I>in quiet, at peace;</I> it is evident, he says, that the &lquo;quarter&rquo; referred to
was that apartment of the castle assigned to the officers on guard, where Othello, after
giving Cassio his orders, had, a little before, left him; and where Iago, with his com-
panions, immediately found him. <SC>Pye</SC> (p. 331): This word, in the military language
of the present day at least, seems to have no very precise meaning; but the meaning
<I>on our station</I> seems the leading signification, for the principal camp-guard of a regi-
ment is called the quarter guard; but a regiment in quarters has no such guard.</CC>

<P>227. <B>it]</B> <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 404: From this passage we may see how unnecessary and re-

<P>275. <B>thee]</B> <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 231: <I>Thou</I>, in Shakespeare's time, was very much like &lquo;du&rquo;

superiority to servants; and contempt or anger to strangers. It had, however, already
fallen somewhat into disuse, and, being regarded as archaic, was naturally adopted in
the higher poetic style and in the language of solemn prayer. . . . . In almost all cases
where <I>thou</I> and <I>you</I> appear at first sight indiscriminately used, further considerations
show some change of thought, or some influence of euphony sufficient to account for
the change of pronoun. [In a foot-note, Abbott says that the Elizabethan distinction
between <I>thou</I> and <I>you</I> is remarkably illustrated in Early English, as detailed by Skeat
in <I>William of Palerne.</I> The passage in <SC>Skeat</SC> is as follows, and is the result of a
tabulation of the best examples in that Romance (about <SC>a. d.</SC> 1350) and also in the
Romance of <I>Alisaunder</I> (about <SC>a. d.</SC> 1340)]: &lquo;<I>Thou</I> is the language of a lord to a
servant, of an equal to an equal, and expresses also companionship, love, permission,
defiance, scorn, threatening; whilst <I>ye</I> is the language of a servant to a lord, and of
compliment, and further expresses honour, submission, entreaty&rquo;&mdash;<I>Preface to William
of Palerne</I>, p. xlii.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>279. <SC>Ottley</SC> (p. 19): Kean said these words, before preparing to go, solemnly and
sadly, as if justifying and explaining a painful act of duty. And then his walk up the
stage! so stately and grand, his cloak swaying gracefully with each well-measured step
&mdash;who that saw it shall forget it?</CC>

<CC><P>281. <B>Sweeting]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: This surfeiting vulgar term of fondness originates from
the name of an apple distinguished only by its insipid sweetness.
<P>283. <B>Lead him off]</B> <SC>Malone</SC>: I am persuaded these words were originally a
stage direction. In our old plays all the stage-directions were couched in imperative
terms:&mdash;Play music.&mdash;Ring the Bell.&mdash;Lead him off. <SC>White</SC> (ed. i): Such is my
opinion, but for a different reason. If Othello had ordered the removal of Montano,
he would have said, not &lquo;Lead him off,&rquo; but &lquo;Lead him <I>away.</I>&rquo; We speak of a man's
being or having been led off, or on, in the sense of away, or onward; but when we
direct a man to be taken from where we are, we say &lquo;away,&rquo; unless we are upon a
staging, or some place of that kind, which, for Shakespeare's purposes, Othello was not.
The rhythm of this command, too, is not like that of Shakespeare's hemistichs. But
as Qq and Ff agree, I do not venture to change it upon mere opinion. <SC>Rolfe</SC>: Ma-
lone may be right.
<P>285. <SC>Booth</SC>: Iago goes off. Cassio braces himself for the sentence, but sinks to
the ground at Othello's exit. At line 288, Iago hurriedly enters to Cassio. In Cassio's
speech &lquo;Reputation,&rquo; &amp;c., don't preach; be not violent; avoid rant; yet be impassioned,
&mdash;feel thoroughly disgusted with yourself, and you'll be natural. Walk about, but don't
stamp or &lquo;saw the air.&rquo;</CC>

<CC><P>296. <B>bodily wound]</B> <SC>Gould</SC> (<I>The Tragedian</I>, p. 87): The simpler meaning is
conveyed by the usual emphasis on &lquo;bodily.&rquo; But this emphasis would oppose bodily
to spiritual wounds, and Iago has no faith in the latter. J. B. Booth, with fine penetra-
tion, emphasized both these words, as if there were no other wounds to suffer from.
<P>296. <B>sence]</B> <SC>Knight</SC>: The <I>sense</I> of a wound is its <I>sensibility.</I>
<P>298, 299. <B>oft . . . deserving]</B> <SC>Booth</SC>: With significant glance at Cassio. Do
not smile, or sneer, or glower,&mdash;try to impress even <I>the audience</I> with your sincerity.
'Tis better, however, always to ignore the audience; if you can forget that you are a
&lquo;shew&rquo; you will be natural. The more sincere your manner, the more devilish your
deceit. I think the &lquo;light comedian&rquo; should play the villain's part, not the &lquo;heavy
man;&rquo; I mean the Shakespearian villains. Iago should appear to be what all but the
audience believe he is. Even when alone, there is little need to remove the mask
entirely. Shakespeare spares you that trouble.

bla/yei, a)\n mh\ su\ qe/lh|s. *to/te de\ e)/sh| beblamme/nos, o(/tan u(pola/bh|s bla/ptesqai</G>&mdash;No
one will hurt thee, unless thou art willing he should. For then only wilt thou be hurt,

<CC><P>342. <B>at a time]</B> This is the Scotch &lquo;ae,&rquo; meaning <I>one.</I> Compare &lquo;Doth not rose-

<P>346. <B>marke]</B> <SC>Knight</SC> says that this is here used as an interjection; &lquo;to make the
matter still more ridiculous&rquo;! exclaims <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Rem.</I>, p. 239), after condemning Knight's
preference for &lquo;devotement&rquo; of F<SUB>1</SUB>.
<P>346. <B>deuotement]</B> <SC>Theobald</SC>: I cannot persuade myself that our Poet would ever
have said any one <I>devoted</I> himself to the <I>devotement</I> of anything. The mistake cer-
tainly arose from a single letter being turned upside-down at press. The three words,
Contemplation, mark, and denotement, are, indeed, in some degree tautological, but the
practice is allowed for the sake of energy. <SC>Malone</SC> notes the frequent occurrence of
this accident in the Qq and Ff. Thus in <I>Merry Wives</I>, IV, vi, 39, &lquo;deuote her to the
doctor;&rquo; <I>Ham.</I> I, ii, 83, &lquo;That can deuote me truly,&rquo; where in both cases it should be
<I>denote.</I> For other instances see his note on the passage in <I>Merry Wives.</I>

<CC><P>the sun. On the contrary, he says &lquo;<I>though other</I> things grow, &amp;c., <I>yet</I>, &amp;c. I believe
the argument is this:&mdash;Iago compares Cassio to one tree, and himself and Roderigo to
another or others. Cassio, he says, &lquo;grew fair against the sun&rquo; while they were in the
shade, i. e., Cassio had an advantage over them in his position in life; but notwith-
standing this, they had &lquo;blossomed first,&rquo; i. e., had by their successful tumbling him out
of his lieutenancy, made better use of their time and opportunities; and arguing from
this, it was likely that they would &lquo;first grow ripe,&rquo; i. e., would ultimately beat him in
the race by attaining their objects, while he would end in failure and disgrace. John-
son's interpretation quite misses the point, while Malone does not touch the first of the
two lines, and fails to explain the blossoming <I>first</I> and getting ripe <I>first</I>, which are im-
portant words here. <SC>Hudson</SC>: The meaning seems to be, &lquo;though in the sunshine of
good luck the other parts of our scheme are promising well, yet we must expect that
the part which first meets with opportunity, or time of blossom, will soonest come to
harvest, or catch success.&rquo;

<P>2. <SC>Theobald</SC> (Nichols's <I>Illus.</I>, ii, 593): The direction for this entrance does not seem
entirely right. The scene should be before Othello's palace. Cassio should speak with
the musicians; after his speech they should play their serenade; and then the Clown
should enter, as from the house. [This scene and the following scene are generally

<P>3. <B>play heere]</B> <SC>Brand</SC> (<I>Pop. Ant.</I>, ii, 176): The custom of awaking a couple the
morning after the marriage with a concert of music, is of old standing. In the letter
from Sir Dudley Carleton to Mr. Winwood, describing the nuptials of the Lady Susan
with Sir Philip Herbert, it is stated that, &lquo;they were lodged in the council chamber,
where the King gave them a <I>reveille matin</I> before they were up.&rquo; <SC>Chappell</SC> (<I>Pop.
Music</I>, &amp;c., p. 61): Any song intended to arouse in the morning was formerly called a
<I>hunt's up.</I> See <I>Rom. &amp; Jul.</I> III, v, 34. Cotgrave de$ines &lquo;Resveil: A Hunts-vp, or
morning song for a new-married wife, the day after the marriage.&rquo; <SC>Ritson</SC>: <I>Haut-boys</I>
are the wind-instruments here meant.
<P>5. <B>Naples]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: A loathsome disease first appeared at the siege of Naples.
<SC>Parr</SC> (p. 36): There are few Clowns in Italy know this; but every clown there knows
that Pulcinella is the Neapolitan mask, and that Pulcinella speaks through the nose.
He generally knows, too, that the man who plays the puppet puts into his mouth a reed
similar to that which is placed in the orifice of the haut-boy. <SC>Cowden-Clarke</SC>: The
Neapolitans have a singularly drawling nasal twang in the utterance of their dialect.</CC>

<P>44. <B>Florentine]</B> <SC>Malone</SC>: In consequence of this line, a doubt has been enter-

appears by I, i, 22, where he is expressly called one. That Iago was a Venetian is
proved by what he says after having stabbed Roderigo, V, i, 112. All that Cassio
means to say here is, &lquo;I never experienced more honesty and kindness even in any one
of my own countrymen than in this man.&rquo;

<CC><P>Folio Desdemona is called <I>Desdemon.</I> The abbreviation was not a capricious one,
nor was it introduced merely for the sake of rhythm. It is clearly used as an epithet
[sic] of familiar tenderness. In the present instance [III, iii, 64] Othello playfully
evades his wife's solicitations with a rarely-used term of endearment. In the next
case, IV, ii, 50, it comes out of the depth of conflicting love and jealousy&mdash;&ldquo;Ah! <I>Des-
demon</I>, away, away, away!&rdquo; In the next place where he employs it, V, ii, 29, it is
used upon the last solemn occasion when he speaks to her, &ldquo;Have you prayed to-night,
<I>Desdemon?</I>&rdquo; And, lastly, it is spoken by him when he has discovered the full extent
of his guilt and misery, &ldquo;O <I>Desdemon!</I> dead <I>Desdemon</I>, dead.&rdquo; The only other occa-
sion on which it is employed is by her uncle Gratiano,&mdash;&ldquo;Poor Desdemon!&rdquo; Surely
we have no warrant for rejecting such a marked peculiarity.&rquo; <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> i, 230)
suggests that Knight supposed the spelling in the present instance, the sixth, &lquo;to be an
erratum&rquo;; but it is not; the verse requires, as Walker says, that we should read <I>Desde-
mon</I>, and assuredly there can be no thought of &lquo;familiar tenderness&rquo; here, from Cassio.
This alone is a serious, perhaps fatal, objection to Knight's theory, which I regretfully
relinquish; nor is the objection lessened when we find, as Walker points out, that a
double form of proper names is by no means uncommon. There are half a dozen
instances of &lquo;Helen&rquo; for <I>Helena</I> in <I>Mid. N. D.</I>, and again in <I>All's Well.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC></CC>

<CC><P><SC>Fechter's</SC> setting of the stage for this scene is noteworthy; some of its details have
been since adopted by eminent actors, and the public has not given due credit to the
originator. It is thus: A Room in the Castle. At the back, an arched opening, look-
ing over the sea. Right and left, in front,&mdash;and facing the public,&mdash;two large doorways
closed with tapestry. At the left, a divan, and table covered with papers, maps, instru-
ments of navigation, &amp;c. On the right a low chair and stool; around and about them,
embroideries, music, musical instruments, &amp;c. As the curtain rises, Desdemona, seated,
winds off silk, which Emilia (sitting on the stool) holds to her; Cassio stands respectfully
before Desdemona, who continues her work as she speaks.
<P>16. <B>strangenesse]</B> The Anonymous conjecture recorded by the <SC>Cambridge Ed-
itors</SC> seems singularly happy.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC></CC>

<CC><P>19. <B>That policie]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: He may either of himself think it politic to keep me
out of office so long, or he may be satisfied with such slight reasons, or so many acci-
dents may make him think my re-admission at that time improper, that I may be quite
forgotten.
<P>24. <B>doubt]</B> <SC>White</SC> (ed. ii): Do not imagine, fear, that.
<P>25. <B>warrant]</B> <SC>Coleridge</SC> (p. 255): The over-zeal of innocence in Desdemona.
<P>28. <B>tame]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: It is said that the ferocity of beasts, insuperable and irre-
claimable by any other means, is subdued by keeping them from sleep. <SC>Steevens</SC>: It
is to the management of hawks and other birds that Shakespeare alludes. So, in Cart-
wright's <I>Lady Errant:</I> &lquo;we'll keep you, As they do hawks, watching until you leave
Your wildness.&rquo; Again, in <I>Monsieur D'Olive</I>, 1606: &lquo;your only way to deal with
women and parrots, is to keep them waking.&rquo; <SC>Harting</SC> (p. 45): A wild hawk was
sometimes tamed by watching it night and day, to prevent its sleeping. So, in &lquo;An
approved treatyse of Hawks and Hawking,&rquo; by Edmund Berk, Gent, 1619:&mdash;&lquo;I have
heard of some who watched and kept their hawks awake seven nights and as many
days, and then they would be wild, rammish, and disorderly.&rquo; <SC>Pye</SC> (p, 335): This
strumpet-like resolution of Desdemona takes off much from the interest we should take
in her fate. [In Pye's Preface, where he is pleased to speak favorably of Shakespeare
(Pye was Poet Laureate, be it remembered), he observes that Shakespeare &lquo;does not
possess the power of Otway, and many inferior poets, in exciting pity.&rquo; Should not a
list of those poets who are superior to Shakespeare in exciting pity include Pye? Is
there anything in Shakespeare that excites more pity than this remark on Desdemona?
Pye says that his Notes are the result of his &lquo;perusal&rquo; of Shakespeare, which has been
&lquo;a favorite amusement in his hours of leisure.&rquo; With what force is not the truth of the
infant hymn driven home to us: &lquo;For Satan finds some mischief still For idle hands
to do&rquo;!&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]</CC>

<CC><P>64. <B>Desdemon]</B> See III, i, 58. <SC>Booth</SC>: He leads her to the couch&mdash;they sit.
<P>67. <B>to night]</B> <SC>Heraud</SC> (p. 278): I know not whether the poet had any design in
it, but it may be, and perhaps profitably, remarked that the action of the Third Act
takes place on a Sunday. . . . . In the arrangements of the scene, the different persons
engaged in it should appear as if coming from their devotions. In the next Act we
find Othello derisively alluding to having seen the meretricious Emilia so engaged;
and this event may have happened on this very Sunday, and probably had.
<P>70. <SC>Lewes</SC> (p. 158): These preceding short, evasive sentences are subtly expressive
of Othello's mind; but Fechter misrepresents them by making Othello free from all
misgiving. He &lquo;toys with her curls,&rquo; and treats her as a father might treat a child who
was asking some favour which could not be granted yet, which called for no explicit
refusal. If the scene stood alone, I should read it differently; but standing as it does
between the two attempts of Iago to fill Othello's mind with suspicion, the meaning is
plain enough. He has been made uneasy by Iago's remarks; very naturally, his bear-
ing towards his wife reveals that uneasiness. A <I>vague</I> feeling, which he dares not
shape into a suspicion, disturbs him. She conquers him at last by her winning ways;
and he vows that he will deny her nothing. If this be the state of mind in which the
great scene begins, it is obviously a serious mistake in Fechter to sit down to his papers,
perfectly calm, free from all idea whatever of what Iago has suggested; and answering
Iago's insidious questions as if he did not divine their import. So clearly does Othello
divine their import that it is <I>he</I>, and not Iago, who expresses in words their meaning.
It is one of the artifices of Iago to make his victim draw every conclusion from prem-
ises which are put before him, so that, in the event of detection, he can say, &lquo;I said
nothing, I made no accusation.&rquo; All he does is to lead the thoughts of Othello to the
conclusion desired.

<P>78. <B>not almost]</B> <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 29: &lquo;Almost&rquo; frequently follows the word which i<*>
qualifies. Hence, in negative sentences &lquo;not-almost,&rquo; where we should use &lquo;almost
not,&rquo; or, in one word, &lquo;scarcely,&rquo; &lquo;hardly.&rquo; Thus, here, in this present instance, it is
equivalent to, &lquo;Is <I>not</I> (<I>I may almost say</I>) fault enough to,&rquo; &amp;c., or, &lquo;is <I>scarcely</I> fault
enough to,&rquo; &amp;c. It was natural for the Elizabethans to dislike putting the qualifying
&lquo;almost&rquo; before the word qualified by it. But there was an ambiguity in their idiom.
&lquo;Not almost-a-fault&rquo; would mean &lquo;not approaching to a fault&rquo;; &lquo;not-almost a fault,
&lquo;very nearly not a fault.&rquo; We have, therefore, done well in avoiding the ambiguity by
disusing &lquo;almost&rquo; in negative sentences.

much curtesie, he might iudge mee wanton.&rquo;

<CC><P>104. <SC>Fechter</SC>: Othello follows her with his eyes, and sends her a last kiss.
<P>104-106. <SC>Booth</SC>: With joyousness,&mdash;yet there should be an undertone of sadness,

<P>104. <B>wretch]</B> <SC>Theobald</SC>: This word can scarce be admitted to be used unless in
compassion or contempt. I make no question but that the Poet wrote <I>wench</I>, which
was not then used in that low and vulgar acceptation as at present. See &lquo;ill-starr'd
wench,&rquo; V, ii, 335. <SC>Upton</SC> (p. 289, n.): Giraldi Cinthio calls Desdemona, in allusion
to her name, <I>la infelice Disdemona.</I> And I make no question but Othello, in his rap-
turous admiration, with some allusion to her name, exclaims, &lquo;Excellent <I>wretch.</I>&rquo;
<SC>Heath</SC> (p. 561): The poison of jealousy has already begun to work in Othello, in-
fused by the artful hints and half sentences of Iago, and by the frank and pressing
solicitations of Desdemona on behalf of Cassio. His assurance in her faith and vir-
tue is already somewhat staggered, and he begins to consider it as a thing possible that
she may be unworthy of his love. To this state of mind this exclamation is admirably
well adapted, expressing the utmost fondness, and at the same time a distrust growing
upon him. If the etymology of the name had been known to Shakespeare, as Upton
suggests, he would not have spoiled it by changing it from Disdemona to Desdemona.
<SC>Johnson</SC>: The meaning of the word &lquo;wretch&rquo; is not generally understood. It is now,
in some parts of England, a term of the softest and fondest tenderness. It expresses
the utmost degree of amiableness, joined with an idea which, perhaps, all tenderness
includes, of feebleness, softness, and want of protection. Othello, considering Desde-
mona as excelling in beauty and virtue, soft and timorous by her sex, and by her situ-
ation absolutely in his power, calls her &lquo;Excellent wretch!&rquo; It may be expressed:
&lquo;Dear, harmless, helpless excellence.&rquo; <SC>Collier</SC>: Such words of endearment are re-
sorted to when those implying love, admiration, and delight seem inadequate. [One
of Collier's best notes in this play.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>] <SC>Hudson</SC>: As here used, &lquo;wretch&rquo; was the
strongest expression of endearment in the language. <SC>White</SC> (ed. ii): It is needless
to point out that &lquo;wretch&rquo; may be used as a term of fondest endearment; but not in

<P>126. <SC>Coleridge</SC> (<I>Note on Winter's Tale</I>, p. 243): The idea of this delightful drama
[<I>The Winter's Tale</I>] is a genuine jealousy of disposition, and it should be immediately
followed by the perusal of <I>Othello</I>, which is the direct contrast of it in every particular.
For jealousy is a vice of the mind, a culpable tendency of the temper, having certain
well-known and well-defined effects and concomitants, all of which are visible in Leon
tes, and, I boldly say, not one of which marks its presence in Othello;&mdash;such as, first,
an excitability by the most inadequate causes, and an eagerness to snatch at proofs;
secondly, a grossness of conception, and a disposition to degrade the object of the pas-
sion by sensual fancies and images; thirdly, a sense of shame of his own feelings
exhibited in a solitary moodiness of humour, and yet from the violence of the passion
forced to utter itself, and therefore catching occasions to ease the mind by ambiguities,
equivoques, by talking to those who cannot, and who are known not to be able to,
understand what is said to them,&mdash;in short, by soliloquy in the form of dialogue, and
hence a confused, broken, and fragmentary manner; fourthly, a dread of vulgar ridi-
cule, as distinct from a high sense of honour or a mistaken sense of duty; and lastly,
and immediately consequent on this, a spirit of selfish vindictiveness.

<CC><P>governed by their passions, can do; while more sanguine tempers reveal themselves at

ing</I> involuntarily <I>from the heart</I>, which, though resolved to conceal the fault, can-
not rule its <I>passion</I> of resentment. <SC>Steevens</SC>: I should willingly have adopted Dr
Johnson's emendation, could I have discovered that the word <I>delation</I> was ever used
in its Roman sense of <I>accusation</I>, during the time of Shakespeare. Bacon frequently
employs it, but always to signify <I>carriage</I> or <I>conveyance.</I> <SC>Malone</SC>: <I>Delation</I> is not
found in any Dictionary that I have seen, nor has any passage been quoted in support
of it. On the contrary, we find in Minsheu the verb &lquo;To delate,&rquo; not signifying to
<I>accuse</I>, but thus interpreted: &lquo;to <I>speak at large</I> of anything, vid. to <I>dilate&rquo;;</I> so that if
even <I>delations</I> were the word of the old copy, it would mean no more than &lquo;dilations.&rquo;
No reasonable objection can be made to <I>denotements</I>, i. e., indications, or recoveries,
not openly revealed, but involuntarily working from the heart, which cannot rule and
suppress its feelings. Nothing is got by the change of the Folio to &lquo;dilations,&rquo; which
was undoubtedly used in the sense of <I>dilatements</I>, or <I>large and full expositions.</I> <SC>Bos-
well</SC>: In Todd's Johnson an authority is given for <I>delations</I> in the sense of <I>accusa-

ingenious suggestion of <I>delations</I>, i. e., secret accusations. <SC>Staunton</SC>: &lquo;Dilations&rquo; may
be a contraction of <I>distillations</I> [see Text. N.], and the meaning of &lquo;close dilations,&rquo;
<I>secret droppings.</I> <SC>White</SC> (ed. i): <I>Delations</I>, i. e., subtle, intimate confessions or in-
formations. <SC>White</SC> (ed. ii): <I>Delations</I>, i. e., revelations. [To me the interpretations,
&lquo;secret accusation,&rquo; and the others, are here barely intelligible. What has frighted
Othello is these &lquo;stops,&rquo; these pauses, of Iago, which he would have disregarded in a
false knave, as a common trick, but in a man that's just, such &lquo;stops,&rquo; such &lquo;dilations&rquo;
indicate something deeper, some horrible conceit which he hesitates to disclose, and
which makes him weigh his words and protract the revelation. For &lquo;dilation&rquo; Shake-
speare had the classical and common Latin word meaning to delay, as Upton pointed
out, and he had, besides, the very same word, exactly so spelled, in French. Cotgrave
gives: &lquo;Dilation: A deferring, delaying, prolonging, protraction.&rquo; I do not think this
explanation pre-eminently happy. I have seen better explanations of difficult passages

<CC><P><SC>Heath</SC> (p. 562): &lquo;Vicious&rquo; doth not signify here, <I>wrong</I> or <I>mistaken</I>, but, apt to put
the worst construction upon everything. The sense then is, &lquo;I beseech you, though I
for my own part am perhaps apt to see everything in the worst light, which is a fault in
my nature that carries its own punishment with it, yet let me intreat you that my imper-
fect conjectures, with the loose and uncertain observations on which they are founded,
may not be the means of raising disquiet in the breast of a person whose wisdom is so
much superior to mine.&rquo; The abrupt and broken character of the sentence was pur-
posely intended, as it represents the artful perplexity of fraud and circumvention prac-
tising on the credulity of an open, honest heart. <SC>Steevens</SC>: Iago seems desirous by
his abruptness and ambiguity to inflame the jealousy of Othello, which he knew would
be more effectually done in this manner than by any expression that bore a determinate
meaning. The jealous Othello would fill up the pause in the speech, which Iago turns
off at last to another purpose, and find a more certain cause of discontent, and a greater
degree of torture in the doubtful consideration how it might have concluded, than he
could have experienced had the whole of what he inquired after been reported to him
with every circumstance of aggravation. We may suppose him imagining to himself
that Iago mentally continued the thought thus, &lquo;Though I&mdash;know more than I choose
to speak of.&rquo; <SC>Malone</SC>: The adversative &lquo;though&rquo; does not appear very proper; but
in an abrupt and studiously clouded sentence like the present, where more is meant
than meets the ear, strict propriety may well be dispensed with. <SC>Knight</SC>: The mod
ern editors enter into a long discussion about abruptness, and obscurity, and regulation
of the pointing, without taking the slightest notice of the perfectly clear reading of the
Folio, which we give without the alteration of a point or letter. <SC>Cowden-Clarke</SC>:
&lquo;Though&rquo; is here used in the sense of &lquo;inasmuch as&rquo; or &lquo;since.&rquo; <SC>Rolfe</SC>: The read-
ing of Q<SUB>1</SUB> for &lquo;that your wisdom,&rquo; line 173, perhaps better suits the broken character
of the sentence. Possibly, in revising the play Shakespeare made the change to the
more logical form of the Folio, and overlooked the &lquo;though,&rquo; which does not suit that
form so well. <SC>Hudson</SC>: Iago here feigns self-distrust, and confesses that he has the
natural infirmity or plague of a suspicious and prying temper, that he may make Othello
trust him the more strongly. So men often prate about, and even magnify, their own
faults, in order to cheat others into a persuasion of their rectitude and candour.

<P>184. <SC>Staunton</SC>: This is invariably printed &lquo;something, nothing&rquo;; but <I>something-

many more examples than have ever been noted. The precise meaning of the phrase
is not easy to determine; the only instance of its use we have met with is the following:
&lquo;Before this newes was stale came a taile of freshe sammon to countermand it with
certain newes of a <I>something nothing</I>, and a priest that was neither dead nor alive, but
suspended between both.&rquo;&mdash;<I>A Watch Bayte to Spare Provender</I>, &amp;c., 1604. It appears,
however, to have been nearly equivalent to the expression, <I>neither here nor there.</I>

<CC><P>188. <B>indeed]</B> <SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 283): There are several passages in Wilson's <I>Rhetorique</I>
which remind one of Shakespeare, so many that it might be affirmed to be a book which
Shakespeare had at some period of his life not only read but studied. The resemblance
of this present passage to the following in the chapter on Amplification is remarkable:
&lquo;The places of Logique help oft for amplification. As, where men have a wrong opin-
ion, and think theft a greater fault than slander, one might prove the contrary as well
by circumstances as by arguments. And first, he might shew that slander is theft, and
every slanderer is a thief. For as well the slanderer as the thief do take away another
man's possession against the owner's will. After that he might shew that a slanderer
is worse than any thief, because a good name is better than all the goods in the world,
and that the loss of money may be recovered, but the loss of a man's good name can
not be called back again; and a thief may restore that again which he hath taken away,
but a slanderer cannot give a man his good name again which he hath taken from him.&rquo;

<P>194. <B>mocke]</B> In a letter to Warburton, dated &lquo;March 31, 1730,&rquo; from his &lquo;most
affectionate and obliged friend and humble servant,&rquo; <SC>Theobald</SC> says: &lquo;I am at a loss
to form any idea to myself, how jealousy mocks its own food, or the cause on which it
subsists. No passion whatever is more in earnest than jealousy, or more intent on the
object which exercises it. But jealousy, we know, is generally mistaken in its object,
and raises to itself uneasinesses from its own mistaken conceptions. What if we should
then read, &ldquo;which doth <I>make</I>,&rdquo; &amp;c., i. e., jealous persons feed on the matter of their
own suspicions.&rquo; Warburton's reply has not been preserved. The future bishop required
the punctilious return of all his letters to &lquo;his dearest friend,&rquo; and perhaps destroyed
them, but it is reasonable to suppose that he failed to commend the emendation, and
probably criticised it with such severity that Theobald did not venture to allude to it in
his edition, nor did Warburton in his edition, where, instead, a note is found justifying
&lquo;mock&rquo; and condemning <I>make</I>, which in the mean time had appeared in Hanmer's text.
Whether or not the emendation is original with Hanmer it is impossible to say. He
rarely gives an authority for his changes. It is possible that he may have received &iacute;t
from Warburton, who may have passed over to him Theobald's letters. It was the use</CC>

<P>by Hanmer of Warburton's notes, without giving him credit, that drove Warburton to

asserts to be the &lquo;surest ever made in Shakespeare,&rquo; and therefore well worth contend-
ing for) has been, I believe, generally accorded to Hanmer down to the appearance of
the invaluable <SC>Cambridge Edition</SC>, where for the first time it is rightly given as a
conjecture of Theobald. Warburton's note in his edition is as follows: &lquo;Mock,&rquo; i. e.,
loaths that which nourishes and sustains it. This being a miserable state, Iago bids
him beware of it. The Oxford Editor [Hanmer] reads <I>make</I>, implying that its sus-
picions are unreal and groundless, which is the very contrary to what he would here
make his General think, as appears from what follows, &lquo;That cuckold lives in bliss,&rquo;
&amp;c. In a word, the villain is for fixing him jealous; and therefore bids him beware
of jealousy, not that it was an <I>unreasonable</I>, but a <I>miserable</I>, state, and this plunges
him into it, as we see by his reply, which is only &lquo;Oh, misery!&rquo; <SC>Grey</SC> (ii, 318): That
is, &lquo;'mock,&rquo; with an apostrophe for <I>mamock</I>, i. e., by continually ruminating or chewing,
it makes <I>mammocks</I> of it, in a metaphorical sense. The verse will bear the whole
word <I>mammock</I>, and will stand thus: &lquo;which doth mamock The meat,&rquo; &amp;c. [This
note is so printed as to imply that it is due to &lquo;Mr <SC>Smith</SC>,&rquo; whom Grey, in his
Preface, pronounced &lquo;the most friendly and communicative man living;&rquo; surely, an
enviable elevation above the vagueness of the patronymic.] <SC>Heath</SC>: &lquo;Mock&rquo; cer-
tainly never signifies to <I>loath.</I> Its common signification is, to disappoint, in which
sense I think it is used here. The proper and immediate destination of food is to sat-
isfy hunger; when this end is not attained by the use of it, the food may be metaphor-
ically said to be mocked or disappointed. So the end proposed by that suspicious
inquisitiveness, which is the natural food of jealousy, is certainty and satisfaction some
way or other. But this end it very rarely attains, and those very doubts and suspicions
are perpetually <I>mocked</I>, and disappointed of that satisfaction they are in such eager pur-
suit of. <SC>Johnson</SC>: I have received Hanmer's emendation; because to &lquo;mock&rquo; does
not signify to <I>loath;</I> and because, when Iago bids Othello &lquo;beware of jealousy, the
green-ey'd monster,&rquo; it is natural to tell why he should beware; and for caution he gives
him two reasons, that jealousy <I>often</I> creates its own cause, and that, when the causes
are real, jealousy is misery. <SC>Farmer</SC>: In this place, and some others, to <I>mock</I> seems
the same with to <I>mammock</I> [vide <SC>Grey</SC>]. <SC>Jennens</SC>: I am apt to think that Shake-
speare had here the Crocodile in his eye, who, by its tears, is said to deceive and entice
its prey. To &lquo;mock&rquo; is used by our Author to signify to <I>delude</I> and <I>deceive.</I> But if
this be the allusion, what is the meat that Jealousy feeds on? And the context seems
to show that Shakespeare makes <I>Love</I> the food of Jealousy. &lquo;That cuckold lives in
bliss. who certain of his fate, loves not his wronger&rquo;; he feels not the pang of Jeal-
ousy, because he wants that which nourishes and supports it, viz.: Love. But how
does Jealousy <I>mock</I> love? By pretending to be its friend, and by seeming to pity and
condole with it, at the same time that it is its great enemy and destroyer. <SC>Steevens</SC>:
If Shakespeare had written <I>a</I> green-ey'd monster, we might have supposed him to
refer to some creature existing only in his particular imagination; but &lquo;<I>the</I> green-ey'd
monster&rquo; seems to have reference to an object as familiar to his readers as to himself.
It is known that the <I>tiger</I> kind have <I>green eyes</I>, and always play with the victim to</CC>

<CC><C>[194. <B>the greene-ey'd Monster, which doth mocke</B>]</C>
<P>their hunger before they devour it. So, in <I>R. of L.</I> 554, &lquo;yet, foul night-waking <I>cat</I>,
he doth but <I>dalty</I>, While in his hold-fast foot the weak mouse panteth.&rquo; Thus, a jeal-
ous husband, who discovers no certain cause why he may be divorced, continues to
sport with the woman whom he suspects, and, on more certain evidence, determines to
punish. There is no beast that can be literally said to <I>make</I> its own food, and there-
fore I am unwilling to receive Hanmer's emendation, especially as I flatter myself that
a glimpse of meaning may be produced from the old reading. One of the ancient
senses of the verb to <I>mock</I> is to <I>amuse</I>, to play with. Thus, in &lquo;A Discourse of Gen-
tlemen lying in London that were better keep House at Home in their Country,&rquo; 1593:
&lquo;A pretty toy to <I>mock</I> an ape withal,&rquo; i. e., a pretty toy to <I>divert</I> an ape, for an ape to
<I>divert</I> himself with. The same phrase occurs in Marston, whose <I>Ninth Satire</I> is en-
titled &lquo;Here's a Toy to mocke an Ape indeede,&rquo; i. e., afford an ape materials for <I>sport</I>,
furnish him with a plaything. In <I>Ant. &amp; Cleo.</I>, &lquo;mock&rquo; occurs again: &lquo;tell him He
<I>mocks</I> the pauses that he makes,&rquo; i. e., he plays wantonly with those intervals of time
which he should improve to his own preservation. Should such an explanation be
admissible, the advice given by Iago will amount to this: Beware, my lord, of yielding
to a passion which, as yet, has no proofs to justify its excess. Think how the interval
between suspicion and certainty must be filled. Though you doubt her fidelity, you
cannot yet refuse her your bed, or drive her from your heart; but, like the capricious
savage, must continue to sport with one whom you wait for an opportunity to destroy.
A similar idea occurs in <I>All's Well:</I> &lquo;so lust doth <I>play</I> With what it loaths.&rquo; Such is
the only sense I am able to draw from the original text. What I have said may be
liable to some objections, but I have nothing better to propose. That jealousy is a
<I>monster</I> which often <I>creates</I> the suspicions on which it feeds may be well admitted,
according to Hanmer's proposition; but is it <I>the</I> monster? (i. e., the well-known and
conspicuous animal), or whence has it <I>green eyes? Yellow</I> is the colour which Shake-
speare usually appropriates to jealousy. It must be acknowledged that he afterwards
characterizes it as &lquo;a monster, Begot upon itself, born on itself.&rquo; But yet &lquo;what damned
minutes tells he o'er,&rquo; &amp;c. is the best illustration of my attempt to explain the passage.
To produce Hanmer's meaning a change in the text is necessary. I am counsel for
the old reading. M. <SC>Mason</SC>: It is so difficult, if not impossible, to extract any sense
from this passage as it stands, even by the most forced construction of it, and the slight
amendment proposed by Hanmer renders it so clear, elegant, and poetical, that I am
surprised the editors should hesitate in adopting it, and still more surprised that they
should reject it. As for Steevens's objection that the definite article is used, not the
indefinite, he surely need not be told in the very last of these plays that Shakespeare
did not regard such minute inaccuracies, which may be found in every play he wrote.
When Steevens compares the jealous man, who continues to sport with the woman he
suspects, and is determined to destroy, to the tiger who plays with the victim of his
hunger, he forgets that the meat on which jealousy is supposed to feed is not the
woman who is the object of it, but the several circumstances of suspicion which jeal-

are not jealous ever for the cause, But jealous, for they are jealous; 'tis a monster

these plays. Mr Steevens, in his paraphrase on this passage, interprets the word <I>mock</I>
by <I>sport;</I> but in what poet or prose writer, from Chaucer and Mandeville to this day,
does the verb <I>to mock</I> signify to <I>sport with?</I> Besides, is it true, as a general position,
that jealousy (<I>as</I> jealousy) <I>sports</I> or <I>plays with</I> the object of love (allowing this not very
delicate interpretation of the words, <I>the meat it feeds on</I>, to be the true one)? The
position certainly is not true. It is <I>Love</I>, not <I>Jealousy</I>, that sports with the object of its
passion; nor can those circumstances which create suspicion, and which are <I>the meat
it feeds on</I>, with any propriety be called the <I>food</I> of <I>Love</I>, when the poet has clearly
pointed them out as the food or cause of <I>Jealousy;</I> giving it not only being, but nutri-
ment. &lquo;There is no beast,&rquo; it is urged, &lquo;that can <I>literally</I> be said to make its own food.&rquo;
It is, indeed, acknowledged that jealousy is <I>a</I> monster which often <I>creates</I> the suspi-
cions on which it feeds, but is it, we are asked, &lquo;<I>the</I> monster? (i. e., <I>a well-known and
conspicuous animal</I>), and whence has it <I>green eyes? Yellow</I> is the color which Shake-
speare appropriates to jealousy.&rquo; To this I answer that <I>yellow</I> is not the only colour
which Shakespeare <I>appropriates</I> to jealousy, for we have in <I>Mer. of Ven.</I> III, ii, 110,
&lquo;shuddering fear, and <I>green-ey'd jealousy&rquo;;</I> and I suppose it will not be contended that
he was <I>there</I> thinking of any of the tiger kind. If our poet had written only &lquo;It is <I>the</I>
green-ey'd monster; beware of it,&rquo; the other objection would hold good, and some par-
ticular monster must have been meant; but the words, &lquo;It is <I>the</I> green-ey'd monster,
<I>which</I> doth,&rquo; &amp;c., in my apprehension have precisely the same meaning as if the poet had
written, &lquo;It is <I>that</I> green-ey'd monster, which,&rquo; or &lquo;it is <I>a</I> green-ey'd monster.&rquo; When
Othello says to Iago in a former passage, &lquo;By heaven, he echoes me, as if there were
some <I>monster</I> in his thought,&rquo; does any one imagine that any <I>animal</I> whatever was
meant? The passage in a subsequent scene, to which Steevens has alluded, strongly
supports the emendation which has been made: &lquo;<I>jealousy</I> . . . . 'tis a <I>monster, Begot
upon itself, born on itself.</I>&rquo; It is, <I>strictly</I> speaking, as false that any monster can be
<I>begot</I>, or <I>born</I>, on itself, as it is that any monster can <I>make</I> its own food; but, poet-
ically, both are equally true of that monster, jealousy. Steevens seems to have been
aware of this, and therefore has added the word <I>literally:</I> &lquo;No monster can be <I>liter-
ally</I> said to make its own food.&rquo; It should always be remembered that Shakespeare's
allusions scarcely ever answer precisely on both sides; nor had he ever any care upon
this subject. Though he has introduced the word <I>monster</I>,&mdash;when he talked of its
<I>making its own food</I> and being <I>begot by itself</I>, he was still thinking of jealousy <I>only</I>,
careless whether there was any animal in the world that would correspond with this de-
scription. That by the words, <I>the meat it feeds on</I>, is meant, not Desdemona herself, as
has been maintained, but <I>pabulum zelotypi&aelig;</I>, may be likewise inferred from a preceding
passage in which a kindred imagery is found: &lquo;That <I>policy</I> may either last so long, Or
<I>feed</I> upon such nice and waterish <I>diet</I>,&rquo; &amp;c. And this obvious interpretation is still
more strongly confirmed by Daniel's <I>Rosamond</I>, 1592, a poem which Shakespeare had
diligently read, and has more than once imitated in <I>Rom. &amp; Jul.:</I> &lquo;O jealousy . . . .</CC>

<CC><P>211. <B>exufflicate]</B> <SC>Hanmer</SC> defines his <I>exsuffolate</I> by &lquo;whisper'd, buzz'd in the
ears; from the Italian verb <I>suffolare.</I>&rquo; <SC>Johnson</SC>: The allusion is to a bubble. Do
not think, says the Moor, that I shall change the noble designs that now employ my
thoughts, to suspicions which, like bubbles <I>blown</I> into a wide extent, have only an
empty show without solidity; or that, in consequence of such empty fears, I will close
with thy inference against the virtue of my wife. <SC>Malone</SC>: Whether our poet had
any authority for the word <I>exsufflicate</I>, which I think is used in the sense of <I>swollen</I>,
and appears to have been formed from <I>sufflatus</I>, I am unable to ascertain. <SC>Boswell</SC>:
This may be traced to the low Latin <I>exsufflare</I>, to spit down upon, an ancient form of
exorcising, and, figuratively, to spit out in abhorrence and contempt. It may thus sig-
nify <I>contemptible.</I> See Du Cange, s. v. <I>exsufflare.</I> <SC>Richardson</SC> (<I>Dict.</I> s. v.): Exsuf-
flare, it is true, is explained by Du Cange (consequentially) to signify <I>contemnere,
despuere, rejicere;</I> arising from the custom in the Romish administration of baptism
of renouncing the devil and all his works, <I>exsufflando et despuendo</I>, by blowing and
spitting him away. Hence, also, the application of <I>exsufflare</I>, and <I>exsufflatio</I> (common
words among early Latin ecclesiastical writers) to a species of exorcism. <I>Exsufflation</I>
is used by Bacon in its ordinary sense. And &lquo;exufflicate&rquo; in Shakespeare is not im-
probably a misprint for <I>exs&ubreve;ffl&amacr;te</I>, i. e., <I>efflated</I> or <I>efflated</I>, puffed out, and consequently
exaggerated, extravagant,&mdash;to which &lquo;blow'd&rquo; is added, not so much for the sake of a
second epithet, with a new meaning, as of giving emphasis to the first. <SC>Collier</SC>: The
meaning of this word is more obvious than its etymology; and if we had any difficulty,
it would be removed, perhaps, by the additional epithet &lquo;blow'd.&rquo; It is one of the words,
the origin of which must not be traced with too much lexicographical curiosity. <SC>Dyce</SC>
(<I>Gloss.</I>): <I>Exsufflicate</I>, swollen, puffed out. For my own part, I can see no reason to
doubt that such was Shakespeare's word, and such the meaning he intended to convey.
<SC>White</SC> (ed. ii): That is, puffed out, thin and bubble-like, or, spat upon, according to
its derivation, as to which, and as to his own exact meaning, I think that Shakespeare
himself was not clear.

gay, dashing fellow on the outside, hiding his malice and treachery under the signs of a
careless honesty and jovial good humour. One point, strictly original, he made, which
powerfully affected Kean. Iago, while working insidiously on the suspicions of Othello,
says to him [lines 226, 227]. All these words, except the last two, Forrest uttered in
a frank, easy fashion; but suddenly, as if the intensity of his under-knowledge of evil
had automatically broken through the good-natured part he was playing on the surface,
and betrayed his secret in spite of his will, he spoke the words <I>nor secure</I> in a husky
tone, sliding down from a high pitch and ending in a whispered horror. This fearful
suggestiveness produced from Kean a reaction so truly artistic and tremendous that the
whole house was electrified. As they met in the dressing-room, Kean said excitedly,
&lquo;In the name of God, boy, where did you get that?&rquo; Forrest replied, &lquo;It is something
of my own.&rquo; &lquo;Well,&rquo; said he, while his auditor trembled with pleasure, &lquo;everybody
who speaks the part hereafter must do it just so.&rquo;

nothing in any other part of the play, properly understood, to imply otherwise.
<P>233, 234. <SC>Booth</SC>: Very confidentially.
<P>235. <SC>Fechter</SC>: With indignant menace. <SC>Booth</SC>: Let your tone express unbounded

<P>237. <B>seem'd]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: This and the following argument of Iago ought to be
deeply impressed on every reader. Deceit and falsehood, whatever conveniences they
may for a time promise or produce, are, in the sum of life, obstacles to happiness.
Those who profit by the cheat distrust the deceiver, and the act by which kindness is
sought puts an end to confidence. The same objection may be made, with a lower
degree of strength, against the imprudent generosity of disproportionate marriages.
When the first heat of passion is over, it is easily succeeded by suspicion, that the same
violence of inclination which caused one irregularity may stimulate to another; and
those who have shown that their passions are too powerful for their prudence, will,
with very slight appearances against them, be censured as not very likely to restrain
them by their virtue.
<P>238. <B>most]</B> <SC>Hudson</SC>: This is one of Iago's artfullest strokes. The instinctive
shrinkings and tremblings of Desdemona's modest virgin love are ascribed to craft,
and made to appear a most refined and elaborate course of deception. His deep sci-
ence of human nature enables him to <I>divine</I> how she appeared.

<CC><P>266. <B>think]</B> <SC>Booth</SC>: Perhaps a slight emphasis on this, though I doubt its value.
<P>267. <SC>Booth</SC>: Referring to his color. (My Father indicated this by a glance at his

<P>269. <B>bold with you]</B> <SC>Booth</SC>: My Father interpreted this as a covert reference to
Brabantio's assertion before the Senate (I, iii, 113) that Desdemona was &lquo;a maiden
never bold,&rquo; an assertion which Othello, with his knowledge of Desdemona's share in
their wooing, might somewhat modify; my Father, therefore, spoke the line not as an
apologetic parenthesis addressed to Othello, as it is usually printed, but as though catch-
ing up and pursuing Othello's own train of thought, and thus insidiously summoning to
Othello's memory secret occasions when Desdemona had shown a &lquo;will most rank,&rquo; and
had been &lquo;bold&rquo; with him. I wish I could describe the white-lipped, icy smile, the
piercing glance at Othello's half-averted face, and eager utterance, with which my
Father said, &lquo;Ay, there's the point; as to be bold with <I>you.</I>&rquo;

<P>335. <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. i): We take this necessary stage direction [&lquo;<I>Let's fall her Nap-
kin</I>&rquo;] from a MS. note, in a hand-writing of the time, in the Duke of Devonshire's Q<SUB>1</SUB>.
<SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Remarks</I>, p. 239): The stage direction inserted by other modern editors is far
better, viz. [&lquo;<I>He puts the handkerchief from him, and it drops</I>&rquo;]. There can be no
doubt that, while Othello pushes away the handkerchief, Desdemona lets it fall: Emilia
(who is now on the stage) says presently: &lquo;<I>she</I> let it drop by negligence; And I,&rquo; &amp;c.
<SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii): This stage direction [&lquo;<I>The napkin falls to the ground</I>&rquo;] and others
[&lquo;<I>Offering to bind his head</I>, after line 333] are from the (MS.) [Where stage directions
occur in the Qq or Ff they are to be reverently accepted, and they are also respectable
in Rowe, as indications of stage tradition, but in other cases, where they are devised by
editors, they are apt to be intrusive and are mostly superfluous. They belong more to
the province of the actor than to that of the editor. We editors readily lose sight of
the fact that we are, for the most part, mere drudges, humble diggers and delvers in
forgotten fields, and from close poring over the words of a dramatic character we are
apt to forget ourselves, and bound in imagination for one wild moment on the stage
to dictate action to the player-folk themselves. Picture Dr Johnson in the r&ocirc;le of
Mercutio! Yet when Dr Johnson modified or inserted stage directions, be they ever
so slight, as he has in Mercutio's speeches, did not his imagination, for an instant,
play him that same fantastic trick? To editorial stage directions far more than to
&aelig;sthetic illustrations the phrase &lquo;sign-post criticisms&rquo; may be properly applied, as it
seems to me. The stage directions of actors stand on a different footing. Here lies
the actor's true province, and to his interpretations must be applied the supreme test
of public judgement, wherein we, as a part of that public, have a right to give our
voice. Here <SC>Fechter</SC> decides that it is Othello who throws down the handkerchief,
and does it in a rage; but <SC>Booth</SC>, with finer insight, lets Othello gently push the hand
kerchief aside and Desdemona drop it.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]</CC>

<CC><P>336. <B>Exit]</B> <SC>Booth</SC>: Take time, gently push the handkerchief from her hand as she
is in the act of binding it on your forehead. Pass her, while on her knees, with forced
indifference, but turn lovingly, and holding your arms for her to enter them, say &lquo;Come,
I'll go in with thee.&rquo; Then with a long soulful look into her eyes, fold her tenderly
to your heart and go slowly off. <I>Keep time.</I> Don't <I>drawl</I> in either speech or move-
ment, yet be not abrupt nor rapid. Every movement, gesture, look, and tone should
be in harmony.
<P>338. <SC>Fechter</SC>: Comes forward with caution, and seizes the handkerchief, which
she has watched narrowly since Othello threw it down. <SC>Booth</SC>: Emilia, by chance,
sees the handkerchief and picks it up.
<P>339. <B>remembrance]</B> <SC>Staunton</SC>: That is, <I>memorial</I>, or <I>forget-me-not.</I>
<P>344. <B>tane out]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: The meaning is not, to have the work picked out and
leave the ground plain, but to have this work copied in another handkerchief. <SC>Steev-
ens</SC>: So in Middleton's <I>Women Beware Women</I>, I, i, &lquo;she intends To <I>take out</I> other
works in a new sampler.&rquo; Again, in the Preface to Holland's Pliny: &lquo;Thus Nicophanes
(a famous painter in his time) gave his mind wholly to antique pictures, partly to exem-
plifie and take out their patternes.&rquo; <SC>Blackstone</SC>: Her first thoughts are to have a
copy made of it for her husband, and to restore the original to Desdemona. But the
sudden coming in of Iago, in a surly humour, makes her alter her resolution, to please
him. <SC>Malone</SC>: This scheme of having the work copied was to render Emilia less
unamiable. It is remarkable that when she perceives Othello's fury on the loss of this
token, though she is represented as affectionate to her mistress, she never attempts to
relieve her of her distress, which she might easily have done. Shakespeare fell into
this incongruity by departing from Cinthio's novel.</CC>

<CC><P>378. <B>my poyson]</B> <SC>Staunton</SC>: The repetition of &lquo;poison&rquo; here is so inelegant that
we may well suspect the word in one line was caught by the compositor's eye from the
other, but it is hard to say in which the corruption lies. <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> i, 287): I
once thought that we should read &lquo;with my <I>practise;</I>&rquo; but it would seem that the word
required should be similar in termination, or general appearance, to &lquo;poison&rquo;; for this
line has dropt out, most probably from that cause, in Q<SUB>1</SUB>. Therefore I conjecture <I>potion.</I>
<P>382. <B>I did say so]</B> To <SC>Blackstone</SC> this exclamation was most unmeaning in the
mouth of such a speaker, at such a time; he therefore suggested that as Iago has the
handkerchief in his hand there may be a reference to it, and that the phrase is &lquo;Hide
it!&mdash;so&mdash;so&rquo;; but he &lquo;readily retracted&rquo; his emendation (though still thinking the
phrase obscure) after reading the following note by <SC>Steevens</SC>: Iago first ruminates on
the qualities of the passion which he is labouring to excite; and then proceeds to com-
ment on its effects. &lquo;Jealousy (says he), with the smallest operation on the blood, flames
out with all the violence of sulphur,&rquo; &amp;c. &lquo;I did say so; Look where he comes&mdash;!&rquo;
i. e., I knew that the least touch of such a passion would not permit the Moor to enjoy
a moment of repose:&mdash;I have just said that jealousy is a restless commotion of the mind;
and look where Othello approaches, to confirm the propriety and justice of my observa-
tion. <SC>Hudson</SC>: The moment Iago's eye lights on Othello, he sees that his devilish in-
sight of things was punctually prophetic of Othello's case; that his words are exactly
verified in the inflamed looks of his victim. <SC>Booth's</SC> dramatic instinct clears any diffi-
culty by a stage direction&mdash;&lquo;Othello groans.&rquo;
<P>383. In a note on <I>Tro. &amp; Cress.</I>, <SC>Dyce</SC>, in his <I>Remarks</I>, p. 147, shows that these
stage directions were not meant to be taken as the actual entrance of the actor, but that
they were merely, as in the present case, to show that towards the end of a soliloquy
the actor who spoke next was to prepare himself (or be summoned) to enter,&mdash;not that
he was to come on the stage before the conclusion of the soliloquy. It is the same in
IV, i, 116, where &lquo;Enter Cassio&rquo; occurs four lines before Iago addresses him. [I sup-
pose it was on this fact that Dyce founded his positive assertion (see note on II, ii, 231)
that F<SUB>1</SUB> was printed from a stage transcript, and not from one where shorthand had been
used. <SC>Knight</SC> was the first to indicate Othello s entrance at the proper word, although
Capell had &lquo;Enter Othello, <I>at a distance.</I>&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<CC><P>or play away any part thereof, or refuse it for his ease, or to avoid paines; wherefore

<P>404 et seq. <SC>Malone</SC> quotes two passages, one from a &lquo;very ancient drama entitled
<I>Common Conditions</I>,&rquo; and another from a <I>Farewell</I> by Peele, which he intimates may
have suggested these lines to Shakespeare. <SC>Steevens</SC>: I know not why we should
suppose that Shakespeare borrowed so common a repetition as those diversified <I>fare-
wells</I> from any preceding drama. A string of <I>adieus</I> is perhaps the most tempting of
all repetitions, because it serves to introduce a train of imagery as well as to solemnify
a speech or composition. Wolsey, like Othello, indulges himself in many <I>farewells;</I>
and the Valete, aprica montium cacumina! Valete, opaca vallium cubilia! &amp;c., are com-
mon to poets of different ages and countries. I have now before me an ancient MS.
English poem, in which sixteen succeeding verses begin with the word <I>farewell</I>, applied
to a variety of objects and circumstances. <SC>Booth</SC>: Utter this, looking off,&mdash;towards
Desdemona. My Father once said to me, &lquo;No human voice could surpass, if equal,
Edmund Kean's in his delivery of this passage.&rquo; Begin slowly, with suppressed emo-
tion; gradually increase the volume and intensity of voice,&mdash;never loud, nor let your
tones be too tearful or tremulous,&mdash;it becomes monotonous.

and queries whether it be a misprint, or a misquotation, or the reading of some copy of

<CC><P>408. <B>Fife]</B> <SC>Warton</SC>: In mentioning the <I>fife</I> joined with the <I>drum</I>, Shakespeare,
as usual, paints from the life; those instruments accompanying each other being used
in his age by the English soldiery. The <I>fife</I>, however, as a martial instrument, was
afterwards entirely discontinued among our troops for many years. It was first used
within the memory of man, among our troops, by the British guards, by order of the
Duke of Cumberland, when they were encamped at Maestricht, in the year 1747.
They took it from the Allies, with whom they served. This instrument, accompanying
the drum, is of considerable antiquity in the European armies, particularly the German.
In a curious picture in the Ashmolean Museum at Oxford, painted 1525, representing
the siege of Pavia by the French King, where the Emperor was taken prisoner, we see
<I>fifes</I> and <I>drums.</I> In Rymer's <I>F&oelig;dera</I>, in a diary of King Henry's siege of Bulloigne,
1544, mention is made of the <I>drommes</I> and <I>viffleurs</I> marching at the head of the King's
army. The <I>drum</I> and <I>fife</I> were also much used at ancient festivals, shows, and pro-
cessions. Gerard Leigh, in his <I>Accidence of Armorie</I>, printed in 1576, describing a
Christmas magnificently celebrated at the Inner Temple, says, &lquo;we entered the prince
his hall, where anon we heard the noyse of <I>drum</I> and <I>fife.</I>&rquo; At a stately masque on
Shrove-Sunday, 1510, in which King Henry VIII was an actor, Holinshed mentions
the entry &lquo;of a <I>drum</I> and <I>fife</I> appareled in white damaske and grene bonnettes&rquo;&mdash;
<I>Chron.</I> III, 805, col. 2. <SC>Knight</SC>: Among the French regiments the fife is not found,
and is so completely unknown to the French in the present day, that M. Alfred de
Vigny, in his translation of this passage of <I>Othello</I>, gives us only the drum. [It is to
be feared that Knight drew a conclusion from insufficient premises. The instrument
was known in France in the days of Shakespeare. Cotgrave gives &lquo;Fifre: m. A Fife;
a Flute, or little pipe accorded with a Drumme, or Taber,&rquo; and that it was never &lquo;com-
pletely unknown&rquo; may be inferred, I think, from the fact that from <SC>Le Tourneur</SC> in
1776, down through <SC>Laroche, Guizot, Hugo</SC>, and <SC>Cayrou</SC>, to <SC>Aicard</SC> in 1882, the
word &lquo;fife&rquo; is translated &lquo;fifre,&rquo; and <SC>De Vigny</SC> is the solitary exception where it is not
found, the omission being presumably due to the exigencies of his rhythm.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
