<CC><P>recent happiness; but, with a terrible spring of the mind, he leaps the chasm of afflic-
tion into which he cannot dare to look, and alights on the other side, amidst the tur-
moils of his youth, amidst the noise and glories of his soldiership. This is the instinct
of the mind to save itself from madness. The mind thus blots out the present from its
view, and takes refuge in the past. Othello will not front his deadliest loss; he shrinks
from it, to grasp with associations which restore him for an instant to the vigorous gran-
deur of his manhood; when <I>that</I> instant is over, his energies collapse; then comes the
depressing sense that for him no more is either hope or action; and so he murmurs
&lquo;Othello's occupation's gone.&rquo; Othello, in this passage, reveals the casuistry with which
the mind blinds itself to ruin; the sophistry in which it quibbles with despair; the
maniac strength with which it wrestles against fate and fact. It is as when we fall
asleep with a heavy trouble on the soul; the soul takes advantage of this silent hour to
escape from its bondage; again it is on the sunny hills; the strength of youth comes
back, with the gladness of love and the hopes of life; not once does the spectre of ill
throw its shadow on the dream; the vision is bright while the eyes are shut; but no
sooner do they open than the dismal reality is present, and it cannot be dismissed.
<P>413. <SC>Gould</SC> (p. 106): In the mere word &lquo;farewell&rquo; his [J. B. Booth's] great heart
seemed to burst as in one vast continuing sigh. The phrase, &lquo;the tranquil mind,&rquo; im-
mediately succeeding, came in clear brain-tones, with a certain involved suggestiveness
of meaning almost impossible to define, but as if the tranquil mind <I>had</I> flown. The
whole passage, with its successive images of glorious war filing and disappearing before
the mind's eye, employed some of the grandest elements of voice, subdued to retro-
spective and mournful cadences. &lquo;Othello's occupation's gone.&rquo; And he stood with a
look in his large blue eyes,&mdash;the bronzed face lending them a strange sadness,&mdash;as if
all happiness had gone after. Kean's manner in this scene was very different. At the
close of the &lquo;farewell&rquo; he raised both hands, clasped them, and so brought them down
upon his head, with a most effective gesture of despair. But the action seems to us like
transferring Othello into Edmund Kean. <SC>Fechter</SC>: Othello falls back on his seat,
quite humbled.
<P>415. <SC>Lewes</SC> (p. 4): Kean's range of expression was very limited. His physical apti-
tudes were such as confined him to the strictly tragic passions; and for these he was
magnificently endowed. Small and insignificant in figure, he could at times become
impressively commanding by the lion-like power and grace of his bearing. I remem-
ber the last time I saw him play Othello, how puny he appeared beside Macready,
until in the Third Act, when, roused by Iago's taunts and insinuations, he moved
towards him with a gouty hobble, seized him by the throat, and, in a well-known explo-
sion, &lquo;Villain! be sure,&rquo; &amp;c., he seemed to swell into a stature which made Macready
appear small. On that very evening, when gout made it difficult for him to display
his accustomed grace, when a drunken hoarseness had ruined that once matchless
voice, such was the irresistible pathos,&mdash;manly, not tearful,&mdash;which vibrated in his tones
and expressed itself in looks and gestures, that old men leaned their heads upon their
arms and fairly sobbed. It was, one must confess, a patchy performance considered as
a whole; some parts were miserably tricky, others misconceived, others gabbled over</CC>

<CC><P>445. <B>My name]</B> <SC>Knight</SC>: There is probably not a more fatal corruption of the mean
ing of the poet [than <I>her</I> of Q<SUB>2</SUB>] amongst the thousand corruptions for which his editors
are answerable. It destroys the master-key to Othello's character. It is his intense
feeling of <I>honour</I> that makes his wife's supposed $ault so terrific to him. It is not that
<I>Desdemona's</I> name is begrimed and black, but that <I>his own name</I> is degraded. This
one thought, here for the first time exhibited, pervades all the rest of the play; and
when we understand how the poison operates upon Othello's mind, we are quite pre-
pared fully to believe him when he says, in conclusion,&mdash;&lquo;For naught I did in hate,
but all in honour.&rquo; The thought that his own name is now tarnished drives him at
once into a phrenzy. He has said, &lquo;<I>I'll have some proof&rquo;;</I> but the moment that the
idea of dishonour comes across his sensitive nature he b<*>rsts into uncontrolled fury:
&lquo;If there be cords, . . . . <I>I'll not endure it.</I>&rquo; <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Remarks</I>, p. 240): The word
&lquo;own&rquo; in the phrase &lquo;mine own face,&rquo; is alone sufficient to refute Knight's long and
laborious defence of &lquo;My.&rquo; Othello would not have said, &lquo;<SC>My</SC> name is now as black
as mine <SC>own</SC> face.&rquo; Mr Knight's text of the present tragedy is, on the whole, as bad
as his text of <I>Hamlet;</I> and a worse text of either play could hardly be produced. [These
harsh expressions of opinion are apt to make one antagonistic and far from willing to
accept them as decisive. In justice to Dyce it should be noted that when, a dozen years
later, he became himself an editor of Shakespeare, his tone to his fellow-editors became
much less supercilious and dogmatic.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<CC><P>457. <SC>Hazlitt</SC> (Hawkins's <I>Life of Kean</I>, ii, 209): Kean was great, as we expected,&mdash;
surpassingly great. In the Third Act he let himself loose on the ocean of his pas-
sion, and drove on in darkness and in tempest, like an abandoned barque. The agony
of his heart was the fiery Moorish agony, not cramped in within an actor's or a school-
man's confines, but fierce, ungovernable, dangerous. You knew not what he would do
next in the madness of his spirit,&mdash;he knew not himself what he should do. One of
the finest instantaneous actions of Kean was his clutching his black hand slowly round
his head as though his brain were turning, and then writhing round and standing in
dull agony with his back to the audience,&mdash;what other performer would so have forgot-
ten himself?
<P>461, 462. <SC>Capell</SC> indicates a quotation by Italics in his text, and thus prints these
two lines: &lquo;More than their own! <I>What then? how then</I>, say you? &verbar; <I>Where's satis-
faction?</I> What shall I say?&rquo; Thereupon he has the following wellnigh unwedge-
able note: What is spoke in another's person ought ever to be distinguish'd from what
a speaker says in his own; and this fitness is greatest in such a case as the present,
where interrogations follow interrogations; for want of such distinction, the two mem-
bers of [line 462] (by what accident transpos'd, we know not; but, probably, of the
press) keep through all prior copies the perverse order that accident put them in, the
latter member preceding: Was all other proof wanting that what is now the first mem-
ber stands in it's due place, we might receive it from what the speaker concludes with,
in which is mention of &lquo;satisfaction&rquo; as a thing of Othello's <I>asking:</I> to which asking
the insertion [of <I>say you</I> in line 461] is as favorable on the score of perspicuousness,
as it is to the verse's numbers which are now first compleated.</CC>

by way of thanksgiving, have complained with a touch of petulance that it was out of

<CC><P>and time. In other lips, indeed, than Othello's, at the crowning minute of culminant
agony, the rush of imaginative reminiscence which brings back upon his eyes and ears
the lightning foam and tideless thunder of the Pontic sea might seem a thing less nat-
ural than sublime. But Othello has the passion of a poet closed in, as it were, and
shut up behind the passion of a hero. For all his practical readiness of martial eye
and ruling hand in action, he is also in his season &lquo;of imagination all compact.&rquo; There-
fore it is that in the face and teeth of all devils akin to Iago that hell could send forth
to hiss at her election, we feel and recognize the spotless exaltation, the sublime and
sunbright purity, of Desdemona's inevitable and invulnerable love. When once we
likewise have seen Othello's visage in his mind, we see, too, how much more of great-
ness is in this mind than in another hero's. For such an one, even a boy may well
think how thankfully and joyfully he would lay down his life. Other friends we have
of Shakespeare's giving whom we love deeply and well, if hardly with such love as
could weep for them all the tears of the body and all the blood of the heart; but there
is none we love like Othello.

<CC><P>instance in Shakespeare where &lquo;marble&rquo; is applied to the &lquo;heavens,&rquo; this fine inter-
pretation might stand without question. But it is used elsewhere in passages where it
cannot have a subjective meaning, and it is these passages and others, which, I think,
should determine its meaning here. In Timon's wild address to the earth (IV, iii, 191)
he bids it &lquo;Teem with new monsters, whom thy upward face Hath to the marbled
mansion all above Never presented;&rquo; again, twice in <I>Cymb.</I> (V, iv) where Sicilius first
invokes Jupiter to &lquo;Peep through thy marble mansion,&rquo; and then when Jupiter retires,
he exclaims, &lquo;The marble pavement closes.&rquo; In these three instances &lquo;marbled&rquo; is, it
seems to me, purely objective, and is not a quality projected by the emotions of the
speaker; it is suggestive of all the imposing pomp of masonry with cloud-capt towers
and glistening domes. Furthermore, Marston uses the same phrase, as Steevens and
Malone pointed out, in <I>Solyman and Perseda</I>, 1599: &lquo;Now by the marble face of
the welkin,&rquo; &amp;c., and in <I>Antonio and Mellida</I>, 1602: &lquo;And pleas'd the marble heavens,&rquo;
&amp;c. Lastly, Milton (<I>Par. Lost</I>, iii, 564) describes how Satan &lquo;into the world's first
region throws His flight precipitant, and winds with ease Through the pure marble air
his oblique way.&rquo; We are safe in ascribing a classic origin to many a Miltonic phrase,
and it was Upton (p. 25) who, in vindicating <I>Paradise Lost</I> from the strictures of
Bishop Burnet, shows that &lquo;marble&rquo; is used by Milton &lquo;in its thoroughly classic sense
from <G>marmai/rw</G>, to sparkle, to glow, or, as in the &ldquo;&aelig;quor marmoreum&rdquo; of Vergil, the
sea shining or resplendent like marble.&rquo; This, then, is the meaning in which, I think,
it was always used by Shakespeare, of course without a thought, or perhaps even know-
ledge, of its classic origin. &lquo;Marble&rquo; refers, I think, to color, aglow with lacing streaks,
and not to texture or to substance.&mdash;<SC>Ed. Schmidt</SC> (<I>Lex.</I> s. v.) queries whether &lquo;mar-
ble&rquo; is applied to the heavens on account of their eternity.
<P>523. <SC>Booth</SC>: Kneels. Both hands above the head, with upturned palms and fingers
towards the back. I used this gesture impulsively, in England first, and it was spoken
of as suggestive of the Orient. Iago watches Othello keenly&mdash;sidewise&mdash;during his
next speech; while Othello seems absorbed and with upturned eyes.

<CC><P>532. <B>And to obey]</B> <SC>Theobald</SC> changed <SC>Pope's</SC> <I>Not</I> to <I>Nor</I>, &lquo;that is, let your com
mands be ever so bloody, remorse and compassion shall not restrain me from obeying
them.&rquo; <SC>Upton</SC> (p. 200): A negative particle has slipped out here, we must read &lquo;And
to obey shall be in me <I>no</I> remorse.&rquo; <SC>Johnson</SC>: Iago devotes himself to wronged
Othello, and says, &lquo;Let him command whatever bloody business, and in me it shall be
an act, not of cruelty, but of tenderness, to obey him; not of malice to others, but of
tenderness to him.&rquo; <SC>Steevens</SC>: &lquo;Remorse&rquo; is used for <I>pity</I> in Surrey's translation of
the Fourth &AElig;neid: &lquo;Sister, I crave thou have remorse of me.&rquo; Again, in <I>King Ed-
ward III.</I> 1599: &lquo;But for yourselves, look you for no remorse,&rquo; and in many more
instances, but I shall content myself to observe that the sentiment of Iago bears no
small resemblance to that of Arviragus in <I>Cymb.</I> IV, ii, 168: &lquo;I'ld let a parish of such
Cloten's blood, And praise myself for charity.&rquo; <SC>Reed</SC> quotes <SC>Mason</SC> as saying that
Shakespeare seldom, if ever, uses the word in any other sense. [It is the only sense
given by <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Gloss.</I>)]. <SC>Tollet</SC>: That is, let him command any bloody business,
and to obey him shall be in me an act of pity and compassion for wrong'd Othello.
<SC>Farmer</SC>: I read, &lquo;let him command <I>An</I>' to obey shall be in me remorse What bloody
business ever &mdash;&rquo; &lquo;And&rquo; for <I>if</I> is sufficiently common; and Othello's impatience
breaks off the sentence, I think, with additional beauty. <SC>Knight</SC>: It is quite clear
that Othello interrupts the conclusion of Iago's speech. At the moment when he has
said that &lquo;obedience to Othello shall stand in the place of remorse (mercy)&mdash;What
bloody business ever&rquo; (Othello may command), Othello, jumping at his meaning, at
once sets him upon the murder of Cassio. <SC>Singer</SC> (ed. ii): &lquo;To remord&mdash;to prey
upon continually and repeatedly; and hence Iago's prefigured remorse; a feeling that
will continually prey upon his mind&mdash;Mordax&mdash;Edax-cara.&rquo; [This Latin I do not
understand.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>] I owe this admirable solution of a difficult passage to the kind-
ness of Dr Richardson. <SC>Hudson</SC>: &lquo;Remorse&rquo; for <I>conscience</I>, simply. Iago has said
before, &lquo;I hold it very stuff o' the conscience to do no contrived murder.&rquo; So the mean-

with me a matter of conscience.&rquo; This explanation is Joseph Crosby's. <SC>White</SC> (ed.

<P>543. <SC>Booth</SC>: Take a liberty here and &lquo;damn her&rquo; <I>four</I> times; the first savagely, the
second time less so, melt with the third, and choke with tears at the fourth; the merest
pause&mdash;then recover and &lquo;Come, go with me,&rquo; &amp;c. Iago shows deep grief till &lquo;Now
art thou my lieutenant,&rquo; then, quickly kneeling, he kisses Othello's hand, and his face
reveals his triumph. <SC>Fechter's</SC> Othello returns as he is going out, and, striking Iago
on the shoulder, with a savage smile of triumph says, &lquo;Now art thou my lieutenant.&rquo;
<P>545. <B>death]</B> <SC>Rymer</SC> (p. 92): Othello is made a Venetian General. We see nothing
done by him, nor related concerning him, that comports with the condition of a General, or,
indeed, of a Man, unless the killing himself, to avoid a death the Law was about to inflict
on him. When his jealousy had wrought him up to a resolution of 's taking revenge
for the suppos'd injury, He sets Jago to the fighting part, to kill Cassio; And he chuses
himself to murder the silly Woman his Wife, that was like to make no resistance.
<P>548. <SC>Booth</SC>: To portray Iago properly you must seem to be what all the characters
think, and say, you are, not what the spectators know you to be; try to win even <I>them</I>
by your sincerity. Don't <I>act</I> the villain, don't <I>look</I> it or <I>speak</I> it (by scowling and
growling, I mean), but <I>think</I> it all the time. Be genial, sometimes jovial, always gen-
tlemanly. Quick in motion as in thought; lithe and sinuous as a snake. A certain bluff-
ness (which my temperament does not afford) should be added to preserve the military
flavour of the character; in this particular I fail utterly, my Iago lacks the soldierly qual
ity. My consolation is that we know him more as a courtier than as a soldier.</CC>

<CC><P>and <I>bid</I> them answer; i. e., the world; those whom he questions. <SC>Henley</SC>: His
design was to propose such questions as might elicit the information sought for from
him, and, therefore, <I>by</I> his <I>questions</I> he might be enabled to answer. <SC>Malone</SC>: That
is, and by them, <I>when answered</I>, form my own answer to you. <SC>Rolfe</SC> states it clearly:
By them be enabled to answer, or get the information to use in my answer.
<P>24. <B>the doing it]</B> For a full exposition of verbals, followed by an object, see

<P>25. <B>should I loose]</B> <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 325: &lquo;Should,&rquo; in a direct question about the past,
seems to increase the emphasis of the interrogation, since a doubt about the past (time
having been given for investigation) implies more perplexity than a doubt about the
future.
<P>25. <B>the]</B> <SC>White</SC> (ed. i): <I>That</I> of the Qq has a loss of significance. To Desde-

<P>27. <SC>Hudson</SC>: Objection has been made to the conduct of Emilia in this scene as
inconsistent with the spirit she afterwards shows. I can discover no such inconsist-
ency. Want of principle and strength of attachment are often thus seen united.
Emilia loves her mistress deeply, but she has no <I>moral</I> repugnance to theft and false
hood, apprehends no <I>fatal</I> consequences from the Moor's passion, and has no soul to
conceive the agony her mistress must suffer by the charge of infidelity; and it is but
natural that when the result comes she should be the more spirited for the very remem-
brance of her own guilty part in the process. <SC>Booth</SC>: Emilia speaks with slight em-
barrassment.

with the same searching intensity; then a kindly doubt seems to rise in his mind, and
he gives her the benefit of it in saying&mdash;&lquo;That <I>commonly</I> (slight pause) <I>rebels.</I>&rquo;
<P>51, etc. <SC>Walker</SC> (iii, 288): Arrange, perhaps,&mdash;&lquo;'Tis a good hand, a frank one. &verbar;
<I>Desd.</I> You may indeed say so; for 'twas that hand &verbar; That gave away my heart.&rquo; [I
record this note, like many another of Walker, simply because I lack the moral cour-
age to omit it. When Walker spends his time and ours in cutting up verses, and frag-
ments of verses spoken by different characters, into lines, what else is it but scanning
by the eye and for the eye? If the words do not flow musically, cutting them into lines
will not make them musical. If they do flow musically, the lines will take care of
themselves. Is it to be imagined that Shakespeare ever followed any guide but his
ear? What does the ear know of lines? recurrent or uncurrent rhythm is all that ever
it can note.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<CC><P>53. <B>You]</B> <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 483: Emphasized pronouns sometimes dispense with the un-
accented syllable. Here <I>you</I> is emphatic. &lquo;A fr&aacute;nk &verbar; one. <I>Y&oacute;</I> &verbar; <I>u</I> m&aacute;y &verbar; ind&eacute;ed &verbar;
say s&oacute;.
<P>55, 56. In these lines <SC>Warburton</SC> discerned a satirical allusion to the creation of
baronets by James the First, and founded on it the date of the composition of the play.
For his arguments in this regard and Malone's reply to them, see Appendix, <I>Date of
the Composition.</I> Warburton also asserted that &lquo;it is evident that line 55 should be
read: &ldquo;The <I>hands</I> of old gave <I>hearts&rdquo;;</I> otherwise it would be no reply to &ldquo;For 'twas
that <I>hand</I> that gave away my heart.&rdquo; Not so, says her husband, &ldquo;The hands of old
indeed gave hearts; but the custom now is to give hands without hearts.&rdquo;&rquo; <SC>Johnson</SC>:
Of emendation there is no need. She says that her hand gave away <I>her heart.</I> He
goes on with his suspicion, and the hand which he had before called <I>frank</I>, he now
terms <I>liberal;</I> then proceeds to remark that <I>the hand was formerly given by the heart;</I>
but now it neither gives it, nor is given by it. <SC>Steevens</SC>: The phrase &lquo;our new her-
aldry&rquo; is only figurative, without the least reference to James's creation of baronets.
The absurdity of making Othello so familiar with British heraldry, the utter want of
consistency as well as policy in any sneer of Shakespeare at the badge of honours
instituted by a Prince whom, on all other occasions, he was solicitous to flatter, and at
whose court this very piece was acted in 1613, most strongly incline me to question the
propriety of Warburton's historical explanation. <SC>Malone</SC>: The hearts of old, says
Othello, dictated the union of <I>hands</I>, which formerly were joined with <I>the hearts</I> of the
parties <I>in them;</I> but in our modern marriages, <I>hands</I> alone are united, without <I>hearts.</I>
Such is the plain meaning of the words. I do not, however, undertake to maintain
that the poet, when he used the word &lquo;heraldry,&rquo; had not the new order of baronets in
his thoughts, without intending any satirical allusion. <SC>Knight</SC>: We do not think that
Shakespeare would have gone out of his way to introduce a covert sarcasm at a passing
event, offensive as it must have been if understood, and perfectly useless if not under-
stood. The obvious meaning of the words, without any allusion, is plain enough; and
&lquo;our new heraldry,&rquo; if it be any more than a figurative expression, may be easily referred
to the practice of quartering or joining the arms of husband and wife. <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Remarks</I>,
p. 241): The reader will probably recollect with dismay the immense mass of annota-
tion which this passage has called forth in consequence of Warburton's ridiculous idea
that the poet alluded here to the new order of baronets created by King James. I have
only to observe: first,&mdash;that the word &lquo;heraldry&rquo; (which the commentators are surprised
at finding here) was evidently suggested to Shakespeare by the words in the preceding
line, &lquo;gave hands&rquo; (to &lquo;give arms&rquo; being a heraldic term); secondly, that Warner, in
his <I>Albion's England</I>, p. 282, ed. 1596, has, &lquo;My hand shall neuer giue my heart, my
heart shall giue my hand.&rquo; <SC>White</SC> (ed. i and ed. ii) adopts Warburton's idea. In his
ed. ii he says: &lquo;This seems to be the new heraldry Othello speaks of; but in that case,
the passage was probably added after the first production of the play.&rquo;</CC>

<CC><P>86. <B>Prophetticke furie]</B> <SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 285): There is something more classical in

<P>88. <B>Mummey]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: The balsamic liquor running from mummies was for-
merly celebrated for its anti-epileptic virtues. This fanciful medicine still holds a place
in the principal shops where drugs are sold. <SC>Dyce</SC>: A preparation for magical pur-
poses, made from dead bodies. Steevens's note seems irrelevant. [I doubt if the word
conveyed, of necessity, any reference to Egyptian mummies; that reference was perhaps
restricted to <I>mummia.</I> Falstaff refers to himself as being turned by drowning into a
&lquo;mountain of mummy,&rquo; and we have &lquo;Witches' mummy&rquo; in <I>Macb.</I> IV, i, 23, which
see with the notes. In Johnson's <I>Dict.</I> s. v. there is a full account of the medicinal
preparation, from Dr Hill's <I>Materia Medica</I>, and in Latham's <I>Johnson</I> a passage is
given from Sir T. Herbert's <I>Travels</I>, &amp;c. 1677, which shows that that traveler not only
did not associate &lquo;mummy&rquo; with Egypt, but not even with dead bodies:&mdash;&lquo;In or near this
place is a precious liquor or <I>mummy</I> growing; . . . . a moist, redolent gum it is, sove-
reign against poisons.&rquo; Steevens cites from <I>The Microcosmos</I> of John Davies of Here-
ford (1603, p. 77, ed. Grosart): &lquo;That's <I>Mummey</I> made of the meere Hart of <I>Love.</I>&rquo;
That Davies was well read in Shakespeare's <I>Sonnets</I> is felt throughout the <I>Microcosm</I>,
but the date of the latter is rather too early to permit the supposition that it had been
influenced by <I>Othello.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>92. <SC>Mrs. Jameson</SC> (ii, 38): Desdemona, whose soft credulity, whose turn for the
marvellous, whose susceptible imagination had first directed her thoughts and affections
to Othello, is precisely the woman to be frightened out of her senses by such a tale as
this, and betrayed by her fears into a momentary tergiversation. It is most natural in
such a being, and shows us that even in the sweetest natures there can be no complete-
ness and consistency without moral energy. There is an incident in the original tale
which could not well be transferred to the drama, but which is very effective, and adds, I

<CC><P>old, whom he trains or bribes to the theft. The love of Desdemona for this child,
her little playfellow,&mdash;the pretty description of her taking it in her arms and caressing
it, while it profits by its situation to steal the handkerchief from her bosom, are well
imagined, and beautifully told; and the circumstance of Iago employing his own inno-
cent child as the instrument of his infernal villainy adds a deeper, and, in truth, an
unnecessary touch of the fiend, to his fiendish character. [It is so common among the
critics to accuse Desdemona of telling a falsehood here, that gratitude is due to Mrs
Jameson for the milder term &lquo;tergiversation.&rquo; Although Desdemona herself says,
&lquo;where should I <I>lose</I> the handkerchief?&rquo; she did not believe it to be actually lost, irre-
coverably gone; it was merely mislaid, and a further search would reward her with
discovery. If she had not been terrified she might have told all this to Othello (and
we should not have had the tragedy, which would be a relief), but, as it is, I think in
her soul she believed she was telling the truth.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>109. When De Vigny makes his dashing attack on the French Classic School, ridi-
culing its horror at the word <I>mouchoir</I>, which, under the hands of the fastidious Ducis,
becomes a &lquo;bandeau de diamants, que l'h&eacute;ro&iuml;ne (as De Vigny says) voulut garder m&ecirc;me
au lit de peur d'&ecirc;tre vue en n&eacute;glig&eacute;,&rquo; our hearts and admiration go entirely with him,
and an almost instinctive contempt arises for any one who can find in such a word, as
&lquo;handkerchief,&rquo; at such a time, anything unworthy of this tragic scene. But will not
the curl of our lips at Ducis straighten, and even some fellow-feeling for him spring
up, if we imagine the word as it is in the Qto, uttered by Othello with passionate vehe-
mence? As this word sounds to us, so must <I>mouchoir</I>, on the stage, have sounded to
Ducis.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>110. <B>A man]</B> <SC>Bodenstedt</SC> (<I>Sh. Jahrbuch</I>, ii, 263): With the same recklessness
and self-will with which Desdemona, out of love to Othello, had exposed herself to
the anger of her Father, she now defies the anger of her husband out of friendship
to Cassio.
<P>115. <B>Away]</B> <SC>Fielding</SC>: Nothing can be more provoking to the human temper, nor
more dangerous to that cardinal virtue, Patience, than solicitations of extraordinary
offices of kindness in behalf of those very persons with whom we are highly incensed.
For this reason Shakespeare hath artfully introduced his Desdemona soliciting favours
for Cassio of her husband, as the means of inflaming not only his jealousy, but his rage,
to the highest pitch of madness; and we find the unfortunate Moor less able to com-
mand his passion on this occasion than even when he beheld his valued present to his
wife in the hands of his supposed rival. In fact, we regard these efforts as insults to
our understanding; and to such the pride of man is with great difficulty brought to
submit.&mdash;<I>Tom Jones</I>, ix, 3, quoted by <SC>Halliwell</SC>.</CC>

<CC><P>120. <SC>Rymer</SC> (p. 126): As if for the first year or two Othello had not been jealous?
This Third Act begins in the morning, at noon she drops the Handkerchief, after dinner
she misses it, and then follows all this outrage and horrible clutter about it. If we
believe a small Damosel, in the last scene of this Act, this day is effectually seven days.
Our Poet is at this plunge, that whether this Act contains the compass of one day, of
seven days, or of seven years, or of all together, the repugnance and the absurdity
would be the same. For Othello, all the while, has nothing to say or to do, but what
loudly proclaim him jealous; her friend and confident Emilia again and again rounds
her in the ear that <I>the Man</I> is jealous; yet this Venetian dame is neither to see, nor to
hear; nor to have any sense or understanding, nor to strike any other note but <I>Cassio,
Cassio.</I> <SC>Steevens</SC>: This line has no reference to the duration of the action, or to the
length of time that Desdemona had been married. What Emilia says is a sort of pro-
verbial remark, of general application, where a definite time is put for an indefinite.
Besides, this &lquo;year or two&rquo; may refer to the beginning of the acquaintance and inti-
macy between the couple. <SC>Pye</SC> (p. 342): Emilia's saying, &lquo;it is not a year or two
shews us a man,&rquo; may be well supposed to insinuate, how then should a month or two,
or even a day or two?
<P>121. <SC>White</SC> (ed. ii): Emilia means, They are nought but stomachs, and we nought
but food. The obscurity results from an inversion of, They are but all stomach, and
we but all food. [There may be an inversion here, but I do not think that it is the
inversion which White points out. &lquo;All&rquo; does not qualify &lquo;stomachs,&rquo; or &lquo;food,&rquo; but
&lquo;They&rquo; and &lquo;we.&rquo; The meaning is that they, every one of them, are merely stomachs
for which we, every one of us, are merely food. When White represents Shakespeare
as making man revert to the Gasteropods or to the Am&oelig;bas, his admiration and exal-
tation of our demi-god go one step farther than mine. &lquo;We know what we are, but
we know not what we may be,&rquo; as Ophelia says, so that I may even yet be brought to
believe that Shakespeare anticipated Darwin,&mdash;but not from this passage.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>125. <SC>Booth</SC>: As if glad to change the subject.</CC>

<CC><P>7 and 9. <B>naked]</B> <SC>Dyce</SC>, in both his Second and his Third Edition, prints these
words with an accent, thus: &lquo;nak&egrave;d.&rquo; I wish I knew why; especially since a similar
forethought for heedless readers of this word is not extended by Dyce elsewhere; after
having learned to lean on our accented <I>&egrave;</I>'s, we are liable to read, in his edition, that
Emilia wishes rascals to be lashed &lquo;nak'd through the world,&rquo; and that Othello threatens
Gratiano that he will assault him &lquo;nak'd as he was.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>10. <B>Diuell]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: This means, hypocrisy to cheat the devil. As common hypo-
crites cheat men by seeming good, and yet living wickedly, these men would cheat the
devil, by giving him flattering hopes, and at last avoiding the crime which he thinks
them ready to commit. <SC>Rymer</SC> (p. 128): At this gross rate of trifling, our General
and his Auncient March on most heroically; till the jealous Booby has his Brains
turn'd; and falls in a Trance. Would any imagine this to be the Language of Vene-
tians, of Souldiers, and mighty Captains? no Bartholomew Droll cou'd subsist upon
such trash. [According to <SC>Allibone</SC> (<I>Dict.</I>), Pope considered Rymer, &lquo;on the whole,
one of the best critics we ever had&rquo;; Dryden and Sir Walter Scott quote him with
respect; Dr Johnson was disgusted at his &lquo;ferocity&rquo;; Sergeant Talfourd praises his
acuteness at the expense of his judgement, and Lord Macaulay deems him &lquo;the worst
critic that ever lived.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>12. <B>Heauen]</B> <SC>Henley</SC>; The true key to the explanation of this passage may be
found in St. Matthew, iv, 7. The poet's idea is, that the devil tempts their virtues
by stirring up their passions, and they tempt heaven by placing themselves in such
a situation as makes it scarcely possible to avoid falling, by the gratification of
them.</CC>

<P>25. <B>Rauen]</B> <SC>Harting</SC> (p. 99): Go where we will over the face of the wide world,
the hoarse croak of the raven is still to be heard. He was seen perched on the bare
rocks, looking over the dreary snows of the highest points visited in Arctic expeditions
Under the burning sun of the equator he enjoys his feast of carrion. He was discov-
ered in the islands of the Pacific by Captain Cook; and in the lowest Antarctic regions
travellers have found him pursuing his cautious predatory life, just as in England. From
the earliest times, with his deep and solemn voice he has always commanded attention,
and in his croakings the superstitious have found something unearthly and ominous. By
the Romans he was consecrated to Apollo and regarded as a prophet of good or of evil.
Through a long course of centuries this character has clung to him; and even at this
day there are many who believe that the raven's croak predicts a death. No wonder
then that Shakespeare has used th&iacute;s widespread belief, and has introduced the raven
into many of the solemn passages of his Plays. <SC>Malone</SC> quotes these fine lines of
Marlowe, <I>Jew of Malta</I>, II, i, 1: &lquo;Thus, like the sad presaging raven, that tolls The
sick man's passport in her hollow beak, And in the shadow of the silent night Doth
shake contagion from her sable wings.&rquo;

<CC><P>33. <B>Conuinced or supply'd]</B> <SC>Theobald</SC>: I read &lquo;convinced or <I>suppled</I>,&rquo; and the
meaning is, there are some such long-tongued knaves in the world, who, if they through
the <I>force of importunity extort</I> a favour from their mistress, or if through <I>her own fond-
ness</I> they make her <I>pliant</I> to their desires, cannot help boasting of their success. To
<I>convince</I>, here, is not, as in the common acceptation, to make sensible of the truth of
anything by reasons and arguments; but to &lquo;<I>overcome, get the better of</I>,&rquo; &amp;c. <SC>Jennens</SC>:
I see no reason for this alteration; Iago is here describing two sorts of gallants; one
who by their importunities have <I>convinced</I>, or overcome, their mistresses; the other, who,
when their mistresses voluntarily doated on them, have <I>supplied</I> them with the effects of
love. <SC>Steevens</SC>: &lquo;Supplied&rquo; is certainly the true reading. See <I>Meas. for Meas.</I> V, i, 212.
<P>44-52. Here, as in <I>Lear</I>, IV, vi, 127, the highest passion of all, as <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 511)
says, is expressed in prose Compare lines 198 et seq. of this Scene.</CC>

<P>50. <B>Instruction]</B> <SC>Warburton</SC>: The starts and broken reflections in this speech
have something very terrible, and show the mind of the speaker to be in inexpressible
agonies. But the words we are upon have a sublime in them that can never be enough
admired. The ridiculous blunder of writing &lquo;instruction&rquo; for <I>induction</I> (for so it should
be read) has, indeed, sunk it into arrant nonsense. Othello is just going to fall into a
swoon; and, as is common for people in that circumstance, feels an unusual mist and
darkness, accompanied with horror, coming upon him. This, with vast sublimity of
thought, is compared to the season of the sun's eclipse, at which time the earth becomes
shadowed by the <I>induction</I> or bringing over of the moon between it and the sun. This
being the allusion, the reasoning stands thus, My nature could never be thus overshad-
owed, and falling, as it were, into dissolution for no cause. There must be an <I>induc-
tion</I> of something; there must be a real cause. My jealousy cannot be merely imagi-
nary. Ideas, <I>words</I> only, could not shake me thus, and raise all this disorder. My
jealousy must be grounded, therefore, on matter of fact. This word is used in this
sense in <I>Rich. III:</I> IV, iv, 5. <SC>Johnson</SC>: This is a noble conjecture, and, whether
right or wrong, does honour to its author. Yet I am in doubt whether there is any
necessity of emendation. There has always prevailed in the world an opinion that,
when any great calamity happens at a distance, notice is given of it to the sufferer by
some dejection or perturbation of mind, of which he discovers no external cause. This
is ascribed to that general communication of one part of the universe with another,
which is called sympathy and antipathy; or to the secret monition, <I>instruction</I>, and
influence of a Superior Being, which superintends the order of nature and of life.
Othello says, Nature could not invest herself in such shadowing passion without
<I>instruction.</I> It is not words that shake me thus. This passion which spreads its
clouds over me is the effect of some agency, more than the operation of words; it is
one of those notices which men have of unseen calamities. <SC>Heath</SC> (p. 569): Othello
feels all his faculties failing him on the sudden, and a cloudy or misty darkness creeping
very fast upon him. This circumstance suggests to him the thought that his very nature,
which sympathizes with him in his present agony, must have received some secret mys-
terious instruction, intimation, or instinctive knowledge of the reality of that calamity
which so deeply oppresses him, otherwise she would never have spontaneously invested</CC>

<CC><P>herself in that horrid darkness which he now felt overwhelming him. <SC>Sir J. Rey-
nolds</SC>: Othello alludes only to Cassio's dream, which had been invented and told him
by Iago. When many confused and very interesting ideas pour in upon the mind all
at once, and with such rapidity that it has not time to shape or digest them, if it does
not relieve itself by tears (which we know it often does, whether for joy or grief) it
produces stupefaction and fainting. Othello, in broken sentences and single words, all
of which have a reference to the cause of his jealousy, shows that all the proofs are
present at once to his mind, which so overpowers it that he falls into a trance, the nat-
ural consequence. <SC>Malone</SC>: <I>Induction</I>, in Shakespeare's time, meant <I>introduction</I> or
<I>prelude</I>, and at no time signified <I>bringing over</I>, as Warburton interprets it.
<P>50. <B>that shakes]</B> See I, iii, 312.
<P>51. <B>Lippes]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: Othello is imagining to himself the familiarities which he
supposes to have passed between Cassio and his wife. If this be not the meaning, we
must suppose he is meditating a cruel punishment for the guilty lovers.
<P>53. <SC>Fechter</SC> here begins his Act IV. Othello and Iago discovered. Othello is
stretched, unconscious, on the divan. Iago behind, contemplating him with a diabol-
ical sneer.
<P>54. <B>workes]</B> An interpolated <I>s</I>, according to <SC>Walker</SC>. See I, i, 31.
<P>57-200. <SC>Salvini</SC> justifies his omission of this portion of the scene on the ground
that it is not in accord with Othello's character. &lquo;Is it to be imagined,&rquo; he asks, &lquo;that
a man of the Moor's haughty and violent temper could command himself during the
recital of his dishonour from the lips of his wronger? Would you not suppose that he
would spring like a tiger on Cassio and tear him to pieces? To be sure, Cassio would
gain enough time to clear up the misunderstanding, and the Tragedy would fall through.
Hence, either this scene must be retained to the injury of Othello's character, or it must
be omitted.&rquo; The gap in the story Salvini considers as filled by Othello's assertion in
the last scene, that he had seen the Handkerchief in Cassio's hand.</CC>

<CC><P>116. See note, III, iii, 383.
<P>118. <B>vnbookish]</B> <SC>Whiter</SC> (p. 112), after citing many instances where Shakespeare
has used the imagery of a <I>book</I> in connection with <I>love</I>, ends with the celebrated
description of Cressida (<I>Tro. &amp; Cress.</I> IV, v, 54) wherein Ulysses speaks of &lquo;unclasp-
ing the tables of their thoughts To every ticklish reader;&rquo; and the same metaphor,
Whiter is persuaded, Iago uses here. &lquo;The &ldquo;unbookish&rdquo; jealousy of Othello,&rquo; says
Whiter, &lquo;is that which confounds his knowledge in the <I>Books of</I> <SC>Love</SC>, and blinds his
discernment respecting the <I>language of</I> <SC>Lovers</SC>. It will cause him to mistake the
artless smiles and gestures of Cassio for the significant expressions of <I>amorous parley.</I>
Whether our Poet intended to comprehend the whole of this meaning, I am not able
to decide: I am convinced, however, that this remote epithet &ldquo;unbookish,&rdquo; as applied
to jealousy, was suggested to his mind by the above very singular imagery of the <I>Lover</I>
and the <I>Book.</I>&rquo; <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> iii, 289) noticed what had escaped Whiter, that &lquo;un-
bookish&rquo; is connected with &lquo;construe,&rquo; but when he adds that &lquo;it is explained by it,&rquo; he
does not take me wholly with him. &lquo;Unbookish&rquo; is certainly used here in an unusual
sense; it is as though there were Books of <I>Jealousy</I>, like Saviolo's <I>Practise of Honorable
Quarrels</I>, which should guide Othello, but did not. <SC>Warburton's</SC> explanation, followed
by Dyce and others, that it is equivalent to <I>ignorant</I>, is scarcely sufficient. The use of
&lquo;bookish&rquo; in the first scene of this play, in its manifest meaning (where Iago talks
of the &lquo;bookish Theoric&rquo;), shows that more is meant by &lquo;unbookish&rquo; than mere lack
of knowledge or of skill. Until a better can be given, Whiter's explanation seems the
nearest, viz.: that Shakespeare having so frequently compared <I>love</I> and <I>lovers</I> to <I>books</I>,
here, by the association of ideas, makes Othello's misconstruction of Cassio's smiles due
to Othello's lack of learning in the books of love.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

<CC><P>ironically. &lquo;Triumph,&rquo; which was a Roman ceremony, brought Roman into his
thoughts. &lquo;What!&rquo; says he, &lquo;you are now triumphing as great as a Roman?&rquo; <SC>Collier</SC>
(ed. ii): The (MS.) informs us that for &lquo;Roman&rquo; we ought to substitute <I>o'er me.</I> This
may be so, and the reason for &lquo;Roman,&rquo; in reference to &lquo;triumph,&rquo; is not obvious; but
as the change is somewhat violent, and in no respect compulsory, we do not make it.

speare and his Birthplace</I>, gives this word as in use in this sense among the peasantry

words, &lquo;you shall marry her,&rquo; and asks, &lquo;Have you made out my reckoning? Are
you finished with me?&rquo; it is not until Othello is out of the way that a marriage with
her is possible. <SC>Hudson</SC>: I am not clear as to the meaning of this. To <I>score</I> was to</CC>

he never <I>pays the score&rquo;;</I> and the context there shows the meaning to be, that when he
has sworn a woman into granting his wish, he never keeps his oaths; or what the Poet
elsewhere calls &lquo;beguiling virgins with the brokens seals of perjury.&rquo; So, in the text,
the meaning may be, &lquo;Have you run up an account against me, which I must pay?
very well, I'll see you paid.&rquo; Or it may be, &lquo;Have you squared the account with me
for cashiering you?&rquo;
<P>159. <B>nose . . . dogge]</B> <SC>Deighton</SC> (p. 62): I see your nose, which I shall soon
tear from your face and fling to the first dog that comes in my way.
<P>162. <B>Before me]</B> <SC>Schmidt</SC> interprets this as equivalent to &lquo;by my soul,&rquo; and refers
to <I>Twelfth Night</I>, II, iii, 194. <SC>Purnell</SC> considers it as a euphemism for &lquo;before God.&rquo;
and refers to <I>Cor.</I> I, i, 124.</CC>

<CC><P>203. <B>your way]</B> <SC>Deighton</SC> (p. 63): That is, it won't do for you to let your thoughts

<P>212. <SC>Mrs Jameson</SC> (ii, 35): Desdemona displays at times a transient energy, arising
from the power of affection, but gentleness gives the prevailing tone to her character,&mdash;
gentleness in its excess,&mdash;gentleness verging on passiveness,&mdash;gentleness which not only
cannot resent, but cannot resist. Here in this passage the exceeding softness of Desde-
mona's temper is turned against her by Iago, so that it suddenly strikes Othello in a new
point of view, as the inability to resist temptation; but to us, who perceive the character
as a whole, this extreme gentleness of nature is yet delineated with such exceeding
refinement that the effect never approaches to feebleness. It is true that <I>once</I> her
extreme timidity leads her, in a moment of confusion and terror, to prevaricate about
the fatal handkerchief.
<P>216. <B>pattent]</B> See <SC>Chalmers</SC>, on Date of Composition, in Appendix.</CC>

<CC><P>237. <SC>Malone</SC>: This does not relate to what Lodovico has just said, but is spoken by
Othello while he salutes him. <SC>Steevens</SC>: I know not how the meaning of this speeh
can be ascertained, unless by reference to the salutation of Lodovico. The distracted
Othello, considering his own happiness at an end in this world, readily catches at the
idea of future felicity suggested by the words: &lquo;'Save you, general!&rquo; In his reply,
therefore, he must be supposed to welcome the pious wish expressed in his behalf. In
<I>Meas. for Meas.</I> II, ii, 157, two replies of Angelo, equally equivocal, are derived from
similar premises: &lquo;<I>Isab.</I> Heaven keep your honour safe! <I>Ang.</I> Amen!&rquo; Again, at
the conclusion of the same scene: &lquo;<I>Isab.</I> 'Save your honour! <I>Ang.</I> From thee: even
from thy virtue!&rquo; If it be urged that &lquo;'<I>save</I> you&rquo; only means <I>preserve you in this</I> world,
my sense of the passage will not be much weakened: as our protection, even &lquo;<I>here</I>,
upon this bank and shoal of time,&rquo; depends on the Almighty.
<P>253. <B>attone]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: Make them <I>one;</I> reconcile them <SC>Henley</SC>: The verb is
formed by the coalesce<*>ce of the words <I>at one.</I></CC>

<CC><P>256. <B>Oth.]</B> <SC>Fechter</SC> gives this speech to Iago, directing him to seize the arm of
Othello across the table and stop him violently. Othello, &lquo;rising furiously,&rquo; had just
uttered line 254. [Much as I dislike the Porte St. Martin, or Bowery, style of Fechter's
Othello, I must confess that here his suggestion strikes me as worthy of consideration.
There is no small degree of propriety in representing the cool Iago as recalling Othello
to his senses; and even if Iago's attempt be obtrusive or unmilitary, it is, perhaps, a
less dramatic fault than what might seem the anticlimax of a sedate expostulation,
addressed to Desdemona after the furious explosion, &lquo;Fire and brimstone.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>259. <SC>Theobald</SC>: Othello is but just arrived at Cyprus; the Senate could hardly
yet have heard of the Ottoman fleet being scattered by the tempest; and Othello is at
once remanded home, without any imputation suggested on his conduct, or any hint
of his being employed in a more urgent Commission. Tis true, the deputation of Cas-
sio in his room seems designed to heighten the Moor's resentment; but some probable
reason should have been assigned for his recall. As to what Iago says afterwards, that
Othello is to go to Mauritania, this is only a lie of his own invention to carry his point
with Roderigo. <SC>Lloyd</SC>: The news that Othello is superseded recalls the impressions
of the judicial deliberations of the Venetian Senate in the First Act, and seems to com-
plete the proof of the infallible instincts of the statesmen.
<P>264. <SC>Cowden-Clarke</SC>: We cannot help thinking that the author probably wrote,

you unwise,&rquo; in reference to his having asked, &lquo;Are you wise?&rquo;

<P>298. <SC>Theobald</SC>: I cannot see, for my heart, the difference betwixt the shot of <I>acci-

but that the Poet intended two different things seems plain from the <I>discretive</I> adverb.
Chance may afflict a man in some circumstances; but other distresses are to be
accounted for from a different cause. I am persuaded our Author wrote: &lquo;nor dart
of <I>change.</I>&rquo; In several other places he industriously puts these two words in opposi-
tion to each other. <SC>Heath</SC> (p. 569): There is no occasion for Theobald's alteration.</CC>

<CC><P>&lquo;Accident&rquo; is commonly used to denote personal calamities; &lquo;chance,&rquo; to distinguish
those in which we are involved in consequence of more general revolutions of fortune.
<P>299. <B>graze]</B> <SC>Warburton</SC>: 'Tis no commendation to the most solid virtue to be free
from the attacks of fortune, but that it is so impenetrable as to suffer no impression.
Now, to &lquo;graze&rquo; signifies only <I>to touch the superficies</I> of anything. That is the attack
of fortune; and by that virtue is try'd, but not discredited. We ought certainly, there-
fore, to read <I>raze</I>, i. e., neither lightly touch upon nor pierce into. The ignorant tran-
scribers being acquainted with the phrase of a <I>bullet grazing</I>, and &lquo;shot&rquo; being men-
tion'd in the line before, they corrupted the true word. <SC>Johnson</SC>: To &lquo;graze&rquo; is not
merely to touch superficially, but to strike not directly, not so as to bury the body of the
thing striking in the matter struck. Theobald trifles, as is usual. &lquo;Accident and &lquo;chance&rquo;
may admit a subtle distinction; &lquo;accident&rquo; may be considered as the <I>act</I>, and &lquo;chance&rquo;
as the <I>power</I> or <I>agency</I> of Fortune; as, It was by <I>chance</I> that this <I>accident</I> befel me.
At least, if we suppose all corrupt that is inaccurate, there will be no end of emenda-
tion. <SC>Malone</SC>: I do not see the least ground for supposing any corruption. As
&lquo;pierce&rquo; relates to &lquo;the dart of chance,&rquo; so &lquo;graze&rquo; is referred to &lquo;the shot of accident.
<P>302, 303. That the punctuation of these lines is puzzling may be inferred from the
fact that the Cambridge Editors, in 1866, did not follow their own punctuation of 1864
I do not think that the F<SUB>1</SUB> can be much improved.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>306, 307. <B>yet . . . worst]</B> <SC>Purnell</SC>: Probably this is an aside.</CC>

<CC><P>317. <SC>Fechter</SC>: They go out as following Othello; who, as soon as they are out of
sight, appears from the tapestry on the left, bringing forward Emilia, and speaks as con-
tinuing to interrogate. [Of course the Scene continues. Here begins <SC>Booth's</SC> Second
Scene, Act Fourth.] <SC>Lloyd</SC>: When this Scene, in which the fainting Othello appears
as the suffering and passive instrument of Iago, is left out in representation, the best
acting in the world, or to be in the world, will not preserve the Scene in the bed-cham-
ber from having, to well-ordered sympathies, all the shockingness of a contrived, cold-
blooded murder.
<P><B>Scena Secunda]</B> <SC>Malone</SC>: There are great difficulties in ascertaining the place
of this Scene. Near the close of it, Iago says to Desdemona, &lquo;Go <I>in</I>, and weep not,&rquo;
which would lead us to place it in the court before Othello's castle. These words
may, indeed, be explained to mean, &lquo;Go <I>into</I> the supper-room&rquo; (though I do not think
that the meaning); but immediately afterwards Roderigo enters and converses with
Iago, which decisively ascertains the scene not to be in Othello's house; for Roderigo,
who had given the first intelligence to Brabantio of his daughter's flight, and had
shortly afterwards drawn his sword on Othello and his partisans, certainly would not
take the liberty of walking into his house at pleasure. On the other hand, what
Othello says early in the scene to Emilia, line 35, &lquo;<I>shut the door</I>,&rquo; and his subsequent
address to her as he goes out, as decisively point out a room in Othello's castle as the
place of the Scene, and compel us to place the several interlocutors there, however
inconsistent with Roderigo's entry and Iago's address to Desdemona. The truth is,
that our poet and his audience, in this instance as in many others, were content, from
want of scenery, to consider the very same spot, at one and the same time, as the
outside and inside of a house. <SC>Cowden-Clarke</SC>: But if it be remembered that a
portion of the mansion is used as a guard-room, it would be natural enough that Rode-
rigo should seek Iago there, and, not finding him, should pursue his search in some of
the apartments adjacent; moreover, it should be remembered that Roderigo is partially
disguised, and therefore not likely to be recognized as the man who gave Brabantio
intelligence of Othello's having married Desdemona.

<CC><P>27. <B>pray]</B> <SC>Heraud</SC> (p. 279): Emilia's supposed hypocrisy embitters Othello both
against her and her calumniated mistress. Perhaps, too, the poet intended his free-
thoughted and noble Moor to entertain a customary protest against superstitious cere-
monies; and here we have a glimpse vouchsafed of his religious tendency. It is in
this furtive manner that Shakespeare always alludes to the theological aspects of his
theme. Never will he altogether neglect them; but nowhere will he thoroughly unveil
them. Both political and religious prudence are evidently observed by Shakespeare in
the treatment of all his subjects. The spirit of the time compelled him to this reticence.
[See <SC>Heraud</SC>, III, iii, 67.]

<P>64, 65. <SC>Steevens</SC>: We call the hour in which we are to die, &lquo;the hour of death,&rquo;&mdash;the
time when we are to be judged, &lquo;the day of judgement,&rquo;&mdash;the instant when we suffer
calamity, &lquo;the moment of evil&rquo;; and why may we not distinguish the time which
brings contempt along with it by the title of &lquo;the time of scorn&rquo;? Othello takes his
idea from a clock. &lquo;To make me (says he) a fixed figure (on the dial of the world)
for the hour of scorn to point and make a full stop at!&rquo; By &lquo;<I>slow unmoving</I> finger&rquo;
our poet could have meant only &lquo;so slow that its motion was imperceptible.&rquo; Thus, in
<I>Ant. &amp; Cleo.</I> III, iii, 22, the messenger, describing the gait of the demure Octavia, says,
she creeps; Her motion and her station are as one,&rquo; i.e., she moved so slowly that she
appeared as if she stood still. <SC>Malone</SC>: Might not Shakespeare have written &lquo;for <I>the
scorn of time</I>,&rquo; &amp;c., i. e., the marked object for the contempt of
all ages and all time?

old copies it may be observed that &lquo;scorn&rquo; is personified in the 88th <I>Sonnet:</I> &lquo;And

<CC><C>[64, 65. <B>time of Scorne . . . slow, and mouing finger.</B>]</C>
<P>support from the 104th <I>Sonnet</I>, in which this very thought is expressed: &lquo;Ah! yet doth
beauty, like a dial-hand, Steal from his figure, and no pace perceiv'd; So your sweet
hue, which methinks still doth stand, Hath motion, and mine eye may be deceiv'd.&rquo;
In the clocks of the last age there was, I think, in the middle of the dial-plate, a
figure of Time, which, I believe, was in our poet's thoughts when he wrote the passage
in the text. The <I>finger</I> of the dial was the technical phrase. So in <I>Albovine</I>, by
D'Avenant, 1629: &lquo;Even as the slow finger of the dial Doth in its motion circular
remove To distant figures.&rquo; The reading of F<SUB>1</SUB>, &lquo;and moving,&rquo; certainly agrees with
the image presented, and its counterpart, better than <I>unmoving</I>, which can be applied
to a clock only by license of poetry (<I>not appearing to move</I>), and as applied to &lquo;scorn&rquo;
has but little force, to say nothing of the superfluous epithet &lquo;slow&rquo;; there needs no
ghost to tell us that that which is <I>unmoving</I> is &lquo;slow.&rquo; &lquo;Slow&rquo; implies some sort of
motion, however little it may be, and therefore appears to me to favour the reading
of F<SUB>1</SUB>. M. <SC>Mason</SC>: Perhaps we should read, &lquo;<I>slowly moving</I> finger at.&rquo; <SC>Hunter</SC> (ii,
287): I have little doubt that the particles &lquo;of&rquo; and &lquo;for&rquo; have changed places; and
that, on the whole, the true reading is, &lquo;The fixed figure of the time, for Scorn To
point his slow and moving finger at.&rquo; It is of the nature of that feeling which leads a
person to suppose himself an object of scorn and derision, to think of himself also as
an object of universal attention. Thus, Othello represents to himself that he shall be
&lquo;the fixed figure of the time,&rquo; the one object of public attention, every passer-by point-
ing at him the finger of scorn. <SC>Knight</SC>: There is certainly the most extraordinary
confusion in Malone's interpretation; if the figure of Time be in the middle, the dial-
hand points from it, and not at it, and there is nothing more remarkable in one numeral
of a clock than in another. But why are we to have the notion of a clock at all? There
is nothing whatever in the passage to warrant us in believing that the poet meant such
a metaphor. By the &lquo;fixed figure&rquo; we understand, literally, a living man exposed to
public shame; or an effigy exhibited to a multitude, as Butler has it, &lquo;To punish in
<I>effigie</I> criminals.&rquo; By &lquo;the time&rquo; we receive the same idea as in <I>Ham.</I> III, i, 70, where
&lquo;time&rquo; is used distinctly to express the <I>times</I>, the <I>age;</I> and it is used in the same way
by Ben Jonson: &lquo;Oh, how I hate the monstrousness of time!&rquo; In the expression before
us, then, the &lquo;time of scorn&rquo; is <I>the age of scorn.</I> The &lquo;slow finger&rquo; is the <I>pausing</I>
finger, pointing at the fixed figure; but while it points it <I>moves in mockery.</I> Shake-
speare was probably thinking of the <I>Digito Monstrari</I> of the ancients, and it may be,
also, of the finger gesticulations of the Italians. <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii) reads, with his
(MS.), &lquo;<I>hand</I> of scorn&rquo; and &lquo;<I>slowly moving</I> finger&rquo;; but returns to the Qq in ed. iii.
<SC>White</SC> (ed. i); &lquo;Unmoving&rquo; may mean either that the finger of scorn does not move
from its object, or that it moves so slowly that its motion is not perceived. So in Lyly's
<I>Euphues:</I> &lquo;You were ignorant of the practices, thinking the Diall stands still, because
you cannot perceive it to move.&rquo;&mdash;Sig. E e, ed. 1597. &lquo;The tongue of a Louer should
be like a poynt in a Dial, which though it goe none can see it going.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Ib.</I> Sig. Y, 3, b.
I was once in favour of Hunter's transposition. But &lquo;the time of scorn&rquo; is a phrase
like &lquo;the day of sorrow,&rquo; &lquo;the hour of joy,&rquo; &lquo;the age of progress.&rquo; <SC>Bailey</SC> (ii, 112)
makes &lquo;the passage run&rquo; thus: &lquo;A fix&egrave;d figure for the time, <I>in</I> scorn, To point his <I>sly
and mocking</I> finger at, &mdash;&rquo; and then adds: &lquo;These epithets greatly enhance the
expression of Othello's horror of the ridicule of the world.&rquo; <SC>Keightley</SC> (<I>Exp.</I> 305):
I see no need of changing the text of the Qto. &lquo;The Time of scorn&rquo; is the scornful
age or world, a frequent sense of &lquo;time&rquo;; and we should print, &lquo;To point his slow&mdash;
unmoving finger at,&rquo; the latter term being a correction of the former. <SC>Delius</SC>: &lquo;Slow</CC>

<CC><P>and moving,&rquo; according to Shakespeare's use of the copula, forms one idea [like &lquo;by

changed &lquo;slow&rquo; to <I>low</I>, asserts &lquo;the image&rquo; to be &lquo;absolutely correct in both sense and

scorn, To point his <I>foul</I> unmoving finger at.&rquo; <SC>Cowden-Clarke</SC>: We take the &lquo;time
of scorn&rquo; to be an impersonation of the scornful spirit of the epoch, and alluding to
the image of Time which many ancient clocks bore. To our minds the combination
&lquo;slow, unmoving,&rquo; serves exactly to describe the hand of a dial, with its onward-stealing
yet apparently still finger; so that, in every way, the idea of the clock is presented to
the imagination by this passage. <SC>John Hunter</SC>: &lquo;For the time of scorn&rquo; is <I>for scorn's
opportunity.</I> <SC>Hudson</SC>: &lquo;The time of scorn&rquo; means, I think, the <I>age</I> of scorn, that is,
the whole period during which scorn may be said to live. The &lquo;fixed figure&rquo; is simply
the speaker himself. As to <I>slow unmoving</I>, the sense of it can be better felt than
expressed; we can see the sneer darting from the inexorable finger, ever slowly moving
<I>with</I> the object, never moving <I>from</I> it. <SC>Rolfe</SC>: That Shakespeare should be supposed
to have written &lquo;slow and moving,&rquo; shows what a poet may suffer at the hands of a pro-
saic critic. The mistake in the Folio was doubtless one of the ear in transcribing the
MS. [I am afraid that this may be classed among those readings to which Steevens
elsewhere refers as having hitherto disunited the opinions of the learned, and which
&lquo;will continue to disunite them as long as England and Shakespeare have a name.&rquo;&mdash;

<P>76. <B>Sommer Flyes]</B> These words might serve, in F<SUB>4</SUB> as an approximate test, among

them a hyphen. In one of my copies of F<SUB>4</SUB>, this hyphen is distinct and unmistaka-
ble; in the second, it is quite faint; in the third, it has vanished, leaving behind a
warning to all not to lean too confidingly on the punctuation of the old texts.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

<P>83. <B>commited]</B> <SC>Malone</SC>: This word, in Shakespeare's time, besides its general
signification, seems to have been applied particularly to unlawful acts of love. [Might
not this have been due to its use in the Seventh Commandment?&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>] <SC>Knight</SC>:
Othello, indignant at Desdemona's question, with a mocking fury repeats it four
times,&mdash;&lquo;what committed?&rquo; The commentators have changed it into an interjectional
phrase, telling us that &lquo;committed&rquo; had a peculiar signification. The plain and natural
interpretation seems the true one. <SC>Deighton</SC> agrees with Knight; &lquo;Othello repeats
interrogatively, over and over again, the last word of Desdemona's speech, which is
here used in its ordinary sense.&rquo;
<P>84. <SC>Booth</SC>: Not too violently,&mdash;more of indignation than anger.
<P>85. <B>my]</B> <SC>White</SC> (ed. i): I suspect that Shakespeare wrote <I>thy.</I> The misprint is
common. Othello has already, when with Iago, spoken Desdemona's imputed deeds
very plainly; and would Shakespeare have forgotten that Othello's cheeks were too
dark to show a blush? or, still more, would he have referred the blush in such a case
to the countenance of the man when the woman was present? In <I>Tit. And.</I> IV, ii,
Aaron the Moor speaks of Chiron's &lquo;beauty&rquo; as a &lquo;treacherous hue, that will <I>betray
with blushing,&rquo;</I> whereas his own blackamoor child is a &lquo;lad fram'd of <I>another leer.</I>&rquo;
<SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. iii): But, as <SC>Lettsom</SC> observes, &lquo;Othello is speaking not of blushes, but of
heat.&rquo; <SC>White</SC> (ed. ii): A doubtful reading. Shakespeare surely may have written
&lquo;<I>thy</I> cheeks.&rquo; Not only was it Desdemona's part to flush, but Othello's cheek was
black.

<P>154. <B>eternall]</B> <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> i, 62) cites this passage and <I>Ham.</I> I, v, 21; V, ii,

&lquo;eternal&rquo; for <I>infernal.</I> See also, to the same effect, <SC>Abbott</SC>, <I>Introduction</I>, p. 16.
[Walker's instances from <I>Hamlet</I> may be well chosen; in &lquo;this eternal blazon,&rquo; and in
&lquo;what feast is toward in thine eternal cell,&rquo; Shakespeare may have used the word inac-
curately; it is also possible that the error is the printer's. But here in <I>Othello</I> and in
<I>Jul. C&aelig;s.</I> (&lquo;There was a Brutus once, that would have brook'd Th' eternal devil,&rquo; &amp;c.)
the supposition of inaccuracy is, I think, far from probable. Walker himself says that the
phrase &lquo;eternal villain&rquo; seems to be still in use among the common people, and antici-
pates the thought which rises in every American mind, when he adds: &lquo;I need scarcely
notice the Yankee '<I>tarnal.</I>&rquo; When needs must, nowadays, we speak of our friends as
&lquo;everlasting fools&rquo;; I think, therefore, that here Emilia means what she says.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>182. <B>discourse of thought]</B> This phrase is no easier of comprehension than the
similar phrase in <I>Ham.</I> I, ii, 150, to which <SC>Malone</SC> refers: &lquo;discourse of reason.&rquo; The
precise meaning which our ancestors attached to &lquo;discourse&rquo; it is now very difficult to
determine, as Gifford says in a note, cited in this edition, on the passage in <I>Hamlet.</I>
Johnson, in his <I>Dict.</I>, defines it as &lquo;the act of the understanding, by which it passes from
premises to consequences,&rquo; which is little else than a paraphrase of his own illustration
from Glanville, which reads: &lquo;The third act of the mind is that which connects propo-
sitions, and deduceth conclusions from them; and this the schools call <I>discourse;</I> and
we shall not miscall it, if we name it reason.&rquo; But that it was not mere &lquo;reason,&rquo; as
Shakespeare used it, is clear from the phrase &lquo;discourse of reason,&rquo; nor that it was merely
&lquo;the reasoning faculty,&rquo; as some have defined it, as is shown by this phrase in <I>Othello</I>,
&lquo;the discourse of thought.&rquo; May it not be that in the few instances where Shakespeare
uses it in reference to the operations of the mind (I speak with great hesitation) that its
Latin origin was uppermost in his thought, vaguely, perhaps, but still operative, espe-
cially if, as is not unlikely, he pronounced the word &lquo;discoorse,&rquo; <I>Hibernic&eacute;?</I> This
would lead to <SC>Singer's</SC> paraphrase, <I>discursive range</I>, which, although somewhat tauto-
logical, is, perhaps, as satisfactory as any that has been yet proposed. Why may we
not omit the <I>discursive</I>, and say that &lquo;discourse when applied to the mind means the
<I>range?</I>&rquo; Thus, &lquo;a beast that wants <I>the range</I> of reason&rquo;; &lquo;he that made us with so
large <I>a range</I>, looking before and after.&rquo; This, too, will explain what Guildenstern
says to Hamlet (III, ii, 320), &lquo;put your discourse into some frame,&rquo; i. e., &lquo;restrict the
range of your fancies.&rquo; And here, too, in <I>Othello</I>, Desdemona says, &lquo;either in range
of thought, or actual deed.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed. Steevens</SC> gives a note, signed &lquo;C,&rquo; to the effect that
the Qq are right, and that Desdemona refers to the three ways of committing sin, men
tioned in the Catholic Catechisms [and in our Liturgy, adds Steevens], viz.: in <I>thought,
word</I>, and <I>deed.</I> <SC>Verplanck</SC> and <SC>Hudson</SC> prefer the Qq. The former says: &lquo;The <I>on</I>
of the Qq appears to me more probable in itself, because more impressive, and more in
unison with the particularity of Desdemona's asseveration of innocence in every possi-
ble manner.&rquo;</CC>

<CC><P>26. <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> i, 92): Whence <I>in them?</I> it is not in the Folio. <I>Qu.</I>, &lquo;have <I>a</I>
grace and favour.&rquo; <SC>Lettsom</SC> (Foot-note to Walker): The words &lquo;in them&rquo; appear in

have written; on the other hand, the additional words do not look either like a sophis-
tication or a printer's blunder.
<P>29. <SC>Cornhill Magazine</SC> (Oct. 1866): This presentiment of Desdemona does not
bear the same tests as that of Romeo [see note <I>ad loc.</I> V, i, 1], nor Hamlet [V, ii, 207].
She had no reason to apprehend a violent death, but she had enough to apprehend from
Othello's anger. He had struck her and called her the vilest names. Naturally, these
unkindnesses would throw her into a deep state of depression. &lquo;A sort of gain-giving&rquo;
would naturally trouble her and exclude every chance of a real presentiment, the essence
of which is, that it shall be spontaneous, at a time when you have no reason to look for
it, when you are not under the influence of any fear or anxiety from known causes, and
when, perhaps, you have some difficulty in its interpretation.

which has improved the play. The rest seem to have been added for the sake of
amplification, or of ornament. When the imagination had subsided, and the mind was
no longer agitated by the horror of the action, it became at leisure to look round for
specious additions. This addition is natural. Desdemona can at first hardly forbear
to sing the song; she endeavors to change her train of thoughts, but her imagination
at last prevails, and she sings it.

<CC><C><B>[Sing Willough, Willough, Willough.]</B></C>
<P>lute, in the British Museum (Addit. MSS. 15,117). Mr Halliwell considers the tran-
script to have been made about the year 1633; Mr Oliphant (who catalogued the
Musical MSS.) dates it about 1600; but the manuscript undoubtedly contains songs
of an earlier time, such as,&mdash;&lquo;O death! rock me asleep, Bring me to quiet rest,&rquo; &amp;c.,
attributed to Anne Boleyn, and which Sir John Hawkins found in a MS. of the reign
of Henry VIII. [&lquo;The music is older than 1600. It is found in Thomas Dallis's MS.
&ldquo;Lute Book,&rdquo; with the title, &ldquo;All a greane willow.&rdquo; Dallis taught music at Cambridge;
and his book, dated 1583, is now in the Library of Trinity College, Dublin.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Shak-
spere's Songs</I>, p. 50, New Sh. Soc. 1884. In this same excellent publication of <I>The
New Shakspere Society</I> ten compositions of this song are enumerated. <SC>Zelter's</SC> com-
position is given in Voss's <I>Othello</I>, Jena, 1806; in Le Tourneur the composition by
<SC>Martini</SC> is given; and for Ducis's <I>Romance du Saule</I> the music was composed by
<SC>Gr&eacute;try</SC>. Of course the song is also to be found in the Opera of <I>Otello</I> by <SC>Rossini</SC>.
The music here given is from Chappell's <I>Popular Music of the Olden Time</I>, i, 207;
however lovely the melody, its charm is heightened by the knowledge that its plaintive
notes once &lquo;sighed along&rquo; the traverses of the Globe Theatre.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>114, 115. <SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 288): Shakespeare having remarked in <I>King John</I>, &lquo;How

these words of Desdemona as, beside their purpose in the drama itself, intended as a

<I>usage</I> is the poet's word. [&lquo;Uses,&rquo; it seems to me, is emphatically right. It is merely
a repetition of Emilia's own word. Emilia has threatened that if &lquo;husbands do not
&ldquo;<I>use</I> us well,&rdquo; it will be their fault if we follow their example.&rquo; Desdemona prays
that she may receive such &lquo;uses&rquo; that, instead of imitating the bad by bad, she may
be able even to mend and become better thereby. The noble, self-forgetting music in
which &AElig;milia dies, goes far to drive away the shadow that envelops her theft of the
handkerchief, for which, in the retrospect, we are ready to make every excuse. But
no excuses can be suggested for her here. Her insidious references to Lodovico, and
her allusion to Othello's blow, while Desdemona's lips are still bruised from it, stone
our hearts, and we can see in her here only the dark foil to Desdemona's snow-white
purity.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC></CC>

<I>rubbed</I> to much <I>sense</I>, but that a man grossly deceived is often called a <I>gudgeon.</I>
Upton reads <I>quail</I>, which he proves, by much learning, to be a very cholerick bird.
Theobald would introduce <I>knot</I>, a small bird of that name. A &lquo;quat&rquo; in the midland
counties is a <I>pimple</I>, which by rubbing is made to smart, or is <I>rubbed to sense.</I> Rode-
rigo is called a &lquo;quat&rquo; by the same mode of speech as a low fellow is now termed in
low language a <I>scab.</I> [Dr Johnson forgot that Shakespeare uses this word too.&mdash;
<SC>Ed.</SC>] To rub to the sense is to rub to the quick. <SC>Steevens</SC> cites several instances of
the use of &lquo;quat&rquo; in Dekker and others, but more to the purpose is it that <SC>Wise</SC> (p. 156)
gives it in his <I>Glossary of Warwickshire Words</I>, as in use at this day, in the same sense
as here.</CC>

<CC><P>79. <SC>Booth</SC>: Cassio takes Desdemona's handkerchief,&mdash;the gift of Othello,&mdash;from

<P>80. <SC>Hawkins</SC> (<I>Life of Kean</I>, i, 253): Previous actors of Iago did not appear to have
remembered that the whole fortune of the Ancient hinged upon this event; they stabbed
Roderigo, and then walked away with perfect ease and satisfaction. Not so Kean. He
gave and repeated the murderous thrust till no life could be supposed to remain; but
feeling this to be too important a matter to be left in doubt, he, though conversing
coolly with those about him, threw his eye continually towards the prostrate body, with
an intensity as if he would pierce its vital recesses to ascertain the important fact.
Sometimes he walked by it carelessly and surveyed it with a glance too rapid to be
observed; sometimes he deliberately approached it and looked at it with his candle, as
if to satisfy the spectators that it was the villain who had attacked his friend Cassio,
and thus he continued to watch and hover over it until he left the stage, his manner
perfectly cool, while his eye expressed the most restless anxiety.
<P>83. <B>be]</B> <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 299: <I>Be</I> is used in questions implying doubt: &lquo;where can they
be?&rquo;
<P>84. <SC>Booth</SC>: As Iago is about to stab Cassio, he sees Lodovico and Gratiano approach-
ing with servants and torches.</CC>

<P>much real information has been added to that which Malone has left us; certainly Dyce
and Collier found nothing to add, and all that Malone was able to discover was, sub-
stantially, that there was a balcony, or upper stage, at the back of the principal stage,
and that, in addition to the principal curtain in the front, there were others, as substi-
tutes for scenes, which were called <I>traverses</I>, and could be drawn aside, disclosing
inner compartments. It is really not difficult to imagine that even these simple resources
were adequate to all the needs of this last scene.&mdash;<SC>Ed. Fechter</SC>: Desdemona's
Chamber. At the back a large window with balcony, overlooking the sea. On the left
of the window an arch discovering an oratory; by the half-raised curtain is seen a prie
Dieu, surmounted by a Madonna, and lighted by a red lamp. On the same side, in front,
a bed raised by two steps. A door at the right. A high and elegant Venetian lamp
burns at the head of the bed, where Desdemona lies asleep; a small toilette glass,
fallen from her hand, lies near her. Her clothes scattered about. On the balcony,
Othello, motionless, enveloped in a long white burnous, is looking at the stars. Far

dentally touches the glass in which he sees his bronzed face,&mdash;(<I>With bitter despair</I>):
&lquo;It is the cause, it is the cause, my soul! (<I>returning to the window, his eyes fixed on the
heavens.</I>) Let me not name it to you, you chaste stars!&mdash;(<I>looking at his face once
again</I>). It is the cause! (<I>He violently throws the glass into the sea, goes to the door,
locks it, advances to the bed, half drawing his sword; then suddenly stops, and returns
it to the scabbard</I>) Yet I'll,&rquo; &amp;c. <SC>Booth</SC>: A Bed-chamber in the Castle. Raised

upon Bed. Door <SC>c.</SC> Divan <SC>c.</SC> A Light burning on Table. Desdemona in Bed, asleep,
discovered. Othello also discovered. <SC>Booth</SC> (MS.): I prefer the bed at the side of
the stage, with the head towards the audience; it is of more importance that Othello's
face should be seen than Desdemona's dead body, and the killing is partly hidden at
the same time. <SC>Mrs F. A. Kemble</SC> (<I>Temple Bar</I>, July, 1884): This last Scene pre-
sents technical difficulties in its adequate representation which have never yet been
even partially overcome. The audience, of course, cannot be expected to sit by and
see Desdemona smothered; the curtains of the alcove in which the bed is, are there-
fore lowered during that operation, but it is very desirable, if not absolutely necessary
that she should be both heard and seen when she gasps out her dying exculpation of
her husband, and while she is perpetually apostrophized by Emilia, Othello, and Lodo-
vico. The lines addressed to the lamp, &lquo;If I quench thee, thou flaming minister,&rquo;
should certainly be spoken with the light in near juxtaposition to the bed, and the
intense pathos of the following ones, &lquo;When I have plucked the rose,&rquo; &amp;c., can only
be given with due effect,&mdash;and what effect Salvini's voice would give to them!&mdash;by
Othello leaning over his sleeping wife. . . . . The position of the bed (which for all the
purposes of the Scene would be altered with advantage to the side of the stage), by
which Othello is constrained to turn his back to the audience while addressing Desde
mona, if she remains in it, has, we suppose, induced Signor Salvini to make her come
from the alcove and speak the greater part of the dialogue standing in front of it; an
alteration of the stage tradition which hurts the effect of the Scene, and is untrue to
the intention of Shakespeare, who makes Othello tell his wife that she is on her death-
bed, and in reply to his furious command, &lquo;Peace, be still,&rquo; receives the answer, &lquo;I
will; what is the matter?&rquo; with which the terrified woman cowers down upon her
pillow like a poor, frightened child. Indeed, the whole Scene loses its most pitiful</CC>
