<P>3, 4. <SC>Johnson</SC>: The abruptness of this soliloquy makes it obscure. The meaning, I
think, is this:&mdash;I am here (says Othello in his mind) overwhelmed with horror. What
is the reason of this perturbation? Is it want of resolution to do justice? Is it the
dread of shedding blood? No; it is not the action that shocks me, but &lquo;it is the
cause, it is the cause, my soul.&rquo; <SC>Steevens</SC>: Othello, full of horror at the cruel action
which he is about to perpetrate, seems at this instant tc be seeking his justification, by
representing to himself <I>the cause</I>, i. e., the greatness of the provocation he had received.
He may, however, mean,&mdash;It is the <I>cause</I> of chastity and virtue that I maintain. <SC>Hud-
son</SC>: Othello means that Desdemona's crime is the sole motive or reason that impels
him to the present act; that in this alone he has a justifying cause, a &lquo;compelling occa-
sion,&rquo; for what he is about to do; so that he cannot justly lie under the reproach
of having acted from any subjective or self-generated <I>animus</I> of revengeful jealousy.
<SC>White</SC> (ed. ii): This is, to me, one of the most doubtful and perplexing passages in
all these plays. Which is the emphatic word, &lquo;it&rquo; or &lquo;is&rquo; or &lquo;cause,&rquo; and what is &lquo;the
cause,&rquo; and of what it is the cause, I confess that I am not ready to decide. That &lquo;it&rquo;
in the second line refers to Desdemona's supposed unchastity is plain enough; but that
her unchastity is &lquo;the cause&rquo; is not so certain. For Othello to say to himself, and at
this moment, that Desdemona's conduct is the cause of his intended murder, seems
very tame; and the [eighth] line, with its conclusion, &lquo;else she'll betray more men,&rquo;
seems to imply that Othello has deluded himself into looking upon his act as providen-
tial rather than retributive, and that &lquo;cause&rquo; is his emphatic word. [If &lquo;cause&rquo; is the
emphatic word, and assuredly it is when it first occurs, it should not receive an equal
emphasis twice in the same line; then White's perplexity falls on all of us. Is the
second &lquo;it&rquo; or the second &lquo;is&rquo; to be emphatic? I should prefer to let the emphasis
fall on &lquo;is.&rquo; But is it necessary to emphasize any one word? Is not the mere repeti-
tion of each word in itself an emphasis of each word?&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>4. <B>chaste Starres]</B> <SC>Hudson</SC>: In classical poetry the Moon is Diana, the goddess
of <I>chastity</I>, and the stars are the train of <I>virgins</I> attending on her. The epithet
&lquo;chaste&rquo; thus applied suggests the nature of the cause which the <I>purity</I> of the stars
forbids to be named in their presence. <I>The Athen&aelig;um</I> (10 April, 1875): After deliv-
ering the speech, &lquo;It is the cause,&rquo; slowly, the first line being spoken close to the door
by which he enters, Othello [Salvini] kisses his sleeping wife, then goes to the window,
and stands with the lightning playing upon his face.

<P>8. <B>more men]</B> <SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 288): I confess the sense is not clear to me. It seems

another man, should die the death.&rquo;&mdash;p. 387.
<P>9. <SC>Upton</SC> (p. 177): Othello enters with a taper (not with a sword, for he intended
all along to strangle his wife in her bed), and in the utmost agony of mind says, he has
cause for his cruelty, a cause not to be named to the chaste stars; 'tis fit, therefore, Des-
demona should die. &lquo;I'll put out the light, and then,&rquo;&mdash;strangle her, he was going to
say; but this recalls a thousand tender ideas in his troubled soul; he stops short&mdash;If I
quench the taper, how easy 'tis to restore,&rquo; &amp;c. <SC>Warburton</SC>: The meaning is, I will
put out the light, and <I>then</I> proceed to the execution of my purpose. But the expression
of <I>putting out the light</I>, bringing to mind the effects of the extinction of the light of
life, he breaks short, and questions himself about the effects of this metaphorical extinc
tion, introduced by a repetition of his first words, as much as to say, But hold, let me
first weigh the reflections which this expression so naturally excites. <SC>Farmer</SC>: War-

<CC><C>[9. <B>Put out the Light, and then put out the Light:</B>]</C>
<P>lines; this was disputed on both sides with a Warmth, which surprised me in Elysium,
till I discovered by Intuition that every Soul retained its principal Characteristic, being,
indeed, its very Essence. The Line was that celebrated one in <I>Othello:</I> &lquo;Put out the
Light, and then put out the Light,&rquo; according to Betterton. Mr Booth contended to have
it thus: &lquo;Put out the Light, and then put out <I>the</I> Light.&rquo; I could not help offering my
Conjecture on this Occasion, and suggested it might perhaps be: &lquo;Put out the Light,
and then put out <I>thy</I> Light.&rquo; Another hinted a Reading very <I>sophisticated</I> in my Opin-
ion, &lquo;Put out the Light, and then put out <I>thee</I>, Light,&rquo; making &lquo;Light&rquo; to be in the voca-
tive Case. Another would have altered this last Word, and read, &lquo;Put out thy Light, and
then put out thy Sight.&rquo; But Betterton said, if the Text was to be <I>disturbed</I>, he saw no
reason why a Word might not be changed as well as a Letter, and instead of &lquo;put out
thy Light,&rquo; you might read, &lquo;put out thy <I>eyes.</I>&rquo; At last it was agreed on all sides to refer
the matter to the decision of Shakespeare himself, who delivered his Sentiments as fol-
lows: &lquo;Faith, Gentlemen, it is so long since I wrote the Line I have forgot my Meaning.
This I know, could I have dreamt so much Nonsense would have been talked and writ
about it, I would have blotted it out of my Works; for I am sure, if any of these be my
Meaning, it doth me very little Honour.&rquo; He was then interrogated concerning some
other ambiguous Passages in his Works, but he declined any satisfactory Answer, saying,
if Mr Theobald had not <I>writ about it</I> sufficiently, there were three or four more new
Editions of his Plays coming out, which he hoped would satisfy every one; Concluding,
&lquo;I marvel nothing so much, as that Men will gird themselves at discovering obscure
Beauties in an author. Certes, the greatest and most pregnant Beauties are ever the
plainest and most striking; and, when two Meanings of a Passage can in the least bal
ance our Judgements which to prefer, I hold it matter of unquestionable Certainty that
neither of them are [<I>sic</I>] worth a farthing.&rquo; <SC>Malone</SC>: The poet, I think, meant merely
to say: &lquo;I will now put out the lighted taper which I hold, and then put out the light
<I>of life;</I>&rquo; and this introduces his subsequent reflection and comparison, just as aptly, as
supposing the latter words of the line to be used in the same sense as in the beginning
of it, which cannot be done without destroying that equivoque and play of words of
which Shakespeare was so fond. I believe, however, that Shakespeare wrote, &lquo;and
then put out <I>thy</I> light&rquo;; and the reading of Q<SUB>1</SUB> in line 12, &lquo;but once put out <I>thine</I>,&rquo;
seems to me to countenance this emendation. [This very line in the Folio <SC>Knight</SC>
adduces as strengthening Warburton's interpretation.] <SC>Boswell</SC>: If Warburton's expla-
nation be an error, it is <I>demptus per vim</I>, and I, for one, am very sorry to part with it.
Broken sentences are very much in Shakespeare's manner, and are surely natural in
the perturbed state of Othello's mind. I am unwilling to persuade myself that a regu-
lation of the text which contains so much beauty could be merely the refinement of a
critic, and that our great author, in one of his most highly-wrought scenes, instead of it,
intended nothing but a cold conceit. [Both Steevens and Malone cite many instances
from Shakespeare, his predecessors, and contemporaries, to prove that &lquo;to put out the
light&rquo; means &lquo;to kill&rquo; or to die. As if the inverted torch were not as old as mortuary
symbolism!&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>] <SC>White</SC> (ed. i): Warburton's ingenious reading makes the second
clause the lively expression of stimulated intelligence; to me it is the despairing utter
ance of the profoundest woe. <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> iii, 291): Read, I believe, &lquo;then put
out <I>thy</I> light!&rquo; or, possibly, &lquo;<I>her</I> light.&rquo; <SC>Cambridge Editors</SC>: Mr Goldwin Smith,
regarding the line in question as a stage direction which has crept into the text, sug-
gests to us that the passage ought to be printed as follows: &lquo;Yet she must die, else
she'll betray more men.&rquo; [<I>Takes off his sword, and then puts out the light.</I>] If I</CC>

<CC><P>23. <B>weepe]</B> <SC>Booth</SC>: Remember how often he is moved to tears,&mdash;therefore I do
not attempt to restrain them in the excess of passion here, in Act III, and elsewhere.
[Yet Othello himself says that his eyes are &lquo;unused to the melting mood.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>24. <B>heauenly]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: &lquo;This tenderness, with which I lament the punishment
which justice compels me to inflict, is a holy passion.&rquo; I wish these two lines could be
honestly ejected. It is the fate of Shakespeare to counteract his own pathos. <SC>Steev-
ens</SC>: The &lquo;cruel tears&rquo; seem adopted from the fabulous history of the crocodile
[<SC>Rolfe</SC> quotes this, and befittingly adds an exclamation mark]; the &lquo;heavenly sor-
row&rquo; from a passage in the Scriptures. <SC>Deighton</SC>: Othello surely means, &lquo;I can-
not help weeping at your fate, but my tears do not soften my heart, so as to change
my determination to kill you.&rquo; <SC>Hudson</SC>: The tears are cruel, because, while heart-
wringing pity is streaming from the eyes, an overmastering strain of duty is forcing
him to what is, objectively, an act of cruelty. And the very loveliness of the victim
only works to intensify his purpose, lest love should usurp the crown that belongs to
a higher passion,&mdash;a passion, too, that <I>must</I> wear the crown, else love itself will fall
from its propriety. Pathos carried to the most soul-searching height! And the &lquo;sor-
row is heavenly,&rquo; because it is baptized and washed into holiness by the sacred and
divine regards of justice.
<P>33. <B>Solicite]</B> <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> iii, 291): That is, <I>plead</I>, as in the old sense of <I>solici-
tor;</I> yet I do not know that <I>plead</I> exactly expresses the meaning.</CC>

<CC><P>80. <B>Sacrifice]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: This line is difficult. &lquo;Thou hast hardened my heart,
and makest me kill thee with the rage of a murderer, when I thought to have sacrificed
thee to justice with the calmness of a priest striking a victim.&rquo; I suspect &lquo;<I>thy</I> heart&rquo;
of Q<SUB>1</SUB> to be genuine. The meaning then will be,&mdash;&lquo;Thou forcest me to dismiss thee
from the world in the state of the murdered without preparation for death, when I
intended that thy punishment should have been a sacrifice atoning for thy crime.&rquo; I
am glad that I have ended my revisal of this dreadful scene. It is not to be endured.
<SC>Halliwell</SC>: Many readers will probably sympathize with Dr Johnson's concluding
observation. Without disputing the masterly power displayed in the composition of the
present tragedy, there is something to my mind so revolting, both in the present Scene
and in the detestable character of Iago, which renders a study of the drama of <I>Othello</I>
rather a painful duty than one of pleasure. [I do not shrink from saying that I wish
this Tragedy had never been written. The pleasure, however keen or elevated, which
the inexhaustible poetry of the preceding Acts can bestow, cannot possibly, to my tem-
perament, countervail, it does but increase, the unutterable agony of this closing Scene.
&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>85-98. <SC>Hales</SC> (p. 112): For the most part Shakespeare delights in tracing the action
of the great moral laws of the world, and showing how fearful is the penalty of trans-
gression. But sometimes he exhibits a yet more dreadful spectacle,&mdash;a spectacle mys-
terious, inscrutable, soul-prostrating. It is Fate blind, inexorable, rapacious. Desde-
mona is one of Fate's choicest victims. Her &lquo;graces serve&rquo; her &lquo;but as enemies.&rquo; Her
very virtues bring on her ruin. What is most innoccnt is construed into evidence
against her. In obeying the best instincts of her clear spirit she excites the evilest
suspicions and secures the bitterest condemnation. The truth from her lips is turned
into a lie. In the present passage, her answers, by an almost incredible infelicity,
are, through the very purity of her nature, just such as to confirm Othello's detestable
impeachment. Could replies be more unfortunate? She lies in the toils of Fate, and
there is no escape for her. We may go further than her name in Greek, <G>dvsdai/mwn</G>,
&lquo;ill-starred,&rquo; and say it is merely a variation of <G>dvsdaimoni/a</G>, &lquo;ill-starredness.&rquo; She is
not only unhappy, she is unhappiness itself.

<P>112. In the Appendix will be found the Ballad which was discovered among the Eger-

<P>her with a dagger,&mdash;drawing blood accounts naturally for gaining power of speech, and

<P>Thus far Editors and Actors, with a ground-tone from the public at large to the effect
that there does seem to be something not altogether true to physiology in the subsequent
revival of Desdemona; yet, such is the Anglosaxon faith in Shakespeare, that, in any
variance between him and Nature, Shakespeare is considered quite able to hold his own.
<P>It was the phrase &lquo;Pale as thy smock&rquo; which first caught my attention; it seemed to
reveal either an oversight on Shakespeare's part, or that he had intended, contrary to the
directions in the QqFf, that Desdemona should be stabbed. As far as I know, no one
has ever noticed the bearing, on the manner of Desdemona's death, of this exclamation.
To my layman's small knowledge there seemed here a violation of physiological laws
so downright, in representing a smothered person as pale, that I knew Shakespeare, who
could note the &lquo;crimson drops i' the bottom of a cowslip,&rquo; never could have committed
it. The reality before our very eyes cannot be as vivid as the coinage of his brain was
to Shakespeare. What he saw, he spoke; so that he must either have known of a case
where congestion of blood in the face did not follow stifling, or he must have intended
Othello to stab Desdemona; which, after all, would only half solve the difficulty; the
stabbing would leave the face pale, but the smock red, as I thought. For Shakespeare's
credit I felt no concern, but I did feel mortified for Nature, on whose behalf it seemed
that if ever our best medical wisdom were to be unmuzzled, this was the hour. To this
trial, in which Nature is the defendant (not Shakespeare, perish the thought!) I hoped
to summon such an array of experts that their verdict would be accepted as final wher-
ever the masters in medicine are known and honored, or any faith exists in diagnosis.
To each one of the following eminent men, whose friendship I am glad to own, I sent
a copy of this last Scene, with the following passages underscored: &lquo;<I>Yet I'll not shed
her blood</I>&rquo;; &lquo;<I>She's Dead</I>&rquo;; &lquo;<I>Ha, No More Moving? Still as the Grave</I>&rquo;;
&lquo;<I>I think she stirs again,&mdash;No</I>&rquo;; all Desdemona's words after the smothering: &lquo;<I>Your
niece, Whose breath, indeed, these hands have newly stopped</I>&rquo;; and lastly, &lquo;<I>Pale as thy
smock</I>,&rquo; accompanying which were these questions: 1. Do you think it likely that</CC>

<P>Othello stabbed Desdemona at &lquo;So, so&rquo;? 2. If he stabbed her, could her smock be
pale? 3. If she were smothered, could she be pale? 4. In either case, could she
speak after apparent death? 5. If she could speak, why did she not quite revive?
6. From what cause, then, did she really die?
<P>To these questions there came the following answers:&mdash;
<P><SC>Dr D. Hayes Agnew</SC>: In answer to your inquiry, I would say that Shakespeare has
been most unfortunate in killing Desdemona. Death by strangulation, inferred from
the language used by Othello: &lquo;<I>Whose breath indeed, these hands have newly stopp'd</I>,&rquo;
cannot readily be reconciled with a temporary revival and ability to speak at three dif
ferent times on the part of the victim, after all signs of life had apparently disappeared
nor with the post-mortem appearances, in which the color of the face and of the smock
are compared (both presumably white).
<P>Against the theory of death by stabbing, we have the declaration of Othello himself,
&lquo;<I>Yet I'll not shed her blood</I>,&rquo; and the supposed absence of blood-stains on the clothing
of Desdemona, indicated by the expression, &lquo;<I>pale as thy smock</I>&rquo;; and yet all the phe-
nomena before and after death are comprehensible on the theory of internal hemor-
rhage, namely, the possibility of a stab in a vital region of the body, without more
than a few drops of blood being seen externally; syncope, resembling actual death,
causing a temporary arrest of bleeding and a return to consciousness and to speech,
followed by the recurrence of a rapidly-fatal hemorrhage, leaving the face bloodless
and pale.
<P>There is, however, a theory which (though somewhat strained) would meet all the
conditions of the text; namely, that death ensued from the secondary effects of injury
to the larynx. It is true that in fatal cases following laceration or fracture of that
organ, the patient dies from a slow asphyxia, and may be rendered voiceless by the
lesion; but surgical writers refer to instances in which, after violence applied to the
neck and the person apparently suffocated, partial recovery has followed with ability to
speak, and yet death suddenly followed from shock, with probably some spasm of the
glottis. In shock the blood retreats from the superficial vessels, giving to the surface
the pallor of death. Probably such were the conditions in the case of Desdemona.
<P><SC>Dr D. G. Brinton</SC>: There is not a word in the text about stabbing, and several
passages make directly against it. In describing Desdemona's death, Othello distinctly
states that he &lquo;stopped her breath,&rquo;&mdash;smothered her. Death by stabbing, therefore,
could not have been in the mind of the author at all.
<P>This leads to the further result that her death is not represented as the immediate act
of her husband; he is not the murderer that he thinks himself; his hands refused the
deed and failed at the second attempt, as they did at the first. Again she moves and
speaks. But her frail body has been put to too severe a strain. Anxiety and fear have
been too much for her debilitated heart, and her last and superhuman effort to exculpate
her loved husband completely exhausts her vital powers; the central organ fails, and
she falls back dead from &lquo;cardiac exhaustion.&rquo; We may call it &lquo;paralysis of the heart,&rquo;
like that brought about by certain potent poisons, or that which supervenes in feeble
subjects on sudden and violent emotions, either of fear or joy. We know little of the
intimate pathology of this fatal process. Writers say that such physical or mental
shocks &lquo;extinguish life by their action on the cardiac plexus.&rquo; The phrase sounds
well, but leaves us where we were before.
<P>Such instances are by no means rare, and must have come to the knowledge of the
author of <I>Othello.</I> A number of them were quoted for the defence in a trial in New</CC>
<PB N=305>
<HE><SC>act v, sc.</SC> ii.] <I>THE MOORE OF VENICE</I> 305</HE>
<FHL>
<CC><C>[112. <B>I would not haue thee linger in thy paine? So, so.</B>]</C>
<P>York City a few years ago. The victim, wife of a physician, was smothered by the
assassin. The defence was, that the attempt at suffocation was abortive, that she revived,
but died of heart-shock from fright and struggling. The theory of her death thus
advanced by the defence is my theory of the death of Desdemona. It consistently
explains the appearance of her face, her smock, her recovery of speech, &amp;c., and relieves
us from the painful and repugnant contemplation of her husband as her actual murderer.
I shall be delighted if these crude remarks aid you in any degree in throwing light on
the train of thought in this wonderful literary creation.
<P><SC>Dr J. M. Da Costa</SC>: The features of Desdemona's death cannot, I believe, be recon-
ciled to strict scientific facts; it is best to accept them as not transgressing poetic license.
That she should have spoken after being smothered is not possible; if she had regained
consciousness sufficiently to speak intelligently, as she did, recovery would have ensued,
though death might have happened, after a time, from injuries induced by the violence.
<P>Concerning the pallor of the countenance, it is contrary to the customary conception
of death by strangulation; the face is held to be suffused and swollen, of dusky or vio-
let hue; but the great poet, in assuming it otherwise, has not been guilty of error. The
countenance in strangulation may be pale and sunken; indeed, so eminent an authority
as Casper declares his observation to have taught him that the greater number of per-
sons strangled have neither a turgid nor a livid countenance, but one simply like that
of any other corpse.
<P>These statements deal with the supposition that Desdemona's death was caused by
strangling. If the stage tradition of her being also stabbed be admitted as correct, a
view suggests itself which removes all difficulties. The effect of the bleeding would
be to relieve the cerebral and pulmonary congestion occurring in strangulation. She
revives sufficiently to speak; the internal hemorrhage continues; she dies exhausted,
and, as always in death from loss of blood, with extreme pallor marked. &lquo;Pale as thy
smock&rquo; Othello might well say; nor need a poet's words be so literally construed as to
exclude the thought of some blood-stains on the white garment; though in point of fact
a stab severing large vessels in the chest may prove fatal without giving rise to external
bleeding.
<P>The stabbing subsequent to the smothering makes, then, the death of Desdemona
one which is described with the closest attention to truth. Whether the stage tradition
represent Shakespeare's thought is, of course, an open question. There is that in the
text, however, which supports the supposition of the stabbing, notwithstanding Othello's
first-declared intention of not shedding blood. He sees her linger, and he determines
on quick, decisive measures. The words &lquo;So, so,&rquo; when he is supposed to stab her,
are short, abrupt expressions, very suitable to rapid, sudden movements as in stabbing.
<P><SC>Dr William A. Hammond</SC>: The matter that engrosses your attention has many
features of interest to me, and your questions lead up to several important points.
<P>Without going into details, I may say, first, I do not think Othello stabbed Desde-
mona; he expressly says, &lquo;I will not shed her blood.&rquo; I am of the opinion that, at the
words &lquo;So, so,&rquo; he pressed the pillow more forcibly against her face.
<P>If he stabbed her, I think it possible, though not probable, that her smock might be
<*>ale.
<P>If she were smothered she might be pale. Persons who are smothered do not ordi-
narily show any signs of having suffered a violent death. For my views in full on this
point, permit me to refer you to my novel, <I>Mr Oldmixon</I>, chap. xiii, in which Hogarth
Oldmixon smothers his wife.</CC>
<PB N=306>
<HE>306 <I>THE TRAGEDIE OF OTHELLO</I> [<SC>act v, sc.</SC> ii.</HE>
<FHL>
<CC><C>[112. <B>I would not haue thee linger in thy paine? So, so.</B>]</C>
<P>If she were smothered sufficiently, she certainly could not speak after the act. A
person smothered, and speaking afterwards, would not die from the smothering. The
mere fact of her speaking shows that she was not smothered to the extent necessary to
cause death.
<P>As to what really killed her, I think it is clearly apparent that Shakespeare was ignor-
ant of the <I>modus operandi</I> of smothering. She ought not to have died at all so far as
any act of Othello's is directly concerned, except, perhaps, from what is called a &lquo;broken
heart,&rquo; or from extreme shock to her nervous system.
<P><SC>Dr William Hunt</SC>: You have asked me some interesting questions about Desde-
mona's death. I am happy to be able to answer you positively and at once; her sad
end is no pathological puzzle to me. She died of fracture of the cricoid cartilage of the
larynx. Shakespeare is entirely consistent, and must have had, as in everything else,
an intuitive, if not practical, knowledge of the subject. Years ago I wrote an Article
upon that fracture, founded upon a case of it. The Article is quoted as authority to this
day. I collected all the reported cases I could find, and several of them were like
Desdemona's. It was a piece of unpardonable oversight in me that I did not put her
in the list. The poet's story is exactly in accordance with the ordinary sequence of
symptoms. There is nothing for a school-boy or anybody else to laugh at in it.
<P>Othello, true to his stated purpose, did not &lquo;shed her blood, nor scar that whiter skin
of hers than snow.&rquo; He first tried a very ineffectual method of smothering with pillows.
His poor victim was simply dazed, &lquo;not dead.&rquo; Seeing this, he grasps her neck with his
powerful hands, his thumbs being over the larynx, and with two strong squeezes and a
&lquo;So, so,&rquo; garrotes her.
<P>The cricoid cartilage breaks, and under the shock there is &lquo;no more moving.&rquo; She
is &lquo;still as the grave.&rquo; But I have no doubt she did &lquo;stir again&rquo;; had any good aus-
cultator placed his ear to her chest he would have heard her heart beating feebly and
rapidly. Paleness, not lividity, would accompany this condition. I have seen it so in
others. A short time passes. Desdemona slowly and temporarily reacts. An exciting
conversation is held in her presence. She hears, and in a smothered, hoarse whisper,
perfectly audible, she speaks; there is a slight spitting of blood, for which, in her nicety,
she uses a handkerchief she had about her, and which must have reminded her of that
other fatal one &lquo;spotted with strawberries,&rquo; and so her smock is left pale and unde-
filed. In my case the patient was pale as a ghost, and his speech as hoarse as a raven's.
Gradually Desdemona succumbs to the pressure of swelling and emphysema, and to the
nervous shock. Tracheotomy was the only thing that might have saved her, but there
was nobody there to perform it, and the chance was slim. I have thus, I think, answered
all your questions. Does not Othello himself acknowledge my method when he says,
&lquo;There lies your niece, whose breath indeed <I>these hands</I> have newly stopped&rquo;? There
was never a clearer case. Is not Shakespeare's universality wonderful?
<P>Rest assured, Desdemona died of fracture of the larynx. The history and the sequences
are without flaws.
<P>In future, let no Othello stab; and let Desdemona learn a hoarse, grating, audible
whisper that will rasp the audience into sympathetic agony.
<P><SC>Dr Ad. Lippe</SC>: To the first question, I answer No; Othello stifles, but does not stab
Desdemona; he had said &lquo;I will not shed her blood&rquo;; at &lquo;So, so,&rquo; he stifles her the
more.
<P>Had she been stabbed, her smock would have been saturated with blood.
<P>If she were smothered, she could be nothing else but pale.</CC>

<CC><P>Had she been stabbed and the dirk or knife not withdrawn, she might have spoken.
If the dagger had been withdrawn, she could not have spoken. If smothered, and,
since Othello says &lquo;I think she stirs again,&rquo; not fully dead, a few drops remaining in
the left heart would permit of a contraction, and the lungs not being completely
clogged would allow the utterance of a few words. These last few contractions of the
left heart must have been caused by the violent mental emotions produced by Emilia's
relation and her questions. These few remaining drops having been expelled, her
ability to speak ceased, and she was fully dead. The real cause of her death was
suffocation and stifling. In Wharton and Still&eacute;'s <I>Medical Jurisprudence</I>, ii, 802, we
find a complete vindication of Shakespeare: &lquo;<I>Homicidal Suffocation.</I> Those who
are usually the victims of this form of murder are infants and the aged, or those
who are otherwise helpless. So slight a degree of resistance is necessary to defeat
the purpose of the assassin, that a great disproportion of strength must exist for the
attempt to be successful. Nevertheless, those miserable wretches, Burke and his
accomplices, reduced murder by suffocation to a system, choosing it as a mode of death
most likely to leave no mark of crime behind it. The murderer bore with his whole
weight upon the breast of his victim, and with his hands forcibly covered the mouth
and nostrils till death came on. The body of one of the victims presented, according
to Dr Christison, so few traces of injury, that without the assistance of proof from other
sources, it would have been impossible to have declared that the death was not a nat-
ural one.&rquo; How well Shakespeare knew the difference between suffocation and stran-
gulation is evident from his masterly description of the latter in the case of Gloucester
in <I>2 Hen. VI:</I> III, ii. Suffocation alone caused the death of Desdemona, and the
suffocation was slow. Violent mental emotion caused the heart to expel the last few
drops of blood, and when the right side of the heart became filled with dark venous
blood, she died. How violent mental emotions can affect the heart belongs to the deep
mysteries of Nature. Materialists cannot solve the question.
<P><SC>Dr S. Weir Mitchell</SC>: I suppose Shakespeare would have put in a stage direction
at &lquo;So, so,&rquo; if he had meant that Othello used a dagger. Were I an actor I should
simply throttle her fiercely again and again as I said &lquo;So, so.&rquo; With this view her
smock need not trouble us. Death by strangling leaves the face horribly congested, not
pale. Believing that Othello simply choked Desdemona, how could she have been
pale of visage and spoken several distinct sentences with so clear a brain as the rele-
vancy of her words displays, and yet have been <I>fatally</I> strangled?
<P>It could not have been; but I fancy Shakespeare cared little for realism when he
desired an explanatory dramatic effect.
<P>If there is evidence that Shakespeare meant that Othello choked her insufficiently, and
finished with a dirk, it becomes clearer, because then speech, partial recovery, death from
bleeding, help us to understand the passage. At the same time the face would have been
paling from blood-loss, and as to the smock, all wounds do not bleed externally; then a
little blood on the smock would not have made less for him its general whiteness.
<P>Again, where Othello says he has &lquo;newly stopp'd her breath,&rquo; he does not speak
of what would have been the more striking object to the spectator, the dagger-wound.
For him, too, that would have been <I>the</I> murder, not the ineffectual throttle.</CC>

<CC><P>me the solitary one worth listening to, on a London Sunday, thirty years ago.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
&lquo;When I returned at 5 <SC>a. m.</SC> next day, copious effusion had taken place in one of the
pleura, and death was close at hand . . . . almost immediately afterwards, without any
struggle, all was over,&mdash;as it seemed. We remained kneeling around the bed. No
sound came from the motionless chest, the beating of the artery under my finger was
no longer perceptible; the hand, which a moment before was grasping mine, had relaxed
its hold; the countenance was no longer scored by lines denoting difficulty in breathing;
the spark in the eye had gone out, and nowhere, so far as I could see, was there any
reason for thinking that the fire of life was still smouldering. I could find no such
reason then, I can find no such reason now. And yet shortly afterwards, he, who
seemed to have died, and to have been dead for several minutes, or moments, minutes
rather than moments, as I remember them, slowly raised himself upon one of his
elbows into a half-sitting posture, and said distinctly, &ldquo;The peace of God, which pass-
eth all understanding, keep your&mdash;<I>our</I>&mdash;hearts and minds in the knowledge and love

Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, be amongst <I>us</I> and remain with <I>us</I> always;&rdquo; and
having so said, without another word, he lay down and died&mdash;again. The voice in
which these words were uttered was the old familiar voice, clear and solemn. . . . .
Between them and the preceding words, which were hurried and scarcely coherent,
and almost lost in distracting sounds connected with lack of breath, a broad line of
separation must be drawn. In uttering these last words no difficulty in breathing or
speaking was noticeable. . . . . I cannot confound these words with any ordinary
death-bed utterances.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Dr C. B. Radcliffe</SC> (<I>Life of Frederick Denison Maurice</I>, 2d

<P>163. <B>Angell]</B> <SC>Hudson</SC>: Emilia evidently means that Desdemona is the more angel
for having spoken the falsehood in question. And surely all well-ordered minds must
agree with her; at all events, I, for one, cannot choose but love and honour Desde-
mona the more for that lie. For, indeed, the sweet, dear sufferer knows that Othello
is driven onward by some monstrous delusion; that some hideous inspiration has put
him clean out of his native self; that he is sure to have the worst of it, and so is even
more an object of compassion than herself; and the unspeakable agony legible in his
features wrings her pure soul with a pity so intense as to take from her all sense of the
pangs of death; and so her last breath is hallowed with a tender yearning to shield
him, as far as she possibly can, from the dreadful retributions which await him, both
from without and from within, when the truth shall be known. So deep and sacred is
the head and spring of Desdemona's dying falsehood! It is a lie born of the very holi-
ness of truth itself!

<CC><P>228. <B>charme]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: I know not whether I have read, or whether my own
thoughts have suggested, an alteration here. It seems to me not improbable that
Shakespeare wrote <I>clam</I> your tongue; to <I>clam</I> a bell is to cover the clapper with felt,
which drowns the blow and hinders the sound [qu., <I>hinders</I> the blow and <I>drowns</I> the
sound? The Cambridge Editors record &lquo;<I>chain</I>, Anon. conj.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>] <SC>Malone</SC>: That
is, compel to be silent, as if by the power of enchantment. <SC>Steevens</SC>: Thus Jonson,
<I>Cynthia's Revels</I> [I, i]: &lquo;Charm your skipping tongue.&rquo; Also <I>Faerie Queene</I>, V, ix
[line 350]: &lquo;That well could charme his tongue, and time his speach.&rquo; [For addi-
tional examples in Shakespeare, see <SC>Schmidt</SC>.]
<P>236. <B>strange]</B> <SC>Staunton</SC>: This is one of the many words which have lost weight
and emphasis since Shakespeare's time. With us it imports no more than <I>unusual, not
customary</I>, &amp;c.; but when Desdemona spoke of the Moor's adventures as &lquo;strange,&rquo;
she meant that they were <I>wonderful, incredible;</I> and it is in this deeper sense of the
word that Gratiano employs it here.

<CC><P>for no honest purpose, and there asks her husband: &lquo;What will you do with it?&rquo; &amp;c.,
III, iii, 366. <SC>Cowden-Clarke</SC>: In allusion to her suspicions at IV, ii, 154; she seems
to be about to say, &lquo;I thought then that there was villainy going on, but little thought
my husband was the author.&rquo; The very thought that Iago could be capable of such
villainy, causes her to interrupt her half-uttered sentence with &lquo;I'll kill myself for
grief.&rquo; <SC>Rolfe</SC> agrees with Cowden-Clarke.
<P>246. <B>I will]</B> <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 319: Some passages which are quoted to prove that Shake-
speare used <I>will</I> with the first person without implying <I>wish, desire</I>, &amp;c., do not warrant
such an inference [see <I>Ham.</I> V, ii, 167]. . . . . There is a difficulty in the expression
&lquo;perchance I <I>will&rquo;;</I> but, from its constant recurrence, it would seem to be a regular
idiom. Compare this passage in <I>Othello</I> with <I>Com. of Err.</I> IV, i, 39: &lquo;Perchance I
will be there as soon as you,&rquo; and <I>Mer. of Ven.</I> II, v, 52: &lquo;Perhaps I will return imme-
diately.&rquo; In all these passages &lquo;perchance&rquo; precedes, and the meaning seems to be in
the last example, for instance: &lquo;My purpose may, perhaps, be fulfilled,&rquo; and &lquo;my pur-
pose is to return immediately,&rquo; or, in other words, &lquo;If possible, I intend to return imme-
diately.&rquo; In all these cases the &lquo;perhaps&rquo; stands by itself. It does not qualify <I>will</I>,
but the whole of the following sentence.

<P>261. <B>Reprobance]</B> In his Article on &lquo;the instance of error in the beginning or

for <I>ation</I> are not infrequent.&rquo; He then gives five or six instances in addition to the

<P>264. <B>thousand]</B> <SC>Pye</SC> (p. 342): This is merely hyperbolical, and is used every day
by impatient men in common speech for <I>five</I> or <I>six.</I> <SC>Cowden-Clarke</SC>: Merely an
indefinite number; used here to convey the effect of long time. See &lquo;a hundred times,&rquo;
III, iii, 339.
<P>265. <B>gratifie]</B> <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> iii, 291): That is, express her gratitude for, recompense.
<P>269. <B>Mother]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: In III, iv, 69, Othello says that &lquo;an Egyptian&rquo; gave this
handkerchief to his Mother; and here he says it was his Father. This has been cen-
sured as an oversight in Shakespeare, but perhaps it is only a fresh proof of his art. The
first account of the handkerchief, as given by Othello, was purposely ostentatious, in
order to alarm his wife the more. When he mentions it a second time, the truth was
sufficient for his purpose. <SC>Cowden-Clarke</SC>: Even this slight deviation from truth
works its own retribution. Had not Othello over-excited Desdemona's fears by his
description of the handkerchief, she might not have been led to prevaricate and into
falsehood.</CC>

<P>292, 293. <SC>Warburton</SC>: Without question Shakespeare wrote and pointed thus:
&lquo;Are there no stones in heaven? For what then serves the thunder?&rquo; i. e. are there
no bolts in heaven for this villain? for what purpose then serves the thunder, that
instrument of vengeance? [Kean adopted this emendation; see Wood's <I>Personal Rec-
ollections</I>, &amp;c., p. 264.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>] <SC>Steevens</SC>: Othello does not demand a thunder-bolt for
Iago. He only asks, if there are no lesser degrees of chastisement more proportioned
to the guilt of mortals, ready to drop down on such villains as Iago, though Omnipo-
tence withholds its thunder as too noble an instrument for the punishment of crimes
like his? Shakespeare might, however, mean, Does heaven reserve its thunder only to
make a noise? has it no implements of mischief to punish as well as terrify? <SC>Malone</SC>:
Has not heaven one supernumerary bolt, to hurl directly at the head of this atrocious
villain? Must all the stores of its arsenal be reserved for common and ordinary thunder?
<P>294. <B>Precious]</B> <SC>Collier</SC>: <I>Pernitious</I> of the Qq does not suit the measure. <SC>Dyce</SC>

below. Collier's metrical objection is &ldquo;naught.&rdquo; See Walker, <I>Vers.</I>, &amp;c., Art. ix.&rquo;&mdash;
<SC>Lettsom</SC>. [I have failed to find this passage in Walker; it certainly is not in Art. ix.

<CC><P>315. <B>Ice brookes]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: Steel is hardened by being put red-hot into very cold
water. <SC>Steevens</SC> identifies the &lquo;ice brook&rquo; with the river called Salo (now Xalon),
near Bilbilis, by citations from Martial [<I>Epig.</I> IV, lv, 15, and I, xlix, 12] and Justin, l,
44. <SC>Pope's</SC> needless change was thus justified by <SC>Blackstone</SC>: I incline to read <B>&lquo;'<I>tis</I></B>
<I>ebroes</I> temper.&rquo; If we suppose that the words, '<I>tis ebroes</I>, were huddled together, either
in transcribing or composing, thus, '<I>tisebroes</I>, the compositor, in running it over with his
eye, might (to make it sense, as he thought) add a couple of letters, and divide the
words thus: th'<I>isebrokes</I>, which is nearly as it stands in the old Qto. I doubt whether
&lquo;ice-brooks&rquo; are usual in the climate of Spain. <SC>Malone</SC>: How this fact may be, I
know not; and I am confident Shakespeare did not inquire.

<P>371. <SC>Swinburne</SC> (p. 179): Iago has within him a sense or conscience of power
incomparable: and this power shall not be left, in Hamlet's phrase, &lquo;to fust in him
unused.&rquo; A genuine and thorough capacity for human lust or hate would diminish and
degrade the supremacy of his evil. He is almost as far above or beyond vice as he is
beneath or beyond virtue. And this it is which makes him impregnable and invulner-
able. When once he has said it, we know as well as he that henceforth he never will
speak word. We could smile almost as we can see him to have smiled at Gratiano's
most ignorant and empty threat, being well assured that torments will in no wise ope
his lips; that as surely and as truthfully as ever did the tortured philosopher before
him, he might have told his tormentors that they did but bruise the coating, batter the
crust, or break the shell of Iago. Could we imagine a far other lost spirit than Fari-
nata degli Uberti's endowed with Farinata's might of will, and transferred from the
sepulchres of fire to the dykes of Malebolge, we might conceive something of Iago's
attitude in hell,&mdash;of his unalterable and indomitable posture for all eternity. <SC>Booth</SC>:
I grind my teeth at this, not because it &lquo;takes,&rquo; but because I feel that it expresses
determination never to speak again.</CC>

<P>421. <B>Iudean]</B> <SC>Pope</SC>: In the first edition it is <I>Judian</I>, occasion'd, probably, by the
word <I>Tribe</I> just after, but the common reading is better; as the word <I>Tribe</I> is applica-
ble to any race of people, and the thought of an ignorant <I>Indian's</I> casting away a pearl
very natural in itself, whereas to make sense of the other, one must presuppose some
particular story of a <I>Jew</I> alluded to, which is much less obvious. <SC>Theobald</SC> adopted
<I>Judian</I> on the grounds that no Indian was so ignorant as not to know the value of
pearls; that an Indian would have been called <I>rude</I> and not &lquo;base&rquo;; that &lquo;pearl&rquo; is
metaphorical, and by it &lquo;our author very properly means <I>a fine woman.</I>&rquo; To Pope's
objection to <I>Judian</I>, that it must contain a reference to some particular Jew, Theobald
opposes the story of &lquo;Herod, who in a fit of blind jealousy threw away such a jewel
of a wife as Mariamne,&rquo; whose story was dramatized in 1613 by Lady Elizabeth Carew.
Lastly, that the accent was no obstacle to a poet who shortens the second syllable in
Euphrates. <SC>Warburton</SC> agrees with Theobald, and adds that from the phrase &lquo;out-
herod Herod&rquo; applied to a poor player in Hamlet, the existence of a tragedy on Herod
is to be inferred. [Malone afterwards showed that the Herod here alluded to was a
character in one of the ancient Mysteries.] <SC>Upton</SC> (p. 255): In the First book of the
Ethiopian romance of Heliodorus there is the story of Thyamis, an Aegyptian robber,
who fell in love with Chariclea; stung with jealousy, and despairing of possessing her
himself, he resolves to murder her; and thinking he had killed her (but it happened to
be another), he cries out, &lquo;Alas, poor maid, these are the nuptial gifts I present thee.&rquo;
This story is alluded to in <I>Twelfth Night</I>, V, i, 121; and it is this same story, it seems
to me, that Othello refers to here, and the phrase should therefore be, &lquo;Like the base</CC>

<P><I>Egyptian</I>, threw,&rquo; &amp;c. This exactly agrees with the Romance. 'Twas Thyamis's own
hand, and he, too, in a strong $it of love and jealousy, that committed this murder.
Brabantio had called Othello &lquo;a foul thief.&rquo; These circumstances crowd into Othello's
mind, and with great propriety he calls himself &lquo;the base <I>Egyptian.</I>&rquo; As for Theo-
bald's reference to Herod and Mariamne, very little will be found in it applicable to
Desdemona's case. Othello was a private murderer, Herod brought his wife to public
justice; Desdemona was fond of the Moor, the Jewess hated her husband, and always
treated him with scorn and contempt. On the other hand, the story of the Egyptian
thief is very minutely applicable, and the passage in <I>Twelfth Night</I> shows that our
author was pleased with the allusion. It seems the corruption was owing to some sort
of ill-written abbreviation, that might be in the original, as <I>Egp<SUP>ian</SUP></I>, and which could
not be easily understood by printer or player. <SC>Heath</SC> (p. 571) defends <I>Indian</I>
against Theobald's objections by asserting, first: That Indians do not know the value
of pearls. &lquo;Nay, even at this day the various tribes of Indians who inhabit the conti-
nent of North America, would joyfully exchange the most valuable pearl that might
accidentally fall into their hands for a bottle of rum, or a flask of gunpowder.&rquo; Sec-
ondly: &lquo;Base&rquo; is used to signify not only villainous and treacherous, but mean, vulgar,
uninstructed in the arts of polished life. Thirdly: That the &lquo;pearl&rquo; doth not mean a
fine woman in virtue of a metaphor, but is only likened to one, to wit, to Desdemona,
in virtue of a comparison or similitude. On the other hand, there are three unanswer-
able objections to <I>Judian.</I> First: There is no such word, and the verse will not permit
<I>Jud&aelig;an.</I> Secondly: It contradicts the probable truth of the manners, as it is in the
highest degree improbable that Othello, born a Negro or Moor, and bred in the tented
field, and rude in speech, should have ever heard of Herod and Mariamne. Thirdly:
There is not the least resemblance between the two stories, except that both Othello
and Herod put their wives to death, the one privately, the other publicly. <SC>Steevens</SC>:
I cannot join with the learned critics in conceiving this passage to refer either to the ig-
norance of the natives of India, in respect of <I>pearls</I>, or to the well-known story of Herod
and Mariamne. The poet might just as fairly be supposed to have alluded to that of
Jephthah and his Daughter. Othello, in detestation of what he had done, seems to com-
pare himself to another person who had thrown away a <I>thing of value</I>, with some cir-
cumstances of the <I>meanest villainy</I>, which the epithet <I>base</I> seems to imply in its general
sense, though it is sometimes used only for <I>low</I> or <I>mean.</I> The Indian could not prop-
erly be termed <I>base</I> in the former and most common sense, whose fault was <I>ignorance</I>,
which brings its own excuse with it; and the crime of Herod surely deserves a more
aggravated distinction. I do not believe the poet intended to make the present simile
coincide with all the circumstances of Othello's situation, but merely with the single act
of having <I>basely</I> (as he himself terms it) destroyed that on which he ought to have set
a greater value. As the <I>pearl</I> may bear a <I>literal</I> as well as a <I>metaphorical</I> sense, I
would rather choose to take it in the <I>literal</I> one, and receive Pope's rejected explana-
tion, <I>presupposing some story of a Jew alluded to</I>, which might be well understood at
that time, though now, perhaps, forgotten, or, at least, imperfectly remembered. I have
read in some book, as ancient as the time of Shakespeare, the following tale, though at
present I am unable either to recollect the title of the piece or the author's name [That
obliging, and yet treacherous, memory!&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]: &lquo;A Jew, who had been prisoner for
many years in distant parts, brought with him at his return to Venice a great number
of pearls, which he offered on the 'change among the merchants, and (one alone
excepted) disposed of them to his satisfaction. On this pearl, which was the largest</CC>

that Othello alludes to no particular story, but to &lquo;the Indian&rquo; as generally described;
and to the passages just cited the following may be added: &lquo;The wretched Indian
spurnes the golden ore.&rquo;&mdash;Drayton, <I>Legend of Matilda</I>, sig. <SC>f</SC>, f 7,&mdash;<I>Poems</I>, n. d.
<SC>White</SC> (<I>Shakespeare Scholar</I>, p. 443): There appears to me not a doubt that F<SUB>1</SUB> is
right, and that the allusion is to Herod and Mariamne. [White here gives a long
extract from George Lunt, of which the following is an abstract]: The expression is
one of generalization, demanding the ready understanding of the reader. Whether he
understand the particular allusion or not, at least it should be of that character that he
might, or ought to have known it; and not drawn from a source so remote as to be out
of his reach. On this ground we are willing to set up any possible <I>Judean</I> against any
<I>Indian</I> that can be imagined. In the first place, &lquo;tribe&rquo; is a word peculiarly appropriate
to the Jewish people. Next, &lquo;base&rquo; would be held peculiarly descriptive of the Jewish
people; in common understanding, it would fit any Jew and all Jews. There would
have been a manifest impropriety in the epithet as denoting the characteristics of East
Indians in general. Lastly, the word &lquo;Judean,&rquo; in reality, means something more than
<I>Jew.</I> A &lquo;Judean&rquo; is, in fact, an <I>inhabitant of Judea;</I> and thus, in correspondence
with Shakespeare's common mode of expression, the word might naturally, and with
more force would, refer to Herod, King of Judea, as the <I>Judean, par excellence</I>,&mdash;as
representing the State. [Thus far Lunt. White then resumes, and emphasizes the abso-
lute necessity of a reference to a particular story. In Boswell's citations and in Dyce's,
not only] is the Indian generally described, but the act. No specific deed is referred to;
there is a mere allusion to a characteristic of the Indian. Not so in Othello's speech.
In that, a particular person and a particular act must be alluded to, because Othello
likens himself, not to the Indian who <I>throws</I> a pearl away, but to &lquo;<I>the base</I> J&uacute;dean&rquo;
who &lquo;<I>threw</I> a pearl away.&rquo; The reference is to some story, specific and unmistakable;
can there be a shadow of a doubt that Herod's was the story referred to, and that we
should not disturb the F<SUB>1</SUB>? [Six years later, in his edition, <SC>White</SC> says]: To my</CC>

who, with <I>his own hand</I>, threw away <I>a treasure</I>, the pearl of his tribe. A story also
well known to Shakespeare, for we find it commented on in his other plays.&rquo; [That
Othello killed his wife, and Jephthah his daughter, does not disconcert M'Grath, for he
philosophically adds, &lquo;we cannot expect every minute detail&rquo; to be exact in counter-

Indian, or to the Indians as generally described, is not quite clear; probably the latter.
<SC>Cowden-Clarke</SC>: Even though we follow the Qq, we confess to entertaining con-
siderable doubts whether the Folio may not, after all, give what Shakespeare wrote.
<SC>Purnell</SC>: Read Jud&aelig;an, and refer to Herod and Mariamne. [In <I>N. &amp; Qu.</I> 6th,
iii, 264, H. K. gives two citations to show the common repute of an Indian's indiffer-

to add, suggestion even in the identity of the two first syllables, <I>Jud</I>as and <I>Jud</I>ean?
Once before in this Scene, Othello's agonized thoughts had turned for a fit comparison
to that dread time when the affrighted globe yawned and darkness covered the face of

<CC><P>425. <B>Medicinable]</B> <SC>Rolfe</SC>: Shakespeare has the word in four other passages

<P>425. <B>gumme.]</B> <SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 289) thinks from the description in <I>The Great Herbal</I>,

Probably not gum arabic, but myrrh.
<P>426. <B>Aleppo]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: I am told that it is immediate death for a Christian to

<P>427. <B>Turbond]</B> <SC>Delius</SC>: Shakespeare seems to have connected the idea of arro-
gance with turbans. See in <I>Cymb.</I> III, iii, 6: &lquo;that giants may jet through And keep
their impious turbans on.&rquo; <SC>Fechter</SC>: Othello here seizes and forces Iago, still bound,
to kneel before Desdemona, but promptly intercepted by Lodovico and Montano, he
draws his poignard, and suiting the action to the word utters the last two lines 429,
430; stabs himself, and throws the dagger at the feet of Iago; then, tottering, walks
to the bed; but, unable to reach Desdemona, falls in despair and dies.
<P>430. <SC>Hawkins</SC>, <I>Life of Kean</I> (i, 75): Kean's falling on his back in the last Scene of
<I>Othello</I> was suggested by an incident in nature. He was giving a young officer some
instruction in fencing, when he accidentally received an alarming wound in the breast,
from the effect of which, becoming insensible, he fell to the ground on his back. When
he recovered his senses he asked, &lquo;How did I fall?&rquo; <SC>Booth</SC>: At the word &lquo;thus&rquo;
Othello stabs himself, cries &lquo;O, Desdemona!&rquo; makes an effort to reach the bed, clutch-
ing (not much) for the curtains as he falls back dead.
<P>430. <SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. iii): When Othello offers to stab Iago he is disarmed by Montano,
but he has &lquo;another weapon,&mdash;a sword of Spain.&rquo; Of that weapon, after wounding
Iago, he is also deprived; this is shown not only by the exclamation of Lodovico,
&lquo;Wrench his sword from him,&rquo; but by the remark of Cassio, &lquo;This I did fear, but
thought he had no weapon.&rquo; The instrument he now uses must, therefore, have been
a dagger, which was concealed about his person. [See <SC>Gould</SC>, line 411.]

<P>448. <SC>Coleridge</SC> (<I>Notes</I>, &amp;c., p. 256): Let me repeat that Othello does not kill Des-
demona in jealousy, but in a conviction forced upon him by the almost superhuman
art of Iago, such a conviction as any man would and must have entertained who had
believed Iago's honesty as Othello did. We, the audience, know that Iago is a villain
from the beginning; but in considering the essence of the Shakespearian Othello we
must perseveringly place ourselves in his situation and under his circumstances. Then
we shall immediately feel the fundamental difference between the solemn agony of the
noble Moor, and the wretched fishing jealousies of Leontes, and the morbid suspicious-
ness of Leonatus, who is, in other respects, a fine character. Othello had no life but in
Desdemona; the belief that she, his angel, had fallen from the heaven of her native
innocence, wrought a civil war in his heart. She is his counterpart; and, like him, is
almost sanctified in our eyes by her absolute unsuspiciousness, and holy entireness of
love. As the curtain drops, which do we pity the most?</CC>

<P>It will be noted that in accordance with the terms of the Entry, no play is included
in this list of which an authentic Quarto had been already printed; yet when the vol-
ume was published, it contained these Quarto plays. From which it is to be presumed
that the interests in these Quartos had become vested in various ways, by purchase,
inheritance, or marriage, in the proprietors of the Folio: Jaggard, Blount, Smithwicke,
and Apsley. But there is a mystery about <I>Othello.</I> It certainly appeared in Quarto,
and it certainly appeared in the Folio, and yet Thomas Walkley had not resigned all
his interest in it in 1623. For in the <I>Stationers' Registers</I> (Arber, iv, 194) we find the
following:
<C>i<SUP>mo</SUP> Martii 1627 [i. e., 1628]</C>
<P>Master <B>Richard</B> Assigned ouer vnto him by Thomas <B>Walkley</B>, and Consent of a
<P><B>Hawkins</B> Court holden this Day all the estate right title and Interest which he
hath in these Copies following . . . . . . . . . xviij<SUP>d</SUP>
<BQ><I>viz<SUP>t</SUP></I><LB>
<I>A kinge and no kinge.</I><LB>
<I><SC>Philaster</SC></I> <I>or love lies ableeding.</I><LB>
<I><SC>Orthello</SC></I> <I>the more of Venice.</I><LB></BQ>
<P>It is not easy to reconcile this proof of property still vested in Walkley with the
appearance of <I>Othello</I> in the First Folio. Collier suggests that, &lquo;most likely, the pub-
lishers of the Folio purchased Walkley's interest at a date posterior to the entry of
their undertaking at Stationers' Hall, and thus became entitled to include it in their
noble volume,&rquo; which does not help us. Although the Folio was issued in 1623, the
printing must have been in hand long before that. Indeed, there are not wanting
<PB N=341>
<HE><I>THE TEXT</I> 341</HE>
<P>copies which are supposed to bear the genuine date 1622, the very year in which
Walkley issued his Quarto, so that the two books must have been in the hands of
the printers at the same time. Can we here infer some private understanding between
the publishers? Was it to emphasize his possession of the Quarto, while acquiesc-
ing in its appearance in the Folio, that Walkley put forth his unusual address &lquo;to
the Reader&rquo;? But speculations are idle; even if they led to assurance, what should
we gain? Merely a better knowledge of the private affairs of Thomas Walkley.
&lquo;When all's done, you look but on a stool.&rquo; Of more importance is it that two
years later, in 1630, Richard Hawkins put his assignment to use by issuing a Quarto
<I>Othello</I> with exactly the same title-page, except that there is a different Vignette, and
that it is stated to be: &lquo;Printed by <I>A. M.</I> for <I>Richard Hawkins</I>, and are to be fold
at &verbar; his $hoppe in Chancery-Lane, neere Sergeants-Inne. &verbar; 1630.&rquo;
<P>This is the <I>Second Quarto</I>, or Q<SUB>2</SUB>.
<P>We next meet &lquo;Orthello&rquo; in the <I>Stationers' Register</I> (Arber, iv, p. 420), when on
the 29&degree; Maij, 1638, <B>vrsula Hawkins</B> widdow (late wife of <B>Richard Hawkins</B>
deceased) assigned to &lquo;Master <B>Mead</B> and Master <B>Meredith</B>&rquo; certain &lquo;Copies&rquo; &lquo;which
did belong vnto her said husband;&rquo; in the list of twenty-five titles, which follows, appears
&lquo;<SC>Orthello</SC> <I>the More of Venice</I> a play.&rquo; Master Mead and Master Meredith did
not long retain possession of <I>Orthello;</I> on the 25th of January of the following year,
1639, they assigned over to Master <B>William Leake</B> &lquo;these Copies,&rquo; &lquo;following which
were Entred vnto them from Mistris <B>Hawkins.</B>&rquo; Again in this list also we have
&lquo;Orthello the More of Venice a Play.&rquo; For sixteen long years did Master Leak
permit the dust to settle on <I>Orthello</I> before he published what he called, on the Title-
page, &lquo;The fourth Edition.&rquo; The rest of the title-page is exactly the same, barring
a Crown for a Vignette, as in the preceding Quartos, except that it is: &lquo;Printed for
<I>William Leak</I> at the <I>Crown</I> in <I>Fleet- &verbar; $treet</I>, between the two Temple Gates,
1655.&rquo;
<P>This is the <I>Third Quarto</I>, or Q<SUB>3</SUB>.
<P>A Player's Quarto appeared in 1681, as &lquo;now [acted] at the Theater Royal, by His
Majesties Servants.&rquo; It is &lquo;Printed for <I>W. Weak</I>, and are to be $old by <I>Richard
Bent</I> &verbar; <I>ley</I> and <I>M. Magnes</I> in <I>Ru$$el Street</I> near <I>Covent- &verbar; Garden</I>, 1681.&rquo; Halliwell
suggests that &lquo;Weak&rquo; is a misprint for <I>Leak.</I> If it be the same W. Leak that published
the Third Qto, who was presumably the same W. Leake that was &lquo;called as an Assist-
ant&rquo; to the Stationers' Company, seventy-seven years before, in 1604, it may be a mis-
print, it cannot possibly, after such a protracted existence, be a misnomer. Reprints of
this Quarto followed in 1687 and 1695.
<P>Meanwhile the <I>First, Second, Third</I>, and <I>Fourth Folios</I> had appeared in 1623, 1632,
1663, and 1685.
<P>Here bibliographic interest in all of them ceases. Their value to us as texts is all
that is of importance now. Although this value is somewhat difficult of adjustment,
there is greater harmony among Editors with regard to it in this play than usually falls
to the lot of a play which has attendant satellites in the shape of Quartos.
<P>We have Four Folios and Three Quartos. How many independent texts are there
and what are their respective values?
<P>The Four Folios are practically one. For any changes introduced after the First
was issued, there is no more authority to be yielded than is due to the intelligence,
more or less keen, of a compositor. For the text of the First Folio there must have
been used either the original MS of Shakespeare (Heminge and Condell asserted that
they had so used it, but then we know that in the case of certain other plays this was
<PB N=342>
<HE>342 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>&lquo;a grace snatched beyond the bounds of truth&rquo;) or else a stage copy, which, perhaps
contained no single word written by Shakespeare's own hand.
<P>Considering the twenty years since Shakespeare's ink was drv on the original, and
considering the burning, between whiles, of &lquo;The Globe&rquo; and its contents (it <I>was</I> a con-
flagration of the world to us), this latter supposition, that the Folio was printed from a
stage copy, seems the more probable. In either case Shakespeare's personal friends
vouched for its accuracy, and no similar authority vouches for any other. This, then,
the text of the Folio of 1623, becomes the text of the play; and in any claim for pref-
erence put forth by other texts the burden of proof lies on the claimants, the presump-
tion of authenticity is all in favour of F<SUB>1</SUB>. As we have seen at II, ii, 231, Dyce, whose
opinion on such matters is of very great weight, asserts that this play in F<SUB>1</SUB> was &lquo;beyond
all doubt printed from a transcript belonging to the theatre.&rquo;
<P>On the other side stand the three Quartos.
<P>The <SC>First</SC>, as we have seen, was issued by a Stationer named Walkley. What manu-
script he used, or how he obtained it, we cannot know. He says in his address &lquo;to the
reader,&rquo; that the author is dead; it is, therefore, not likely that he received the MS
from Shakespeare during Shakespeare's lifetime and kept it lying idle for five or six
years. Nor is it likely that Walkley's text was taken down surreptitiously by short-
hand from a performance on the stage: the stage directions are not sufficient in number,
nor descriptive enough in character, to indicate an eye-witness; and although four of
the Acts are noted, there are no divisions into Scenes. Yet there can be no doubt that
Walkley's text is an original text, and that it is not the same as that of the Folio. In
a comparison of the two, mere omissions go for nothing. Counting every line of the Folio,
not as verses but as lines, as is done in the preceding pages of this volume, and count-
ing the lines in the Quarto in the same way, there are, roughly speaking, more than
three hundred and fifty lines in the Folio that are omitted in the Quarto. Knight, who
with closer accuracy, computed the verses, reckons the number at &lquo;a hundred and sixty-
three.&rquo; But additions are important; they are presumably from the hand of the author;
and in the way of additions there are ten or fifteen lines in the Quarto, Knight says less
than ten, which are not to be found in the Folio. This alone goes far to stamp the Qto
as an independent text. But the most noticeable difference, one that strikes every reader
at once, from the beginning to the end, in the first speech of Iago and among the last
speeches of Emilia, and in Cassio's drunken scene, lies in the use of oaths and adjurations.
&lquo;Zounds,&rquo; &lquo;God,&rquo; &lquo;'Sblood,&rquo; etc., scattered through the First Quarto, are either omitted
altogether or are toned down, in the Folio. Hence there can be no reasonable doubt
that in the First Quarto we have a genuine text, and since it cannot be supposed to have
come from Shakespeare, and was not taken down by short-hand, we are forced to con-
clude that it too was a play-house copy, and, I think, an old one, possibly &lquo;stolne.&rquo; It
is not worth while here to enter upon a minute comparison of the two texts. The very
purpose of the Textual Notes in the foregoing pages is to enable the student to do that
for himself. It is not hard to grow interested in minute collation, but then one must do
it for himself, at first hand. Simply to repeat another's work is most tolerable and not
to be endured. It is no better than proof-reading, proof-reading, too, uncheered by the
hope of blunders.
<P>The older Editors, from <SC>Johnson</SC> to the time of <SC>Knight</SC>, were influenced in favour of
this Qto, which they considered older and more authentic. Knight followed the Folio,
upholding its text always through thick, and sometimes through thin. <SC>Collier</SC> leaned
to the Second Qto, but since his time the balance of favour has been on the side of the
Folio, which is, to me, far and away the better.
<PB N=343>
<HE><I>THE TEXT</I> 343</HE>
<P>Perhaps it is well to mention that Pope, in his &lquo;Table of the Several Editions&rquo; which
he had used, closed his list with the title of an <I>Othello</I>, undated, but &lquo;Published by
Tho. Walkely, Quarto, (soon after his Death, as appears by the Preface.)&rquo; Overlooking
Pope's somewhat startling announcement of &lquo;Walkely's&rquo; posthumous performance,
Malone conjectured that this Quarto was simply Q<SUB>1</SUB>, whose date had been &lquo;cut off,
which frequently happens in old plays.&rquo; Capell, both in his &lquo;Table of Plays&rquo; and in
his Appendix, refers to this undated Qto, but it is on the authority of Pope. The
Cambridge Editors think that the reference to the publisher's preface is conclusive that
Pope's Qto was the Qto of 1622. No undated Qto having been discovered from Pope's
day to the present, we may safely acquiesce in Malone's opinion.
<P>The <SC>Second Quarto</SC> appeared in 1630. Have we here an independent text, or
merely a reprint? <SC>Malone</SC> dismissed it as &lquo;an edition of no authority,&rquo; but <SC>Collier</SC>
espoused its cause with zeal, on the ground that it &lquo;was unquestionably printed from
a manuscript different from that used for the Qto of 1622 or for the Folio of 1623;
and presents a number of various readings, some of which singularly illustrate the
original text of <I>Othello.</I>&rquo; Collier cites III, iii, 518, where Q<SUB>2</SUB> gives the word <I>feels</I>
adopted by the majority of Editors, instead of &lquo;keepes,&rquo; of the Ff. <SC>Grant White</SC>,
however, does not estimate this Qto as highly as Collier does (<SC>Dyce</SC> and <SC>Staunton</SC> do
not even mention it in their Prefaces); he says, in reference to it, in his Introduction:
&lquo;After a careful consideration of its readings, I have come to the conclusion that it is
&lquo;only a reprint of the Qto of 1622, corrected by the text of the Folio, having some
&lquo;typographical errors peculiar to itself, and a very few unimportant corrections and
&lquo;sophistications, such as crept into almost every dramatic reprint of the period. I
&lquo;therefore regard it as of no authority, and make no mention of its readings.&rquo; The
<SC>Cambridge Editors</SC> agree in the main with Grant White. &lquo;After a minute compari-
&lquo;son,&rquo; they say, &lquo;of the two [Quartos] it appears to us clear that the Quarto of 1630
&lquo;must have been printed from a copy of the Quarto of 1622, which had received addi-
&lquo;tions and corrections in manuscript. The resemblances between the two are too close
&lquo;to allow of any other supposition. These additions and corrections, though agreeing
&lquo;for the most part with the First Folio, which had appeared in the interval, were derived
&lquo;from an independent source.&rquo;
<P>It by no means follows that &lquo;this independent source&rquo; was Shakespeare or his
MS.; a compositor or an actor would be competent to have suggested the changes.
With this understanding, I quite agree with this conclusion, to which, I think, any one
would the more readily come if the two copies and the Folio were placed open side by
side. Where F<SUB>1</SUB> supplies the omissions of Q<SUB>1</SUB>, Q<SUB>2</SUB> follows F<SUB>1</SUB>, and even where it differs
from F<SUB>1</SUB> there seems to be more an attempt to correct than to rewrite. For instance,
II, i, 45, &lquo;Euen till we make the Maine, and th' Eriall blew,&rquo; is not in Q<SUB>1</SUB>; in Q<SUB>2</SUB> the
line is found, but it is evidently an attempt to convert nonsense into sense, and not an
original reading: &lquo;Euen till we make the Maine and th' Ayre all blue.&rquo; Again, oaths
and adjurations are sometimes omitted and sometimes retained, even on the same page,
as though the excision had been attempted but done carelessly. Once more, let the
Textual Notes suffice for any further investigation, if the subject be worth it.
<P>The <SC>Third Quarto</SC> is a reprint of Q<SUB>2</SUB>; if it were a good reprint, it would be to that
extent respectable; as it is, it is worthless. I have recorded its separate readings only
here and there as mere curiosities. I can say nothing worse of it than that, having
been issued in the same year with the Third Quarto of <I>King Lear</I>, I think Jane Bell
must have printed them both, and tried her 'prentice hand on <I>Othello.</I>
