<C>THE DATE OF COMPOSITION.</C>
<P><SC>The</SC> earliest attempt to fix the Date of the Composition of this Play was made by
<SC>Warburton</SC>, who asserted that there was an allusion to the creation of baronets by
James the First, in the words of Othello to Desdemona in III, iv, 55: &lquo;The hearts
of old, gaue hands: But our new Heraldry is hands, not hearts.&rquo; &lquo;The expression
&lquo;of &ldquo;new heraldry,&rdquo;&rquo; says Warburton, &lquo;was a satirical allusion to the times. Soon after
&lquo;King James the First came to the crown, he created the new dignity of baronets for
&lquo;money. Amongst their other prerogatives of honour, they had an addition to their
&lquo;paternal <I>arms</I>, of a <SC>hand</SC> <I>gules</I> in an Escutcheon <I>argent.</I> And we are not to doubt
&lquo;but that this was the <I>new heraldry</I> alluded to by our author: by which he insinuates
&lquo;that some then created had <I>hands</I> indeed, but not <I>hearts;</I> that is, <I>money</I> to pay for
&lquo;the <I>creation</I>, but no <I>virtue</I> to purchase the <I>honour.</I> But the finest part of the poet's
&lquo;address in this allusion is the compliment he pays to his old mistress, Elizabeth. For
&lquo;James's pretence for raising money by this creation, was the reduction of Ulster, and
&lquo;other parts of Ireland; the memory of which he would perpetuate by that addition
&lquo;to their arms, it being the arms of Ulster. Now the method used by Elizabeth in the
&lquo;reduction of that Kingdom was so different from this, the dignities she conferred being
&lquo;on those who employed their <I>steel</I>, and not their <I>gold</I>, in this service, that nothing could
&lquo;add more to her glory, than the being compared to her successor in this point of view:
&lquo;nor was it uncommon for the dramatic poets of that time to satirize the ignominy of
&lquo;James's reign. So, Fletcher, in <I>The Fair Maid of the Inn.</I> One says, &lquo;I will send
&lquo;&lquo;thee to Amboyna in the East Indies for pepper.&rquo; The other replies, &lquo;To Amboyna?
&lquo;&lquo;so I might be pepper'd.&rquo; Again, in the same play, a Sailor says, &lquo;Despise not this
&lquo;&lquo;pitch'd canvas, the time was, we have known them lined with Spanish ducats.&rquo;&rquo;
<P>This &lquo;satirical allusion&rquo; of Warburton would fix the date at 1611, the year in which
James instituted the order of Baronets, and in this date there arose general acquiescence.
<SC>Malone</SC>, in his first edition, 1790, accepted it, but under protest. After quoting War-
burton's note, &lquo;our Hibernian coadjutor,&rquo; as Steevens calls him, proceeded thus to criti-
cise it:
<P>&lquo;By what chemistry can the sense which Warburton has affixed to this passage be
&lquo;extracted from it? Or is it probable that Shakespeare, who has more than once
&lquo;condescended to be the encomiast of the unworthy founder of the order of Baronets,
&lquo;who had been personally honoured by a letter from his majesty, and substantially
&lquo;benefited by the royal license granted to him and his fellow-comedians, should have
&lquo;been so impolitic, as to satirize the king, or to depreciate his new-created dignity?
&lquo;. . . . On every marriage the arms of the wife are <I>united</I> to those of the husband.
&lquo;This circumstance it was, that suggested <I>heraldry</I> in this place. . . . . It was the office
&lquo;of the herald to <I>join</I>, or, to speak technically, to <I>quarter</I> the arms of the new-married
&lquo;pair. Hence with his usual license, Shakespeare uses &lquo;heraldry&rquo; for <I>junction</I>, or
&lquo;<I>union</I> in generall. Thus in <I>R. of L.</I> 64, the same term is employed to denote that
&lquo;<I>union</I> of colours which constitutes a beautiful complexion. This passage not afford-
&lquo;ing us any assistance, we are next to consider one in <I>The Alchemist</I>, by Ben Jonson,
&lquo;which, if it alluded to an incident in <I>Othello</I>, as Steevens seems to think it does,
&lquo;would ascertain this play to have appeared before 1610, in which year <I>The Alchemist</I>
&lquo;was first acted: &lquo;<I>Lovewit.</I> Dids't thou hear a cry, says't thou? <I>Neighbour.</I> Yes, sir,
&lquo;&lquo;like unto a man that had been strangled an hour, and could not speak.&rquo; But I doubt
&lquo;whether <I>Othello</I> was here in Jonson's contemplation. Old Ben generally spoke out;
&lquo;and if he had intended to sneer at the manner of Desdemona's death. I think he
<PB N=345>
<HE><I>DATE OF COMPOSITION</I> 345</HE>
<P>&lquo;would have taken care that his meaning should not be missed, and would have writ-
&lquo;ten&mdash;&lquo;like unto a <I>woman</I>,&rquo; &amp;c.&rquo; Although <I>Othello</I> was not printed until 1622, Malone
said &lquo;it was acted at court early in the year 1613&rquo;; and, as an authority for this state-
ment, cited &lquo;MS. Vertue,&rquo; for an account whereof see Chalmers, <I>post.</I> Malone con-
tinues: &lquo;I have persuaded myself that <I>Othello</I> was one of Shakespeare's latest per-
&lquo;formances; a supposition to which the acknowledged excellence of the piece gives
&lquo;some degree of probability. It is here [i. e., in Malone's edition of 1790] attributed
&lquo;to the year 1611, because Warburton's comment on the passage may convince others,
&lquo;though, I confess it does not satisfy me. <I>Emilia</I> and <I>Lodovico</I>, two of the characters
&lquo;in this play, are likewise two of the persons in <I>May-day</I>, by Chapman, first printed in
&lquo;1611.&rquo;
<P>The value of Warburton's citation from Fletcher's <I>Fair Maid of the Inn</I>, Malone
destroyed in his note on III, iv, 55, where he says &lquo;that play indeed never was per-
&lquo;formed before King James, being the last play but one that Fletcher wrote, and not
&lquo;produced till the 22nd of Jan. 1625-6, after the death both of its author and King
&lquo;James; but when it was written, he must, from the circumstances already mentioned,
&lquo;have had the court before his eyes.&rquo;
<P>Malone died in 1812, and when the Variorum of 1821 appeared, it was found that
he had abandoned the date of 1611 and adopted 1604, but before this change became
known, two other dates had been proposed.
<P>First: <SC>Chalmers</SC> (<I>Supplemental Apology</I>, 1799, p. 457) urged a date later even than
Warburton, &lquo;who,&rquo; said Chalmers, &lquo;is partly right, and partly wrong. By what chem-
&lquo;istry could this critic extract such a sense from this passage? asks Mr Malone. The
&lquo;answer must be, the same sort of chemistry, which so frequently enabled the observant
&lquo;dramatist to captivate his audience, by his striking allusions to the passing scene; to
&lquo;satyrise without lampoon; and to throw out sarcasms without scoffing. In IV, i, Iago,
&lquo;working on the jealousy of Othello, artfully remarks: &lquo;If you are so fond over her
&lquo;&lquo;iniquity, give her [a] <I>patent</I> to offend.&rquo; The audience, who knew from their feel-
&lquo;ings, how much vexation had arisen from the <I>patents of monopoly</I>, which Queen Eliz-
&lquo;abeth and King James had so frequently granted, and so often retracted, must have
&lquo;been electrified by this fine stroke of well-timed satire. . . . . Warburton was right in
&lquo;supposing that the stroke at the <I>new</I> heraldry was, incidentally, aimed at the creation
&lquo;of baronets, which was attended with uncommon circumstances. The epoch of this
&lquo;order was undoubtedly May, 1611. But, unluckily, for the speculation of Warburton,
&lquo;the additional armorial bearing, of the bloody hand, was not given by the patent of
&lquo;creation. The order had scarcely been created when a dispute arose, during those
&lquo;punctilious times, about precedence, between the baronets and the younger sons of
&lquo;viscounts, and barons. On this difficult point King James sat <I>personally</I>, during three
&lquo;several days, to hear the learned counsel; to take the information of Heralds; and to
&lquo;consider the proofs: And, in the end, he decided against the baronets, declaring he
&lquo;had not had any purpose to wrong <I>third parties tacitly</I>, whatever he might intend to
&lquo;confer, by his creation, on others: But the King, wishing to ampliate his favour towards
&lquo;the baronets, granted them by a <I>second</I> patent, dated 28 May, 1612, among other <I>pre-
heminences</I>, &lquo;the arms of Ulster, that is, in a field argent, a hand <I>geules</I>, or a <I>bloudie
&lquo;hand.</I>&rquo; Spenser will inform us, in his <I>State of Ireland</I>, &lquo;that the <I>bloody hand</I> is
&lquo;<I>O'Neel's badge.</I>&rquo; Such, then, was the <I>new</I> heraldry, which Shakespeare played with,
in order to please his audience! Yet we see clearly, from the second patent, in 1612,
that the epoch, which was assigned to <I>Othello</I> in 1611, cannot be supported. And we
must, therefore, look for the true date in some subsequent year. The fact is, that the
<PB N=346>
<HE>346 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>&lquo;baronets had to encounter a severer shock. A great noise was made in the House of
&lquo;Commons on the 23 May, 1614, about the creation of Baronets. This clamour against
&lquo;the King's right to create such an order was silenced in committee. . . . . There was,
&lquo;a few days before, a still louder outcry raised, in the House of Commons, with much
&lquo;greater cause, against patents of monopoly. Owing to those remarkable coincidences,
&lquo;and powerful reasons, I am of opinion, that <I>Othello</I> was written in 1614; and, being
&lquo;written at this epoch, was the last, as it was one of the greatest, of his labours.&rquo;
<P>Malone had stated, as we have seen, that <I>Othello</I> &lquo;was acted at Court early in the
year 1613,&rquo; and gave as his authority &lquo;Vertue's MS.&rquo; This date, if authentic, would
overthrow Chalmers's chronology; wherefore Chalmers set to work &lquo;making some
&lquo;inquiries by a friend what manuscript of Vertue's it were, which I saw so often quoted
&lquo;about scenic matters, and Mr Steevens was so obliging as to say: &lquo;The books, from
&lquo;&lquo;which those extracts were made, with several others lost, belonged to Secretary Pepys,
&lquo;&lquo;and afterwards to Dr Rawlinson, who lent them to Mr Vertue. There is a MS note
&lquo;&lquo;subjoined to the MSS of Vertue, which, about thirty years ago, were lent to Mr Steev-
&lquo;&lquo;ens by Mr Garrick.&rquo; Much is it to be lamented that any MS or book which furnished
&lquo;an illustration of Shakespeare, and having once been seen, should ever disappear. I
&lquo;would bow to any register of the time; but I will not allow Vertue, though a very dili-
&lquo;gent collector, to draw deductions for me which are to militate against the strongest
&lquo;probabilities.&rquo;
<P>Second: though Chalmers discarded Vertue's MS, <SC>Drake</SC> (<I>Shakespeare and his
Times</I>, ii, 528) accepted it; and taking its date, viz: the &lquo;1st of January, 1613,&rquo; as a
final limit in one direction, and the date of the &lquo;<I>Second</I> Patent&rquo; to the Baronets, viz:
the &lquo;28th of May, 1612, as a starting-point on the other, Drake felt &lquo;no hesitation in
expressing &lquo;the belief that <I>Othello</I> was written in the interval between the two.&rquo;
<P>We now come to <SC>Malone's</SC> final decision in the Variorum of 1821; a decision,
which, although formed on evidence now lost, has been generally concurred in down
to the present day. To his note in 1790 (quoted above), Malone now adds: &lquo;A passage
&lquo;in the Essays of Sir Wm Cornwallis, the younger, 1601, may have suggested to Shake-
&lquo;speare the mention of the new heraldry upon which Warburton has put, what I think,
&lquo;a most erroneous interpretation: &lquo;We of these later times full of a nice curiositie mis-
&lquo;&lquo;like all the performances of our <I>forefathers;</I> we say they were honest plaine men,
&lquo;&lquo;but they want the capering wits of this ripe age. . . . . <I>They had wont to give their
&lquo;&lquo;hands and their hearts together, but we think it a finer grace to looke asquint, our
&lquo;&lquo;hand looking one way and our heart another.</I>&rquo; If the simile of the &lquo;Pontick Sea,&rquo;
&lquo;in III, iii, is an allusion to Pliny, translated by Philemon Holland in 1601, this will
&lquo;assist us further in ascertaining the date of this play. We know it was acted in 1604,
&lquo;and I have, therefore, placed it in that year.&rquo;
<P>On this last very noteworthy sentence, <SC>Boswell</SC> has the following: &lquo;Mr Malone
&lquo;never expresses himself at random. I therefore lament deeply that I have not been
&lquo;able to discover upon what evidence he <I>knew</I> this important and decisive fact.&rquo;
<P>Here, for the moment, we must leave the discussion of this final date of Malone, and
proceed chronologically.
<P>In 1836, <SC>Collier</SC> (<I>New Particulars</I>, p. 58) announced his discovery of the proof
that <I>Othello</I> was written not in 1604, according to Malone's chronology, but as early as
1602. This fact was obtained from the Accounts preserved at Bridgewater House in
the handwriting of Sir Arthur Mainwaring, of the expenses incurred by Sir Thomas
Egerton, afterwards Lord Ellesmere, in entertaining Queen Elizabeth and her Court
for three days at Harefield. &lquo;It is headed, &lquo;31&degree; July et 1&degree; et 2&degree; Augusti, 1602, the
<PB N=347>
<HE><I>DATE OF COMPOSITION</I> 347</HE>
<P>&lquo;&lquo;Queenes Ma<SUP>tie</SUP> beeing at Harefield iij nights,&rquo; and among the particulars is the fol-
&lquo;lowing: &lquo;6 Aug. 1602. Rewardes to the Vaulters Players and Dauncers. Of this &pound;10
&lquo;&lquo;to Burbidge's players for Othello . . . . 64 18 10.&rquo;&rquo; &lquo;It is indisputable,&rquo; says Collier,
&lquo;from this evidence, that <I>Othello</I> was acted at Harefield in 1602.&rquo;
<P><SC>Knight</SC> accepted this date in his edition which followed shortly after Collier's an
nouncement.
<P>A few years after this, <SC>Peter Cunningham</SC>, a man of literary and antiquarian tastes,
was appointed to a situation in the Audit Office, Somerset House, and forthwith started
on a search for &lquo;old papers,&rquo; rummaging &lquo;in dry repositories, damp cellars, and still
damper vaults, for books of accounts, for warrants, and for receipts.&rquo; He found many
documents of value, but still nothing of commanding interest, until at last his perse-
verance was rewarded. &lquo;My last discovery,&rquo; he says, &lquo;was my most interesting; and
&lquo;alighting as I now did upon two official books of the Revels,&mdash;one of Tylney's and
&lquo;one of Buc's,&mdash;which had excaped both Musgrave and Malone, I at last found some-
&lquo;thing about Shakespeare,&mdash;something that was new, and something that was definitive.
&lquo;This was my little Guanahana&rquo; [<I>sic</I>]. And this was all. Cunningham was destined
to find no more. Still it was a great &lquo;find&rquo;; any &lquo;find&rquo; connected with Shakespeare is
great. Malone's Transcripts from ten of the Books of the Revels are printed in vol. iii
of the Variorum of 1821, pp. 364-409, and at the close of the last, ending in 1587-88,
Malone adds: &lquo;There is no subsequent Revels Account in the reign of Queen Eliza-
&lquo;beth now extant,&rquo; wherein he was probably correct. Cunningham's discovery, which
he calls &lquo;Book XII,&rquo; opens with November, 1605.
<P>These &lquo;Revels Books&rquo; are the Accounts of the expenses incurred for the entertain-
ment of Royalty by the Master of the Revels, a title which sufficiently defines itself.
From 1579 to 1610 this office was filled by one man, Edmund Tylney, who deserves
a fame which has not been vouchsafed to him. His term extended over nearly the
whole of Shakespeare's dramatic life; through his hands and under his eyes must
have passed the original manuscripts (&lquo;O happy reader, by no critic vex't!&rquo;) of upwards
of thirty of those immortal plays. Since Edmund Tylney adorns no tale, let him at
least point a moral. The first, fresh inhalation of Shakespeare's poetry in Shake-
speare's own handwriting ought to have proved a liberal education, but, alack the
day! in Tylney's case it did not; witness the following uncouth description of his
office; its lack of polish can be accounted for, I fear, only by the fact that he read the
text without the help of the commentators: &lquo;The Office of y<SUP>e</SUP> Revells consistethe of
&lquo;a Wardropp, and other several Roomes, for Artificers to worke in, viz. Taylors, Im-
&lquo;brotherers, Propertimakers, Paynters, Wyerdrawers, and Carpenters, togeather with a
&lquo;convenient place for y<SUP>e</SUP> Rehearsalls and settinge forthe of Playes and other Showes
&lquo;for those Services.&rquo; It is the infinite variety of expenses, big and little, necessarily
connected with these duties that composes these Revels Books, whereof the whole
Series was printed by <I>The Shakespeare Society</I> in 1842 under Cunningham's editorial
supervision. For the most part it is weary, dreary reading, wherein it is inconceivable
that human intelligence can find present interest, an endless repetition of the most insig-
nificant items, which would require Dickens's immortal &lquo;pair of million-magnifying gas
microscopes, of hextra power&rquo; to enlarge into even a languid interest. We find page
after page embalming the facts that the Master of the Revels spent so many pence for
&lquo;A peece of small corde,&rquo; &lquo;A pound of glewe,&rquo; &lquo;A peece of greate corde,&rquo; &lquo;For pynnes,&rquo;
&lquo;For allom,&rquo; &lquo;For broomes,&rquo; &amp;c., &amp;c., &amp;c. But on pp. 203, 204, we are startled broad
awake by the sight of the &lquo;greatest name in all literature;&rquo; it is true that in &lquo;Shaxberd&rquo;
its favour, like Roderigo's, is defeated, literally, with an vsurp'd beard,&mdash;but it is there

<P>We read:

<P>(In the original, &lquo;Shaxberd&rquo; is not placed here, but opposite the play of <I>Mesur for
Mesur.</I>) Then follows a list of twelve or thirteen plays, such as &lquo;the Merry Wiues of
Winsor,&rquo; &lquo;Mesur for Mesur,&rquo; &lquo;The Plaie of Errors,&rquo; &lquo;How to larne of a woman to wooe,&rquo;
&amp;c., with the names of &lquo;Shaxberd,&rquo; &lquo;Hewood,&rquo; &amp;c., in the margin, a practice observed
nowhere else in the volume. Although this is headed 1605, internal evidence in the
rest of the entries shows that the true date is 1604.
<P>This date of the performance of <I>Othello</I> in 1604, of course, corroborated Collier's of
1602, and it is safe to say that it influenced every editor down to, and including, Dyce
in 1866. The original MS volume, from which Cunningham printed, disappeared.
<P><SC>Verplanck</SC>, who wrote shortly after Cunningham's publication, unwillingly, on &aelig;s-
thetic grounds, relinquished the later dates of Malone and Chalmers. The emotions and
passions depicted in <I>Othello</I> are not, so he thought, such as could be reasoned out from
a young Poet's mind, or portrayed by any effort of an inexperienced imagination.
&lquo;Richard and Romeo, and <I>The Tempest</I> (whatever may have been their actual dates)
&lquo;might have been the creations of youthful genius, but <I>Othello</I> required actual experi-
&lquo;ence, or close observation, of the workings of bitter passions, in however humble a
&lquo;form, yet in actual life.&rquo; So impressed was Verplanck with this belief that, in order
to reconcile the <I>Othello</I> of 1602 with the <I>Othello</I> of 1622, he suggested that the former
&lquo;may have been, like the original <I>Hamlet</I>, barely an outline, sufficient for dramatic
&lquo;effect, containing all the incidents and characters, but wanting some of the heightened
&lquo;poetry and intense passion of the drama we now read.&rquo;
<P>The controversy that arose in 1859 over the genuineness of the MS Corrections in
Collier's Second Folio, extended to the other Shakespearian documents put forth by Col-
lier in his <I>New Facts</I> and <I>New Particulars,</I> and among them to the papers in Bridge-
water House, with the item of &pound;64 paid to &lquo;Burbidge's players for <I>Othello</I>&rquo; in 1602,
the only one which concerns us here. I do not find that this paper is anywhere, early
in the controversy, specifically mentioned as spurious. Halliwell, to whose opinion as
to the genuineness of the five Bridgewater documents great weight is deservedly attached,
did not see this <I>Othello</I> item (Hamilton's <I>Inquiry</I>, p. 81), and although Hamilton, in
his <I>Inquiry</I> (p. 84), says that &lquo;these [five] documents are given in Appendix I,&rquo; yet
when we turn to Appendix I, this <I>Othello</I> item is not there, and it is stated (p. 109)
that there are <I>six</I> documents, and when we come to count them we find that there are,
in all, <I>seven</I> documents; and had the <I>Othello</I> item been given, there would have been
<I>eight.</I> I dare say this confusion, or discrepancy, is all my own, and shall accept with
equanimity any imputation on my editorial fidelity or capacity. I might as well con-
fess, at once, not merely to an indifference, but to an aversion, to all this discussion over
the authorship of these documents. It is one thing to prove a document a forgery, but
it is another, and a very different thing, to say who is the forger. The imputation of
dishonesty, and a motiveless dishonesty at that, cast upon one to whom every student
of dramatic history is under lasting obligations, is so painful that I have always avoided
the whole matter; and while ready to accept results, as to genuineness, arrived at by my
betters, must beg to be suffered to retain my private judgement as to the hand by which
the dishonesty was committed. While thus confessing that my reading has not been
<PB N=349>
<HE><I>DATE OF COMPOSITION</I> 349</HE>
<P>thorough, I wish it understood that, from what I have read, I have received the deep
impression that if these documents, and the MS corrections in F<SUB>2</SUB>, are forged, it was not
Collier who was guilty; he must have been the dupe, not the forger. In the department
of &lquo;the Collier controversy&rquo; my library is incomplete, and will remain so. I have felt
that this obtrusive personal reference is necessary to explain the omission of all discus-
sion as to the character, genuine or otherwise, of this reference by Collier to the per-
formance of <I>Othello</I> in 1602. <SC>Dyce</SC>, in his first edition (vol. i, p. lxix), quotes Collier,
but with a <I>caveat.</I> <SC>Staunton</SC> is more outspoken. In his Preface to <I>Othello</I>, alluding
to this Bridgewater item, he says, &lquo;the suspicion long entertained that the Shakespear-
ian documents in that collection are modern fabrications having now deepened almost
into certainty, the extract in question is of no historical value.&rquo; <SC>Halliwell</SC>, in his
Folio Edition (1865, vol. i, p. 188), while stating the questionable character of all the
Bridgewater documents, passes no judgement on the <I>Othello</I> item, because that one,
as he says, he had not seen. In his Preface to <I>Othello</I> in that same edition, he
passes it over in silence. <SC>Dyce</SC>, in his Second Edition (1866, vol. i, p. 77), quotes
Staunton's verdict, and adds, from Hardy's <I>Review of the Present State of the Shake-
spearian Controversy</I>, p. 60: &lquo;The writing, the ink, and the signature [of the paper
containing the <I>Othello</I> item] equally condemn it at once.&rquo; I can find no notice of it
in <SC>Halliwell-Phillipps's</SC> <I>Outlines of the Life of Shakespeare</I>, 1885, 5th edition.
<P>Here we must leave its further consideration, and turn to the Editors in chronolog-
ical order. The next in point of time is <SC>Grant White</SC>, who, in his First Edition, was
strongly influenced by Warburton's theory, and inclined to place the date in 1611.
&lquo;It seems impossible to avoid the conclusion that this passage [i. e., &lquo;our new heraldry
&lquo;&lquo;is hands, not hearts&rquo;] was written after the creation of the first baronets&rquo;; &lquo;although
&lquo;it is possible that the play was written before the creation, and that the allusion was
&lquo;introduced immediately afterwards, it is not probable.&rquo; Collier's Bridgewater docu-
ment has been &lquo;pronounced a forgery,&rquo; but even should it &lquo;prove genuine, the perform-
&lquo;ance of a play called <I>Othello</I> by &lquo;Burbidge's players,&rquo; in 1602, cannot, for reasons to
be presently given, be accepted as conclusive evidence that Shakespeare's tragedy was
&lquo;then written. As to the genuineness&rquo; of Cunningham's item from the Revels Account,
there can be no doubt; and &lquo;the probability seems strong that the play in question was
&lquo;Shakespeare's <I>Othello.</I> But is it certain? Not quite, in my opinion. It may have
&lquo;been a play founded on Giraldi Cinthio's story, and called <I>The Moor of Venice</I>, which
&lquo;was written by another playwright, and which, being the property of his company,
&lquo;Shakespeare afterwards entirely re-wrote, taking the names of Othello and Iago from
&lquo;the <I>History of the Prince of Denmark</I>, before mentioned. This supposition is so
&lquo;much in accordance with Shakespeare's practice, and the heraldic allusion before
&lquo;mentioned is entitled to such weight in the decision of the question, that, although
&lquo;there seems no sufficient ground for a fixed opinion upon the subject, I am inclined to
&lquo;place the date of the composition of this tragedy rather after 1611 than before that
&lquo;year. There is yet another fact which leads towards this conclusion. . . . . <I>Troilus
&lquo;and Cressida</I> and <I>Pericles</I> were published in 1609; and after a lapse of thirteen
&lquo;years without the appearance of one of Shakespeare's dramas from the press, this trag-
&lquo;edy was published in 1622, although there were then nineteen of no inferior rank
&lquo;among his works which were known to the public only upon the stage. Why this
&lquo;long interval passed thus unimproved by the dealers in dramatic literature, and why
&lquo;this play was chosen from among so many, to be published only a year before the
&lquo;appearance of the collected edition, (the intentions in regard to which could hardly
&lquo;have been unknown to the trade, or even to the public,) can only be a matter of very
<PB N=350>
<HE>350 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>&lquo;vague conjecture. We know that it was high in general favour; but I am inclined
&lquo;to the opinion that in addition to this claim upon a publisher's notice, it had also that
&lquo;of being one of its author's very latest productions. It certainly seems strange that
&lquo;after thirteen years had passed without the publication of one of Shakespeare's plays,
&lquo;during the first half of which period he produced works which were as well adapted for
&lquo;the press as any that had previously been issued, a publisher should go back at least
&lquo;eighteen years for one, which was the case if <I>The Moor of Venise</I> performed before King
&lquo;James, in 1604 was Shakespeare's <I>Othello</I>, in the only form in which it is known to us.&rquo;
<P>If there were in those days only one play called <I>The Moor of Venis</I>, and if the
heraldic allusion were not a later insertion, it was reserved for <SC>Sir Frederic Madden</SC>
to overthrow completely Warburton's date of 1611. Among the MSS in the British
Museum there is an account of the journey in England of Lewis Frederick, Prince of
Wirtemberg, in 1610, &lquo;which has been briefly penned in the French language by me,
Hans Jacob Wurmsser von Vendenheym.&rquo; In this journal Madden found the follow-
ing entry in the month of April: &lquo;Lundi, 30. S. E. alla au Globe lieu ordinaire ou l'on
joue les Commedies, y fut represent&eacute; l'histoire du More de Venise.&rquo;
<P><SC>Halliwell</SC> in his Folio edition, relying on the Revels Book, puts the date of com-
position &lquo;some time previously to November 1st, 1604,&rquo; and adds a reference to the per-
formance of the play seen by the Prince of Wirtemberg; and, &lquo;again, in an account of
&lquo;plays acted before Prince Charles, the Lady Elizabeth, and the Prince Palatine Elector,
&lquo;early in the year 1613, in both instances under its title of the &lquo;Moor of Venice.&rquo; . . . .
&lquo;The twelfth Public Act, which was passed in the first Parliament of James, some time
between March 19th and July 7th, 1604, was levelled &lquo;against conjuration, witch-
&lquo;&lquo;crafte, and dealinge with evill and wicked spirits.&rquo; [Cited by <SC>Grey</SC>, see I, iii, 76.]
&lquo;In the course of this Act it is enacted, that &lquo;if any person or persons shall, from and
&lquo;&lquo;after the feaste of Saint Michaell, the Archangell next comminge, take upon him or
&lquo;&lquo;them <I>by witchcrafte, inchantment, charme or sorcerie</I>, to tell or declare in what place
&lquo;&lquo;any treasure of golde or silver should or might be founde or had in the earth or other
&lquo;&lquo;secret places, or where goodes or thinges loste or stollen should be founde or become,
&lquo;&lquo;<I>or to the intent to provoke any person to unlawfull love</I>,&rquo; then such person or persons,
&lquo;if convicted, &lquo;shall for the said offence suffer imprisonment by the space of one whole
&lquo;&lquo;yere without baile or maineprise, and once in everie quarter of saide yere shall, in some
&lquo;&lquo;markett towne upon the markett day, or at such tyme as any faire shal be kepte there,
&lquo;&lquo;stande openlie upon the pillorie by the space of sixe houres, and there shall openlie
&lquo;&lquo;confesse his or her error and offence.&rquo; It seems probable that part of the First Act
&lquo;of <I>Othello</I> would not have assumed the form it does, had not the author been familiar
&lquo;with the statute, in common with the public of the day, the Duke referring to such
&lquo;a Law when he tells Brabantio, that his accusation of the employment of witchcraft
&lquo;shall be impartially investigated. If this be the case, the date of the composition of
&lquo;this tragedy may be positively assigned to the year 1604.&rquo; To this note Halliwell-
Phillipps adds in his <I>Outlines</I>, &amp;c., 5th ed., p. 541: &lquo;Although the offence named in
&lquo;the statute refers not to the use of charms to make people love one another, but to the
&lquo;employment of them for the provocation of unlawful love, yet still this may be said to
&lquo;have an oblique application to the story of the tragedy in the surreptitious marriage of
&lquo;Othello. By the Act of James, a previous one, 5 Eliz. c. 16, of a similar character
&lquo;was &lquo;utterlie&rquo; repealed, and the object of the second Act appears to have been to
&lquo;punish the same offence more severely.&rquo; [The existence of an Act of a &lquo;similar
character&rquo; already in force, somewhat weakens this argument, as it seems to me.]
<P>In a note on III, iii, 183: &lquo;Who steals my purse steals trash,&rquo; Halliwell observes

<P>&lquo;This is imitated by one J. M. in an unpublished manuscript, &lquo;<I>The Newe Metamor-

This imitation would give the date of the play to an earlier period than is stated

<P><SC>Staunton</SC> in his note on the same passage cites this reference of Halliwell, and
adds: &lquo;But the reflection is sufficiently trite, and in both instances, as in many others
&lquo;where it occurs, was probably founded&rquo; on passages in <I>Homily</I> XI, pt. 2, <I>Homily</I> XII,
pt. 1. <SC>Halliwell-Phillipps</SC> (<I>Outlines</I>, p. 163, first ed.) now pronounces the passage

&lquo;on the title-page of that poem, the manuscript itself contains a distinct allusion by name
&lquo;to Speed's <I>Theatre of Great Britaine</I>, a work first published in 1611.&rquo; (For a fuller

<P>In 1868, <I>The Athen&aelig;um</I> (20th of June) announced a painful discovery in connection
with the Revels Books, edited for <I>The Shakespeare Society</I> by Cunningham. In <I>The
Galaxy</I> of November following, the story of the discovery was re-told by <SC>Grant White</SC>
with fuller details, which he had &lquo;learned from authentic sources.&rquo; It is substantially
as follows: &lquo;The story about the finding of the Revels Book had passed out of mind,
&lquo;though not out of memory, when about three months ago an oldish man, broken down
&lquo;by hard drinking, appeared at the British Museum and presented for sale an old manu-
&lquo;script volume, which contained, he said, records of much value about the early English
drama, and which &lquo;his friend, Mr Collier, said was worth sixty guineas.&rquo; It was Peter
Cunningham, and the volume was that one of the &lquo;Revels Accounts,&rquo; which contained
the record of the performance of nine plays by Mr Shaxberd. The volume was retained
for examination before purchase, was found to be public property, and was, of course,
held as such. So interesting a volume attracted at once the attention of the experts
of the Audit Office, and they at once discovered that, although the book was genuine,
that part of it which was of greater interest than all the rest, the leaves containing the
&lquo;record of the performance of Shakespeare's plays, was a forgery, a gross forgery from
&lquo;beginning to end. Mr Duffus Hardy, of the Rolls Court, than whom there is no better
&lquo;authority in England, not excepting Sir Frederic Madden himself, so pronounces it,
&lquo;and so do the distinguished Shakespearian scholars, the Rev Alexander Dyce and Mr
&lquo;J. O. Halliwell, although they have founded part of their editorial labours upon it.....
&lquo;It is to be remarked, that the important entries are made upon two leaves lying loose
&lquo;in the volume, and that these leaves, and these only of all the volume, have in the
&lquo;margin the names of the writers of the plays. There is other writing upon the mar-
&lquo;gins, usually mere index words for convenience of reference; but here only in the
&lquo;course of thirteen books, which when put into print make two hundred and twenty-
&lquo;six octavo pages, is the name of the author of a play, mask, or interlude given. This
&lquo;circumstance in itself, of which no notice seems to have been taken, casts great sus
<PB N=352>
<HE>352 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>&lquo;picion upon the pages on which these records appear, and when it is found that they
&lquo;are loose and were never bound into the volume, suspicion approaches certainty. But
&lquo;the evidence of the writing itself is said to settle the question at once for any person
&lquo;familiar with old manuscript.....And now who is the forger? The conclusion that
&lquo;Peter Cunningham is the man seems unavoidable.&rquo;
<P>From an Article in <I>The British Quarterly Review</I> of January, 1869, we learn, in
reference to this MS volume which Cunningham offered to the British Museum, that
&lquo;it only required a glance of the experts to discover that the list of Shakespeare's plays
&lquo;performed before the Court in the years alluded to, had been appended to the old doc-
&lquo;uments by a modern hand. The trifling and uninteresting items of expenditure are
&lquo;genuine, but the book containing these appears to have also contained some blank
&lquo;pages, into which the forger has crammed the whole of the writings referring to
&lquo;Shakespeare.&rquo;
<P>But the mystery connected with these entries in the Revels Book by no means ends
here. Recent revelations have shown that Malone was right when he said that he
knew <I>Othello</I> was acted in 1604; and the proof of this knowledge, which Boswell
failed to find, has been discovered, and it turns out to be this very list, which, or a copy
of it, Cunningham is accused of forging in 1842. These revelations are made in that
inestimable volume, for which too much gratitude to the author cannot be shown, espe-
cially by us Americans, debarred as we are from all access to original records, the <I>Out-
lines of the Life of Shakespeare</I>, by Halliwell-Phillipps. From the Fifth Edition, 1885,
p. 607, I quote the following:
<P>&lquo;There are substantial reasons for believing, that although the manuscript [of the
&lquo;pages of Cunningham's Revels Book] itself is spurious, the information which it yields
&lquo;is genuine.
<P>&lquo;In the year 1791 Sir William Musgrave, the First Commissioner of the Board of
&lquo;Audit, made arrangements for Malone's inspection of the ancient manuscripts then in
&lquo;his office, these including what he termed &lquo;records of the Master of the Revels for
&lquo;&lquo;1604 and 1605.&rquo; These facts are derived from explicit notes that will be found in
&lquo;the Variorum Shakespeare, ed. 1821, iii, 361, 363. That Malone availed himself of
&lquo;the opportunity, and visited Somerset House for the express purpose of examining
&lquo;the whole collection of the documents that pertained to the Office of the Revels, is
&lquo;evident from his own statement in the work just quoted, iii, 361; and amongst the
&lquo;papers that came with that portion of his library which was added to the treasures of
&lquo;the Bodleian in 1821 is a leaf which contains the following memoranda no clue, how-
&lquo;ever, being given to the source whence they were derived:&mdash;&lquo;1604 &amp; 1605&mdash;Ed<SUP>d</SUP>.
&lquo;&lquo;Tylney&mdash;Sunday after Hallowmas&mdash;Merry Wyves of Windsor perf<SUP>d</SUP> by the K's play-
&lquo;&lquo;ers&mdash;Hallamas&mdash;in the Banquetting ho<SUP>s</SUP>. at Whitehall the Moor of Venis&mdash;perf<SUP>d</SUP>. by
&lquo;&lquo;the K's players&mdash;on S<SUP>t</SUP>. Stephens Night&mdash;Mesure for Mesur by Shaxberd&rquo;&rquo; [as in the
case of the Revels Book, only so much is cited here as applies to <I>Othello</I> and Shax-
berd].
<P>&lquo;Although the contents of this leaf are not in Malone's handwriting, there is no
&lquo;doubt whatever that it belonged to his collection of materials, it being one with others
&lquo;of an analogous character that were in a loose bundle of scraps which formed part of
&lquo;the original gift to the Bodleian, and had remained uncatalogued and inaccessible to
&lquo;students until they were bound in recent years under the direction of Mr H. S. Har-
&lquo;per, one of the officials of that library. The leaf containing the abridged transcript
&lquo;just given is now preserved in MS. Mal. 29; and Mr Harper, who well recollects
arranging the papers for the formation of that volume, assures me that there is no
<PB N=353>
<HE><I>DATE OF COMPOSITION</I> 353</HE>
<P>&lquo;possibility of any of its contents having been acquired subsequently to the reception
&lquo;of the Malone Collection in 1821. There is nothing either in the character of the
&lquo;handwriting or in the form of the transcript, to justify the faintest suspicion that it is
&lquo;in itself a forgery. It has, on the contrary, every indication of being a faithful abridge-
&lquo;ment, sent most probably to Malone from the Audit Office, of the list which was
&lquo;printed in 1842. There now arises the crucial enquiry for the period at which
&lquo;Malone became acquainted with the information yielded by that list, for, unless he
&lquo;met with the latter for the first time nearly at the end of his career, it is incredible
&lquo;that he should have accepted the genuineness of any of its important details without
&lquo;a personal examination of the original. Such an assumption is incompatible with the
&lquo;numerous traces of the unwonted assiduity that pervaded his Shakespearian researches.
&lquo;Now, although there is at present no direct evidence of the fact, the little that is known
&lquo;favours the belief that he was in possession of the contents of the existing forgery
&lquo;within a few years after his invitation to the Audit Office in 1791, while nothing has
&lquo;been produced which is in the slightest degree inconsistent with that opinion. Let
&lquo;the following intimations be carefully weighed: The material novelties that are intro-
&lquo;duced into that forgery are restricted to the dates therein given of the performances
&lquo;of <I>Othello</I> and <I>Measure for Measure</I>, and the entries respecting these are the only
&lquo;items which Malone would have been absolutely compelled to notice in his disserta-
&lquo;tion on the order of Shakespeare's plays. With respect to the first, he took the new
&lquo;chronological fact for granted when he made the following decisive statement,&mdash;&lquo;we
&lquo;&lquo;<I>know</I> it (<I>Othello</I>) was acted in 1604, and I have therefore placed it in that year,&rquo;&mdash;
&lquo;important words that were penned before his death in 1812 (<I>Variorum Shakespeare</I>,
&lquo;ed. 1821, ii, 404); and there can hardly be a reasonable doubt that he was relying on
&lquo;the same testimony when he observed in another work: &lquo;I formerly thought that
&lquo;&lquo;<I>Othello</I> was one of our great dramatic poet's latest compositions, but I now know,
&lquo;&lquo;from indisputable evidence, that was not the case&rquo;&mdash;note to a passage in Dryden's
&lquo;<I>Grounds of Criticism</I>, ed. 1800, pp. 258, 259. If the former work, the Variorum of
&lquo;1821, had not been impaired by the disadvantages attending its posthumous com-
&lquo;pilation, it being the product of Malone's imperfectly revised text and essays, the con-
&lquo;firmation of his assertion respecting the date of the tragedy would no doubt have been
&lquo;given; and to the same unfortunate accident must be imputed the circumstance of his
&lquo;observations on the date of <I>Measure for Measure</I> in that edition being a mere reprint
&lquo;of those which had appeared in 1790. It is altogether impossible that so experienceo
&lquo;a record-student as Malone could have been even transiently deceived by the forgery
&lquo;now in existence, while the character of its ink encourages the suspicion that it could
&lquo;not have been perpetrated until long after his death in 1812. The latter opinion is to
&lquo;some extent supported by its entries not belonging to the more graphic species of lite-
&lquo;rary frauds that were current before that period. Then there is the extreme improb-
&lquo;ability that Malone should have lighted upon two documents, each of them yielding
&lquo;the unexpected information of the early date of <I>Othello</I>, while his acknowledged rigid
&lquo;integrity excludes the very thought that he would have been accessory to a deception
&lquo;in the matter. It may, therefore, on the whole, be fairly presumed that he had access
&lquo;in or before 1800 to a genuine manuscript that included in some form the entries that
&lquo;are given in the abridged transcript; for we may feel sure that he would never have
&lquo;used the words &lquo;indisputable evidence&rquo; in respect to one of them until he had made
&lquo;a personal scrutiny of the original, even if his residence had not been, as it was, within
&lquo;less than an hour's walk from the Audit Office. There appears to be only one solution
&lquo;that reconciles all the known facts of the case. It is that the forger had met with,
<PB N=354>
<HE>354 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>&lquo;and reproduced in a simulated form, trustworthy extracts from a genuine record that
&lquo;had disappeared from that Office. This view of the case is essentially supported by
&lquo;what is, in respect to the present inquiry, the important discovery at Hatfield of the
&lquo;note of Sir Walter Cope, which mentions the revival of <I>Love's Labour's Lost</I> by the
&lquo;King's Company in or shortly before January, 1605, an evidence that could not have
&lquo;been known to the imposter, and one of a fact that would have been beyond even the
&lquo;remote probability of a successful conjecture. On the other hand, with the single excep-
&lquo;tion of the day assigned for the performance of that comedy, there are no questionable
&lquo;indications of any kind in the contents of the fabricated list, nothing that cannot be either
&lquo;explained or corroborated. The only other feature that could really justify a suspicion
&lquo;is the quaint orthography of the poet's name, but this no doubt is to be ascribed to the
&lquo;illiteracy of the original scribe; and it may be added that similar forms were in pro-
&lquo;vincial use, e. g., <I>Shaxber</I>, Chapel-lane deed, 1572, and Stratford MS., 1704; <I>Shax-
&lquo;bere</I>, Henley-street conveyance, 1573; <I>Shaxbeer</I>, Stratford MS., 1737.&rquo; [Halliwell-
Phillipps here gives six confirmatory facts of the performance of the plays from the
accounts of the <I>Treasurer of the Chambers</I>, and two for the performance of the maskes
from Winwood's <I>Memorials;</I> four of these confirmatory facts from the accounts of the
Treasurer of the Chambers, Cunningham also reprinted in the Preface to his Revels
Books, pp. xxxvi, xxxvii. Halliwell-Phillipps then continues]: &lquo;It would appear from
&lquo;these notices either that the fabricator had not before him a complete list of the plays
&lquo;that had been acted, or that he intentionally omitted a number of entries. Whatever
&lquo;may have been the exact nature of his proceedings, it is certain that the particulars
&lquo;of the forgery were not based upon the defective information given in the official
&lquo;accounts of the <I>Treasurer of the Chambers.</I> If that had been the case, it would be
&lquo;necessary to assume that he went recklessly out of his way to insert a fictitious notice
&lquo;of a performance on a day that was not sanctioned by those accounts, the high proba-
&lquo;bility of the accuracy of that solitary discrepancy having, moreover, been lately revealed
&lquo;by the discovery of an evidence to which he could not have had access. This singular
&lquo;coincidence may fairly be held to outweigh the suspicion attending the omission in the
&lquo;Treasurer's ledger, an oversight of a very unusual character, and yet an error infinitely
&lquo;more likely to occur than the preternatural ratification of what would have been by
&lquo;itself an extravagant conjecture. Upon a balance of probabilities there can thus
&lquo;hardly be a doubt that <I>Love's Labour's Lost</I> was revived at Court very early in Janu-
&lquo;ary of 1605 in a representation that was not honoured by the presence of the Queen.
&lquo;When, therefore, a play was to be selected almost immediately afterwards for the
&lquo;entertainment of Her Majesty at Lord Southampton's, it was natural that Burbadge,
&lquo;who had only one day's notice of the intended performance, should have recom-
&lquo;mended a drama which his company had just then in hand, and which at the same
&lquo;time would have been a novelty to the only spectator whose approval was regarded.&rquo;
<P><SC>Ward</SC>, whose valuable <I>History of English Dramatic Literature</I> preceded Halli-
well-Phillipps's discovery of Malone's transcript, says: According to internal evidence
of character and manner there can be no difficulty in assigning to this play a date not
far removed from those of <I>Macbeth</I> and <I>Lear</I>, a conclusion fairly supported by the
&lquo;tests&rquo; of versification. No trustworthy external evidence exists as to the date of
<I>Othello</I>, unless importance be attached to the [passage in <I>The Newe Metamorphosis</I>,
cited by Halliwell. But Halliwell, as we have seen, subsequently withdrew all belief
in its critical value].
<P><SC>Hudson</SC>, on the strength of the performances before the Duke of Wirtemberg in 1610,
and before Prince Charles in 1613, from Burbadge's Elegy (see <I>post</I>), and from the lack
<PB N=355>
<HE><I>DATE OF COMPOSITION</I> 355</HE>
<P>of other authentic contemporary notices, is inclined to give a late date, either 1609 or
early in 1610. &lquo;And the internal evidence of style and manner is, I think, in entire
&lquo;harmony with that conclusion; the diction, versification, and psychologic inwardness
&lquo;being such as to speak it into close chronological neighbourhood with <I>Cymbeline</I> and
&lquo;<I>Coriolanus.</I>&rquo;
<P>In the <I>New Shakspere Society's Transactions</I>, 1874, p. 10, <SC>Fleay</SC>, by the application
of <I>Metrical Tests</I>, puts the date of <I>Othello</I> as 1605, and <I>Ib.</I>, p. 450, <SC>Ingram</SC>, in his tabula-
tion of the Plays according to the <I>Numbers of Light and Weak Endings</I>, gives <I>Othello</I>
the Twenty-first place, between <I>Julius C&aelig;sar</I> and <I>Lear.</I>
<P><SC>Dowden</SC> (<I>Shakspere, His Mind and Art</I>, p. 223): Around the year 1600 are
grouped some of the most mirthful comedies that Shakspere ever wrote. Then a little
later, as soon as <I>Hamlet</I> is completed, all changes. From 1604 to 1610 a show of tragic
figures, like the kings who passed before Macbeth, filled the vision of Shakspere.....
During these years the imaginative fervour of Shakspere was at its highest, and sus-
tained itself without abatement. There was no feverish excitement in his energy, and
there was no pause.....During a certain brief season it may have been that Shak-
spere altogether ceased to write for the stage. But now in unbroken series, year by
year, one great tragedy succeeds another. Having created <I>Othello</I>, surely the eye of a
poet's mind would demand quietude, passive acceptance of some calm beauty, a period
of restoration. But <I>Othello</I> is pursued by <I>Lear, Lear</I> by <I>Macbeth, Macbeth</I> by <I>Antony
and Cleopatra, Antony and Cleopatra</I> by <I>Coriolanus.</I>
<P>The <SC>Cambridge Editors</SC> were, I think, the first to call attention to &lquo;many oaths
and expletives&rquo; in Q<SUB>1</SUB> (see <I>Text</I>, p. 342) which, in all the later editions, are altered or
omitted. &lquo;This shows,&rquo; they continue, &lquo;that the MS. from which it was printed had
&lquo;not been recently used as an acting copy.&rquo; (From which I infer that they would
throw back the date of composition to the early years of the century.)
<P><SC>Knight</SC> had noticed long ago this difference in one particular passage between the
Folio and Quarto (see I, i, 4), and had conjectured therefrom that the First Quarto was
written before the passage of the Statute 3 Jac., 1605, against profanity on the stage.
<P><SC>Furnivall</SC> places it in Shakspere's <SC>Third Period</SC> (1601-1608), as a companion to
<I>Macbeth</I> in <I>The Tempter-yielding Group</I>, with the date (? 1604).
<P><SC>Rolfe</SC> groups this play with <I>Lear</I> and <I>Macbeth</I>, &lquo;when Shakespeare was in the full
maturity of his powers.&rquo;
<P><SC>Grant White's</SC> latest conclusion is that while the allusion to the &lquo;new heraldry&rquo;
points to 1611, we have an authentic record of its performance in April, 1610. &lquo;It is
&lquo;more than possible, then, that the tragedy was originally written before 1606 (in 1605
&lquo;or 1604), and that it afterwards received additions on some special occasions.&rquo;
<P>If &lquo;time will unfold what plighted cunning hides,&rquo; we need but cross our hands and
wait. (Will not a few shreds of Shakespeare's mantle suffice to cover me, if, patterned by
his fondness for quibbles, I suggest that &lquo;time will unfold what plighted Cunningham
hides&rquo;?) Nothing else but time, I fear, will ever solve the mystery of these forged
leaves in the Revels Book. That they are forged is a settled fact. But, unlike other
forgeries, their substance is genuine. Their items are all authenticated by extrinsic
evidence. The rough transcript found by Halliwell-Phillipps among Malone's papers
repeats every item, except three, word for word. If this transcript is a true copy from
a genuine original, then are Cunningham's pages a true copy from the same; and, as
we have seen, in Malone's transcript Halliwell-Phillipps puts entire faith. When a
scholar so learned and so cautious leads the way, ought we not to follow? Were we
all to trust ourselves unreservedly to his guidance, it is doubtful if Shakespearian liter-
<PB N=356>
<HE>356 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>ature would ever receive a single harmful bias &lquo;down the ringing grooves of change.&rquo;
Yet, at the same time, may we not be permitted, just by way of showing off an inde-
pendence which we do not possess, to scrutinize somewhat closely for a minute or two
that same transcript of Malone?
<P>One argument in favour of its being a draft from a genuine original, which has great
weight with Halliwell-Phillipps, is that Malone said he <I>knew Othello</I> was acted in 1604,
which he would not have said without the fullest documentary proof, such proof as an
inspection of the original would alone have afforded. We all know how thoroughly
trustworthy Malone is, and nothing can be farther from my intention than to impugn
his accuracy; and yet, although it is not likely, it is not inconceivable that Malone's
knowledge extended no farther than to this rough transcript. Malone had the
same confidence in Sir William Musgrave that we all have in Malone, and if Sir
William had sent the transcript to him as a memorandum of a document awaiting his
inspection, it is perfectly consistent with honesty that Malone should refer to the con-
tents of this transcript as &lquo;known&rquo; even before he had examined the original, or even
if he had never examined the original. Granting that this transcript came from Som-
erset House, (and it is not easy to see whence else it could have come,) Malone would
not hesitate on the strength of it to believe in the existence of the original document.
Indeed my supposition receives some faint colour from a letter of Malone to Sir Wil-
liam Musgrave in my possession. In it Malone says: &lquo;I mean to print Queen Eliza-
beth's letter to Lady Paget as it stands in <I>Nichols's Progresses</I>, copied from a MS of
Dr Birch in the Museum; surely there can be no harm in saying that the original <I>is
still extant.</I>&rquo; (The Italics are Malone's.) I also happen to have Sir William Mus-
grave's reply to this very letter, in which he shows more caution than Malone, for he
says: &lquo;I certainly have not any objection against your saying, &ldquo;That you have been
informed that the original is still extant.&rdquo;&rquo; Although this correspondence refers to facts
which it was necessary to keep secret, and therein is somewhat removed from ordinary
cases, yet it is, perhaps, worth citing, as showing that Malone, like all the rest of us,
was willing to accept as fact that which was known to be such by one in whom he had
an absolute trust. Do we not all accept <I>The Outlines of the Life of Shakespeare</I> in
the same faith? What the original document could have been from which this rough
transcript was taken, it is hard to imagine. I do not see how it could have belonged
to the Accounts either of the Treasurer of the Chambers or of the Master of the Revels.
The fact that it gives the names of the authors of the plays renders it wholly unlike
either; it is anomalous in that regard. Could it have been the hasty memorandum of the
Revels accountant, from which he intended afterwards to fill out his books, and for that
purpose left the blank pages subsequently utilized by Cunningham; who, having found
the memorandum, fulfilled the long-neglected duty, and then destroyed the original?
But these imaginings are idle, and particularly idle in one as ignorant in such matters
as myself. It was the mistrust in this transcript of Malone, written in an unknown
hand, of an unknown date, from an unknown source, save that it was among Malone's
papers, and unknown, apparently, even to Boswell, that led me to give as large a space
as I did to Halliwell-Phillipps's defence of it, which, be it distinctly remembered, is
based mainly on Sir Walter Cope's notice of the revival of <I>Love's Labour's Lost.</I>
<P>In dealing with questions like this of the date of the composition of a play, it seems
to me that it is of the first moment to keep before us the end and aim which gives the
subject its importance; we ought to adjust our lines of perspective and so arrange our
objects in view that each shall have its true relative value, and that we be not in danger
of confounding nearness with magnitude or importance. Every one has a right to select
<PB N=357>
<HE><I>DATE OF THE ACTION</I> 357</HE>
<P>his vanishing-point, and arrange his lines as suit him best; to me it is a great charm in
the study of Shakespeare that the number of points from which that myriad-minded
man can be studied are as myriad as his mind. If we are searching for the facts of
his outward life, then the days and months and years when he wrote his plays are of
essential importance. But if the outward conditions of his muddy vesture of decay do
not attract us, and we are straining to catch sound of immortal harmony, what profit
to us then is there in tides and times? Would a year or two, one way or the other,
in the composition of <I>Othello</I>, or a dozen years, for that matter, bring us any nearer to a
knowledge of the Moor? Would a single throb be added to Romeo's last farewell to
Juliet if we knew the very day, or the very hour of the day, when Shakespeare wrote
the scene? We must beware that we do not confound in any question like this, the
essential and the accidental. Does the history of the Koh-i-nor add one doit to its
value or one tint to its rays? It is not the knowledge that it was written in 1604 or in
1704 that fills our theatres when <I>Othello</I> is on the stage.
<P>Accepting the date of 1604, I began with a reliance on time, and a trust in Halli-
well-Phillipps; there we may safely remain, &lquo;enshelter'd and embay'd.&rquo;

<P><SC>Malone</SC> (Note on II, i, 1): All the modern editors following Rowe have supposed
the capital of Cyprus to be the place where the scene of <I>Othello</I> lies during the last four
Acts, but this could not have been Shakespeare's intention; <I>Nicosia</I>, the capital city
of Cyprus, being situated nearly in the centre of the island, and thirty miles distant
from the sea. The principal sea-port town of Cyprus was <I>Famagusta</I>, where there was
formerly a strong fort and commodious haven,&mdash;the only one of any magnitude in the
island; and there undoubtedly the scene should be placed. &lquo;Neere unto the haven
(says Knolles), standeth an old <I>castle</I>, with four towers after the ancient manner of
building.&rquo; To this castle we find Othello presently repairs.
<P>It is observable that Cinthio, whose novels were first published in 1565, makes no
mention of any attack being made on Cyprus by the Turks. From our poet's having
mentioned the preparations against this island, which they first assaulted and took from
the Venetians in 1570, we may suppose that he intended that year as the era of his
tragedy; but by mentioning Rhodes as also likely to be assaulted by the Turks, he has
fallen into an historical inconsistency, for they were then in quiet possession of that
island, of which they became masters in December, 1522; and if, to evade this diffi-
culty, we refer <I>Othello</I> to an era prior to that year, there will be an equal incongruity;
for from 1473, when the Venetians first became possessed of Cyprus, to 1522, they had
not been molested by any Turkish armament.
<P><SC>Reed</SC>: The time of this play may be ascertained from the following circumstances
Selymus the Second formed his design against Cyprus in 1569, and took it in 1571.
This was the only attempt the Turks ever made upon that island after it came into the
hands of the Venetians (which was in the year 1473), wherefore the time must fall in
with some part of that interval. We learn from the play that there was a junction of
the Turkish fleet at Rhodes in order for the invasion of Cyprus; that it first came sail-
ing towards Cyprus, then went to Rhodes, there met another squadron, and then re-
sumed its way to Cyprus. These are real historical facts which happened when Mus-
tapha, Selymus's general, attacked Cyprus in May, 1570, which, therefore, is the true
period of this performance. (See Knolles's <I>History of the Turks</I>, pp. 838, 846, 867.)
<PB N=358>
<HE>358 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P><SC>Knight</SC>: The Republic of Venice became the virtual sovereign of Cyprus in 1471,
when it assumed the guardianship of the son of Catharine Cornaro, who, being left a
widow, wanted the protection of the Republic to maintain the power which her husband
had usurped. The island was then first garrisoned by Venetian troops. Catharine, in
1489, abdicated the sovereignty in favour of the Republic. Cyprus was retained by
the Venetians till 1570, when it was invaded by a powerful Turkish force, and was
finally subjected to the dominion of Selim II in 1571. From that period it has formed
[until it was acquired a few years ago by England] a part of the Turkish Empire.
Nicosia, the inland capital of the island, was taken by storm; and Famagusta, the
principal sea-port, capitulated after a long and gallant defence. It is evident, there-
fore, that we must refer the action of <I>Othello</I> to a period before the subjugation of
Cyprus by the Turks. The locality of the scenes after the First Act must be at Fama-
gusta, which was strongly fortified,&mdash;a fact which Shakespeare must have known, when
in III, ii, Othello says: &lquo;I will be walking on the <I>works.</I>&rquo;
<P><SC>Staunton</SC> gives a long extract from Knolles's <I>History</I> narrating the &lquo;circumstances
originating the siege of Nicosia, &ldquo;the chief and richest citie of all the Island,&rdquo; and the
ultimate conquest of Cyprus by the Turk, (for there was no &ldquo;segregation of the Turk-
ish fleet&rdquo; as the play supposes,) of which the most important, it might be said the only
important, items, (and Italicized by Staunton,) are as follows: &lquo;For Mustapha, author of
that expedition, had before appointed Piall Bassa at a time prefixed <I>to meet him at the
Rhodes, and that he that came first should tarrie for the other, that so they might
together saile into Cyprus.</I>&rquo; And again: &lquo;The whole fleet at that time consisted of <I>two
hundred galleys</I>, amongst whom were diverse galliots,&rquo; &amp;c.
<SHL>
<C>DURATION OF THE ACTION</C>
<P><SC>Shakespeare's</SC> art in dealing with Time was first noticed by <SC>Halpin</SC> and Professor
<SC>Wilson</SC>, and was referred to in the Preface of <I>Hamlet</I>, where is given a brief exposition
of their views. According to Professor Wilson, Shakespeare counts off days and hours,
as it were, by two clocks, on one of which the true Historic Time is recorded, and on
the other the Dramatic Time, or a false show of time, whereby days, weeks, and months
may be to the utmost contracted. It is as though the hour-hand pointed to historic
time, while the minute-hand, recording fresh sensations with every swing of the pendu-
lum, tells dramatic time. While the former has traveled from one figure to another,
the latter has traversed the whole twelve, and is true to the hour when the hammer
falls. We know that but an hour has passed, and yet, following the minute-hand, we
have lived through the whole twelve. In no one way, it is submitted, does Shake-
speare show more emphatically than in this, that he wrote his plays to be heard and
not read. In the theatre no trace is noted of this art, or even trick (be it respectfully
termed); while on the printed page it may be detected in almost every Scene. In no
play is this glamour carried to greater lengths than in <I>Othello.</I> That Desdemona
should be murdered within thirty-six hours after landing in Cyprus is what no spec-
tator of the play can readily believe; and yet to the reader of the tragedy this headlong
speed is so real that it was proclaimed two hundred years ago by Rymer, who hissed
and cackled over what he considered an absurdity so glaring, that he believed the
exposure would forever disgrace and dethrone Shakespeare. Perhaps it is well that
Professor Wilson did not know in whose footsteps he was unconsciously treading&mdash;but
to what a different goal!
<PB N=359>
<HE><I>DURATION OF THE ACTION</I> 359</HE>
<P>Whilst this legerdemain in regard to dramatic or llusory time is thus pronounced in
<I>Othello</I>, in scarcely any other is the historic or real time more clearly noted. We can
follow the characters through each day, nay, we can discover even the very days of the
week, and that Othello landed in Cyprus on Saturday afternoon.
<P>In the foregoing pages no notes in regard to this question of time have been included,
except one or two here and there, enough to recall to the student's memory that such a
question exists, and should be borne in mind.
<P>It is but fair to say, at the outset, that there are not wanting good scholars who deny
this theory of Double Time, and who variously interpret the allusions which Halpin
and Wilson consider indications of it. It will be, of course, my endeavour duly to set
forth their opposition; but, for the present, let the correctness of the theory be assumed,
and let it be taken for granted that here, in <I>Othello</I>, Shakespeare has interwoven two
different computations of time, the historical or real, the dramatic or illusory.
<P>I propose first to note the passages which point to <I>Historic Time</I>, and as briefly as
possible; the whole play is at hand and compression is obligatory.
<P>The drama opens at night. Within an hour after the council is adjourned, Othello
and Desdemona start for Cyprus. This night we may fancifully call the <I>First Day.</I>
<P>How long the voyage from Venice to Cyprus lasts, we have no means of knowing.
The distance was great, thirteen or fourteen hundred miles, and the labouring barks
were slow and delayed by a tempest; ten days or a fortnight is none too long. Iago's
arrival anticipated Cassio's expectation by a <I>se'en nights' speed.</I> The desperate tem-
pest had lasted during the night, when the wind-shak'd surge had seemed to cast
water on the burning Bear; it had evidently cleared up in the afternoon, and the a&euml;rial
blue appeared. The afternoon was Saturday. At five o'clock the Herald announced
that, upon certain tidings <I>now arrived</I> of the perdition of the Turkish fleet, there was
to be sport and revels till the bell have tolled eleven. Othello tells Cassio to look to
the guard <I>to-night</I>, and before ten o'clock Iago has begun his temptation of Cassio,
from which hour the action steadily proceeds through the night, until Cassio, after his
disgrace, resolves to beseech the virtuous Desdemona to undertake for him betimes in
the morning. Although on parting Iago wishes him good-night, yet the day was break-
ing, and Cassio did not go to bed. As soon as he thinks Emilia is stirring, he appears
before Othello's dwelling with some musicians, to give his General the good-morrow
customary on the morning after marriage.
<P>This is the beginning of the <I>Second Day</I>, and in Cyprus, and Sunday.
<P>Emilia admits Cassio, and promises to bestow him where he should have time to
speak his bosom freely to Desdemona. The great Third Scene of the Third Act opens
with this interview between Desdemona and Cassio; which is broken off by the return of
Othello, with Iago, from an inspection of the works; the gentle lady intercedes for the
disgraced Lieutenant, and here we learn the days of the week: &lquo;<I>Des.</I> Good love, call him
&lquo;back. <I>Oth.</I> Not now, sweet Desdemona, some other time. <I>Des.</I> But shall't be shortly?
&lquo;<I>Oth.</I> The sooner, sweet, for you. <I>Des.</I> Shall't be to-night [Sunday], at supper? <I>Oth.</I>
&lquo;No, not to-night. <I>Des.</I> To-morrow [Monday] dinner then? <I>Oth.</I> I shall not dine at
&lquo;home; I meet the Captains at the citadel. <I>Des.</I> Why then to-morrow [Monday] night,
&lquo;on Tuesday morn. On Tuesday noon or night, on Wednesday morn. I prithee thee
name the time, but let it not exceed three days.&rquo;
<P>Before this scene closes Othello has become Iago's victim, and withdraws to furnish
nimself with some swift means of death for Desdemona, but first he wishes to discover
the truth of Iago's assertion that Cassio has the handkerchief; to Desdemona he there-
fore goes at once. That Othello goes instantly to Desdemona, I infer not only from
<PB N=360>
<HE>360 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>the eternal fitness of things, (he never could have been in her company one minute
without resolving his doubts), but also from his <I>Aside</I> when he first greets her: &lquo;Oh
hardness to dissemble!&rquo; This is his first attempt at dissembling, therefore the first time
that he had seen her. He finds that the handkerchief is gone, and leaves her in fury.
Cassio sees Bianca and promises to call on her that evening, which is of course Sunday
evening, and with this interview between Cassio and Bianca the Third Act closes.
<P>The only chance thus far, it seems to me, for any time to elapse is between the close
of the Third and the beginning of the Fourth Act. I was at one time in great hopes
that at least some days could be wedged in here, especially since the conversation, with
which the Act opens, between Iago and Othello is not only general in its character, as
though they were discussing some abstract question of morality, but Othello had actually
forgotten all about the handkerchief. I was the victim of Shakespeare's art, and two
little words of Bianca's bind the two Acts together as one in point of time. Bianca
asks Cassio what he meant by that same handkerchief which he gave her <I>even now;</I>
so that we are still in Sunday, in the afternoon, after the generous islanders invited by
Othello had had their dinner. Bianca repeats her invitation to Cassio to come to supper
<I>to-night.</I> To supper likewise Othello invites Lodovico, who arrives from Venice before
this Scene closes. Before the next Scene closes the trumpets summon to this very
supper. After Bianca's supper Cassio is wounded, and after the supper to the Vene-
tian Ambassadors, Desdemona is smothered,&mdash;<I>on Sunday night, within</I> thirty-six hours
after her arrival in Cyprus.
<P>The indications of <I>Dramatic Time</I> are not so easily enumerated; they are often mere
hints, vanishing touches, leaving an impression not by their force, but by their frequent
and varied repetition.
<P>It is not till the Moor is caught in the whirlwind of passion raised by Iago that any
necessity arises for these hints of Protracted Time. But, when once caught up, it is
of the utmost necessity that the action should drive ahead in storm; one minute's calm
would explain everything; yet the delusion must be complete that Othello's passion is
of gradual growth. Before our eyes it must be made to pass through all stages of devel-
opment. In the First Act, therefore, there are but few indications, that I can detect,
of this Dramatic Time. There are one or two towards the close of it, where Iago tells
Roderigo that &lquo;It cannot be that Desdemona should long continue her love to the
Moor, nor he his to her, it <I>was</I> a violent commencement, and thou shalt see an answer-
able sequestration.&rquo; The past tense flits by us, and the marriage of the Moor, within
the hour, seems already like an old story. Again, before the Senate, Othello speaks as
though this were not the first campaign in which he had been accompanied by his wife.
He promises for himself with an assurance, clearly born of experience, when he repels
the thought that &lquo;Light-winged toys of feathered Cupid&rquo; could &lquo;seel his speculative and
officed instruments.&rquo; Again, Iago, at the very close, leaves us with the impression that
his knavery will be slow in its advances. &lquo;Let's see: <I>After some time</I> to abuse Othello's
ear.&rquo; Trusting in this promise that the process will be slow, we accept the order of the
subsequent events as in fulfilment of it.
<P>Of one fact in this First Act it is important to be sure, before we leave it, and this is
that Othello's marriage takes place on the very night that it was discovered by Brabantio;
the first words that Roderigo utters refer to it as an end of all his hopes, and Iago tells
Cassio shortly afterwards that Othello &lquo;is made forever if the land carack prove lawful
prize which he has secured <I>to-night.</I>&rquo; If we may suppose that Othello and Desdemona
were married for some time before the night on which the play opens, then many of the
difficulties of the Short Time in Cyprus disappear. This theory was started and dis-

&lquo;that, with his creative powers, if he was determined to have Two Calendar Months

&lquo;suspicion sown and the murder done, nothing could have been easier to him than to

&lquo;would have been bound to prefer this course to that inexplicable marriage and no mar-

&lquo;be sustained in the bosoms of his audience required a rapidity of movement in his
&lquo;Murder-Plot, and it moves on feet of fire.

<P>I am afraid that Daniel doth protest a tiny bit too much. When he says that &lquo;it offers

the only <I>possible</I> way in which Iago could have persuaded Roderigo of his power to help

his unbounded influence with the Magnifico and his daughter? I am much afraid that
if we give ourselves up to this supposition, the Gull will have companions.

<P>&lquo;Why, in all the world, do they thus suddenly depose him, and put Cassio in his place?
&lquo;You cannot very well think that the next measure of the Senate, after entrusting the
&lquo;command of Cyprus, their principal Island, to their most tried General, in most criti-
&lquo;cal and perilous times, was to displace him ere they hear a word from him. They
&lquo;have not had time to know that the Turkish Fleet is wrecked and scattered, unless
&lquo;they sit behind Scenes in the Green-room.
<P>&lquo;<I><SC>Talboys</SC>.</I> We must conclude that the Senate must give weeks or months to this
&lquo;New Governor ere interfering with him.&mdash;To recall him before they know he has
&lquo;reached Cyprus&mdash;nay, to send a ship after him next day&mdash;or a day or two following
&lquo;his departure&mdash;would make these &lquo;most potent, grave, and reverend Signors,&rquo; enig-
&lquo;mas, and the Doge an Idiot. What though a steamer had brought tidings back to
&lquo;Venice that the Turks had been &lquo;banged&rquo; and &lquo;drowned?&rquo; That was not a sufficient
&lquo;reason to order Othello back before he could have well set his foot on shore, or taken
&lquo;more than a look at the state of the fortifications, in case the Ottoman should fit out
&lquo;another fleet.

&lquo;<I>what I have seen and known.</I>&rquo; Lodovico says, &lquo;The noble Moor, whom our Senate
&lquo;call all in all sufficient.&rquo; Then they have not quarrelled with him, at least&mdash;nor lost
&lquo;their good opinion of him! Iago answers, &lquo;He is much changed?&rquo; What, in a day?
&lquo;And again&mdash;&lquo;It is not honesty in me to speak what I have seen and known.&rquo; What,
&lquo;in a day? Lodovico comes evidently to Othello after a long separation&mdash;such as
&lquo;affords room for a moral transformation; and Iago's words&mdash;lies as they are&mdash;and
&lquo;seen to be lies by the most unthinking person&mdash;yet refer to much that has passed in
&lquo;an ample time&mdash;to a continued course of procedure. But in all the Play, nothing is
&lquo;so conclusive of long time as IV, ii, 3-14. If all this relates to their residence at
&lquo;Cyprus, it indicates many weeks. Then a word about Emilia. Now, consider, first,
&lquo;her character. She seems not very principled, not very chaste. Yet how strong her
&lquo;affection for Desdemona, and her faith in her purity! She witnesses for her, and she
&lquo;dies for her! I ask, how long did that affection and that opinion take to grow? a few
&lquo;days at Venice, and a week while they were sea-sick aboard ship? No. Weeks&mdash;

&lquo;&lquo;worth in herself, but is raised into worth by her contact with Desdemona&mdash;into heroic
&lquo;&lquo;worth!&rquo; &lquo;I care not for thy sword&mdash;I'll make thee known, though I lost twenty
&lquo;&lquo;lives.&rquo; The impure dying a voluntary martyr for the pure is to the highest degree

&lquo;&lquo;and-key of villainous secrets: and yet she'll kneel and pray; I have seen her do't.&rquo;

&lquo;is his treatment of one whom he supposes to have been serviceable to his wife's and

<I>She</I> could not before. He speaks to her as <I>professional</I> in such services, therefore

<P>helpfulness to his wife and her paramour, and at Cyprus&mdash;there&mdash;only there. Nothing

<P>In that storehouse of information, <I>The Shakespeare Key</I> (p. 217), <SC>Cowden-Clarke</SC>
