much lapse of time is <I>implied;</I> for Cassio speaks of his &lquo;former suit,&rquo; and Desdemona
sends for him to inform him of the progress she has made in her advocacy on his
behalf, although there is no absolutely-stated interval since she begged Othello to let
Cassio come and plead for recall, and her husband refused to allow this return to be
made either &lquo;to-night,&rquo; &lquo;to-morrow,&rquo; or within the next &lquo;three days.&rquo; So systematically
is Long Time <I>implied</I> while Short Time is <I>preserved</I>, that it is impossible not to believe
in this having been the author's thorough intention and artistic plan.&rquo; Also, III, iv,
145; IV, ii, 163; <I>Ib.</I>, 182; <I>Ib.</I>, 207-212.
<P>Even in addition to these enumerated by Wilson and Cowden-Clarke, it seems to
me that a few other instances which intimate Long Time may be gleaned. Thus,
II, ii, 345, on the very first evening in Cyprus, after Cassio's disgrace, Iago speaks
of Othello's having given himself up to the contemplation of Desdemona's graces to
such an extent that the general's wife is now the general; such an assertion seems
to require a long course of marked attention, in public and in private, to justify it.
Again, Roderigo was a man of wealth; in the pursuit of his pleasure he could afford
to buy jewels rich enough to half corrupt a votarist; before he left Venice he may be
supposed to have fulfilled his promise to Iago, and to have converted all his land into
money; his last words were, &lquo;I'll go sell all my land.&rquo; Iago speaks of the amount
of his gold and jewels as large; and yet he has been in Cyprus but a few hours before
he tells Iago that his money is almost spent, that he has not more than enough to last
him to get back to Venice; and in referring to himself as hunting in a chase we have
visions of a lavish expenditure, day after day, and week after week; nor does Iago
diminish this impression when he speaks of the <I>dilatory</I> time and of the <I>patience</I> which
their work demands. Again, Cassio expresses to Desdemona a fear that the policy
which obliges Othello to treat him coldly may last <I>so long</I> that Othello will <I>forget</I> him.
<P>This question of Shakespeare's use of these Two Times is so important (of more
importance in this than in almost any other play) that it is incumbent on us to give
good heed to Wilson's explanation of it, whereof the substance I have here endeav-
oured to extract.
<PB N=368>
<HE>368 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>&lquo;The usefulness of the Two Times is palpable from first to last&mdash;of the Short Time
&lquo;for maintaining the tension of the passion&mdash;of the Long for a thousand general needs.
&lquo;Thus Bianca must be used for convincing Othello very potently, positively, unanswer
&lquo;ably. But she cannot be used without supposing a protracted intercourse between
&lquo;her and Cassio. Iago's dialogue with him falls to the ground if the acquaintance
&lquo;began yesterday. But superincumbent over all is the <I>necessity of our not knowing</I>
&lquo;that Iago begins the Temptation, and that Othello extinguishes the Light of his Life,
&lquo;all in one day. And observe how this concatenation of the passionate scenes operates.
&lquo;Let the Entrances of Othello be four&mdash;A, B, C, D. You feel the close connection of
&lquo;A with B, of B with C, of C with D. You feel the coherence, the nextness, and all
&lquo;the force of the impetuous Action and Passion resulting. But the logically-consequent
&lquo;near connection of A with C, and much more with D, as again of B with D, you <I>do
&lquo;not feel.</I> Why? When you are at C, and feeling the pressure of B upon C, you have
&lquo;lost sight of the pressure of A upon B. At each entrance you go back one step&mdash;you
&lquo;do not go back two. The suggested intervals continually keep displacing to distances
&lquo;in your memory the formerly felt connections. This could not so well happen in real
&lquo;life, where the relations of time are strictly bound upon your memory, though some-
&lquo;thing of it happens when passion devours memory. But in fiction, the conception
&lquo;being loosely held, and shadowy, the feat becomes easily practicable. Thus the Short
&lquo;Time tells for the support of the Passion, along with the Long Time, by means of vir-
&lquo;tuous installations from the hand or wing of Oblivion. From one to two you feel no
&lquo;intermission&mdash;from two to three you feel none&mdash;from three to four you feel none; but
&lquo;I defy any man to say that from one to four he has felt none. I defy any man to say
&lquo;honestly that &lquo;sitting at the Play&rquo; he has kept count from one to four. Besides every
&lquo;past Scene, constituting a marked moment in the progress of the Play, has the effect for
&lquo;the Poet, as well as for you, of protracting the time in retrospect,&mdash;throwing everything
&lquo;that has passed further back. The goings-out and re-enterings of Othello have a
&lquo;strangely deluding effect&mdash;they disconnect the time more than you can think&mdash;and all
&lquo;the changes of persons on the stage, all shiftings of scenes and droppings of curtains,
&lquo;break and dislocate and dilate the time to your imagination, till you do not in the least
&lquo;know where you are. In this laxity of your conception, all hints of extended time
&lquo;sink in and spring up, like that fungus which, on an apt soil, in a night grows to a
&lquo;foot diameter. Shakespeare, we have seen, in his calmer constructions, shows, in a
&lquo;score of ways, weeks, months; that is therefore the true time, or call it the historical
&lquo;time. Hurried himself, and hurrying you on the torrent of passion, he forgets time,
&lquo;and a false show of time, to the utmost contracted, arises. I do not know whether
&lquo;he did not perceive this false exhibition of time, or perceiving, he did not care. But
&lquo;we all must see a reason, and a cogent one, why he should not let in the markings of
&lquo;protraction upon his dialogues of the Seduced and the Seducer. If you ask me, How
&lquo;stood the time in the mind of Shakespeare? I answer, I do not know. The ques
&lquo;tion splits itself into two: first, &lquo;How did he <I>project</I> the time?&rquo; Second, &lquo;How did
&lquo;&lquo;he conceive it in the progress of the Play?&rquo; My impression is, that he projected
&lquo;extended time. If so, did he or did he not know tha<*> in managing the Seduction he
&lquo;departed from that design by contracting it into a Day? Did he deliberately entertain
&lquo;a double design? If he did, how did he excuse this to himself? Did he say, &lquo;A
&lquo;&lquo;stage necessity, or a theatrical or dramatic necessity&rquo;&mdash;namely, that of sustaining at
&lquo;the utmost possible reach of altitude the tragical passion and interest&mdash;&lquo;requires the
&lquo;&lquo;precipitation of the passion from the first breathing of suspicion&mdash;the &lquo;Ha! Ha! I
&lquo;&lquo;like not that,&rquo; of the suggesting Fiend&mdash;to the consecrated &lquo;killing myself, to die upon
<PB N=369>
<HE><I>DURATION OF THE ACTION</I> 369</HE>
<P>&lquo;&lquo;a kiss!&rquo;&mdash;all in the course of fifteen hours&mdash;and this tragical vehemency, this impet-
&lquo;&lquo;uous energy, this torrent of power I will have; at the same time I have many reasons
&lquo;&lquo;&mdash;amongst them the general probability of the action&mdash;for a dilated time; and I, being
&lquo;&lquo;a magician of the first water, will so dazzle, blind, and bewilder my auditors that
&lquo;&lquo;they shall accept the double time with a double belief&mdash;shall feel the unstayed rush-
&lquo;&lquo;ing on of action and passion, from the first suggestion to the cloud of deaths&mdash;and
&lquo;&lquo;yet shall remain with a conviction that Othello was for months Governor of Cyprus
&lquo;&lquo;&mdash;they being on the whole unreflective and uncritical persons?&rquo;
<P>&lquo;<I><SC>Talboys</SC>.</I> And, after all, who willingly criticises his dreams or his pleasures?
<P>&lquo;<I><SC>North</SC>.</I> And the Audience of the Globe Theatre shall not&mdash;for &lquo;I hurl my dazzling
&lquo;&lquo;spells into the spungy air,&rquo; and &lquo;the spell shall sit when the curtain has fallen.&rquo; Shake-
&lquo;speare might, in the consciousness of power, say this. For this is that which he has&mdash;
&lquo;knowingly or unknowingly&mdash;done. Unknowingly? Perhaps&mdash;himself borne on by
&lquo;the successively rising waves of his work. For you see, Talboys, with what prolonged
&lquo;and severe labour we two have arrived at knowing the reality of the case which now
&lquo;lies open to us in broad light. We have needed time and pains, and the slow settling
&lquo;of our understandings, to unwind the threads of delusion in which we were encoiled
&lquo;and entoiled. If a strange and unexplained power could undeniably so beguile us&mdash;a
&lquo;possibility of which, previously to this examination, we never have dreamt, how do we
&lquo;warrant that the same dark, nameless, mysterious power shall not equally blind the
&lquo;&lquo;Artificer of Fraud&rquo;? There <I>are</I> the Two Times, the Long and the Short; and each
&lquo;exerts upon you its especial virtue. I can believe that Shakespeare unconsciously did
&lquo;what Necessity claimed,&mdash;the impetuous motion on, on, on of the Passion,&mdash;the Long
&lquo;Time asked by the successive events; the forces that swayed him, each in its turn, its
&lquo;own way. And put up with these Two Times we must,&mdash;one for our sympathy with
&lquo;Othello's tempest of heart,&mdash;one for the verisimilitude of the transaction.
<P>&lquo;Illusion, a constituent of Poetry, is <SC>when the same thing is, and is not</SC>. Pa&mdash;
&lquo;God bless him!&mdash;makes believe to be a Lion. He roars, and springs upon his prey.
&lquo;He at once believes himself to be a Lion, and knows himself to be Pa. Just so with
&lquo;the Shakespeare Club&mdash;many millions strong. The two times at Cyprus <I>are there;</I>
&lquo;the reason for the two times&mdash;to wit, probability of the Action, storm of the Passion&mdash;
&lquo;<I>is there;</I> and if any wiseacre should ask, &lquo;How do we manage to stand the <I>known</I>
&lquo;together-proceeding of two times?&rquo; the wiseacre is answered&mdash;&lquo;We don't stand it&mdash;
&lquo;for we know nothing about it. We are held in a confusion and a delusion about the
&lquo;time.&rquo; We have effect of both&mdash;distinct knowledge of neither. We have suggestions
&lquo;to our Understanding of extended time&mdash;we have movements of our Will by precipi-
&lquo;tated time. Does any man by possibility ask for a scheme and an exposition, by which
&lquo;it shall be made luminous to the smallest capacity <I>how</I> we are able distinctly all along
&lquo;to know, and bear in mind, that the preceding transactions are accomplished in a day,
&lquo;and at the same time and therewithal, distinctly all along to know and bear in mind
&lquo;that the same transactions proceeding before our eyes take about three months to
&lquo;accomplish? Then, I am obliged&mdash;like the musicians, when they are told that, if
&lquo;they have any music that may not be heard, Othello desires them to play it&mdash;to make
&lquo;answer, &lquo;Sir, we have none such.&rquo; It is to ask that a deception shall be not only
&lquo;seemingly but really a truth! If you ask me&mdash;which judiciously you may&mdash;what or
&lquo;how much did the Swan of Avon intend and know of all this astonishing legerdemain,
&lquo;when he sang thus astonishingly? Was he, the juggler, juggled by a&euml;rial spirits,&mdash;
&lquo;as Puck or Ariel? I put my finger to my lips, and nod on him to do the same; and
if I am asked, &lquo;Shall a modern artificer of the Drama, having the same pressure from
<PB N=370>
<HE>370 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>&lquo;within and from without, adopt this resource of evasion?&rquo; I can answer with great
&lquo;confidence, &lquo;He had better look before he leap.&rquo;
<P>&lquo;<I><SC>Talboys</SC>.</I> Assume, sir, that Shakespeare knew what he was doing.
<P>&lquo;<I><SC>North</SC>.</I> Then the Double Time is to be called&mdash;an Imposture.
<P>&lquo;<I><SC>Talboys</SC>.</I> Oh, my dear sir,&mdash;oh, oh!
<P>&lquo;<I><SC>North</SC>.</I> A good-natured Juggler, my dear Talboys, has cheated your eyes. You
&lquo;ask him to show you how he did it. He does the trick slowly&mdash;and you see. &lquo;Now,
&lquo;&lquo;good Conjurer, <I>do it slowly, and cheat us.</I>&rquo; &lquo;I can't. I cheat you by doing it quickly.
&lquo;&lquo;To be cheated, you must <I>not</I> see what I do; but you must <I>think</I> that you see.&rquo; When
&lquo;we inspect the Play in our closets the Juggler does his trick slowly. We sit at the
&lquo;Play, and he does it quick. When you see the trick again done the right way,&mdash;that
&lquo;is, quick,&mdash;you cannot conceive how it is that you no longer see that which you saw
&lquo;when it was done slowly! Again the impression returns of a magical feat.
<P>&lquo;<I><SC>Talboys</SC>.</I> I doubt, if we saw <I>Othello</I> perfectly acted, whether all our study would
&lquo;preserve us from the returning imposture.&rquo;
<P>For me, after this revelation, &lquo;the rest is silence.&rquo; The only time when Wilson does
not take me with him is when he suggests that Shakespeare's use of these Two Times
may have been unconscious. The more I study Shakespeare, the more profoundly do
I become impressed with the evidences on every hand of his consummate art. From
the bias to the world's estimate of him which Milton gave us we have scarcely yet
recovered. There are not wanting those who even at this late day believe that Shake-
speare warbled his native wood notes wild with as much unconsciousness as does a song-
sparrow. It will be many a long day yet, I think, before we exhaust the evidences
of his myriad-sided art. There can be no subtle effect produced on us by the inter-
lacing of these Two Times which Shakespeare himself did not feel, and did not fore-
cast.
<P>Daniel, however, does not believe in these Two Times, and is inclined to attribute
the discrepancies, which a disbelief in them detects, to the imperfect state of the text,
an asylum always at hand and wide open as a retreat from any and every Shakespearian
difficulty; lest I do injustice to a scholar whose opinion is entitled to more weight than
mine, let me quote his words:
<P><SC>Daniel</SC> (<I>New Shakespere Soc. Trans.</I>, 1877-79, Part ii, p. 231): &lquo;But though I think
&lquo;it must be admitted that long time at Venice before marriage is an element worthy of
&lquo;consideration as affording some explanation of many otherwise simply impossible inci-
&lquo;dents of the play, I am forced to admit that this explanation is far from satisfactory.
&lquo;Incidents such as the recall of Othello by the Senate before it could be known that
&lquo;he had landed in Cyprus are not affected by it in the least. Long time at Cyprus <I>after
&lquo;marriage</I> is absolutely necessary for the probability of the plot; but before I seek refuge
&lquo;in the....inexplicable mystery of &lquo;double time,&rquo; I should like to be convinced that
&lquo;the author himself did not provide it. I say, with Professor Wilson, that &lquo;with his
&lquo;creative powers, if he was determined to have Two Calendar Months from the First
&lquo;of May to the First of July, and then in One Day distinctly the first suspicion sown
&lquo;and the murder done, nothing could have been easier to him than to have imagined,
&lquo;and indicated, and hurried over, the required gap of time.&rquo; Long familiarity with
&lquo;Shakespeare's work has convinced me, as it must have convinced most students, that
&lquo;we cannot with certainty affirm that any of his plays have reached us in the state in
&lquo;which they left his hands: in some cases their corruption and mutilation for stage pur-
&lquo;poses can be proved to demonstration, and it is quite possible that in <I>Othello</I> some
&lquo;scenes may have been struck out and others so run together as to confuse the time-
<PB N=371>
<HE><I>DURATION OF THE ACTION</I> 371</HE>
<P>plot originally laid down by the author. The links in the chain of time, the absence
&lquo;of which so startles the reader, would not be, and indeed are not, missed in the visible
&lquo;action on the stage; but we should not, therefore, rashly jump to the conclusion that they
&lquo;never existed, and therefore that the author deliberately designed an impossible plot.&rquo;
<P><SC>Fleay</SC> (<I>Robinson's Epitome of Literature</I>, 15th June, 1879) proposes a third solu-
tion, which partakes somewhat of the nature of Daniel's, in so far as it suggests a divis-
ion of the Acts different from that in the QqFf. Convertite as I am to Wilson's Double
Time, I find answers therein, in the foregoing pages, to Fleay's arguments. After a rapid
review of the First and Second Acts, and Scenes i, ii, and iii of Act Third, Fleay pro-
ceeds: &lquo;So far the commentators and I are agreed, but I do not agree that a consider-
&lquo;able time must have elapsed since the landing, to render the dialogue intelligible.
&lquo;They allege, for instance, that Roderigo's money could hardly have been spent on the
&lquo;first night of his arrival. Why not? The voyage has been tempestuous, and, unless
&lquo;I quite misinterpret the allusions to it, has occupied not less than a week. Roderigo
&lquo;is just the man to empty his purse in one night's gaming, and Iago would not procras-
&lquo;tinate in that matter. Moreover, he may have been spending heavily at Venice before
&lquo;the marriage.
<P>&lquo;Iago has asked Emilia a hundred times to steal the &lquo;hankercher.&rquo; When? says
&lquo;Daniel. On the voyage, surely.&rquo; [Daniel, in a foot-note, p. 231, says, &lquo;Mr. E. H.
&lquo;Pickersgill calls attention to the time occupied by the voyage to Cyprus as suggesting
&lquo;a <I>possible</I> explanation with reference to Emilia's &lquo;hundred times.&rquo;&rquo;]
<P>&lquo;Iago says: &lquo;I lay with Cassio lately.&rquo; But Cassio has not been abed in Cyprus,
&lquo;says Daniel again. And what then? Does this over-careful critic take this statement
&lquo;for a narrative of fact? or does he imply that Shakespeare must have made all his
&lquo;villains lie so carefully as never to clash with possibility?
<P>&lquo;Up to this point the arguments for a long residence in Cyprus seem to me over-
&lquo;strained and futile: and at this point comes in the same question I raised as to <I>A
&lquo;Midsummer Night's Dream:</I> &lquo;are the present divisions into acts to be regarded as
&lquo;&lquo;authentic&rquo;? Why should they be, since they can in no instance be traced to Shake-
&lquo;speare's lifetime? I would therefore end the Third Act here, and allow a week's
&lquo;interval between this Scene and the next. There is no reason for the immediate con-
&lquo;secution of the Scenes, except Wilson's opinion, regarded as cogent by Daniel, that
&lquo;Othello would not have let an hour elapse before inquiring about the &lquo;hankercher.&rquo;
&lquo;Perhaps Othello would not: but Othello <I>under Iago's inspiration</I> probably would.
&lquo;And, besides, we have the positive statement of Bianca that Cassio has been away
&lquo;<I>for a week;</I> and, moreover, time is absolutely necessary for the Senate to hear of the
&lquo;loss of the Turkish fleet, and to send to recall Othello. These are positive integral
&lquo;parts of the plan, not to be neglected in any scheme.
<P>&lquo;And why are scholiasts&rquo; opinion of what their author should, must, or ought to have
&lquo;done, to be preferred to the direct allegations of the text? In IV, i, again, we hear
&lquo;that Othello had a fit <I>yesterday.</I> This at once disproves Daniel's notion that Acts III,
&lquo;IV, V, all take place on one day, and gives us a reason for Othello's delay in inquir-
&lquo;ing about the &lquo;hankercher.&rquo; Othello, under Iago's guidance, has, it seems to me,
&lquo;been waiting (after III, iii) to let Desdemona betray herself: after some days she does
&lquo;so by a <I>repeated</I> application on Cassio's behalf (III, iv, 18). The first application had
&lquo;been utilized by Iago to excite Othello, and so produced the first fit. But this is con-
&lquo;jectural. My main object is not to add more guesses to Shakespearian criticism, but
&lquo;to submit the following scheme of time for this play,&mdash;not founded on my own preju-
&lquo;dications, but taken from the text itself:

<P><SC>Pope</SC>: The Story is taken from Cynthio's Novels. <SC>Theobald</SC>: Cinthio Giraldi
seems to have designed his Tale as a Document to young Ladies against dispropor-
tioned Marriages: <I>di non se accompagnare con huomo, cui la Natura, &amp; il Cielo, &amp;
il modo della Vita disgiunge da noi;</I> that they should not link themselves to such,
against whom Nature, Providence, and a different way of Living have interposed a
Bar. Our Poet inculcates no such Moral; but rather, that a Woman may fall in Love
with the Virtues and shining Qualities of a Man, and therein overlook the Difference
of Complexion and Colour.
<P><SC>Farmer</SC>: I have seen a French translation of Cynthio, by Gabriel Chappuys, Paris,
1584. This is not a faithful one, and I suspect through this medium the work came
into English. [This translation is reprinted by <SC>Francois-Victor Hugo</SC> in his edition
of Shakespeare, Paris, 1868, vol. v, pp. 443-458.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P><SC>Simrock</SC> (<I>Quellen des Shakespeare</I>, &amp;c., Berlin, 1831, iii, 181) ridicules the idea that
it is necessary to find a translation into English of Giraldi Cinthio. &lquo;As if,&rquo; he says in
scorn, &lquo;it would not have been mere child's play for such a genius as Shakespeare to
have mastered Italian and French! .... It is as probable that the story of Cinthio
&lquo;was founded in fact as in fiction. Waiblinger, in the <I>Taschenbuch, Penelope</I>, 1831,
&lquo;asserts that there is an Italian ballad on this subject of Othello, but we have looked
&lquo;for it in vain in Wolff's <I>Egeria.</I> At all events, the style of the &ldquo;novel&rdquo; renders it not
&lquo;unlikely that it originated in some popular romance, such as minstrels, who wandered
&lquo;around the country with painted placards, were wont to sing. This &ldquo;novel&rdquo; belongs
&lquo;to the best of Cinthio's, whose skill as a narrator we do not highly prize.&rquo; [While

&lquo;ceived through a mistaken interpretation of his name.&rquo;
<P><SC>Knight</SC>: It is not improbable that [Cinthio's novel] is of Oriental origin; the re-
venge of the Moor, as there described, is of that fierce and barbarous character which
is akin to the savage manner in which supposed incontinence is revenged amongst the
Arabs. The painfully affecting tale of <I>The Three Apples</I>, in <I>The Thousand and One
Nights</I>, is an example of this; and, further, there is a similarity between the stolen
apple and the stolen handkerchief. The malignity of the slave in the Arabian tale,
too, is almost as motiveless as that of Iago; [but the Iago of Cinthio was not motive-
less.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P><SC>Collier</SC>: Shakespeare may have read Cinthio's story in the original language; it is
highly probable that he was sufficiently acquainted with Italian for the purpose.
<P>[In 1837, <SC>Rawdon Brown</SC> published, at Venice, <I>Ragguagli sulla Vita e sulle Opere
di Marin Sanuto, &amp;c.</I>, wherein (i, 226-235) he conjectured that a certain &lquo;Christophal
Moro,&rquo; a &lquo;Luogotenente di Cipro,&rquo; who returned from Cyprus in 1508 after having

<P>lead him to suppose that the story was popular enough to have supplied the details to

&lquo;to England years and years afterwards, was translated and read by Shakespeare. <I>Ven-

<P><SC>Klein</SC> (<I>Geschichte des Dramas. Das Italienische Drama</I>, ii, 384) finds a resem-
blance which he deems quite striking between several passages in <I>Othello</I> and Ludov-

ing on his tragedy may have had the Italian in view.
<P>In <I>Marianna</I> there is one situation which resembles <I>Othello.</I> Salome, Herod's
sister, has secretly accused Marianna, Herod's wife, of having bribed his cup-bearer to
poison him. Erode (Herod) cross-questions the cup-bearer, who confirms the charge.
Like Othello, Herod demands proofs. &lquo;The Cup-bearer envelops Erode's soul in his
&lquo;snaky coils, until, like Iago, he finds the chance to dart his poisonous fang. &lquo;They
&lquo;&lquo;who brood on crime,&rquo; he hisses; &lquo;play the game so close that one hand knows not
&lquo;&lquo;what the other does.&rquo;&rquo; Erode is determined that the cup-bearer shall repeat the
accusation in the presence of the Queen, and Marianna is called.
<P>Erode addresses her:
<BQ>&lquo;Marianna, io torrei perder il regno,<LB>
E insieme rimaner mendico e nudo<LB>
Prima, ch'aver cagion, come n' ho troppa<LB>
D' imputarti, o crudel, delitto alcuno.&rquo;<LB></BQ>
<P>To which Marianna replies:
<BQ>&lquo;Se delitto &egrave; d' avervi amato sempre<LB>
Con quello amor, ch' amar si dee consorte,<LB>

Avete alta cagion d' odiarmi ognora.&rquo;<LB></BQ>
<P>(&lquo;Marianna, I would gladly lose my kingdom, And remain for aye a beggar and
unclad, Rather than have cause, as but too much I have, To impute to thee, O cruel
one, any crime.&rquo; The parallel passage, which will occur to every one, is, of course:
&lquo;Had it pleas'd Heaven,&rquo; &amp;c., IV, ii, 57. Marianna's reply is in the same scene: &lquo;If
it be a crime to have always loved you With that love with which one should love a
husband, And to have honoured you as my lord, You have deep cause to hate me
always.&rquo;)

<P>While noting these parallelisms, and suggesting, as I have said, that Shakespeare
may have used Marianna as a lay figure in draping his tragedy, Klein acknowledges
the grander scale on which Shakespeare worked and the loftier key in which his
drama is pitched; whereby &lquo;the wild, gloomy, hellish temperament of a Herod is trans-
$igured into the lofty, noble, clear soul of a grand-hearted, g<*>ileless man.&rquo; To me it
would be impossible in Shakespeare's case to infer any familiarity with Dolce, even
were the parallelisms many times more numerous and more exact. But Klein's opin-
ions on dramatic subjects are always to be respectfully heard, and treated with the
deference due to an antagonist whose weapon, were he living, would be &lquo;the whole
tree of knowledge torn up by the roots.&rquo;
<P>In <I>The Academy</I> (9th January, 1875) appeared the letter above referred to, written
in Venice, from <SC>Rawdon Brown</SC>, which gives interesting and fuller details from early
Venetian documents concerning the bearers of the name of &lquo;Moro,&rquo; in one of whom,
Christopher, as we have seen, the writer finds the original Othello. After giving some
proofs of credulity, on the part of the Venetian Senate, in stories quite as marvellous as
any in Othello's travels' history, Brown proceeds: &lquo;Fronting the summit of the &ldquo;Giants'
&lquo;Stair,&rdquo; where the Doges of Venice were crowned, there are still visible four shields
&lquo;&ldquo;spotted with mulberries&rdquo; (&ldquo;strawberries&rdquo; in the description of Desdemona's hand-
&lquo;kerchief), indicating that that part of the palace portal on which they are carved was
&lquo;terminated in the reign of Christopher Moro, whose insignia are three mulberries sable
&lquo;and three bends azure on a field argent; the word &ldquo;Moro&rdquo; signifying in Italian either
&lquo;mulberry-tree or blackamoor.
<P>&lquo;In July, 1469, this Doge .... Christopher Moro effected indirectly the annexation of
&lquo;Cyprus to Venice, and in May, 1505, as a reward for military and diplomatic services,
&lquo;the Grand Council elected his namesake&mdash;Christopher Moro, son of Lorenzo&mdash;lord-
&lquo;lieutenant of the island, where he remained, after his term of service had expired, and
&lquo;by reason of his being thus accidentally on the spot, he was appointed to defend it from
&lquo;an hypothetical attack which, according to report, was meditated either by the Soldan,
&lquo;the Sofi, or the Turk. This statement exists in the summary of a dispatch from Chris-
&lquo;topher Moro's successor, the Lord-Lieutenant Lorenzo Giustinian, who adds that he
&lquo;and the counsellors had &ldquo;elected Christofal Moro captain of the fourteen ships detained
&lquo;by them for fear;&rdquo; and it is a curious coincidence that the tenour of the official advices
&lquo;from Cyprus corresponds precisely with the causes assigned for the subsequent dispatch
&lquo;of Othello from Venice for the defence of that island, as in Act I, Scene iii, of Shake-
&lquo;speare's tragedy. And, finally, the return of Christopher Moro to Venice is recorded in
&lquo;Marin Sanuto's Diaries thus: <SC>a. d.</SC> 1508, October 22. &ldquo;Item. The ship from Syria
&lquo;arrived, having on board Christopher Moro, on his return from the Lord-Lieutenancy
&lquo;of Cyprus. 1508, October 26. In the morning there presented himself to the College,
&lquo;Christopher Moro, returned Lord-Lieutenant from Cyprus, and elected Captain in Can-
&lquo;dia, <I>wearing his beard for the death of his wife</I> [Desdemona?] <I>on her way from Cyprus,
&lquo;as heard previously, and he made his report.</I>&rdquo; .... To return to Christopher Moro. He
&lquo;was decidedly a lady's man, as according to Barbaro's genealogies he was married four
&lquo;times. Nor should it be forgotten that the tale, whether told by Cinthio or Shake-
&lquo;speare, must have its incidents dated between 1486, when Catherine Cornaro abdicated
&lquo;in favour of Venice, until the fall of Famagosta, in 1571. Further, Moro's military
&lquo;exploits in the Romagna, against C&aelig;sar Borgia, and subsequently during the League
of Cambrai, as recorded by the Venetian historians, and by an inscription which once
&lquo;existed in the Palazzo Pretorio at Padua, would warrant his saying of himself, &lquo;I have
done the State some service, and they know it.&rquo;

<P>&lquo;Cinthio s novel, it may be added, would never have sufficed Shakespeare for his
<I>Othello.</I> The Italian described Desdemona's handkerchief as a &lquo;nose-napkin&rquo; (<I>pan-
nicello da naso</I>), and says it was most delicately wrought, but does not give the design,
which reveals the whole thing. Had he called things by their right names, the sale
&lquo;of his book in Venice would have been prohibited..... Among the Venetians in Eng-
&lquo;land from 1603 to 1615 there were the secretary Scaramelli, and the ambassadors Duodo,
&lquo;Correr, Francesco Contarini, and Foscarini, from one or other of them, or from some
&lquo;of their attendants, Shakespeare&mdash;who may, perhaps, have been struck by some Eng-
&lquo;lish translation of Cinthio's tales&mdash;might easily have ascertained the true story of <I>his</I>
&lquo;Othello.&rquo;
<P>In <I>The Academy</I> of 20 February, 1875, E. H. <SC>Pickersgill</SC> replied to Rawdon
Brown, and among other arguments gives a shrewd reason for Shakespeare's conversion
(if it be a conversion) of the &lquo;three mulberries sable&rquo; into &lquo;strawberries.&rquo; By the
&lquo;assumption that the &ldquo;strawberries&rdquo; were Othello's insignia <I>at all</I>, we should involve
&lquo;Shakespeare in a gross inconsistency. For, of course, in that case, Cassio, when he
&lquo;found the handkerchief dropped in his bed-chamber, could not have been in doubt
&lquo;respecting its ownership; he would have recognized it, at once, as the property of
&lquo;Desdemona. In Cinthio's novel, Cassio actually does recognize it, not by any insig-
&lquo;nia upon it, but by the curious inwrought &ldquo;Moresco work.&rdquo;&rquo; Furthermore, Pickers-
gill asks: &lquo;If Shakespeare was acquainted with the historical Moro's military exploits
&lquo;in the Romagna, why does he prefer to mention Rhodes, Cyprus, and Aleppo as the
&lquo;scenes of the exploits of his Othello?&rquo; The most conclusive argument against Brown's
theory Pickersgill finds in the actual date, settled by Reed, of Othello's dispatch to
Cyprus [see p. 357], which was sixty years after Christopher Moro's governorship of
the island.
<P>Lastly, in <I>The Athen&aelig;um</I>, 18 September, 1875, C. <SC>Elliot Browne</SC> asks: &lquo;Was
&lquo;Shakespeare indebted for any part of the conception of Othello to the story of Sam-
&lquo;piero, the famous Corsican leader? .... The hint was thrown out more than a cen-
&lquo;tury ago by the anonymous writer of a paper in Dodsley's <I>Museum</I>, when replying to
&lquo;some of Rymer's criticisms upon this drama. He said (in substance), why this con-
&lquo;tinual cry about the unnaturalness of Othello, when there is evidence from real life
&lquo;that a brave soldier, whose character resembled in many points that which Shake-
&lquo;speare has given to the Moor, being placed in similar circumstances of terrible per-
&lquo;plexity, behaved almost exactly as Othello is represented to have done?
<P>&lquo;There is some resemblance between the careers of Sampiero and Othello. Sam-
&lquo;piero, or, as the name is more correctly written, San Pietro di Bastelica, was an Italian
&lquo;adventurer in the service of France, who had arrived at high distinction by conduct
&lquo;and valour; and he had married, against the wish of all her relatives, the beautiful
&lquo;Corsican heiress, Vanina d'Ornano..... In 1563, Sampiero, leaving his wife in France,
&lquo;went to Constantinople to beg assistance for the Corsicans from the Turks. During
&lquo;this absence his Genoese enemies are said to have tampered with some servants of his
&lquo;wife's household, and caused a report to reach Constantinople that she was living on
&lquo;too intimate terms with his secretary, Antonio. Immediately returning to France,
&lquo;Sampiero came up with his wife at Aix; and after a scene which all accounts agree
to have been characterized on his part by a strange mixture of passionate tenderness
&lquo;and brutal ferocity, and on hers by gentle, uncomplaining submiss on, he asked pardon
&lquo;upon his knees for the deed he was about to commit, and deliberately strangled her
&lquo;with her handkerchief. It is proper to add, that there is in existence another version
&lquo;of the affair, in which the cause of Vanina's fate is attributed to her husband's indig-

<P>&lquo;nation at some secret advances which she had made to the Genoese government for
&lquo;the purpose of obtaining his pardon, thus excluding altogether the motive of jealousy.
<P>&lquo;Although wanting in several important points of resemblance, this story comes

<P><I>The Hecatommithi</I> of <SC>Giouanbattista Giraldi Cinthio</SC> are divided into Ten
Decades, each Decade devoted to a particular subject, whereto ten Stories or Novels
furnish the appropriate illustrations.
<P>The Third Decade deals with &lquo;The Unfaithfulness of Husbands and of Wives,&rquo; and
is dedicated, let us hope with permission, to the &lquo;Illvstrissima Signora la Signora Laura
Eustochia da Este.&rquo;
<P>The Seventh Novel in this Decade is here faithfully reprinted from the original edi-
tion, issued &lquo;In Venegia M&dot;D&dot;LXVI.&rquo; Here and there the ampersands are changed
to <I>e</I> and <I>et;</I> and <I>u</I> is changed to <I>v.</I>

lation was reprinted by Collier in the first edition of <I>Shakespeare's Library</I>, and again
by W. C. Hazlitt in the second. Lastly, in 1855, by <SC>John Edward Taylor</SC>. This
translation is here reprinted on the same page with the Italian.

der Shakespeare</I>, Berlin, 1831.
<P>Of the author, Giraldi Cinthio, <SC>Taylor</SC>, in the Introduction to his Translation, says
that he &lquo;was a nobleman of Ferrara, and a Professor of Philosophy in that city;&rquo; and

&lquo;composition of his work, in connection with his &lquo;grave studies of philosophy,&rquo;&mdash;by
&lquo;the light of which, the fount and origin of laudable habits, and of all honest disci-
&lquo;pline, and likewise of every virtue, I have sought to perfect my work, which is wholly
&lquo;directed, with much variety of examples, to censure vicious actions and to praise honest
&lquo;ones,&mdash;to make men fly from vice and embrace virtue.&rquo; What could the reader expect
&lquo;from this proem (which is found <I>totidem verbis</I> in all the books of this school), but a

<P>There once lived in Venice a Moor, who was very valiant and of a handsome person;
and having given proofs in war of great skill and prudence, he was highly esteemed by
the Signoria of the Republic, who in rewarding deeds of valour advanced the interests
of the State.
<P>It happened that a virtuous lady of marvellous beauty, named Disdemona, fell in love
with the Moor, moved thereto by his valour; and he, vanquished by the beauty and the
noble character of Disdemona, returned her love; and their affection was so mutual that,
although the parents of the lady strove all they could to induce her to take another hus-
band, she consented to marry the Moor; and they lived in such harmony and peace in
Venice that no word ever passed between them that was not affectionate and kind.
<P>Now it happened at this time that the Signoria of Venice made a change in the troops
whom they used to maintain in Cyprus, and they appointed the Moor commander of the
soldiers whom they dispatched thither. Joyful as was the Moor at the honour proffered
him, such dignity being only conferred on men of noble rank and well-tried faith, and
who had displayed bravery in arms,&mdash;yet his pleasure was lessened when he reflected
on the length and dangers of the voyage, fearing that Disdemona would be pained at
his absence. But Disdemona, who had no other happiness in the world than the Moor,
and who rejoiced to witness the testimony of his valour her husband had received from
so powerful and noble a Republic, was all impatient that he should embark with his troops,
and longed to accompany him to so honourable a post. And all the more it vexed her
to see the Moor so troubled; and not knowing what could be the reason, one day, when
they were at dinner, she said to him, &lquo;How is it, O Moor, that when so honourable a post
has been conferred on you by the Signoria, you are thus melancholy?&rquo;
<P>The Moor answered Disdemona, &lquo;My pleasure at the honour I have received is
disturbed by the love I bear you; for I see that of necessity one of two things must
happen,&mdash;either that I take you with me to encounter the perils of the sea, or, to save

<P>The next morning the tidings of this affair spread through the whole city, and reached

<P>Then they consulted of one means and another&mdash;poison and daggers&mdash;to kill poor

we can pull down a portion of the ceiling, and thus make it seem as if a rafter falling
on her head had killed the lady. Suspicion cannot rest on you, since all men will
impute her death to accident.&rquo;
<P>This cruel counsel pleased the Moor, and he only waited for a fitting time to execute
the plot. One night, when he and Disdemona had retired to bed, the Ensign, whom
the Moor had concealed in a closet which opened into the chamber, raised a noise in

not hear that noise?&rquo;

<P>On the following day Disdemona was buried, followed to the grave by the universal

wicked a deed should go unpunished. Ere long the Moor, whom Disdemona had
loved more than her own life, began to feel such sorrow at her loss that he went
wandering about as one bereft of reason, searching in every part of the house. And
reflecting in his thoughts that the Ensign had been the cause that he had lost, with

not bear to set eyes on him, and had it not been for his fear of the inviolable justice
of the Signoria of Venice, he would have slain him openly. But being unable to do
this with safety, he deprived him of his rank, and would not allow him to remain in
his Company; whereat such an enmity arose between the two that no greater or more
deadly can be imagined.

<P>The Captain of the troop, whose anger returned fiercely, but without knowing why,

his wife, and called the Ensign to witness the truth of what he said. The Ensign
declared both charges to be true, for that the Moor had disclosed to him the whole
plot, and had tried to persuade him to perpetrate both crimes; and that, having after-
wards killed his wife out of jealousy he had conceived, he had narrated to him the
manner in which he had perpetrated her death.
<P>The Signoria of Venice, when they heard of the cruelty inflicted by a barbarian upon
a lady of their city, commanded that the Moor's arms should be pinioned in Cyprus, and
he be brought to Venice, where, with many tortures, they sought to draw from him the
truth. But the Moor, bearing with unyielding courage all the torment, denied the whole
charge so resolutely that no confession could be drawn from him. But, although by
his constancy and firmness he escaped death, he was, after being confined for several
days in prison, condemned to perpetual banishment, in which he was eventually slain
by the kinsfolk of Disdemona, as he merited. The Ensign returned to his own coun-

<P><SC>John Galt</SC> (<I>Lives of the Players</I>, London, 1831, i, 268): It would be a curious
speculation to attempt to determine the cause of Garrick's failure in Othello, for a fail-
ure it must be considered, as compared with his transcendency in other parts. In the
just and natural inflection of the voice, we have no cause to doubt that he was equally
excellent. The probability, therefore, is that he failed in the expression of the coun-
tenance alone, and that this default and short-coming to expectation was entirely owing
to the black disguise he was obliged to assume.
<P>On the epithet &lquo;thick-lips,&rquo; applied, I, i, 72, by Roderigo to Othello, <SC>Coleridge</SC>
(p. 249) has the following: Roderigo turns off to Othello; and here comes one, if not
the only, seeming justification of our blackamoor or negro Othello. Even if we sup-
posed this an uninterrupted tradition of the theatre, and that Shakespeare himself, from
want of scenes, and the experience that nothing could be made too marked for the
senses of his audience, had practically sanctioned it,&mdash;would this prove aught concern-
ing his own intention as a poet for all ages? Can we imagine him so utterly ignorant
as to make a barbarous negro plead royal birth,&mdash;at a time, too, when negroes were not
known except as slaves? As for Iago's language to Brabantio, it implies merely that
Othello was a Moor, that is, black. Though I think the rivalry of Roderigo sufficient
to account for his wilful confusion of Moor and Negro, yet, even if compelled to give
this up, I should think it only adapted for the acting of the day, and should complain
of an enormity built on a single word, in direct contradiction to Iago's &lquo;Barbary horse.&rquo;
Besides, if we could in good earnest believe Shakespeare ignorant of the distinction,
still why should we adopt one disagreeable possibility instead of a ten times greater and
more pleasing probability? It is a common error to mistake the epithets applied by the
<I>dramatis person&aelig;</I> to each other as truly descriptive of what the audience ought to see
<PB N=390>
<HE>390 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>or know. No doubt Desdemona saw Othello's visage in his mind; yet, as we are con
stituted, and most surely as an English audience was disposed in the beginning of th<*>
seventeenth century, it would be something monstrous to conceive this beautiful Vene-
tian girl falling in love with a veritable negro. It would argue a disproportionateness,
a want of balance, in Desdemona, which Shakespeare does not appear to have in the
least contemplated.
<P><SC>Hawkins</SC> (<I>Life of Edmund Kean</I>, i, 221): Kean regarded it as a gross error to
make Othello either a negro or a black, and accordingly altered the conventional black
to the light brown which distinguishes the Moors by virtue of their descent from the
Caucasian race. Although in the tragedy Othello is described with a minuteness which
leaves no doubt that Shakespeare intended him to be black, there is no reason to sup-
pose that the Moors were darker than the generality of Spaniards, who, indeed, are
half Moors, and compared with the Venetians he would even then be black. There is
some variety in the colour of the Moors, but it never approaches so deep a hue as to
conceal all change of colour. Betterton, Quin, Mossop, Barry, Garrick, and John
Kemble all played the part with black faces, and it was reserved for Kean to innovate,
and Coleridge to justify, the attempt to substitute a light brown for the traditional black.
The alteration has been sanctioned by subsequent usage.
<P><SC>Hunter</SC> (<I>New Illust.</I>, ii, 280): Shakespeare, in IV, ii, 257, seems to point to Mau-
ritania as the native country of Othello, who is hence to be regarded as a Moor in the
proper sense of the word, a native of the northern coast of Africa, towards the west;
and the expression &lquo;black&rquo; is to be interpreted as meaning no more than <I>very dark</I>,
and this in comparison with the fair European. <I>Moor</I>, however, it may be observed,
was used by English writers very extensively, and all the dark races seem, by some
writers, to be regarded as comprehended under it. Sir Thomas Elyot calls the Ethi-
opians, Moors. A distinction was sometimes made between black Moors and white
Moors.
<P><SC>Knight</SC> (<I>Note</I> on I, i, 72): This passage has been received as indicating the inten-
tion of Shakespeare to make Othello a Negro. It is very probable that the popular
notion of a Moor was somewhat confused in Shakespeare's time, and that the descend-
ants of the proud Arabs, who had borne sovereign sway in Europe (&lquo;men of royal
siege&rquo;), and, what is more, had filled an age of comparative darkness with the light
of their poetry and their science, were confounded with the uncivilized African, the
despised slave. We do not think, however, that Shakespeare had any other intention
than to paint Othello as one of the most noble and accomplished of the proud children
of the <I>Ommiades</I> and <I>Abbasides.</I> The expression &lquo;thick-lips,&rquo; from the mouth of Rod-
erigo, can only be received dramatically, as a nick-name given to Othello by the folly
and ill-nature of this coxcomb. Whatever may have been the practice of the stage,
even in Shakespeare's time,&mdash;and it is by no means improbable that Othello was repre-
sented as a Negro,&mdash;the whole context of the play is against the notion. [The fol-
lowing observations were communicated to Knight by a friend:] In the ages of her
splendour, Venice was thronged with foreigners from every climate of the earth; and
nowhere else, perhaps, has the prejudice of colour been so feeble. A more important
fact, as regards Desdemona's attachment, is that it was the policy of the Republic to
employ foreign mercenaries, and especially in offices of command, for the obvious pur-
pose of lessening to the utmost the danger of cabal and intrigue at home. The fami-
lies of Senators, or other chief citizens, were in the habit of seeing, in their dark-com-
plexioned guests, those only who were distinguished by ability and by the official rank
thereby gained,&mdash;picked men, whose hue might be forgotten in their accomplishments.

<P><SC>Verplanck</SC>: There was nothing in the Moor's descent so to affect his social position
in the eyes of Cinthio's readers or Shakespeare's audience, as to surprise them at his
being received on equal footing in the family of a Venetian noble, or attaining the
highest military rank in the service of the Republic. Yet it is equally clear that, in
regard to Desdemona, his race and colour are not a matter of indifference; they are
especially dwelt upon as one of the grounds of jealousy; they place between the Moor
and the Venetian lady a natural barrier, which it requires a &lquo;downright violence and
storm of fortune&rquo; to break down. It is the admiration of high intellect, of heroic qual-
ities and achievements,&mdash;such as has been sometimes known in real life to overcome
most strange disparities of age, character, and external circumstances,&mdash;which gives
the lady to see Othello's visage only &lquo;in his mind.&rquo; She does not lose her own social
position by marriage with one under whom Italian and Cypriot nobles (Cassio, Iago,
Montano) are ambitious to serve, and with whom the princes and rulers of the State
associate as companions; yet her love to him would appear in itself strange and unac-
countable, had not the Poet opened to us &lquo;the pure recesses of her mind,&rquo; and showed
us whence it sprung.
<P><SC>Wilson</SC> (<I>Blackwood's Maga.</I>, April, 1850, p. 484):

&lquo;saw Othello's visage in his mind&rdquo; is nothing, unless the visible visage is one to be

&lquo;contrast, and a thought of the immense love that has overcome it.
<P>&lquo;<I><SC>North</SC>.</I> White and Black is the utter antithesis,&mdash;as, at intensity, Night and Day.
&lquo;Yes, Talboys,&mdash;every jot of soot you take from his complexion, you take an iota from
&lquo;the signified power of love.
<P>&lquo;<I><SC>Talboys</SC>.</I> As you say, sir, the gap which is between the Stage and Reality must
&lquo;prevent, in our hearts, anything like loathing of the conjunction.
<P>&lquo;<I><SC>North</SC>.</I> The touch of such an emotion would annul the whole Tragedy. A dis-
&lquo;parity, or a discrepancy, vast as mysterious,&mdash;but which love, at the full, is entitled to
&lquo;overlook&mdash;overstep! Whether Fate dare allow prosperity to a union containing so
&lquo;mighty an element of disruption, is another question. It seems like an attempt at
&lquo;overruling the &ldquo;&AElig;terna f&oelig;dera rerum.&rdquo; . . . . Talboys, I cannot help thinking that
&lquo;Shakespeare shows up in Othello foul passions,&mdash;that you see in him two natures con-
&lquo;joined,&mdash;the moral Caucasian White and animal tropical Black. In the Caucasian,
&lquo;the spiritual or angelical in us attains its manifestation. In the offspring of the trop-
&lquo;ics, amongst the sands and under the suns of Africa, the animal nature takes domina-
&lquo;tion. The sands and suns that breed Lions, breed men with Lions' hearts in them.
&lquo;The Lion is for himself noble, but blood of the Irrational in the veins of the Rational
&lquo;is a contradiction. The noblest moral nature and the hot blind rage of animal blood!
<P>&lquo;<I><SC>Talboys</SC>.</I> Ay, the noblest moral nature, and high above every other evidence of it,
&lquo;his love of <SC>Her</SC>,&mdash;which, what it was, and what it would have remained, or become,&mdash;
&lquo;and what he was and would have been, had Iago not been there, we may imagine!
&lquo;With all the power of a warrior, and a ruler, he has the sensibility of a Lover,&mdash;with
&lquo;all spontaneous dignity and nobility, he has the self-mastery of reason,&mdash;before his
&lquo;overthrow.
<P>&lquo;<I><SC>North</SC>.</I> Wherefore, my dear Sheriff, I prefer Othello as a specimen of the <I>Ethical
&lquo;Marvellous.</I> Like, as in another kingdom, a Winged Horse, or a Centaur,&mdash;the meet-
&lquo;ing of two natures which readily hold asunder. All this has under the &AElig;thiop com-
&lquo;plexion its full force,&mdash;less if you mitigate,&mdash;if not mitigate merely, but take away,
&lquo;where are we all? The innate repugnance of the White Christian to the Black Moor-
&lquo;ish blood, is the ultimate tragic substratum,&mdash;the &ldquo;<I>must</I>&rdquo; of all that follows. Else,&mdash;
&lquo;<I>make</I> Othello White,&mdash;and, I say again, <I>see</I> where we are!
<P>&lquo;<I><SC>Talboys</SC>.</I> Shakespeare, sir, was not one to flinch from the utmost severity of a
&lquo;Case.
<P>&lquo;<I><SC>North</SC>.</I> Not he, indeed,&mdash;therefore I <I>swear</I> Othello is a Blackamoor.
<P>&lquo;<I><SC>Talboys</SC>.</I> And I take it, sir, that Othello's natural demeanour is one of great grav-
&lquo;ity, to which the passionate moods induced are in extremity of contrast. I conceive
that, by these mixtures and contrasts, he is rendered picturesque and poetical.
<P>&lquo;<I><SC>North</SC>.</I> I swear Othello was a Blackamoor,&mdash;and that Desdemona was the Whitest
&lquo;Lady in Europe.&rquo;
<P><SC>Grant White</SC> (<I>Shakespeare's Scholar</I>, 1854, p. 432): Shakespeare nowhere calls
Othello an Ethiopian, and also does not apply the term to Aaron in the horrible <I>Titus
Andronicus;</I> but he continually speaks of both as Moors; and as he has used the first
word elsewhere, and certainly had use for it as a reproach in the mouth of Iago, it
<PB N=393>
<HE><I>OTHELLO'S COLOUR</I> 393</HE>
<P>seems that he must have been fully aware of the distinction in grade between the two
races, although his notion of their distinctive traits was, perhaps, neither very true nor
very clear. Indeed, I could never see the least reason for supposing that Shakespeare
intended Othello to be represented as a negro. With the negroes the Venetians had
nothing to do, that we know of, and could not have, in the natural course of things;
whereas, with their over-the-way neighbours, the Moors, they were continually brought
in contact. These were a warlike, civilized, and enterprising race, which could furnish
an Othello; whereas, the contrary has always been the condition of the negroes. The
reasons for supposing Othello to be a negro are few and easily set aside, which is not
the case of those which show him to be a Moor. The most conclusive of the former
is Roderigo's calling Othello &lquo;thick lips&rquo;; but this is the result of Shakespeare's want
of exact informat&igrave;on. He had, doubtless, never seen either a Moor or a negro, and
might very naturally confuse their physiological traits; but a man of his knowledge
and penetration could not fail to know the difference between the position and the
character of the nation which built the Alhambra and that which furnished their stock
in trade to the Englishmen who, when he wrote <I>Othello</I>, were supplying the planta-
tions in the West Indies with slaves, and, soon after his death, introduced negro slavery
into Virginia. In addition to this epithet &lquo;thick lips,&rquo; there are several allusions to
Othello as having the visage of the devil, as black, and as being, therefore, the very
reverse of attractive to a woman like Desdemona. But this proves nothing; for
Shakespeare has applied these identical epithets to so eminent and undeniable a Moor
as the Prince of Morocco. In the <I>Mer. of Ven.</I> I, ii, Portia says, upon the announce-
ment of the royal Moor, &lquo;if he have the condition of a saint and the complexion of a
devil, I had rather he would shrive me than wive me.&rquo; He himself prays her, &lquo;Mis-
like me not for my complexion&rquo;; and she, when he has selected the wrong casket,
says, &lquo;May all of his complexion choose me so&rquo;; and yet he was not jetty black like
a negro, but tawny; for the stage direction in II, i, in the Qq is, &lquo;<I>Enter</I>, Morochus, <I>a
tawny Moor, all in white.</I>&rquo; Plainly, then, the devilish visage attributed to Othello, and
the assumed repulsiveness of his colour, makes him out, in Shakespeare's estimation,
only a Moor, and not even a very black Moor at that. But there is direct evidence
that he was a Mauritanian [from Iago's calling him a &lquo;Barbary horse,&rquo; and from his
telling Roderigo that Othello was going to Mauritania].
<P><SC>Henry Reed</SC> (<I>Lectures on Tragic Poetry</I>, p. 268): The repulsive notion that Othello
was a black,&mdash;a coarse-featured African,&mdash;seems to me directly at variance with the requi-
sitions of both poetry and history; and I cannot but think it is an error, which may be
traced either to some false critical theory, or else more probably to the too literal inter-
pretation of passages in the play, the unimaginative reading which is fatal so often to
the spirit of poetry. The hero is styled &lquo;Othello, <I>the Moor;</I>&rquo; such is his title and
familiar designation throughout. He was one of that adventurous race of men who,
striking out from the heart of Arabia, had made conquest of Persia and Syria; and,
overturning the ancient sovereignty of Egypt, swept in victory along the whole north-
ern coast of Africa; and, passing thence across the narrow frith of the Mediterranean,
scattered the dynasty of the Goths with Roderic at their head. . . . . How true to his
nature was it for Othello to stand in conscious pride,&mdash;the descendant of a race of
kings, the representative of the Arabs who had been sovereigns of Europe,&mdash;his spirit
glowing with noble ancestral memories! And, on the other hand, how perfectly con-
sistent it was with the debasing malignity of Iago, and with the petulant disappoint-
ment of Roderigo, to be blind to all that ennobled and dignified the Moorish name&mdash;
to see no distinction between the chivalrous Moor, the chieftain of Christian armies,
<PB N=394>
<HE>394 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>and the barbarous Ethiop,&mdash;the despised slave. It was natural that vulgar words should
be uttered from the lips of such men, and also that the parental frenzy of Desdemona's
father should find relief in the same strain of vituperative misrepresentation, the pro-
pensity of a fresh and angry grief to magnify its injury. Such are the authorities that
have led to the supposition that Othello was black. In one scene, indeed, he speaks
so of himself; but it is when he is in Iago's grasp,&mdash;when he is &lquo;changing with the
poison.&rquo; The agony of doubt has heaved over the lofty complacent bearing of his
happier moments, and his speaking of himself as black is,&mdash;what is very natural to
such condition of mind,&mdash;a piece of morbid exaggeration; just as when, in the same
scene, he describes himself as &lquo;declined into the vale of years.&rquo; On every account, it
is better to clear the fancy of this false conception of Othello's colour, most of all for
the sake of our sympathies with the gentle Desdemona; for if we are brought to be-
lieve that this bright, this fair-faced, Venetian lady was wedded to a black, we should
almost be tempted to think that the monstrous alliance was fitly blotted out in its fear-
ful catastrophe. . . . . The Moorish complexion of Othello, not intended to produce in
our minds disgust at Desdemona's choice, is made to serve an important dramatic pur-
pose, in that it greatly ministers to his suspicions of his wife's fidelity. It is the first
unprompted argument for doubt; the first suggested by Othello's own thoughts, and,
of course, quickly seized on and fomented by Iago. It serves, too, to account for the
extreme sensitiveness of Othello's sense of honour,&mdash;that which is a prime element in
his character.
<P>J. E. <SC>Taylor</SC> (<I>Introduction to Trans. of Cinthio</I>, p. 13): We have merely to deal
with the poet's own conception of the character, and to take this as the standard by
which to judge its delineation: the drama, as a work of art, is simply amenable to the
rules of art. And this is an instructive instance of the fact that artistic truth may con-
sist with accidental errors which lie beyond the pale of art; the character of Othello
may be in itself perfect,&mdash;faultless; and yet, when a nationality is affixed to it, it may
violate the physical and moral laws of nature displayed in the distinction of races.
This is a very minor point of mere speculation, not of criticism; still it is open to dis-
cussion. The novelist speaks of the <I>blackness</I> (negrezza) of the Moor, and that Shake-
speare had the outward figure of a black present to his thoughts appears more than
probable from numerous allusions in the Play. . . . . Nothing can be more conclusive
than these expressions, and the tradition of the Stage (there is reason to believe) has
uniformly represented Othello as a black from Shakespeare's day to the present.
Nevertheless, this in no degree affects the character of the Moor, for the reasons just
stated.
<P><SC>Halliwell</SC>: The reference to &lquo;Mauritania,&rquo; IV, ii, 257, surely settles the disputed
question, Was Othello a negro? Certainly not. He was a Moor of lofty lineage, with
thick lips and a very dark complexion. &lquo;Black Othello&rquo; was the dark-complexioned
Othello. So the word &lquo;black&rquo; was employed in Shakespeare's time, as in the follow-
ing extract: &lquo;<I>Quest.</I> Why do some women love men that bee blacke, and other, those
that be faire and well coloured? <I>An.</I> Women of feeble sight love them that bee blacke,
because blacknesse doth joyne and unite the sight too much disparkled, and by this
meanes doth comfort the same. Or else we may well say that every thing doth love
and desire his like. They therefore which be hote of nature love them that be blacke,
because they be more prone to heate. Other which be of colder nature do love them
that be white, because they be of cold complexion, the mother of whitenesse.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Delect-
<*>ble Demaundes and Pleasant Questions</I>, 1596, p. 10.
<P><SC>Hudson</SC> (also in reference to &lquo;Mauritania&rquo;): This passage proves, so far as anything
<PB N=395>
<HE><I>OTHELLO'S COLOUR</I> 395</HE>
<P>said by Iago may be believed, that Othello was not meant to be a Negro, as has been
represented, both on the stage and off, but a veritable Moor. His kindred, the Mauri-
tanians,&mdash;from whose &lquo;men of royal siege he fetched his life and being,&rquo; and among
whom he was about to retire,&mdash;though apt enough to be confounded with the negroes,
were as different from them externally as brown is from black; internally, in mind and
character, the difference was far greater. [In his <I>Preface</I>, p. 33, Hudson writes:] The
difference of Moors and Negroes was as well known in Shakespeare's time as it is now;
and that he thought them the same is no more likely from this play than from <I>The Mer-
chant of Venice</I>, where the Prince of Morocco comes as a suitor to Portia, and in a stage
direction of the Qto is called &lquo;a <I>tawny</I> Moor.&rquo;
<P><SC>Mary Preston</SC> (<I>Studies in Shakespeare</I>, 1869, p. 71): In studying the play of
<I>Othello</I>, I have always <I>imagined</I> its hero <I>a white</I> man. It is true the dramatist paints
him black, but this shade does not suit the man. It is a stage decoration, which <I>my
taste</I> discards; a fault of colour from an artistic point of view. I have, therefore, as I
before stated in <I>my readings</I> of this play, dispensed with it. Shakespeare was too cor-
rect a delineator of human nature to have coloured Othello <I>black</I>, if he had personally
acquainted himself with the idiosyncrasies of the African race.
<P>We may regard, then, the daub of black upon Othello's portrait as an <I>ebullition</I> of
fancy, a <I>freak</I> of imagination,&mdash;the visionary conception of an ideal figure,&mdash;one of
the few erroneous strokes of the great master's brush, the <I>single</I> blemish on a faultless
work.
<P>Othello <I>was</I> a <I>white</I> man! [The Authoress dates her Preface from &lquo;Oaklands, Har-
ford County, Maryland.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P><SC>Lewes</SC> (<I>On Actors and the Art of Acting</I>, p. 145): Othello is black,&mdash;the very trag-
edy lies there; the whole force of the contrast, the whole pathos and extenuation of his
doubts of Desdemona, depend on this blackness. Fechter makes him a half-caste, whose
mere appearance would excite no repulsion in any woman out of America.
<P><SC>Erl Rygenhoeg</SC> (<I>Am. Bibliopolist</I>, Dec., 1875): A thousand examples might be
quoted to show that in Shakespeare's time a dark or <I>brunette</I> complexion was indicated
by calling a person &lquo;black.&rquo; Thus, in the English Bible, 1611, <I>Song of Solomon</I>, i, 6, 7;
and in the very play under consideration, II, i, Desdemona asks, &lquo;How if she be <I>black</I>
and witty?&rquo;
<P><SC>Snider</SC> (i, 105): Othello was not a Hottentot on the one hand, nor was he a Cauca-
sian on the other; he was, however, born in Africa, and his physiognomy is thoroughly
African. The point which the Poet emphasizes so often and so strongly is the differ-
ence of race between him and Desdemona. He is her equal in rank, for he comes of
royal lineage; he is the peer of her family in honor and fame, for he is the most dis-
tinguished man in Venice. The sole difference which is selected as the ground of the
collision is the difference of race. This fact is sufficient for all dramatic purposes, to
ascertain the exact shade of his skin may be left to those who have leisure to play with
probabilities.
<P><SC>Grant White</SC> (<I>Note in 2d Edition on</I> &lquo;thick lips,&rquo; I, i, 72): Shakespeare's notions
about Moors and Negroes were, we may be sure, far from being clear and discrimi-
nating; and it is to be remarked that even Moors have thicker lips than the white
European races.
<P>[That Shakespeare meant to represent Othello as &lquo;black,&rquo; I cannot but think, and
&lquo;black&rquo; in the full meaning of the word, not &lquo;dark-complexioned&rquo; as Desdemona uses
it in &lquo;How if she be black and witty,&rquo; nor &lquo;tawny,&rquo; but thoroughly <I>black.</I> Disregard-
ing the &lquo;thick lips&rquo; of Iago, or the &lquo;sootie bosome&rquo; of Brabantio, or any phrase uttered

<P>by Othello's enemies in moments of passion, to me, beyond a peradventure, Othello

<P>The name of <SC>Nathan Field</SC> appears among the list of Actors, prefixed to the First
Folio. Collier in his <I>Hist. of Dram. Poetry</I> (iii, 437, 2d ed.) has the following con-

<P><SC>Halliwell-Phillips</SC> (<I>Outlines</I>, 5th ed., p. 177): The Tragedy of <I>Othello</I>, orig-
inally known under the title of the Moor of Venice, . . . . was very popular, Leonard
Digges speaking of the audiences preferring it to the laboured compositions of Ben
Jonson. In 1609, a Stage-loving parent, one William Bishop of Shoreditch, who had
perhaps been taken with the representation of the tragedy, gave the name of Othello's
perfect wife to one of his twin daughters. . . . . These scattered notices, accidentally
preserved, doubtlessly out of many others that might have been recorded, are indicative
of its continuance as an acting play; a result that may, without disparagement to the
author, be attributed in some measure to the leading character having been assigned to
the most accomplished tragic actor of the day,&mdash;Richard Burbage. The name of the
first performer of Iago is not known, but there is a curious tradition, which can be traced
as far back as the close of the Seventeenth century, to the effect that the part was orig-
inally undertaken by a popular comedian, and that Shakespeare adapted some of the
<PB N=397>
<HE><I>ACTORS</I> 397</HE>
<P>speeches of that character to the peculiar talents of the actor. [Hereupon are given
the two following Illustrative Notes:] According to Wright's <I>Historia Histrionica</I>,
1699, p. 4, Taylor was distinguished in this part [Iago], but probably not until after
the death of Shakespeare. The insertion of Taylor's name in the list of Shakespear-
ian actors in ed. 1623, merely proves that he had been one of them in or before that
year. &lquo;I'm assur'd, from very good hands, that the person that acted Iago was in
much esteem of a comedian which made Shakespear put several words and expressions
into his part, perhaps not so agreeable to his character, to make the audience laugh,
who had not yet learnt to endure to be serious a whole play.&rquo;&mdash;Gildon's <I>Reflections on
Rymer's Short View of Tragedy</I>, 1694.
<P><SC>Malone</SC> (<I>Hist. Account of the English Stage</I>, Var. '21, vol. iii, p. 126): The first
woman that appeared in any regular drama on a public stage, performed the part of
Desdemona; but who the lady was, I am unable to ascertain. The play of <I>Othello</I> is
enumerated by Downes as one of the stock-plays of the King's Company on their open-
ing their theatre in Drury Lane in 1663; and it appears from a paper found with Sir
Henry Herbert's Office-book, that it was one of the stock-plays of the same company
from the time they began to play without a patent at the Red Bull in St. John Street.
Mrs Hughs performed the part of Desdemona in 1663, when the company removed to
Drury Lane, and obtained the title of the King's Servants; but whether she performed
with them while they played at the Red Bull, or in Vere Street, has not been ascer-
tained. Perhaps Mrs Saunderson made her first essay there, though she afterwards
was enlisted in D'Avenant's Company. The received tradition is, that she was the
first English actress. [Mrs Saunderson afterwards married Betterton. Unmarried
women were not called <I>Miss</I> &lquo;until after the Revolution,&rquo; says Davies in his edition
of Downes, p. 28; the first instance of its use which he found was in Flecknoe's Epi-
grams, 1669.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>] The verses which were spoken by way of introducing a female
to the audience were written by Thomas Jordan, printed, I believe, in 1662. [Malone
here reprints the whole Prologue, but I think a short extract will satisfy all demands
of curiosity or of refinement:]

<P>From a paper in Sir Henry Herbert's handwriting, I find that <I>Othello</I> was performed
by the Red Bull Company (afterwards his Majesty's Servants) at their new theatre in
Vere Street, near Clare Market, on Saturday, December 8, 1660, for the first time that
winter. On that day, therefore, it is probable an actress first appeared on the English
stage.
<P><SC>Collier</SC> (<I>New Facts</I>, &amp;c., 1835, p. 6) stated that he had been permitted to examine
at Bridgewater House the manuscripts of Lord Ellesmere, the Keeper of the Great
Seal to Queen Elizabeth and Lord Chancellor to James I; among the papers, there
preserved, he found a volume of MS Ballads; collected, as he conjectured, &lquo;about the
date of the Protectorate, when old broadsides were becoming scarce, and new ones far
from abundant, as the Puritans set their faces against anything like popular amusements.
I apprehend that most of those in the volume were copied from printed originals, many
of which are now lost.&rquo; In the list of these Ballads, as given by Collier (<I>New Particu-
lars</I>, &amp;c., 1836, p. 45), there appeared the following: &lquo;Tragedy of <I>Othello</I> the Moor.
&lquo;Anonymous, but following Shakespeare's Tragedy very closely. Not printed.&rquo;
<P>&lquo;There can be no doubt,&rquo; Collier goes on to say, &lquo;that this Ballad was written subse-
quently to Shakespeare's tragedy; it was founded upon the play in consequence of its
popularity, and not the play upon it. . . . . It varies slightly from the play, and makes
Iago a Spaniard, as indeed his name indicates. The change was, perhaps, made in
accordance with the prejudice of the time when it was written, possibly about 1625,
after the breaking off of the Spanish Match. It is as follows, and here I preserve the
spelling of the MS, since it may aid in some degree in fixing the age of the production:
<C>THE TRAGEDIE OF OTHELLO THE MOORE</C>
<BQ>The foule effects of jealousie,<LB>
Othelloe's deadly hate,<LB>
Iagoe's cruell treacherie,<LB>
And Desdemonae's fate,<LB>
In this same ballad you may reade,<LB>
If soe you list to bye,<LB>
Which tells the blackest, bloodiest deede<LB>
Yet ever seen with eye.<LB>
In Venice City, long time since,<LB>
A Noble Moore did live,<LB>
Who to the daughter of a Prince<LB>
In secrecie did wive.<LB>
She was as faire as he was blacke,<LB>
A sunshine and a cloude:<LB>
She was as milde as playfull childe,<LB>
But he was fierce and proude.<LB>
And lovede he her, as well he might,<LB>

<P>[In a foot-note on the fourth line of the last stanza, Collier says:] &lquo;As Burbage
&ldquo;began his course&rdquo; as an actor many years before <I>Othello</I> was written, the meaning
of the author of this ballad may be that Burbage played the part of Othello originally,
and retained it until his death. Otherwise, we must take it as a mere guess, and not a
happy one, that Burbage commenced as an actor in <I>Othello.</I> The great probability is,
that Burbage was upon the stage, as a boy, when Shakespeare first joined the company
in 1586 or 1587.&rquo; [Collier reiterates in the text that] &lquo;Burbage was, of course, dead,
and it is certainly a mistake to assert that he began his course with Othello.&rquo; [Some
of the other ballads in this volume have been held to be spurious, and, I suppose, on
the principle of <I>noscitur ex sociis</I>, doubts have been cast on the foregoing. Indeed,
<SC>Ingleby</SC> publicly challenged its genuineness in <I>The Academy</I> in 1876. The stanza
which he selected as proving its &lquo;very modern composition&rquo; is the tenth, and the line
which he therein italicised is, &lquo;<I>He whisper'd at Othelloe's backe&rquo;;</I> he also italicised, in
the same stanza, the words &lquo;<I>much preferrd.</I>&rquo; He then justifies his challenge and mar-
shals his proof that the whole ballad is a forgery, as follows: &lquo;The first line of this
&lquo;stanza [viz. the line just quoted in Italics] might have been suggested by the second
&lquo;of Retsch's Outlines to Schiller's <I>Fridolin</I>, of which Mr Collier published a transla-
&lquo;tion of great merit in 1824.&rquo; This is all the proof, which I can find, that he adduces.
That a scholar so eminent and a critic so keen should, with apparent gravity, give us
this hypothetical pluperfect subjunctive <I>might have been</I>, after whetting our appetites
for a downright perfect indicative <I>was</I>, lay beyond my comprehension, till my eye
caught the date of the Number of <I>The Academy</I>&mdash;the First of April!&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
