<P><SC>Wilhelm Oechelh&auml;user</SC> (<I>Othello, f&uuml;r die deutsche B&uuml;hne bearbeitet</I>, Weimar
1876. Einleitung, p. 13): Othello is above all things hero and warrior. Before Des-
demona's charms had kindled the flame of love in his heart, warlike exploits, battles.
and adventures, were the element in which he lived. The African retired into the
background behind his position in the military service of the Christian Republic of
Venice, to which he was devoted body and soul; to have vindicated the honor of
which was his last proud recollection before death. When, therefore, actors, as many
do, seek to give to the personation a dash of Muli Hassan, and to make the African
blood of Othello a prominent quality, it is an error, mere clap-trap. Only in the
Third and in the beginning of the Fourth Act, where Iago with cynical calculation
speculates upon the warmth of his senses, the southern passion of Othello may be,
somewhat beyond our European limits, moderately personated. For the rest, he who
forgets his paint represents Othello best. It is not the design of the tragedy to illustrate
the Moorish character; every European of like quality would, in like circumstances, do
just as Othello did. It is not the peculiar jealousy of a Moor, but jealousy in a
character little disposed to it, that the poet depicts. He did not make Othello a Moor
(or, as Schlegel thinks, he mistook the Saracen of novels for a Moor) in order to mark
the representation of him with the stamp of his race. He had a far deeper ethical aim,
namely, to contrast the greatness of Othello's character with the ideal purity of Desde-
mona's love.
<P>Othello, then, should be personated not with the bizarre hastiness and vivacity of the
African, but with the quiet, nay aristocratic bearing of the hero, of the mature man of
high position, who has &lquo;declined into the vale of years.&rquo; Such is the manner in which
he presents himself before us in the beginning of the piece; the dignity and repose
with which he confronts the enraged father, the manly self-consciousness, and the
noble modesty and simplicity which mark his story of his love, reveal to us the essen-
tial qualities of his character. In Othello there is no trace of the <I>parvenu</I>, who feels
himself uncertain of the high position which he has reached, alternating between bully-
ing and cringing, as is often witnessed in real life. He is conscious of his royal de-
scent and of his services, and with just pride takes for granted their silent recognition,
without any thought of forcing it by boasting and importunity.
<P>(P. 20.) The direct opposite to the part of Othello must stand boldly out in the
thoroughly <I>plebeian</I> bearing of Iago. Othello is an aristocrat and a gentleman;
Iago, from crown to sole, a plebeian, no trim, knightly villain like Edmund. His
vulgar bearing, with which his dress even should be in accord, must be represented as
auxiliary to his cunning. Herein is the point where most personators of Iago entirely
fail,&mdash;the like is most frequently the case in the personation of Richard III,&mdash;namely,
in the skilful wearing of the mask of an honest man. . . . . A plebeian, countrified
behaviour, a homely, careless dress, a tone, now of broad cynicism and soldierly
jest, and then of honesty, of fellow-feeling, of unselfish friendship (a masterpiece in
this respect is the great Act III, Scene iii) must illustrate the personation of this r&ocirc;le.
Admirably does he hit the right tone for every person and every situation; the keenest
knowledge of men underlies his diabolical speculations on the weakness of every indi-
vidual. His long and frequent dialogues with Roderigo show us an original <I>nuance</I>
of his ordinary bearing. To all others he is always on the <I>qui vive;</I> only with this
gull has he an easier task. He ill-treats and plucks this pigeon with the keenest
humour, as if to refresh himself, all in the tone of the consideration of a well-meaning
older friend. Humour and sarcasm form the salient qualities of his character; he
takes thorough delight in his devil's work, which breaks out in his humour.
<PB N=443>
<HE><I>GERMAN CRITICISMS&mdash;FRIESEN</I> 443</HE>
<P>(P. <*>1.) Iago is to be represented as at least of the same age as Othello,&mdash;that is, as
of ripe manhood.
<P>(P. 26.) Generally speaking, too little attention is paid to the part of Emilia, the
wife of the infamous Ensign. Most of the adaptations for the stage omit too large a
portion of her r&ocirc;le; and stage managers assign it to inferior talent, as if any soubrette
of the theatre were equal to it. The important part which Emilia takes in the catas-
trophe, her touching devotion to her mistress, the moral courage with which she con-
fronts the deluded Moor and her guilty husband, should indicate that here is work for
a skilful and gifted artist. Emilia, in the drama, is in the position of a servant; in
Cinthio's novel she appears more as a friend. On the stage she should be represented
in a character between the two, as this finds its justification in Italian manners at that
period. Her notions of conjugal fidelity, as she airs them in the last Scene of the
Fourth Act, are of no account, and stand in sharpest contrast with the ideal which
her infinitely finer natured mistress has of the marital relations. But nowhere is there
found any ground for supposing, as Schlegel does, that Emilia's practice was in accord-
ance with her loose talk. Cinthio in the novel calls her &lquo;a beautiful and honourable
person.&rquo; How often do women talk in a light-minded fashion, which authorizes no
unfavourable inferences as to their actual characters.
<P>In her whole conduct Emilia is chargeable with only one fatal weakness: obtaining
at her husband's wish the lost handkerchief upon which hangs such a fearful tragedy.
She certainly had no suspicion of the evil purpose of Iago, to whom she stands in a
relation of cold indifference. Putting this one error out of sight, she is the faithful,
devoted servant and friend of Desdemona, the unterrified asserter of her innocence,
even when she is threatened with death; first by the Moor, and then by her husband,
showing therein great moral courage. Her position in the last Scene can be made of
commanding importance.&mdash;Emilia is to be represented as young, but certainly older
than Desdemona.
<P><SC>Herm. Freih. von Friesen</SC> (<I>Shakspere-Studien</I>, Wien, 1876, iii, 132): In connec-
tion with the character of Othello, composed as it is of so many elements, there comes
the question whether this drama, in opposition to the other works of Shakspere, is to be
regarded as illustrative of character or of intrigue. It must be granted that if the fate
of Othello and Desdemona is determined by Iago's intrigues, then the essential ele-
ment of a tragedy,&mdash;namely, the tragic fault of the sufferers,&mdash;is wanting, and the Poet
is exposed to an undeniable reproach. Apparently, the predominance of intrigue over
the whole development of the action of the play is not to be questioned. We must, first
of all, agree as to what is to be understood by intrigue, if it is to be rejected as a mo-
tive power to a tragic result. Under all circumstances it is indispensable that, in a true
tragedy, the person in whom the interest centres must be led to his fate without loss of
his free will and choice. Certainly, then, the voluntary and deliberate proceedings of
one or more persons, by which another individual is deprived of his freedom of thought
and action, and is thereby doomed to destruction, excludes the tragic fault. But it does
not follow that in tragedy the cunning, lies, and plots of one individual practised upon
another are not to be introduced. Only the influence of these must be so related to
the character of the person suffering under <*>t that he shall be driven to his fate, not
irresistibly, but only through the passion which has already shaken his freedom to the
utmost, so that in truth he yields only to the impulse of his own will.
<P>This being premised in regard to Iago's influence upon the fate of Othello, no one
<PB N=444>
<HE>444 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>will be disposed to deny the power of Iago. Yet there is still the question whether the
criminality of the intrigue and its fatal effect rests only upon Iago, or whether the actual
ground of this effect lies not in Othello's personal character. (P. 135.) Notwithstand-
ing the righteous indignation with which we regard Iago, upon Othello's head falls the
chief fault. The right to lay it to his account begins in the natural qualities of his
character, and gains in weight, by the circumstances just mentioned, from the wonder-
ful, or at least unusual, excitement of his mind. As in all Shakspere's creations, we
cannot help confessing that such an individuality as Othello's,&mdash;not only endowed
with the most distinguished gifts, but having qualities and ways of thought even an-
tagonistic,&mdash;that such a character, and such a character alone, would lie open to the
diabolical influence of Iago. All so happens as to remind us, step by step, that for any
other to ward off Iago's assaults would have been easy; and if, full of sympathy for
Othello and full of indignation at Iago, we are blind to this possibility, and seem to see
Othello helplessly entangled in the net which Iago weaves, the reason of it is in the
impression which the finished work of the Poet makes on us, in the brilliancy of
Othello's speeches, in the poetic force of the emotions which gush involuntarily from
within him, contrasted with the coarse hints of Iago, sounding, as it were, from the
nether world. While the former delights us and the latter stirs our indignation, we
take sides and pardonably overlook the Poet's hint that, although Othello is caught in
an almost inextricable net, he has not lost his freedom. With what skill does the Poet
use, among other circumstances, everything which he found in the novel! In the
novel, Cassio steals away from Othello's sight when he knocks secretly at the back
door of the house to return the handkerchief to Desdemona, which is sufficient to
increase the jealousy of Othello after it has already been awakened by Iago. In the
drama (III, iii) his withdrawal from Desdemona's presence at the appearance of
Othello is suspicious, and only on this account affords Iago a circumstance for the first
step in his plot because the mind of the Moor is in a state of intense excitement. Fur-
thermore, how narrowly Othello escaped hearing what Iago and Cassio are talking
about (IV, i). A word that he might have caught would have been enough to con-
vince him of Iago's treachery. Even the way in which the fatal handkerchief makes
its appearance is, in the drama, with fine poetic instinct, entirely different from that of the
novel. In the novel, a counterfeit of it is shown to Othello through a window. Thus,
Othello was not at all in a position to penetrate the deception, while here he has only
to demand an explanation to rend the whole plot to pieces. Equally ingenious is it
that the handkerchief in the drama is lost through Othello's and Desdemona's care-
lessness; while in the novel, Iago gets possession of it by cunning. The whole devel-
opment of the tragic result hangs upon the finest threads. And here it is especially
that the connection of Iago's relation to Roderigo appears of the greatest significance.
That in the first examination of Cassio the inquiry into the disturbance does not extend
to the question who the man was whom Cassio had beaten, and what cause he had given
therefor, is a circumstance only possible from Othello's unsuspicious disposition; while,
had the inquiry been pushed that far, Iago's villainy would have been laid bare at the
outset. In what danger Iago was in this respect we can surmise when Roderigo (IV, ii),
in his distrust of Iago, threatens to go directly to Desdemona. A spark of this distrust
in the soul of Othello would have saved him and Desdemona. The struggle of Othello
before the murder is at once most significant and most touching. Throughout, the tragic
event tends to a catastrophe which results not from accident or the overpowering force
of another person, but only from a destiny originating in the inmost nature of the indi-
vidual. To the very last moment of this fearful scene the threads are not severed
<PB N=445>
<HE><I>GERMAN CRITICISMS&mdash;GENSICHEN, BULTHAUPT</I> 445</HE>
<P>by which Othello and Desdemona might be saved. This possibility, presented before
our eyes with masterly power, is what moves us most painfully with mingled emotions
of fear and sympathy. Let the calm judgement of the spectator be blinded and over-
come by the powerful tones which the Poet draws forth from the instrument of his
genius; I yet venture to maintain that the catastrophe finds its necessity in the nature of
Othello. Even if the demoniac power of Iago drove him to the fatal act, the ground
therefor lies only in Othello's personal nature and disposition. In the freedom with
which the Poet changes the catastrophe as it is in the novel, we have an unquestionable
proof of his poetic art in this direction.
<P>O. F. <SC>Gensichen</SC> (<I>Studienbl&auml;tter</I>, Berlin, 1881, p. 67): In the last Act, after the
heart-breaking scene in which the whole fabric of her happiness falls in ruins before
her, Desdemona can with the guileless innocence of a child,&mdash;fall asleep.
<P>Wonderful, indeed, appears this sleep. No reconciling word between herself and
Othello has been spoken; she knows that Othello will appear again in a moment, that
he wishes to speak with her alone, and for that reason Emilia is dismissed. His com-
ing must explain the terrible change that came over him,&mdash;why his love and reverence
have been turned into contempt and rage. Desdemona, whose perfect devotion finds
that even the stubbornness, the checks, the frowns of her husband &lquo;have grace and
favour,&rquo; must await with the most painful impatience this critical interview; what rest
could she find before peace was restored between her and Othello? And yet she can
fall asleep, and so profound is her slumber that she is disturbed neither by the tumult
in the street nor by the entrance of Othello into her chamber. Even his kisses fail to
awaken her.
<P>Here we see the contrast between her genuine woman's nature and the full man's
nature in Othello. His &lquo;bloody passion shakes his very frame,&rquo; his &lquo;eye rolls,&rquo; he
&lquo;gnaws his nether lip&rquo;; Desdemona peacefully sleeps, and awakes to receive him with,
&lquo;Will you come to bed, my lord?&rquo; instead of seeking to deliver him from his unworthy
suspicions. Here, too, we find that lovely freedom from care which, in the conscious-
ness of her purity, takes not upon itself the trouble of considering the individual differ-
ence of temperament. And it is just this point which renders intelligible the possibility
of a rupture of her relation to Othello.
<P>[In their zealous and praiseworthy pursuit of &lquo;the tragic fault&rquo; which shall, by refer-
ring all our misfortunes to our own misdeeds, harmonize Shakespeare's tragedies with
human life, some of our German brothers are inclined to push the search to its remotest
bounds. Thus <SC>Gensichen</SC> finds that the tragic termination of Othello's wedded life
might have been avoided had he only kept up such observances as fit the bridal. &lquo;Had
Othello retained a trace,&rquo; he says (p. 83), &lquo;of the gallantry of a lover, he would have
picked up the handkerchief which Desdemona let fall when she tenderly wished to bind
it round his forehead. It was through this neglect of a courteous act that Othello him-
self provided Iago with the weightiest proof of his wife's infidelity.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P><SC>Heinrich Bulthaupt</SC> (<I>Dramaturgie der Classiker</I>, Oldenburg, 1883, p. 222): A
villainous knavery, a combination of accidents, is Desdemona's ruin. Her horrible and
unmerited end excites the most painful emotion. Cordelia's moral elevation, her nature,&mdash;
which, notwithstanding her womanly tenderness, so far from shrinking from the conflict
with life advances to meet it,&mdash;stands in a much more intimate relation to the dark powers
<PB N=446>
<HE>446 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>of Fate than this fine, sensuous character of Desdemona, made, as she is, for the full-
est enjoyment of life. Cordelia's death affects us tragically. Desdemona's is simply
horrible. Can any one who is not infatuated take, with Otto Ludwig, a different view?
Can it be seriously maintained that sin and punishment are, in her case, skilfully propor-
tioned, and that her punishment for no heinous fault was &lquo;mild&rquo;? Mild,&mdash;this horrible
death? Granting that mere physical destruction by murder amounts to nothing, but,
for this young creature, who is pure love, pure devotion, can anything be more terrible
than to find herself treated as a harlot, and to be deliberately strangled by the hands of
that man for whom she had sacrificed everything? In her last moments, from her awak-
ing to her death, did not a whole hell yawn before her? How is it possible to misunder-
stand this awful martyrdom! The very circumstance that there is no proportion be-
tween her fate and her fault affects us only the more profoundly. This unmerited
suffering ennobles her, creates the deepest sympathy, and wins every heart. We forget
every error that, in the thoughtlessness of youth, she may have committed. We can only
bend the knee before her. Her loveliness, like a saint's, is transfigured by her tears, by
her death. From the same source from which has come all that she has done, or left
undone, comes her last word, &lquo;Farewell! Commend me to my kind lord.&rquo; Her kind
lord! Him who has murdered her! This unconquerable love, to my feeling, is appa-
rent in a slight, thoroughly Shakespearian touch, than which nothing can be more
beautiful. When the Willow Song of poor Barbara occurs to her, when her heart is
full to overflowing of suffering, she suddenly remarks, apparently without connection,
&lquo;Lodovico is a proper man.&rquo; The whole scene of her ill-treatment at the hand of her
husband, the coming of her relative, like a true knight, to her defence,&mdash;all is present
to her again and to us. But she will not complain of her loved husband, who has
done the worst to her, who has <I>struck</I> her. She thinks, as the memory of the bitter
scene fills her mind with grief and her eyes with tears, only of him who had so kindly
taken her part, &lquo;He is a proper man!&rquo; &lquo;And he speaks well!&rquo; she adds.

<P>J. F. <SC>Ducis</SC> (<I>Othello. Repr&eacute;sent&eacute;e pour la premi&egrave;re fois en 1792. Avertissement.</I>)
La trag&eacute;die d'Othello est une des plus touchantes et des plus terribles productions
dramatiques qu'ait enfant&eacute;e le g&eacute;nie vraiment cr&eacute;ateur de ce grand homme. L'ex&eacute;-
crable caract&egrave;re de Jago y est exprim&eacute; surtout avec une vigueur de pinceau extraordi-
naire. Avec quelle souplesse effrayante, sous combien de formes trompeuses, ce ser-
pent caresse et s&eacute;duit le g&eacute;n&eacute;reux et trop confiant Othello! Comme il l'infecte de tous
ses poisons! comme il l'enveloppe de tous ses replis! enfin, comme il le serre, comme
il l'&eacute;touffe et le d&eacute;chire dans sa rage! Je suis bien persuad&eacute; que si les Anglais peuvent
observer tranquillement les man&oelig;uvres d'un pareil monstre sur la sc&egrave;ne, les Fran&ccedil;ais ne
pourraient jamais un moment y souffrir sa pr&eacute;sence, encore moins l'y voir d&eacute;velopper
toute l'&eacute;tendue et toute la profondeur de sa sc&eacute;l&eacute;ratesse. C'est ce qui m'a engag&eacute; &agrave; ne
faire conna&icirc;tre le personnage qui le remplace si faiblement dans ma pi&egrave;ce, que tout &agrave; la
fin du d&eacute;no&ucirc;ment, lorsque le malheur d'Othello est consomm&eacute; par la mort de la plus
fid&egrave;le, de la plus tendre amante, qu'il vient d'immoler aux aveugles transports de sa
jalousie. Je me suis bien gard&eacute; de le faire para&icirc;tre du moment qu'il est connu, du
moment que je r&eacute;v&eacute;l&eacute; au public le secret affreux de son caract&egrave;re. Je n'ai pas manqu&eacute;
non plus, d&egrave;s que je l'ai pu, dans un court r&eacute;cit, d'instruire ce m&ecirc;me public de sa puni-
tion, de sa mort cruelle dans les tortures. J'ai pens&eacute; m&ecirc;me que si le spectateur avait
pu, dans le cours de la trag&eacute;die, le soup&ccedil;onner seulement, au travers de son masque,
d'&ecirc;tre le plus sc&eacute;l&eacute;rat des hommes, puisqu'il est le plus perfide des amis, c'en &eacute;tait fait
du sort de tout l'ouvrage, et que l'impression pr&eacute;dominante d'horreur qu'il e&ucirc;t inspir&eacute;e
aurait certainement amorti l'int&eacute;r&ecirc;t et la compassion que je voulais appeler sur l'amante
d'Othello et sur ce brave et malheureux Africain. Aussi est-ce avec une intention tr&egrave;s-
d&eacute;termin&eacute;e que j'ai cach&eacute; soigneusement &agrave; mes spectateurs ce caract&egrave;re atroce, pour ne
pas les r&eacute;volter.
<P>Quant &agrave; la couleur d'Othello, j'ai cru pouvoir me dispenser de lui donner un visage
noir, en m'&eacute;cartant sur ce point de l'usage du th&eacute;&acirc;tre de Londres. J'ai pens&eacute; que le
teint jaune et cuivr&eacute;, pouvant d'ailleurs convenir aussi &agrave; un Africain, aurait l'avantage
de ne point r&eacute;volter l'&oelig;il du public, et surtout celui des femmes, et que cette couleur
leur permettrait bien mieux de jouir de ce qu'il y a de plus d&eacute;licieux au th&eacute;&acirc;tre, c'est-
&agrave;-dire de tout le charme que la force, la vari&eacute;t&eacute; et le jeu des passions r&eacute;pandent sur le
visage mobile et anim&eacute; d'un jeune acteur, bouillant, sensible et enivr&eacute; de jalousie et
d'amour. . . . .

<P>J'ai maintenant &agrave; parler de mon d&eacute;no&ucirc;ment. Jamais impression ne fut plus terrible.
Toute l'assembl&eacute;e se leva, et ne poussa qu'un cri. Plusieurs femmes s'&eacute;vanouirent.
On e&ucirc;t dit que le poignard dont Othello venait de frapper son amante &eacute;tait entr&eacute; dans
tous les c&oelig;urs. Mais aux applaudissemens que l'on continuait de donner &agrave; l'ouvrage
se m&ecirc;laient des improbations, des murmures, et enfin m&ecirc;me une esp&egrave;ce de soul&egrave;vement.
J'ai cru un moment que la toile allait se baisser. D'o&ugrave; pouvait na&icirc;tre une impression
si extraordinaire, une agitation si tumultueuse? Me tromperais-je, en croyant qu'elle
venait de l'extr&ecirc;me int&eacute;r&ecirc;t que j'avais inspir&eacute; pour H&eacute;delmone [Desdemona]; de ce
que mon spectateur avait d&eacute;sir&eacute; trop passionn&eacute;ment qu'elle p&ucirc;t d&eacute;sabuser Othello de
son erreur; de ce que je l'avais tenu trop long-temps dans les angoisses de la terreur
et de l'esp&eacute;rance; de ce que son d&eacute;sir, tromp&eacute; au moment du coup de poignard, s'&eacute;tait
tourn&eacute; en une sorte de d&eacute;sespoir, et avait r&eacute;volt&eacute; sa douleur m&ecirc;me contre l'auteur de
l'ouvrage?
<P>Comment se fait-il cependant que le public, apr&egrave;s avoir eu tant de peine &agrave; me par-
donner mon d&eacute;no&ucirc;ment, soit revenu le voir encore pendant le cours de douze repr&eacute;sen-
tations? Ne serait-ce pas qu'il a &eacute;t&eacute; averti par la r&eacute;flexion qu' Othello n'est point un
homme f&eacute;roce, mais un amant &eacute;gar&eacute;, un Africain jaloux, un More, qui frappe ce qu'il a
de plus cher, et qui ne survivra pas &agrave; sa victime? Ne serait-ce pas qu'il a senti par
instinct que les naturels les plus tendres et les plus sensibles, une fois pouss&eacute;s dans les
exc&egrave;s, sout quelquefois les plus pr&egrave;s de la barbarie, par la raison peut-&ecirc;tre qu'ils en
&eacute;taient les plus &eacute;loign&eacute;s?
<P>Cependant quoique le public ait le droit, sous tous les climats, de tracer aux auteurs
les limites de la terreur et de la piti&eacute;, ces limites pourtant sont plus ou moins recul&eacute;es
selon le caract&egrave;re des diff&eacute;rentes nations. Mon d&eacute;no&ucirc;ment a eu de la peine &agrave; passer &agrave;
Paris; et &agrave; Londres, les Anglais soutiennent tres-bien celui de Shakespeare. Ce n'est
point avec un poignard qu' Othello, sur leur th&eacute;&acirc;tre, immole son innocente victime; il
lui presse, dans son lit, et avec force, un oreiller sur la bouche, il le presse et le represse
encore jusqu' &agrave; ce qu'elle expire. Voil&agrave; ce que des spectateurs fran&ccedil;ais ne pourraient
jamais supporter. Un po&egrave;te tragique est donc oblig&eacute; de se conformer au caract&egrave;re de
la nation devant laquelle il fait repr&eacute;senter ses ouvrages. C'est une v&eacute;rit&eacute; incontest-
able, puisque son principal but est de lui plaire. Aussi, pour satisfaire plusieurs de mes
spectateurs, qui ont trouv&eacute; dans mon d&eacute;no&ucirc;ment le poids de la piti&eacute; et de la terreur
excessif et trop p&eacute;nible, ai-je profit&eacute; de la disposition de ma pi&egrave;ce, qui me rendait ce
changement tr&egrave;s-facile, pour substituer un d&eacute;no&ucirc;ment heureux &agrave; celui qui les avait
bless&eacute;s; quoique le premier me paraisse toujours convenir beaucoup plus &agrave; la nature et
&agrave; la moralit&eacute; du sujet, et que je l'aie eu sans cesse en vue, comme il est facile de le
remarquer d&egrave;s le commencement et dans le cours de ma trag&eacute;die. Mais comme je l'ai
fait imprimer avec les deux d&eacute;no&ucirc;mens, les directeurs des th&eacute;&acirc;tres seront les ma&icirc;tres de
choisir celui qu'il leur conviendra d'adopter.

d'aventures plus ou moins touchantes; c'est par la cr&eacute;ation de l'homme lui-m&ecirc;me

<P>Qu'on appelle l'un apr&egrave;s l'autre tous les personnages de la trag&eacute;die, depuis ses h&eacute;ros
jusqu'aux moins consid&eacute;rables, Desdemona, Cassio, Emilia, Bianca; on les verra par-
a&icirc;tre, non sous des apparences vagues, et avec les seuls traits qui correspondent &agrave; leur
situation dramatique, mais avec des formes pr&eacute;cises, compl&egrave;tes, et tout ce qui constitue
la personnalit&eacute;. Cassio n'est point l&agrave; simplement pour devenir l'object de la jalousie
d'Othello, et comme une n&eacute;cessit&eacute; du drame, il a son caract&egrave;re, ses penchants, ses qual-
it&eacute;s, ses d&eacute;fauts; et de l&agrave; d&eacute;coule naturellement l'influence qu'il exerce sur ce qui arrive
Emilia n'est point une suivante employ&eacute;e par le po&euml;te comme instrument soit du n&oelig;ud,
soit de la d&eacute;couverte des perfidies qui am&egrave;nent la catastrophe; elle est la femme de
Iago qu'elle n'aime point, et &agrave; qui cependant elle ob&eacute;it parce qu'elle le craint et
quoiqu'elle s'en m&eacute;fie; elle a m&ecirc;me contract&eacute;, dans la soci&eacute;t&eacute; de cet homme, quelque
chose de l'immoralit&eacute; de son esprit; rien n'est pur dans ses pens&eacute;es ni dans ses paroles:
cependant elle est bonne, attach&eacute;e &agrave; sa ma&icirc;tresse; elle d&eacute;teste le mal et la noirceur.
Bianca elle-m&ecirc;me a sa physionomie tout &agrave; fait ind&eacute;pendante du petit r&ocirc;le qu'elle joue
dans l'action. Oubliez les &eacute;v&eacute;nements, sortez du drame; tous ces personnages demeur-
eront r&eacute;els, anim&eacute;s, distincts; ils sont vivants par eux-m&ecirc;mes; leur existence ne s'&eacute;van-
ouira point avec leur situation. C'est en eux que s'est d&eacute;ploy&eacute; le pouvoir cr&eacute;ateur du
po&euml;te, et les faits ne sont, pour lui, que le th&eacute;&acirc;tre sur lequel il leur ordonne de monter.&rquo;
<PB N=450>
<HE>450 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>It was with a translation of <I>Othello</I> that, over fifty years ago, in 1829, Le Comte
<SC>Alfred de Vigny</SC> undertook to break the Academic chains which enfettered the French
drama. His struggle and final triumph, aided by <SC>Victor Hugo, &Eacute;mile Deschamps,
le duc de Broglie, Charles Nodier, B&eacute;ranger</SC>, and others, form an exceedingly
instructive and interesting chapter in the History of the French Stage, but which
scarcely comes within the scope of the present work. All that I can do here, is again
to refer the student to <SC>Lacroix's</SC> admirable <I>M&eacute;moire</I>, p. 292 et seq.; and to quote
from De Vigny's Preface the terms of the problem which he submitted to the French
public, from which an idea may be formed of the plan of the whole campaign.
<P>&lquo;Or, voici le fond de ce que j'avais &agrave; dire aux intelligences, le 24 octobre, 1820.
<P>&ldquo;Une simple question est &agrave; r&eacute;soudre. La voici:
<P>&ldquo;La sc&egrave;ne fran&ccedil;aise s'ouvrira-t-elle, ou non, &agrave; une trag&eacute;die moderne produisant:&mdash;
dans sa conception, un tableau large de la vie, au lieu du tableau resserr&eacute; de la catas-
trophe d'une intrigue;&mdash;dans sa composition, des caract&egrave;res, non des r&ocirc;les, des sc&egrave;nes
paisibles sans drame, m&ecirc;l&eacute;es &agrave; des sc&egrave;nes comiques et tragiques;&mdash;dans son ex&eacute;cution,
un style familier, comique, tragique, et parfois &eacute;pique?&rdquo;&rquo;
<P>It is not difficult to see what the result must have been when <I>Othello</I> was brought
forward as an answer to these questions. Our Gallic brothers are not stocks and
stones, and the contest was as short as it was sharp. Academic frigidity melted under
the rays of a warmth which, springing from Nature, was directed by Art, Shakespeare's
art, the finest the world has known.
<P>In the following January, in 1830, an Article appeared in the <I>Revue fran&ccedil;aise</I> by
M. le duc <SC>de Broglie</SC>, which I should like to transfer bodily to these pages. I admire
it for its style, its boldness, its liberality, its admiration of Shakespeare even while con-
fessing a fidelity to certain convictions which are opposed to Shakespeare. Herewith
are passages which we cannot afford to overlook:
<P>Le Th&eacute;&acirc;tre Fran&ccedil;ais s'est rendu, faute d'avoir &eacute;t&eacute; secouru &agrave; propos et ravitaill&eacute; en
temps opportun. Dans la soir&eacute;e du 25 octobre dernier, Attila-Shakespeare en a pris
possession avec armes et bagages, enseignes d&eacute;ploy&eacute;es, au fracas de mille fanfares.
Pauvres po&euml;tes de la vieille roche, qu'allez-vous devenir? Il ne reste plus aux &acirc;mes
faibles qu'&agrave; se rendre, &agrave; sacrifier sur l'autel des faux dieux, et aux vrais croyants qu'&agrave;
s'envelopper la t&ecirc;te de leur manteau.
<P>Plaisanterie &agrave; part, la r&eacute;volution qui s'op&egrave;re depuis quelque temps dans le go&ucirc;t du
public est un ph&eacute;nom&egrave;ne curieux et singuli&egrave;rement digne d'attention. Jamais plus
notable changement ne s'est prononc&eacute; avec plus d'&eacute;clat et de rapidit&eacute;.
<P>(P. 53.) Que cet homme [Shakespeare] est un &eacute;tonnant peintre de la nature hu-
maine! combien il est vrai qu'il a re&ccedil;u d'en haut quelque chose de cette puissance cr&eacute;a-
<*>rice qui souffle sur un peu de poussi&egrave;re, et qui l'anime pour la vie et l'&eacute;ternit&eacute;!
<P>Dans l'entrevue avec Brabantio, Othello ne prononce pas quinze vers; devant le
s&eacute;nat, Desd&eacute;mona n'en prof&egrave;re pas vingt; et pourtant d&eacute;j&agrave; Othello existe tout entier,
Desd&eacute;mona existe tout enti&egrave;re; ils sont l&agrave;, l'un et l'autre, vivant sous nos yeux, se
d&eacute;ployant sans contrainte, dans toute la gr&acirc;ce et la singularit&eacute; de leur caract&egrave;re, dans
toute leur individualit&eacute; na&iuml;ve et imp&eacute;rissable. Supprimez le reste de la pi&egrave;ce, vous
n'effacerez de notre m&eacute;moire ni Desd&eacute;mona ni Othello; placez-les &agrave; plaisir dans un
autre ordre de circonstances; allez, &eacute;vertuez-vous: ma&igrave;s ne vous trompez pas, car nous
les connaissons, nous savons d'avance ce qu'ils peuvent dire ou faire.
<P>Et pourtant, dans ces caract&egrave;res, que de complexit&eacute;, que de contrastes, que de finesse
et de nuances!
<P>(P. 57.) Figurez-vous un homme qui n'aurait v&eacute;cu depuis longtemps qu'&agrave; la clart&eacute;
<PB N=451>
<HE><I>FRENCH CRITICISMS&mdash;DE VIGNY</I> 451</HE>
<P>des bougies, des lampions ou des verres de couleur, qui n'aurait vu que des cascades
d'op&eacute;ra, des montagnes de toile peinte et des guirlandes de fleurs artificielles, et qui se
trouverait transport&eacute; tout-&agrave;-coup, par une magnifique matin&eacute;e du mois de juillet, au
souffle de l'air le plus pur, sous les tranquilles et gracieux noyers d'Interlaken, en face
des glaciers d'Oberland; et vous aurez une assez juste id&eacute;e de la situation morale d'un
habitu&eacute; de nos premi&egrave;res repr&eacute;sentations lorsqu'il vient &agrave; se trouver, &agrave; l'improviste, en
pr&eacute;sence de ces beaut&eacute;s si simples, si grandes et si naturelles.
<P>Un second point sur lequel le sentiment involontaire du public fran&ccedil;ais s'est trouve
tout-&agrave;-fait en d&eacute;saccord avec les admirateurs de Shakespeare, c'est le r&ocirc;le d'Iago. Ce
r&ocirc;le, qui est la cheville ouvri&egrave;re de la pi&egrave;ce, est grandement c&eacute;l&egrave;bre en Angleterre et
ailleurs; tous les critiques sans exception, anglais, allemands ou fran&ccedil;ais, ne tarissent
pas dans leurs &eacute;loges. A la sc&egrave;ne, il nous a paru d&eacute;plaire g&eacute;n&eacute;ralement; d&eacute;plaire
d'une mani&egrave;re tr&egrave;s-prononc&eacute;e, et qui allait croissant d'acte en acte, tellement que, s'il
e&ucirc;t &eacute;t&eacute; jou&eacute; avec moins d'aplomb et de d&eacute;cision, il lui serait certainement arriv&eacute; mal-
heur. Pourquoi a-t-il d&eacute;plu?
<P>Il &eacute;tait assez curieux, &agrave; la fin de chaque acte, d'entendre chaque spectateur donner
la raison de sa r&eacute;pugnance, le motif de son aversion. Celui-ci trouvait Iago trop im-
moral; celui-l&agrave;, au contraire, ne le trouvait pas assez habile hypocrite: on ne se vante
pas ainsi de sa sc&eacute;l&eacute;ratesse, disait-il; un troisi&egrave;me &eacute;tait r&eacute;volt&eacute; de voir commettre le
crime en plaisantant; ainsi de suite.
<P>Selon nous, le r&ocirc;le a d&eacute;plu parce qu'il n'est pas bon; parce qu'il est, non pas incon-
s&eacute;quent (quoi de plus naturel &agrave; l'homme que l'incons&eacute;quence?) mais incoh&eacute;rent, parce
que les parties dont il se compose ne tiennent pas ensemble, et qu'&agrave; son &eacute;gard, on ne
sait vraiment &agrave; quelle id&eacute;e se prendre. Telle est du moins notre mani&egrave;re de voir. Que
les d&eacute;vots &agrave; Shakespeare nous anath&eacute;matisent, si c'est leur bon plaisir.
<P>Qu'est-ce qu'Iago?
<P>Est-ce le malin esprit, ou du moins son repr&eacute;sentant sur la terre? Othello a-t-il
raison quand il le regarde aux pieds pour voir s'il ne les aurait pas fourchus? Est-ce
un &ecirc;tre qui fait le mal pour l'amour du mal, et qui vient souffler des poisons sur l'union
d'Othello et de Desd&eacute;mona, par ce seul motif que Desd&eacute;mona est une cr&eacute;ature ang&eacute;-
lique et qu'Othello est un homme loyal, brave et g&eacute;n&eacute;reux?
<P>Alors pourquoi donner &agrave; Iago des motifs humains et int&eacute;ress&eacute;s? Pourquoi nous
montrer en lui une basse cupidit&eacute;, le ressentiment d'une injure faite &agrave; son honneur,
l'envie d'un poste plus &eacute;lev&eacute; que le sien? Pourquoi le voyons-nous d&eacute;valiser ce pauvre
Roderigo, comme Scapin ou Sbrigani escamotent &agrave; un imb&eacute;cile la bourse qu'il a dans
son pourpoint? Ces passions de bas aloi d&eacute;truisent tout le fantastique du r&ocirc;le; le
d&eacute;mon n'a ni humeur ni honneur; il n'a ni rancune, ni col&egrave;re, ni convoitise; c'est un
personnage d&eacute;sint&eacute;ress&eacute;; il fait le mal parce que le mal est le mal, et qu'il est, lui, le
malin.
<P>Iago est-il, au contraire, comme il s'en fait gloire, le parfait &eacute;go<*>ste, l'homme qui sait,
au supr&ecirc;me degr&eacute;, s'aimer lui-meme, l'&ecirc;tre qui sait subordonner hi&eacute;rarchiquement ses
d&eacute;sirs, selon leur degr&eacute; d'importance, et disposer ensuite ses actions de mani&egrave;re &agrave; tendre
invariablement &agrave; sa plus haute satisfaction, co&ucirc;te que co&ucirc;te &agrave; autrui, sans scrupule, sans
remords, et aussi sans se laisser d&eacute;tourner par des vell&eacute;it&eacute;s d'un ordre inf&eacute;rieur?
<P>Alors pourquoi poursuit-il en m&ecirc;me temps trois ou quatre buts distincts, et d'une
importance pour lui tr&egrave;s-in&eacute;gale? Pourquoi entreprend-il coup sur coup vingt projets
diff&eacute;rents qu'il abandonne l'un apr&egrave;s l'autre? Pourquoi surtout prodigue-t-il, dans
chaque occasion, cent fois plus de m&eacute;chancet&eacute; que le besoin de la circonstance ne le
comporte?

<P>(P. 62.) Il [Iago] r&eacute;ussit, dira-t-on.
<P>Il r&eacute;ussit, ainsi le veut l'auteur. Mais le bon sens, qu'en dit-il?
<P>L'auteur lui-m&ecirc;me r&eacute;ussit, mais d'o&ugrave; vient? C'est parce que telle est la prodondeu<*>
et la vivacit&eacute; de sa conception premi&egrave;re que les invraisemblances les plus choquantes,
les absurdit&eacute;s les plus inconcevables passent inaper&ccedil;ues; c'est parce que personne n'a
l'envie ni le loisir de regarder aux ressorts du drame. Autre chose est pourtant de
nous donner ces absurdit&eacute;s pour des m&eacute;rites.
<P>Oui, cela est tr&egrave;s-vrai; depuis le premier moment o&ugrave; la premi&egrave;re insinuation s'&eacute;chappe
des l&egrave;vres d'Iago pour atteindre l'oreille du More, depuis ces paroles fatales: &lquo;Ah! ceci
me d&eacute;pla&icirc;t,&rquo; jusqu' au moment solennel o&ugrave; le rideau tombe sur les cadavres des deux
amants, le spectateur n'a pas la possibilit&eacute; de respirer. Vous entendriez voler une
mouche dans la salle, et bien maladroits sont les amis dont le z&egrave;le s'efforce d'inter-
rompre par des applaudissements cette anxi&eacute;t&eacute; qui va croissant de minute en minute.
<P>D&egrave;s le premier mot, tout est dit, tout est d&eacute;cid&eacute;.
<P>Adieu pour jamais, Desd&eacute;mona, adieu Othello. Desd&eacute;mona n'appara&icirc;t plus que
comme l'innocent oiseau qui se d&eacute;bat faiblement sous la serre d'un vautour, mais d'un
vautour qui se d&eacute;bat lui-m&ecirc;me en furieux sous la serre d'un autre vautour, et se venge,
sur la pauvre victime, des effroyables tortures auxquelles il est en proie.
<P>Le spectateur contemple ce tableau, non point avec cette curiosit&eacute; inqui&egrave;te qui passe
tour &agrave; tour de la crainte &agrave; l'espoir, mais, s'il est permis de le dire, et en tenant compte
de toutes les diff&eacute;rences, avec quelque chose de cette angoisse inexprimable qui s'empare
de nous lorsque, dans une cour de justice, nous assistons aux vains efforts de malheureux
entra&icirc;n&eacute;s vers une condamnation fatale et indubitable.
<P>(P. 69.) La sc&egrave;ne o&ugrave; Desd&eacute;mona se d&eacute;shabille, avant de se mettre au lit, est donc
bien v&eacute;ritablement, pour elle, ce quart d'heure de gr&acirc;ce que l'on accorde aux con-
damn&eacute;s avant de les conduire au supplice; en vain essaie-t-elle de donner le change
&agrave; Emilia, de se faire illusion &agrave; elle-m&ecirc;me, de d&eacute;tourner sa pens&eacute;e sur quelque sujet
frivole; le plus intime de son &acirc;me reparait et surgit &agrave; chaque mot. Et telle est aussi
cette sc&egrave;ne pour le spectateur &eacute;perdu; il compte les minutes; il s'attache au moindre
incident; il se cramponne &agrave; la moindre chose; il demande pourquoi pas encore ce n&oelig;ud,
pourquoi pas encore cette agrafe; il voudrait, en quelque sorte, saisir Desd&eacute;mona par
sa robe et la retenir.
<P>Po&euml;tes tragiques, voil&agrave; votre ma&icirc;tre; prenez le&ccedil;on de lui, si vous savez en prendre.
<P><SC>Victor Hugo</SC> (<I>William Shakespeare</I>, Paris, 1864, p. 321): Maintenant qu'est-ce
qu'Othello? C'est la nuit. Immense figure fatale. La nuit est amoureuse du jour.
La noirceur aime l'aurore. L'africain adore la blanche. Othello a pour clart&eacute; et pour
folie Desd&eacute;mona. Aussi comme la jalousie lui est facile! Il est grand, il est auguste,
il est majestueux, il est au-dessus de toutes les t&ecirc;tes, il a pour cort&eacute;ge la bravoure, la
bataille, la fanfare, la banni&egrave;re, la renomm&eacute;e, la gloire, il a le rayonnement de vingt vi<*>
toires, il est plein d'astres, cet Othello, mais il est noir. Aussi comme, jaloux, le h&eacute;ros
est vite monstre! le noir devient n&egrave;gre. Comme la nuit a vite fait signe &agrave; la mort!
<P>A c&ocirc;t&eacute; d'Othello, qui est la nuit, il y a Iago, qui est le mal. Le mal, l'autre forme
de l'ombre. La nuit n'est que la nuit du monde; le mal est la nuit de l'&acirc;me. Quelle
obscurit&eacute; que la perfidie et le mensonge! avoir dans les veines de l'encre ou la trahison,
c'est la m&ecirc;me chose. Quiconque a coudoy&eacute; l'imposture et le parjure, le sait; on est &agrave;
t&acirc;tons dans un fourbe. Versez l'hypocrisie sur le point du jour, vous &eacute;teindrez le soleil.
C'est l&agrave;, gr&acirc;ce aux fausses religions, ce qui arrive &agrave; Dieu.

<P><SC>In</SC> proof of the difficulties attending the translation of Shakespeare into German, <*>
gave in <I>Macbeth</I> eighteen or twenty German versions of &lquo;Double, double toil and
trouble,&rquo; &amp;c.; which was well enough chosen as an instance where foreigners have to
contend with a difficulty that might be termed merely technical. The lines, to Eng-
lish ears, convey but little definite meaning; their vagueness, combined with the bub-
bling sound as of boiling, imparts the Abracadabra suggestion of a witch's charm. I am
not sure that some of the versions there given do not fulfil the essential conditions of a
translation where, as I have said, the difficulty is technical. A fairer test of translation
is to be found in lines where words have a peculiar signification and an inherent charm
to English ears, without which the whole passage is naught, and where, if a single word
be changed, the spell is snapt, just as the fractured point of a Prince Rupert's tear
reduces the crystal globule to sand. For instance, take those lines which Iago utters as
he sees Othello approaching, after the first administration of the &lquo;poisonous mineral&rquo;:
<BQ>&lquo;Look where he comes: Not poppy, nor mandragora,<LB>
Nor all the drowsy syrups of the world,<LB>
Shall ever medicine thee to that sweet sleep<LB>
Which thou owd'st yesterday.&rquo;<LB></BQ>
<PB N=454>
<HE>454 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>It seems sheer impertinence to attempt to point out to English readers any especial
charm where every phrase is full of beauty, but for my present purpose I must be par-
<*>oned for calling attention to three words here. Is there any other word in the Eng-
lish tongue that can be substituted for &lquo;drowsy&rquo;? <I>Sleepy</I> certainly cannot. There is no
resistance in <I>sleepy.</I> For <I>sleep</I> one composes his limbs, and repose is wooed. <I>Narcotic</I>
is worse, it has a repulsive odor; and <I>soporific</I> is pedantic. But in &lquo;drowsy&rquo; there is
half-wakefulness, utter weariness, and nodding resistance to the potent drug. Thus,
also, &lquo;syrup,&rquo; which is not <I>juice</I>, or <I>potion</I>, or <I>essence</I>, or <I>extract</I>, nor anything but that
heavy liquid sweetness whose very sluggishness suggests its power in reserve, whose
inertness by contrast renders its essence more quick, and it is redolent of its home in the
East. Lastly comes &lquo;medicine,&rquo; with its suggestion of illness, and dis-ease, and resto-
ration. Of course all the other words in these lines are exquisitely chosen, but then
they are such as can be transferred readily from one language to another. The vague
sonorousness of &lquo;mandragora&rquo; speaks quite as powerfully, it may be supposed, to French
or German or Italian ears as to ours. But the three words which I have specified,
&lquo;drowsy,&rquo; &lquo;syrup,&rquo; and &lquo;medicine,&rquo; must be felt, or the translation falls short; it may
be through the fault of the translator or through the deficiency of his mother tongue.
<P>Furthermore, in examining the following translations, another question suggests
itself,&mdash;a question which I have never been able to answer satisfactorily. Should a
translation of poetry be in prose or rhythm? A discussion of this far-reaching ques-
tion is hardly germane here; my present purpose is fulfilled in calling attention to
what seems to me to be the fact, that in the prose translations which follow, the sug-
gestions of the original are reproduced somewhat more completely than in those in
rhythm. But, alack the day, what does the passage amount to without the exquisite
cadence of &lquo;Nor all the drowsy syrups of the world&rquo;? which seems, in its undulation
merely, to suggest the quiet &lquo;unfurling&rquo; of twilight and the solemn tolling of the cur-
few. &lquo;In every language,&rquo; said Southey, &lquo;there is a magic of words as untranslatable
as the <I>Sesame</I> in the Arabian tale,&mdash;you may retain the meaning, but if the words be
changed the spell is lost.&rquo; Of course, this is true in German. Not while the world
lasts will Gretchen's song be translated: &lquo;Meine Ruh ist hin, Mein Herz ist schwer.&rquo;
<P><SC>Le Tourneur</SC>, Paris, 1776: Va, ni l'opium, ni la mandragore, ni toutes les potions
assoupissantes de l'univers ne te rendront jamais ce doux sommeil que tu go&ucirc;tas hier

<P>In the Textual Notes the symbol Ff indicates the agreement of the Second, Third,
and Fourth Folios. The agreement of the three Quartos is indicated by Qq.
<P>The frequent omission of the apostrophe in the Second Folio, a peculiarity of that
edition, is not generally noted.
<P>The sign + indicates the agreement of <SC>Rowe, Pope, Theobald, Hanmer, War-
Burton</SC>, and <SC>Johnson</SC>.
<P>When <SC>Warburton</SC> precedes <SC>Hanmer</SC> in the Textual Notes, it indicates that <SC>Han-
mer</SC> has followed a suggestion of <SC>Warburton's</SC>.
<P>The words <I>et cet.</I> after any reading indicate that it is the reading of <I>all other</I>
editions.
<P>The abbreviation (subs.) indicates that the reading is <I>substantially</I> given, and that
immaterial variations in spelling, punctuation, or stage directions are disregarded.
<P><S>Coll.</S> (<I>MS</I>) refers to <SC>Collier's</SC> annotated Second Folio.
<P><I>Quincy</I> (<I>MS</I>) refers to <SC>Quincy's</SC> annotated Fourth Folio.
<P>An Emendation or Conjecture which is discussed in the Commentary is not repeated
in the Textual Notes; nor is &lquo;conj.&rquo; added to any name in the Textual Notes unless
it happens to be that of an editor, in which case its omission would be misleading.
<P>All citations of Acts, Scenes, and Lines in <I>Romeo and Juliet, Macbeth, Hamlet</I>,
and <I>Lear</I> refer to this edition of those plays; in citations from other plays the <SC>Globe
Edition</SC> is followed.
<P>I have not called attention to every little misprint in the Folio. A reference to the
Textual Notes will always show them to be misprints by the agreement of all the
Editors in their correction.
<P>Nor is notice taken of the first Editor who adopted the modern spelling, or who
substituted commas for a parenthesis, or changed? to !. At the same time some
comparatively trifling peculiarities are noted, such as the use of hyphens, to which
some Editors, Staunton, for instance, attach value. The variations in the spelling
of the word &lquo;murther,&rquo; where it occurs so frequently in Act V, is not noted. The
spelling is almost uniformly <I>murder</I> in the Quartos, but in the Folios it is apparently
arbitrary; in V, ii, 145, it is &lquo;Murther,&rquo; and in the second line after, we have &lquo;murder'd.&rquo;
<P>Otherwise, even the most manifest misspellings in the Quartos and Folios are re-
corded, to supply what aid they may in estimating the value of the texts or their indi-
viduality; for instance, &lquo;Cyprus&rquo; and &lquo;Lieutenant&rquo; are almost invariably spelled, in the
First Quarto, <I>Cypres</I> and <I>Leiutenant.</I> I have tried always to record every instance in
the Quartos, especially in the First, of any really intelligent punctuation.
<PB N=461>
<HE><I>EDITIONS COLLATED IN THE TEXTUAL NOTES</I> 461</HE>
<P>It may well be conceived that no part of my labours is more onerous than this of
collation; for which there is so little to show, and at which I do not suppose that
one reader in a hundred, or in five hundred, ever even as much as glances. But the
work has to be done, somebody must do it, and I seem to have drawn the unhappy lot.
Wherefore let me say that, thus far, I have not flinched, but, to ensure accuracy, I have
gone over every syllable of the collation, in these forty, and more, editions, <I>twice</I>, sev-
eral months apart, and have arisen from the task with the conviction that I have, after
all, by no means evaded the inexorable law of imperfection.
<P>It once occurred to me that if I ever hereafter edit another play, which is very
doubtful, I might abridge the labour by disregarding the successive editions put forth
by the same editor, and take only his last edition, in which, presumably, his maturest
judgement is to be found. But this attempt, I am afraid, would be vain. Editors have
rights which those who collate them are bound to respect, and foremost among these
rights is that of credit for precedence in emendation; this can be respected only by noting
the first editions. If therefore of a modern Editor his first edition must be recorded, it
is equally incumbent to note his last. Nigh twenty years of close study passed between
Dyce's First Edition and his latest, over thirty-five between Collier's, and shall we take
the sallet days and disregard the ripened judgement? Wherefore I see no chance to
ease the task in this direction,&mdash;nor in any other. If this burdensome collation is to
be done at all, it must be done so thoroughly that future students may begin where we
leave off.
<P>In the collation of the Quartos and Folios I have allowed myself no discretion;
what has attracted my attention, I infer would attract any one else's. In these days,
when Shakespeare's mood is to be detected in the number of syllables in his lines, I
shrink from fathoming the issues which may depend on the spelling of a word.
<P>I have taken no notice of the commentaries on the text given by <SC>Robert Deverell</SC>
in the annotated <I>Othello</I> contained in the Third Volume of his <I>Hieroglyphics;</I> of course
they illustrate nothing but the midsummer madness of the poor fellow whose pure
lunacy explains all difficulties by &lquo;appearances in the moon.&rquo; For instance, I open
the volume at random: &lquo;There has been much question about the manner of pro-
&lquo;nouncing the line, &ldquo;If I quench thee,&rdquo; &amp;c.; but if the first part of it be referred to
&lquo;the taper only (as formed out of the streaks of light on Cassio's body), and the latter
&lquo;part not merely to the death of Desdemona (in character), but to the obscuration, or
&lquo;extinction rather, of the part of the moon which forms her prototype, the difficulty will
&lquo;be removed.&rquo; It is not easy at first to repress a smile,&mdash;it is impossible, over some of
the many grotesque wood-cuts,&mdash;but the pathos of the jangled bells drowns all sense
of the ludicrous, and we can only close the book with a sigh.
<P>Although in the Preface I have referred to the notes which my friend <SC>Edwin Booth</SC>
prepared for me, and which enrich the foregoing pages, yet I wish again, for his sake, to
emphasise the fact that their informal, off-hand style is due to the circumstances under
which they were written, with no thought on his part that they were to be seen by any
one but by him at whose request they were made. On the last page of the Prompt
Book wherein they were written is the following note, which, I think should be given
here, as it explains and justifies what I have just said: &lquo;Some Notes for y<SUP>e</SUP> Novice, H.
H. F. I have jotted here some of the odd notions that flit through my head while act-
ing. In cold blood 'tis difficult to recall them, but I think I've done pretty well. Much
may be stale,&mdash;I've often found my &lquo;original&rquo; ideas very well moth-eaten and musty with
<PB N=462>
<HE>462 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>age, and 'tis long since I have overhauled the Commentators. I find that I've repeated
myself often, and in my &lquo;fidgets&rquo; have left out words in many sentences, while the
grammar (which I abhor) will doubtless confuse you. However, I have kept my
promise as best I can. I hope when you act Othello or Iago, or any other character
in this play, that my suggestions may be of service.&rquo;
<P>In the Commentary I have, in many a place, put <SC>Ed.</SC> where I should much prefer to
have omitted it. But I beg to have it understood that it is present not as a claimant,
but as a safeguard, that upon none of my betters may be fathered my folly. Partly for
the same reason, I have in my notes used the First Person Singular, but mainly because
if anywhere we are restricted to the expression of our own individual opinions, it is in
the interpretation of Shakespeare; there, as in the Republic of Letters, each man can
speak but for himself alone, and the monarchical &lquo;we&rquo; is an assumption of authority
without the substance.
<P>[In this closing hour of my labour, and since the foregoing has been put in type,
the mail brings me the Facsimile of the First Quarto, &lquo;publisht&rquo; by C. Praetorius in
London, with an admirable Introduction by <SC>Herbert A. Evans</SC>, M. A., which gives,
clearly and succinctly, all needful information in regard to this particular Text, and a
comparison of it and the First Folio. This Facsimile is one of a series of all the
Shakespearian Quartos, now issuing in London, whose excellence is to be paralleled
but by its cheapness. If any word of mine can extend a knowledge of this most
commendable publication, I can only wish that I were &lquo;trumpet-tongued.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
